c-001.title: Use baking soda and vinegar separately, not mixed
c-001.summary: Mixing them just makes foam and the two cleaning powers cancel out. Use baking soda for grease and vinegar for limescale, one at a time.
c-001.principle: A weak base (NaHCO₃) and a weak acid (CH₃COOH) neutralize into near-neutral sodium acetate: NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂↑
c-001.example: Mixing 1 tbsp (about 12g) of baking soda with 1/2 cup of vinegar leaves a nearly neutral liquid once the fizz stops, so it dissolves neither grease nor scale well. Used separately, the same amounts handle both kinds of dirt.
c-001.actionItem: Today, use only a baking soda paste on greasy sink areas and only a vinegar-soaked paper towel on tap limescale.

c-002.title: Never use bleach together with acidic cleaners
c-002.summary: Mixing sodium hypochlorite (bleach) with an acidic toilet cleaner releases toxic chlorine gas. Use one product at a time and rinse well in between.
c-002.principle: On contact with acid, hypochlorite turns into chlorine: NaOCl + 2HCl → NaCl + Cl₂↑ + H₂O
c-002.example: Chlorine irritates eyes and throat at about 3ppm and causes severe coughing and breathing trouble above 30ppm. In a small bathroom it can reach dangerous levels within minutes.
c-002.actionItem: Store bleach and acidic cleaners (hydrochloric or citric) on separate shelves today, and check the 'do not mix' warning on each label.

c-003.title: Bleach plus ammonia or glass cleaner is also dangerous
c-003.summary: Mixing bleach with an ammonia-based glass cleaner produces toxic chloramine gas. Ventilate, and avoid using the two products back to back.
c-003.principle: NaOCl + NH₃ → NH₂Cl + NaOH forms chloramine (NH₂Cl), which irritates the airways.
c-003.example: Even a splash of bleach into a cleaner with about 5% ammonia can cause coughing and stinging eyes within minutes in a closed bathroom. Bleach on urine-soiled spots releases the same kind of gas.
c-003.actionItem: Look for 'ammonia' on your cleaner labels, note not to use them with bleach on the same day, and open a window when cleaning.

c-004.title: Pick a travel hand sanitizer with at least 60% ethanol
c-004.summary: Alcohol gel is the fallback when there is no water, but below 60% ethanol it works much worse. For flights, decant it into containers of 100mL or less.
c-004.principle: Ethanol denatures microbial proteins and dissolves lipid membranes. It is flammable: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
c-004.example: A 60-80% ethanol product must be rubbed in for about 20 seconds and left until fully dry. For visibly dirty hands, soap and water beat sanitizer.
c-004.actionItem: Check the ethanol percentage on the label of the sanitizer you will pack, and decant it into a container of 100mL or less.

c-005.title: Read the pH on the label when choosing a cleaner
c-005.summary: Kitchen and bathroom cleaners differ in pH by purpose. Pick alkaline for grease and acidic for scale to get more cleaning for the same money.
c-005.principle: pH = -[H⁺], so each drop of 1 pH unit means 10 times more H⁺. Fats saponify in alkali: RCOOR' + NaOH → RCOONa + R'OH
c-005.example: A pH 11-12 alkaline cleaner suits grease, while a pH 2-3 acidic one suits limescale. Neutral (pH 6-8) dish soap is gentle on hands but slower on baked-on grease.
c-005.actionItem: On your next shop, check the pH and intended use on cleaner labels, and note the pH of three cleaners you already own.

c-006.title: Cut heating energy with 30°C washes
c-006.summary: Modern detergents have enzymes that work well around 30°C, so everyday laundry rarely needs 60°C. The less water you heat, the less electricity you use.
c-006.principle: Heat needed is Q = mcΔT (c = 4.18kJ/(kg · K)), and protein-digesting enzymes work best around 30-40°C.
c-006.example: Heating 10L of water from 15°C to 30°C takes about 627kJ, but to 60°C takes about 1,881kJ, three times more. At four loads a week, the savings add up over 200 loads a year.
c-006.actionItem: Set your washer to 30°C (or cold) today, and raise it to 40°C only for heavily sweaty clothes.

c-007.title: Remove kettle limescale with a spoon of citric acid
c-007.summary: The white crust inside a kettle dissolves in citric acid. It smells less than vinegar and costs little, so try it before buying a new kettle.
c-007.principle: Calcium carbonate scale dissolves in acid: 3CaCO₃ + 2C₆H₈O₇ → Ca₃(C₆H₅O₇)₂ + 3H₂O + 3CO₂↑
c-007.example: Boiling 500mL of water with 1 tbsp (about 10g) citric acid and leaving it 20 minutes loosens most scale around 1mm thick. One kilogram of citric acid lasts for dozens of descalings.
c-007.actionItem: Today, boil water with 1 tbsp citric acid in the kettle, leave it 20 minutes, then pour it out and rinse two or three times.

c-008.title: What the white soap scum on laundry and tiles really is
c-008.summary: In hard water, the fatty acids in soap bind calcium and become an insoluble residue. Synthetic detergents or a vinegar rinse can reduce it.
c-008.principle: Ca²⁺ + 2C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻ → Ca(C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂↓ forms a precipitate and lowers lather.
c-008.example: In areas with hardness above 200mg/L (as CaCO₃), the same amount of soap may produce less than half the lather. The white film on bathroom tiles dissolves in acidic cleaner.
c-008.actionItem: Spray vinegar or citric acid solution on the white film on your bathroom tiles today, wait 5 minutes, then wipe.

c-009.title: Reduce residual chlorine in tap water by standing or boiling
c-009.summary: Tap water keeps a small amount of chlorine for disinfection. It is safe, but if you dislike the smell, leaving it uncovered or boiling lowers it.
c-009.principle: Hypochlorous acid breaks down with time or light: 2HOCl → 2HCl + O₂↑
c-009.example: Residual chlorine at the tap is usually 0.1-0.5mg/L. Letting water stand a few hours in a jug, or boiling it 5 minutes uncovered, clearly reduces the smell.
c-009.actionItem: Fill a jug tonight, leave it uncovered, and compare the smell before drinking tomorrow.

c-010.title: Why hair feels stiff after showering in hard-water destinations
c-010.summary: Water in places like parts of Europe is rich in calcium and magnesium, so shampoo lathers less and hair feels stiff. An acidic final rinse helps.
c-010.principle: Hard-water Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ bind the anionic surfactants in shampoo and form a residue. Hardness is expressed in mg/L CaCO₃.
c-010.example: Above 300mg/L water is classed as very hard, more than three times typical Korean tap water (about 50-100mg/L). A final rinse with 1 tbsp of apple cider vinegar per liter of water reduces the stiffness.
c-010.actionItem: Pack a small amount of citric acid powder or a tiny vinegar bottle on your next trip, and ask your lodging about the local water hardness.

c-011.title: Ion-exchange softener resin is recharged with salt
c-011.summary: Shower softening filters and some water systems capture calcium with ion-exchange resin. Some types regenerate with brine while others are replaced, so check before buying.
c-011.principle: The resin grabs calcium and releases sodium: 2R-Na + Ca²⁺ → R₂Ca + 2Na⁺. After saturation it is restored with strong brine.
c-011.example: If a replacement cartridge costs 10,000 won and is changed monthly, that is 120,000 won a year. A regenerating system can run for years on a few kilograms of salt.
c-011.actionItem: Compare the replacement interval and regeneration option of the softener you are considering, and calculate the yearly cost.

c-012.title: A scaled-up heater uses more energy and fails sooner
c-012.summary: When limescale builds up on a kettle or humidifier heating plate, less heat reaches the water, heating takes longer and parts overheat. Regular descaling helps both energy use and lifespan.
c-012.principle: Heat transfer is q = (kAΔT / d), and scale (k ≈ 1-3W/(m · K)) is an insulating layer that blocks heat far more than metal does.
c-012.example: With scale over 2mm thick, heating time to the same temperature can rise by a few percent while element temperature climbs and shortens its life. A citric acid wash once a month is enough.
c-012.actionItem: Add a recurring calendar entry 'first Sunday of each month: descale kettle and humidifier with citric acid'.

c-013.title: Melt ice with salt, but spread a little before it freezes
c-013.summary: A small sprinkle of salt before snow or just before freezing uses far less than melting ice already formed, because it lowers the freezing point.
c-013.principle: Freezing-point depression ΔT_f = i K_f m (K_f = 1.86K · kg/mol, i ≈ 2 for NaCl)
c-013.example: A 10% by mass brine has m ≈ 1.9 mol/kg, giving ΔT_f ≈ 7 °CmathrmC, so it starts freezing near -7°C. Below about -10°C salt loses effect, so use sand instead.
c-013.actionItem: If tonight's forecast is below freezing, lightly spread a handful of salt on your entry steps.

c-014.title: Calcium chloride vs rock salt: what to use where
c-014.summary: Calcium chloride works at lower temperatures but is harsher on concrete and metal. Choose by temperature and location.
c-014.principle: Calcium chloride releases heat as it dissolves: CaCl₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻, ΔH ≈ -82kJ/mol
c-014.example: In practice NaCl works down to about -10°C and CaCl₂ to about -25°C. Near new concrete or iron railings, use less chloride and prefer sand.
c-014.actionItem: Check the ingredient (sodium chloride or calcium chloride) on your de-icer bag today and mark it as not for use near iron railings.

c-015.title: Rinse de-icer off pet paws and hands
c-015.summary: Chloride de-icers on the road dry out paw pads and can cause vomiting if licked. Rinse with lukewarm water after walks.
c-015.principle: Chlorides draw moisture out of skin and dry it. Dissolved salt remains as brine, the same colligative effect as ΔT_f = i K_f m.
c-015.example: Calcium chloride gives off heat as it dissolves, so on damp skin it can sting. Rinsing paws in lukewarm water for 30 seconds and drying them solves most problems.
c-015.actionItem: After today's walk, rinse your pet's paws in lukewarm water, and wipe your own shoe soles with a damp cloth.

c-016.title: Check windshield washer fluid freezing point before winter road trips
c-016.summary: Washer fluid that is just water freezes at 0°C and blocks your view. Winter fluid uses alcohol to lower the freezing point.
c-016.principle: Since ΔT_f = K_f m, more alcohol means a lower freezing point, but also flammability (C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O).
c-016.example: A label of -20°C or -30°C means it should not freeze down to that temperature, but diluting it with water raises the freezing point. Methanol fumes are toxic, so keep the cabin ventilated.
c-016.actionItem: Before leaving, check the fluid level and the freezing-point rating on the label.

c-017.title: Check mix ratio and spec when buying antifreeze
c-017.summary: Mixing antifreeze (ethylene glycol) into coolant lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point. Follow the ratio and specification, and never mix different types.
c-017.principle: With ΔT_f = i K_f m, about 50 vol% ethylene glycol freezes near -37°C and boils near 106°C.
c-017.example: Using straight concentrate actually raises the freezing point and lowers heat transfer. Ethylene glycol tastes sweet and is lethal to pets, so wipe spills immediately.
c-017.actionItem: Check your car manual for the recommended antifreeze specification and mix ratio, and ask about it at your next service.

c-018.title: Predict winter window condensation with the dew point
c-018.summary: When humid indoor air touches cold glass, droplets form and cause mold and heat loss. Keeping indoor humidity moderate also wastes less heating.
c-018.principle: Dew point is roughly T_d ≈ T - 100-RH5 (RH>50%), and condensation is H₂O(g) → H₂O(l).
c-018.example: At 22°C indoors and 60% humidity, the dew point is about 14°C. If the inner glass surface is 10°C, it will condense; lowering humidity to 40-50% drops the dew point to about 10-12°C and prevents most of it.
c-018.actionItem: Set your humidifier target to 40-50% today and check the hygrometer this evening.

c-019.title: Safely remove bathroom silicone mold with diluted bleach
c-019.summary: Black mold on silicone fades with oxidizing bleach. Always ventilate and keep it away from acidic products.
c-019.principle: Hypochlorite oxidation: NaOCl → Na⁺ + OCl⁻, and OCl⁻ oxidizes mold pigment and cells.
c-019.example: Dilute household bleach (about 4-5%) 1:10 with water, apply, wait 10 minutes, then rinse well. Mold grows above about 60-70% relative humidity, so ventilating after showers prevents recurrence.
c-019.actionItem: Today, open the bathroom window, wear gloves, wipe the silicone with 1:10 diluted bleach, and rinse after 10 minutes.

c-020.title: Use sodium percarbonate to lift mold and yellow stains safely
c-020.summary: Oxygen bleach (sodium percarbonate) is gentler than chlorine bleach with no chlorine gas risk, and is easier to use on colored fabrics. It works best in warm water.
c-020.example: Dissolve 1 tbsp (about 10g) in 1L of 40-50°C water and soak 30-60 minutes to remove sweat and mold stains. Do not use it on wool or silk.
c-020.actionItem: Today, soak a yellowed white sock or dish cloth in 40-50°C water with 1 tbsp of percarbonate for 30 minutes.

c-021.title: A closet dehumidifier lasts longer in a small space
c-021.summary: Calcium chloride dehumidifier packs absorb moisture from the air until they liquefy. Used in small closed spaces like closets and shoe cabinets rather than large rooms, they work more efficiently.
c-021.principle: CaCl₂(s) + 6H₂O(g) → CaCl₂ · 6H₂O, and with more moisture it dissolves into liquid.
c-021.example: Calcium chloride takes up several times its weight in water. Placed where doors open often it saturates fast, so a closed small space for a month or more gives the best value. Dispose of the collected liquid away from skin and metal.
c-021.actionItem: Put one dehumidifier pack on the bottom of your closet today and open the doors less often.

c-022.title: The little packet in snacks: silica gel vs quicklime
c-022.summary: Food packaging desiccants are commonly silica gel or quicklime, and neither should be eaten. Quicklime heats up in water, so especially protect eyes and mouth.
c-022.principle: Quicklime: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (exothermic, ΔH ≈ -64kJ/mol). Silica gel adsorbs water molecules on its surface.
c-022.example: Silica gel can be reused after drying 1-2 hours in a 100-120°C oven. A wet quicklime packet becomes strongly alkaline liquid, so keep it from water when discarding.
c-022.actionItem: Take desiccant packets from your kitchen drawer, check whether they say silica gel or quicklime, and keep them out of children's reach.

c-023.title: Stop glasses and goggles from fogging with a drop of surfactant
c-023.summary: When you step from cold outdoors into a warm room, lenses fog because of tiny droplets. A surfactant film makes the water spread into a thin sheet so you can still see.
c-023.principle: The larger the contact angle, the more droplets bead up. A surfactant lowers surface tension γ so water spreads out.
c-023.example: One drop of dish soap thinly spread on the lens and buffed with a dry cloth reduces fogging for hours. On coated lenses it may damage the coating, so check the maker's instructions.
c-023.actionItem: Before going out today, seal your mask tight over the nose, and wipe your glasses with a thin film of dish soap.

c-024.title: Freeze food thin and fast to keep it fresher
c-024.summary: Slow freezing makes large ice crystals that tear cells, so food weeps and turns tough after thawing. Spreading it thin and freezing quickly makes small crystals that keep quality.
c-024.principle: Crystal size depends on cooling rate. The phase change H₂O(l) → H₂O(s) requires removing ΔH_fus = 6.01kJ/mol.
c-024.example: Spreading leftover soup or meat 2cm thick in a zip bag on a metal tray freezes hours faster than a thick block and cuts drip loss on thawing. Store at -18°C or colder.
c-024.actionItem: Pack one leftover into a zip bag, flatten it thin, label the date, and freeze it today.

c-025.title: How to handle sprouted or green potatoes
c-025.summary: Potato sprouts and green patches contain high levels of the toxin solanine. Boiling or frying does not easily destroy it, so cut it out generously.
c-025.principle: Solanine is heat-stable and breaks down only near 290 °CmathrmC. Light increases both chlorophyll and solanine formation.
c-025.example: Cutting away at least 1cm around sprouts and green areas removes most of it. Discard potatoes that are green all over or taste bitter. Storing them dark and cool (8-10°C) slows sprouting.
c-025.actionItem: Wrap potatoes in newspaper and store them in a dark, cool place today, and cut away or discard sprouted ones.

c-026.title: Slow apple and avocado browning with a drop of lemon juice
c-026.summary: Cut fruit turns brown through an enzyme reaction with oxygen. Adding acid slows it, and it is safe to eat.
c-026.principle: Polyphenol oxidase: 2 catechol + O₂ → 2 o-benzoquinone + 2H₂O. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) reduces the quinone back.
c-026.example: Enzyme activity drops greatly below pH 4. Sprinkling 1 tsp lemon juice on one sliced apple delays browning by 2-3 hours. Browned portions are not a big issue for nutrition or safety.
c-026.actionItem: If you cut an apple or avocado today, add a few drops of lemon juice or dip it briefly in salt water.

c-027.title: A pressure cooker raises the boiling point to save time and gas
c-027.summary: In a sealed pot pressure rises and water boils above 100°C. Higher temperature speeds up chemical reactions.
c-027.principle: By the Clausius-Clapeyron relation, at about 2atm (absolute) water boils near 120 °CmathrmC. Rate follows k = Ae⁻E_a/RT.
c-027.example: Each 10°C rise roughly doubles the reaction rate, so 20°C gives about 4 times. Beans or tough meat that take 60 minutes in an open pot take around 20 in a pressure cooker, cutting gas use greatly.
c-027.actionItem: Try a long-simmer food (beans, shank) in the pressure cooker today and compare the time.

c-028.title: Why high-sugar jam keeps without mold
c-028.summary: Sugar binds water, leaving less for microbes to use. Sterilizing jars and keeping the sugar ratio lets you keep jam a long time in the fridge.
c-028.principle: When water activity a_w = (p / p₀) falls below 0.85, most bacteria cannot grow, though molds can survive near 0.8.
c-028.example: Jam with about 60% sugar has a_w ≈ 0.80, which suppresses bacteria but still allows some mold. Use sterilized jars, refrigerate, and eat within 2-3 weeks after opening to cut waste.
c-028.actionItem: Cook leftover fruit with 40-50% sugar into jam today and store it in a sterilized jar labeled with the date.

c-029.title: Wipe greasy pans first, then wash in warm water
c-029.summary: Cooled fat hardens and resists soap and water. Wiping with a paper towel first and then washing in warm water saves soap and water.
c-029.principle: Fats react with alkali and surfactants to form washable soap: C₃H₅(OOCR)₃ + 3NaOH → C₃H₅(OH)₃ + 3RCOONa
c-029.example: Lard begins to melt around 30-40°C, so water near 40°C loosens grease. Wiping first can halve the washing water and prevents drain clogs.
c-029.actionItem: Before washing up today, wipe the grease off the pan with a paper towel first, then wash in warm water.

c-030.title: Stop frying and baking at light golden to cut acrylamide
c-030.summary: Cooking potatoes or bread at high heat to dark brown increases acrylamide. Stopping at golden keeps the taste while reducing formation.
c-030.principle: Asparagine and reducing sugars undergo the Maillard reaction above 120 °CmathrmC, forming acrylamide (C₃H₅NO).
c-030.example: Frying chips below 175°C to golden and not refrigerating potatoes keeps sugars low and can cut formation a lot. It is better not to eat dark brown or burnt parts.
c-030.actionItem: Take toast or roast potatoes out before they turn dark brown today and cut off any burnt bits.

c-031.title: A disposable hand warmer is heat from iron rusting
c-031.summary: The iron powder in a hand warmer oxidizes with oxygen from the air and gives off heat. It is handy on winter trips, but long skin contact risks low-temperature burns.
c-031.principle: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃ is exothermic, and activated carbon and salt speed the reaction.
c-031.example: The peak is about 50-60°C and lasts for hours. Stick it on the outside of clothing and remove it when sleeping to prevent low-temperature burns. Its sealed wrapper blocks air before opening.
c-031.actionItem: When using a hand warmer today, stick it on top of clothing and check your skin every hour.

c-032.title: Charcoal deodorizers adsorb, they do not decompose
c-032.summary: Charcoal and activated carbon trap odor molecules on their surface to reduce smell. They stop working when saturated, so respect the replacement or regeneration schedule.
c-032.principle: Adsorption is molecules sticking to a surface, and activated carbon has a specific surface area of 500-1500m²/g.
c-032.example: 100g of activated carbon can have the surface area of a football field, enough to tackle one fridge shelf. Drying charcoal in the sun once a month partly regenerates it, and replacing every 3-6 months is enough.
c-032.actionItem: Write the date you replaced your fridge deodorizer on its label and set a reminder for 3 months later.

c-033.title: Soaking rice for 30 minutes cuts cooking energy
c-033.summary: Soaked rice has already absorbed water, so heating takes less time and cooks more evenly. You use a little less electricity or gas.
c-033.principle: Starch absorbs water and gelatinizes: (C₆H₁₀O₅)_n + nH₂O → a swollen gel. Gelatinization occurs at about 60-70 °CmathrmC.
c-033.example: Rice soaked 30 minutes takes up about 20-25% of its weight in water so water reaches the core. Cooking time drops by a few minutes versus unsoaked, which adds up to dozens of minutes saved a month if cooked daily. In winter lukewarm water is quicker.
c-033.actionItem: Wash and soak rice for 30 minutes this evening, cook it, and compare the cooking time.

c-034.title: Washing hands for 20 seconds gives soap time to surround dirt
c-034.summary: Soap molecules love oil on one end and water on the other, so they wrap dirt and germs and wash them away. This takes friction and time.
c-034.principle: Above the critical micelle concentration (CMC), soap forms micelles that enclose grease: RCOONa → RCOO⁻ + Na⁺
c-034.example: Lathering palms, backs, between fingers and under nails for 20 seconds (two rounds of the birthday song) greatly lowers common germs. Choose water temperature for skin comfort rather than effect.
c-034.actionItem: Count 20 seconds with a timer or a song when you wash your hands today, including under the nails.

c-035.title: Winter lip balm forms a barrier rather than adding moisture
c-035.summary: Hydrocarbon balms such as petroleum jelly form a hydrophobic film that slows water loss from the lips. They work better on slightly damp lips than on dry flakes.
c-035.principle: Evaporation scales with the water vapor pressure difference at the surface, and a petroleum hydrocarbon C_nH₂ₙ₊₂ film does not mix with water, so it slows that loss.
c-035.example: In dry winter indoor air (about 20% relative humidity) bare lips lose water quickly. A thin layer of petroleum jelly noticeably reduces evaporation and cracking.
c-035.actionItem: Tonight, dampen your lips with water and apply one thin layer of lip balm before bed.

c-036.title: Apply hand cream on damp skin to make it last
c-036.summary: On damp hands, moisturizer traps water better. The same amount keeps skin moister, so you use less cream.
c-036.principle: Skin water loss follows Fick's law J = -D(dC / dx), with glycerin drawing in water and petrolatum blocking evaporation.
c-036.example: Within 3 minutes of showering or washing, patting lightly with a towel and applying a pea-sized amount can cut how often you reapply even in dry winter. Wearing gloves overnight boosts the effect.
c-036.actionItem: After washing your hands today, apply a pea-sized amount of hand cream before drying them completely.

c-037.title: Choose a cleanser close to skin's mildly acidic pH (around 5.5)
c-037.summary: Skin has a mildly acidic protective layer that high-pH soap can disrupt. In dry winter a mildly acidic cleanser is less irritating.
c-037.principle: pH = -[H⁺]. Skin surface is pH 4.5-5.5 while regular soap is pH 9-10, with [H⁺] about ten thousand times lower.
c-037.example: pH 5.5 versus pH 9.5 is a 10⁴-fold difference in hydrogen ion concentration. A cleanser labeled mildly acidic causes less tightness after washing and reduces how much moisturizer you need.
c-037.actionItem: When buying your next cleanser, check the pH on the product description and note how your skin feels after washing.

c-038.title: Why power banks lose capacity in the cold
c-038.summary: In low temperatures, chemical reactions and ion movement in lithium-ion cells slow down, so usable capacity drops. Keeping them in an inner pocket reduces drain.
c-038.principle: With rate k = Ae⁻E_a/RT, a lower T makes k smaller and raises the cell's internal resistance.
c-038.example: Near 0°C capacity can fall 20-30%, and more at -10°C. A 10,000 mAh power bank may deliver only around 7,000 mAh outdoors in winter, so it seems to need recharging more often.
c-038.actionItem: Keep your power bank and phone in an inner coat pocket today so body heat keeps them warm.

c-039.title: Calculate power bank flight limits in Wh
c-039.summary: Lithium batteries are allowed only in carry-on, not checked baggage, and the limit is in Wh. mAh alone is confusing, so calculate it yourself.
c-039.principle: Wh = V × Ah (nominal 3.7V for lithium-ion). Up to 100Wh is allowed; 100-160Wh needs airline approval.
c-039.example: 20,000 mAh = 20 Ah × 3.7V = 74Wh, which is fine, while 27,000 mAh gives 99.9Wh, right at the limit. 30,000 mAh (111Wh) needs approval.
c-039.actionItem: Today, multiply your power bank's mAh by 3.7V to get Wh and check whether the label shows Wh.

c-040.title: Prevent carbon monoxide poisoning from winter heating and charcoal
c-040.summary: Fuel burned incompletely in poor ventilation produces odorless carbon monoxide. Never use charcoal, briquettes or camping heaters indoors.
c-040.principle: With too little oxygen, 2C + O₂ → 2CO forms carbon monoxide, which binds to hemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen.
c-040.example: At 200ppm CO, headaches appear within hours, and above 800ppm it becomes dangerous within an hour. Check boiler flue connections and ventilation, and install a CO alarm.
c-040.actionItem: Check your boiler flue connection and your CO alarm battery today.

c-041.title: A yellow gas flame means wasted fuel
c-041.summary: A healthy gas flame is blue. Yellow or orange means incomplete combustion with soot and more carbon monoxide. Cleaning the burner restores efficiency.
c-041.principle: Complete combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. With too little oxygen: CH₄ + 32O₂ → CO + 2H₂O.
c-041.example: A yellow flame that blackens the pot bottom transfers less heat and uses the same or more fuel. Clearing food debris from burner ports with a toothpick usually brings back the blue flame.
c-041.actionItem: Clean your stove burner ports with a toothpick today and check the flame color.

c-042.title: Avoid winter car battery drain and save on replacement
c-042.summary: Cold weather and repeated short trips run down lead-acid batteries and shorten their life. A discharged battery has weaker electrolyte and can freeze in sub-zero weather.
c-042.principle: Discharge: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Sulfuric acid is consumed, so the electrolyte freezing point rises.
c-042.example: A fully charged battery freezes around -60°C, but a discharged one can freeze near -7°C. Driving 30 minutes or more once a week, or topping up with a charger, can postpone a replacement costing around 100,000 won.
c-042.actionItem: Before starting the car today, switch off heater, heated seat and audio, and schedule a weekly 30-minute drive.

c-043.title: Seasoning a cast-iron pan is oil polymerizing into a hard film
c-043.summary: Baking a thin layer of oil on at high heat forms a hard coating that reduces rust and sticking. A thick coat turns sticky.
c-043.principle: Unsaturated fatty acids react with oxygen and polymerize. Rust forms by 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃.
c-043.example: Wipe on a tiny amount of cooking oil, wipe it off with a paper towel, and bake at 220°C for 1 hour to form the film. Drying it right after use lets one seasoned pan last years, making it cheap to own.
c-043.actionItem: After washing a cast-iron or carbon steel pan today, dry it over heat and wipe on a thin film of oil.

c-044.title: Clean tarnished silver with aluminum foil and baking soda
c-044.summary: This electrochemical reaction turns black silver sulfide on silver back into silver. No rubbing means less silver is scrubbed away. Ventilate, since it smells of sulfur.
c-044.example: Dissolve 1 tbsp baking soda in 500mL hot water and soak the silver so it touches the foil for 2-5 minutes. Do not use it on pearls, gemstones or glued handles.
c-044.actionItem: Soak one tarnished silver spoon in hot baking soda water with foil today.

c-045.title: Do not eat from the blue-green patina on copper pots
c-045.summary: When copper meets acid and moisture, a toxic blue-green patina (verdigris) forms. Do not leave acidic food in copper cookware, and check the inner lining.
c-045.principle: Copper oxide dissolves in vinegar: CuO + 2CH₃COOH → Cu(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂O. Verdigris is Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃.
c-045.example: Copper pots are safe only if the inside is lined with tin or stainless steel. Remove patina on the outside by rubbing a 1:1 vinegar and salt paste for 5 minutes and rinsing. Do not cook in it if the lining has worn through.
c-045.actionItem: Check the inner lining of your copper pot today, and stop cooking in it if it has worn off.

c-046.title: Soaking burnt pans with simmered baking soda takes less effort and energy
c-046.summary: Simmering in a mild alkaline solution loosens burnt residue with little force, rather than long scrubbing under hot water. Avoid it on aluminum pans, which discolor.
c-046.principle: On heating, 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂↑ forms sodium carbonate and raises the pH to about 11.
c-046.example: Simmering 2 tbsp baking soda in 500mL water for 10 minutes loosens burnt marks. This uses less water, soap and hot water than scrubbing under a running tap.
c-046.actionItem: Today, simmer a burnt pot with 2 tbsp baking soda and water for 10 minutes, let it cool, then wipe it clean.

c-047.title: Rinse bloodstains in cold water first
c-047.summary: Blood comes out of fabric with cold water (below 20°C), not warm water.
c-047.principle: Blood proteins such as hemoglobin and fibrinogen denature and coagulate with heat, bonding to the fibers. Hydrogen peroxide is broken down by the catalase in blood: 2H₂O₂ ―(catalase)→ 2H₂O + O₂↑
c-047.example: A cotton shirt rinsed with 60°C water sets a brown stain, but soaking it 5 minutes in 15°C water and dabbing 3% hydrogen peroxide makes it fizz (oxygen) and lifts most of the stain. Use on whites only, and test colored fabric on a hidden spot first.
c-047.actionItem: If a stain happens today, run cold water through it from the back of the fabric instead of using warm water.

c-048.title: Dose detergent to your water hardness
c-048.summary: Doubling detergent barely improves cleaning; it just costs more and needs more rinsing.
c-048.principle: Surfactants stop lifting extra soil once above their critical micelle concentration (CMC). Calcium ions in hard water precipitate soap: Ca²⁺ + 2C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻ → Ca(C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂↓
c-048.example: Using 80mL instead of the recommended 40mL cleans about the same but leaves residue that needs an extra rinse cycle. Saving 40mL per load over 20 loads a month is 9.6L a year, roughly 15 USD.
c-048.actionItem: Check the cap markings on your detergent before today's wash and measure only the recommended amount.

c-049.title: Fine dust is made in the air
c-049.summary: Much of PM2.5 forms in the atmosphere by chemical reactions, so a well-fitted KF94 mask helps on high-dust spring days.
c-049.principle: Sulfur and nitrogen oxides react with ammonia to form secondary particles: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃, 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄
c-049.example: In severe Korean PM2.5 episodes, ammonium nitrate and sulfate can make up nearly half of the particle mass. KF94 filters at least 94% of 0.4μm particles, but only if it seals to the face.
c-049.actionItem: If today's air forecast says Bad, press the mask's nose clip so there is no gap before going out.

c-050.title: Windshield water-repellent coating is a thin silane film
c-050.summary: Water-repellent coatings build a siloxane or fluorinated molecular film on glass so rain and sleet bead up and roll off. Better visibility makes winter driving safer.
c-050.principle: Silanes bond to the glass Si-OH groups to form Si-O-Si links, and the outward hydrophobic chains raise the water contact angle θ to roughly 100^° or more.
c-050.example: Bare glass has a contact angle near 30^° so water spreads, while coated glass at 100^° or more lets droplets blow off at 60-80km/h. The coating usually wears off after a few months.
c-050.actionItem: This week, clean off the oily film on the windshield, apply a thin coat of water repellent and buff it with a dry cloth.

c-051.title: Why cotton and polyester dry differently
c-051.summary: Choose polyester for workouts and cotton for underwear and towels to handle sweat and moisture.
c-051.principle: Cotton cellulose has many -OH groups that hydrogen-bond to water, absorbing up to ~25% of its weight, while hydrophobic polyester absorbs only ~0.4%. HO-R + H₂O ⇌ HO-R · sH₂O
c-051.example: A sweat-soaked 100g cotton tee can take over 2 hours to dry, while polyester dries in about an hour. Polyester, though, holds onto odor molecules and needs washing.
c-051.actionItem: Next time you shop, read the fiber label and pick a high polyester share for sportswear.

c-052.title: City gas bills charge for heat content, not just volume
c-052.summary: City gas is billed on volume (m³) multiplied by a heating-value factor (MJ/m³), so the bill reflects energy. Knowing the unit helps you compare heating use month to month.
c-052.principle: Methane combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH ≈ -890kJ/mol. One cubic meter of city gas holds about 42MJ.
c-052.example: Using 50m³ a month is about 50 × 42 = 2100MJ. Cutting use by 10% with a lower boiler setpoint saves roughly 210MJ.
c-052.actionItem: Today, find this month's usage (m³) on your gas bill and note how it compares with last month.

c-053.title: Dissolving rust with citric acid
c-053.summary: Red rust on small steel tools mostly disappears after a soak in citric acid solution.
c-053.principle: Iron(III) oxide dissolves and is chelated by citrate: Fe₂O₃ + 6H⁺ → 2Fe³⁺ + 3H₂O, then Fe³⁺ binds citrate ions.
c-053.example: Dissolve 25g citric acid in 500mL water (5%), soak rusty scissors for 4-6 hours, and scrub. Never combine with chlorine cleaners; dry right away and wipe on a thin film of oil.
c-053.actionItem: Put one rusty small tool in 5% citric acid today, then dry and oil it tomorrow.

c-054.title: Oxygen bleach works best in warm water
c-054.summary: Sodium percarbonate is most active near 40°C and cheaply revives whites.
c-054.principle: Sodium percarbonate splits in water into hydrogen peroxide and sodium carbonate: 2Na₂CO₃ · 3H₂O₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + 3H₂O₂, then H₂O₂ → H₂O + 12 O₂
c-054.example: Dissolve 25g in 5L of 40°C water and soak yellowed white socks for 1 hour. It is cheaper than branded whiteners and has no chlorine smell, but do not use on wool or silk.
c-054.actionItem: Soak one load of whites today in 40°C water with 5g/L percarbonate.

c-055.title: Pollen season: rinse your nose with saline
c-055.summary: For spring allergies, a 0.9% saline rinse washes pollen off the nasal lining.
c-055.principle: 0.9% NaCl is isotonic with body fluids, so it neither swells nor shrinks mucosal cells. Osmotic pressure: = iMRT
c-055.example: Dissolve 4.5g salt in 500mL boiled, cooled water (0.9%). Do not use raw tap water; plain water is hypotonic and stings.
c-055.actionItem: After coming home today, rinse each nostril once with a store-bought saline spray.

c-056.title: Shoe odor comes from bacteria feeding on sweat, not sweat itself
c-056.summary: Sweat is nearly odorless; bacteria in shoes break down its fats and proteins into smelly fatty acids. Baking soda neutralizes these acidic odors and absorbs moisture.
c-056.principle: Odor molecules such as short-chain fatty acids (for example isovaleric acid) react with a weak base: RCOOH + NaHCO₃ → RCOONa + H₂O + CO₂.
c-056.example: Leaving 1-2 teaspoons of baking soda in each shoe overnight reduces acidic odor and soaks up moisture. Shake it out the next day before wearing.
c-056.actionItem: When you take your shoes off today, sprinkle a spoonful of baking soda inside and leave it overnight.

c-057.title: The plastic number on the bottom and microwaves
c-057.summary: The recycling number on a container tells you whether it is safe for microwaves and hot food.
c-057.principle: PP (#5) melts around 160°C and is used for microwave-safe ware, while foam PS (#6) deforms near 80°C. Polymerization: n CH₂=CHCH₃ → [-CH₂-CH(CH₃)-]_n
c-057.example: A PP lunch box tolerates soup above 100°C with little change, but heating a hot greasy meal in a disposable PS cup noodle tub can melt it. Also look for a microwave-safe symbol.
c-057.actionItem: Check the bottom number on 3 containers you use often and keep non-#5 ones out of the microwave.

c-058.title: Vitamins A, D, E and K absorb best with some fat
c-058.summary: Fat-soluble vitamins barely dissolve in water, so they need dietary fat to be carried into the gut lining inside micelles. Taking them on an empty stomach can lower absorption.
c-058.principle: Nonpolar molecules dissolve inside micelles formed by bile acids. Without fat, fewer micelles form and absorption drops.
c-058.example: Beta-carotene from carrots cooked in a teaspoon of olive oil is absorbed several times better than from raw carrots. Vitamin D supplements are also better taken with a meal.
c-058.actionItem: If you take vitamin D or another fat-soluble supplement today, take it with a meal that contains fat.

c-059.title: Tea-stained cups and baking soda
c-059.summary: Brown tea and coffee film inside mugs comes off with baking soda paste thanks to mild abrasion and alkalinity.
c-059.principle: Tea tannins and polyphenols dissolve better in mild alkali. NaHCO₃ ⇌ Na⁺ + HCO₃⁻, a weakly alkaline pH of about 8.3
c-059.example: Mixing 1 tablespoon of baking soda with 1 teaspoon of water and scrubbing a sponge for 1 minute removes most of the brown film, even on years-old mugs, with no special cleaner to buy.
c-059.actionItem: Scrub one stained mug with baking soda paste today.

c-060.title: Coffee grounds are not instant fertilizer
c-060.summary: Dry coffee grounds and mix in small amounts; heavy use causes mold and stunted growth.
c-060.principle: Composting works best at a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio (C/N) of about 25-30:1. Grounds are around 20:1, nitrogen-rich, and residual caffeine can inhibit seedlings.
c-060.example: Keep dried grounds under 10% of the soil volume (100mL per 1L of soil) to be safe. A thick wet layer grows mold.
c-060.actionItem: Spread today's coffee grounds on newspaper to dry.

c-061.title: When aspirin smells like vinegar
c-061.summary: If an aspirin bottle smells of vinegar, moisture has broken it down; do not take it and discard it.
c-061.principle: Acetylsalicylic acid reacts with water: C₉H₈O₄ + H₂O → C₇H₆O₃ + CH₃COOH (salicylic acid + acetic acid)
c-061.example: On a bathroom shelf above 80% humidity, hydrolysis can progress within months. Store with the cap closed in a cool, dry drawer, with one silica gel packet if possible.
c-061.actionItem: Move medicines and supplements from the bathroom to a dry drawer today.

c-062.title: Revive a waterproof jacket's coating with heat
c-062.summary: If water no longer beads on a rain jacket, washing and gentle heat can restore the water-repellent coating.
c-062.principle: DWR coatings stand up hydrophobic chains on fabric so water beads by surface tension. Contact angle θ>90^°, Young's equation: θ=γ_SV-γ_SLγ_LV
c-062.example: Soap residue and dirt flatten the chains. After a mild-detergent wash, 20 minutes in a medium-heat dryer (about 40-60°C) or a gentle iron stands the chains up so water beads again. If not, use a retail repellent spray.
c-062.actionItem: Splash water on your rain jacket today and see whether it beads.

c-063.title: What does 20-10-10 on a fertilizer bag mean
c-063.summary: The N-P-K numbers on a fertilizer bag give the percentage of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, so match them to your crop.
c-063.principle: Plants use nitrogen (NO3−, NH4+) for leaves, phosphorus (H₂PO₄⁻) for roots and flowers, potassium (K⁺) for stems and fruit. Urea hydrolysis: CO(NH₂)₂ + 2H₂O → 2NH₄⁺ + CO₃²⁻
c-063.example: 1kg of 20-10-10 fertilizer holds 200g N, 100g P2O5, and 100g K2O. Leafy greens suit high N; flowers and fruit suit higher P and K. Overapplying beyond the label burns roots.
c-063.actionItem: Look up the best N-P-K ratio for one plant you grow today.

c-064.title: Alkaline versus lithium AA batteries
c-064.summary: Alkaline suits remotes; lithium primary cells last longer in cold or high-drain devices.
c-064.principle: Alkaline: Zn + 2MnO₂ + H₂O → ZnO + 2MnO(OH). Aqueous electrolyte slows in the cold, but lithium primary cells use non-aqueous electrolyte and work to -40°C.
c-064.example: In a digital camera, 2 alkaline AAs often give about 300 shots while lithium AAs give 800 or more. For low-drain items such as remotes and wall clocks, cheap alkaline is the better value.
c-064.actionItem: Write down today which of your devices should use alkaline and which lithium.

c-065.title: Soil acidity decides hydrangea color
c-065.summary: Blue or pink hydrangeas depend on soil pH, so you can steer the color by adjusting the soil.
c-065.principle: In acidic soil (pH below about 5.5), aluminum dissolves as Al³⁺ and binds anthocyanin to give blue; in neutral to alkaline soil it precipitates as Al(OH)₃, so flowers stay pink: Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Al(OH)₃↓
c-065.example: Watering pink hydrangeas monthly with aluminum sulfate at about 3g per liter turns them bluer in a few months. Raising pH above 6.5 with lime gives pink. Overdoses harm roots.
c-065.actionItem: Test your pot soil with a pH strip today and decide the color you want.

c-066.title: Why wool sweaters shrink
c-066.summary: Wool shrinks from hot water and friction, so hand wash it in lukewarm water with neutral detergent.
c-066.principle: Wool is the protein keratin, and its scaly surface tangles with agitation in felting. Alkali and heat hydrolyze peptide bonds: R-CO-NH-R' + H₂O → RCOOH + R'NH₂
c-066.example: Press-wash 2-3 minutes in water under 30°C with neutral detergent, do not wring, blot with a towel, and dry flat for almost no shrinkage. A 40°C regular machine cycle can shrink a size at once and ruin an expensive sweater.
c-066.actionItem: Check the care label on a wool garment today and set aside neutral detergent.

c-067.title: Vitamin C is fragile to light and air
c-067.summary: Keep vitamin C supplements in a dark bottle, tightly closed, away from sunlight and moisture.
c-067.principle: Ascorbic acid oxidizes in air: C₆H₈O₆ → C₆H₆O₆ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ (dehydroascorbic acid), and heat and light speed it.
c-067.example: Powdered vitamin C left in an open bottle at 25°C and 70% humidity turns brown and loses potency within weeks. Stored cool, the same product stays stable until its expiry date.
c-067.actionItem: Move your supplements from the windowsill or kitchen shelf to a cool drawer today.

c-068.title: Choosing DEET or picaridin repellent
c-068.summary: Before outdoor trips, a 20-30% DEET or 10-20% picaridin product protects for hours.
c-068.principle: DEET (N,N-diethyl-m-toluamide, C₁₂H₁₇NO) disrupts mosquito odor receptors so they cannot locate you. Higher concentration lasts longer, but the benefit levels off.
c-068.example: 30% DEET typically protects ~6 hours and 10% ~2 hours; above 50% adds little. Apply from your hands, not sprayed on the face, and do not use on babies under 2 months.
c-068.actionItem: Check the active ingredient and concentration on your repellent today and pack it in your outdoor bag.

c-069.title: Stainless steel 304 versus 316: reading the label
c-069.summary: For seaside or salty-food use, 316 stainless with molybdenum resists corrosion better.
c-069.principle: Stainless forms a Cr₂O₃ passive film from at least ~10.5% chromium: 4Cr + 3O₂ → 2Cr₂O₃. 316 adds 2-3% molybdenum to resist chloride (Cl−) attack.
c-069.example: 304 (18-8) is fine for ordinary kitchenware but can pit in salty environments. A 316 flask costing 20-30% more lasts longer at the beach.
c-069.actionItem: Find the 304 or 316 marking on the bottom of a stainless item you use today.

c-070.title: Fluoride in toothpaste turns enamel into a tougher crystal
c-070.summary: Fluoride ions convert the hydroxyapatite in enamel into fluorapatite, which resists acid better. Rinsing lightly after brushing keeps more fluoride on the teeth.
c-070.principle: Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂ + 2F⁻ → Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆F₂ + 2OH⁻. Fluorapatite starts dissolving near pH 4.5, compared with about pH 5.5 for hydroxyapatite.
c-070.example: Use a pea-sized amount of 1000-1500ppm fluoride toothpaste and rinse just once lightly with water to keep its residual protective effect.
c-070.actionItem: After brushing tonight, rinse only once lightly instead of swishing water several times.

c-071.title: Why aluminum pots darken
c-071.summary: Acidic food left in an aluminum pot darkens it, so store leftovers in another container.
c-071.principle: The Al₂O₃ film on aluminum dissolves in acid: Al₂O₃ + 6H⁺ → 2Al³⁺ + 3H₂O, 2Al + 6H⁺ → 2Al³⁺ + 3H₂. Alkaline cleaners also damage it.
c-071.example: Tomato sauce (pH about 4.5) left in an aluminum pot overnight can discolor it and add a metallic taste. Boil 2 tablespoons of citric acid or cream of tartar per liter of water for 10 minutes to remove most of the dullness.
c-071.actionItem: Transfer today's leftover soup or sauce from the pot to a glass or stainless container.

c-072.title: What the yellow underarm stain really is
c-072.summary: The yellow underarm stain on white shirts comes from sweat and aluminum in antiperspirant, and oxygen bleach works on it.
c-072.principle: Sweat proteins and fatty acids combine with aluminum salts into insoluble deposits, and oxygen bleach oxidizes the organics: H₂O₂ → H₂O + [O]
c-072.example: Mix 1 tablespoon percarbonate with a cup of 40°C water into a thick paste, leave on the stain for 30 minutes, then wash; most color lifts. Chlorine bleach can actually turn protein stains yellower.
c-072.actionItem: Apply an oxygen bleach paste to the underarms of today's white shirt before washing.

c-073.title: A new-furniture smell signals formaldehyde
c-073.summary: The smell of new furniture or wallpaper is volatile organic compounds (VOCs), so air them out with open windows for days.
c-073.principle: Urea resins in plywood adhesive break down and release formaldehyde, HCHO. Emission rises with temperature and humidity.
c-073.example: For the first 2 weeks after new furniture arrives, ventilate for 30 minutes three times a day and add a bake-out at 25-30°C; levels drop sharply. The indoor guideline is 0.1ppm or lower.
c-073.actionItem: Ventilate today with cross-ventilation three times, at least 10 minutes each.

c-074.title: Travel water: boiling versus purification tablets
c-074.summary: Unsafe water can be disinfected by boiling at least 1 minute or with chlorine tablets, killing most pathogens.
c-074.principle: Chlorine tablets form hypochlorous acid in water, which oxidizes microbes: NaDCC + H₂O → HOCl + · s, HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻
c-074.example: Add 1 tablet to 1L of clear water and wait 30 minutes (longer for Cryptosporidium). Cloudy water should be strained through cloth first, and above 2,000m extend boiling to 3 minutes.
c-074.actionItem: Pack a purification tablet or portable filter in your travel bag today.

c-075.title: Fleece wash bags reduce microplastics
c-075.summary: Washing synthetic clothes in a bag in cold water sharply cuts the microfibers they shed.
c-075.principle: Polyester is an ester polymer that does not degrade but fragments by abrasion: n HOOC-C₆H₄-COOH + n HOCH₂CH₂OH → [-OC-C₆H₄-COO-CH₂CH₂O-]_n + 2n H₂O
c-075.example: A single fleece jacket wash can release thousands to hundreds of thousands of microfibers. A wash bag or filter catches a fair share and keeps them out of rivers, and a colder wash also saves energy.
c-075.actionItem: Zip up fleece and polyester clothes, put them in a wash bag, and run a cold wash today.

c-076.title: Choose low-self-discharge NiMH rechargeable batteries
c-076.summary: Ordinary NiMH cells lose about 20% of their charge per month even when unused. Low-self-discharge types keep 70-85% after a year, which suits remotes and clocks.
c-076.principle: NiMH reaction: NiOOH + MH ⇌ Ni(OH)₂ + M. Self-discharge happens as hydrogen slowly shifts between the electrolyte and the electrodes.
c-076.example: One low-self-discharge AA cell (about 2000 mAh) recharged 500 times can replace hundreds of disposable alkaline cells, cutting long-term cost sharply.
c-076.actionItem: Today, if any remote or clock uses disposable batteries, plan to switch it to low-self-discharge rechargeables.

c-077.title: Ballpoint ink stains come out with alcohol, not water
c-077.summary: Ballpoint ink is an oil-based ink with dye dissolved in organic solvent, so water barely moves it. Dabbing with a cloth wet with rubbing alcohol dissolves the dye.
c-077.principle: Similar polarity mixes well. Oil-based dyes dissolve far better in ethanol (ε ≈ 25) than in water (ε ≈ 80).
c-077.example: Place dry paper towel under the stain and dab from the outside inward with a swab of 70% alcohol; the ink transfers to the towel instead of spreading. Test a small hidden spot first.
c-077.actionItem: Today, if you have a ballpoint mark on fabric or furniture, test alcohol on a hidden spot first.

c-078.title: Wilted vegetables revive after a soak in cold water
c-078.summary: Wilted lettuce and spinach are limp because their cells have lost water. Soaking in cold water for 20-30 minutes lets osmosis refill the cells and restore crispness.
c-078.principle: Water moves into cells when the solute concentration inside is higher than outside. The osmotic pressure = iMRT builds the turgor that stiffens the leaf.
c-078.example: A handful of lettuce left a day too long gains about 5-10% in weight and regains its crunch after a 30-minute soak. Leaves that are slimy or spoiled do not recover.
c-078.actionItem: Today, soak wilted leafy greens from your fridge in cold water for 30 minutes, then shake them dry.

c-079.title: Dust mite allergens fall only with washing at 60°C or hotter
c-079.summary: Mites and allergen proteins in bedding barely drop with cold-water washes. Water near 60°C denatures the proteins, killing mites and reducing allergens.
c-079.principle: Heat unfolds the tertiary structure of proteins so they lose function (thermal denaturation). Mites usually die within minutes at 55-60°C.
c-079.example: Washing sheets and pillowcases at 60°C cuts allergens substantially, while a 30°C wash helps little. If the care label forbids it, a hot dryer cycle is an alternative.
c-079.actionItem: Today, wash your pillowcases or sheets on the hottest cycle the care label allows.

c-080.title: Camp fuel and winter butane
c-080.summary: Isobutane canisters weaken near freezing, so use propane-blend fuel for late-winter camping.
c-080.principle: Liquefied gases do not vaporize below their boiling points: butane about -1°CmathrmC, isobutane -12°CmathrmC, propane -42°CmathrmC. Combustion: C₄H₁₀ + 132O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O
c-080.example: Below 0°C a butane canister loses pressure, the flame weakens, and boiling water can take twice as long. Keep the can warm in a sleeping bag or close to your body, and ventilate in a tent to avoid CO poisoning.
c-080.actionItem: Check the butane/propane ratio on your camp fuel canister today.

c-081.title: Reading sunscreen ingredients
c-081.summary: Before spring UV climbs, learn the difference between mineral (zinc oxide) and chemical filters when you choose.
c-081.principle: Zinc oxide (ZnO) reflects and scatters UV, while organic filters such as avobenzone absorb it and release heat: h + filter → filter^* → heat
c-081.example: SPF 50 blocks about 98% of UVB and SPF 30 about 97%, a small gap. For the face you need about 0.5g (two finger lengths) reapplied every 2-3 hours.
c-081.actionItem: Squeeze two finger lengths of sunscreen and apply it before going out today.

c-082.title: Draining food waste cuts both its smell and its weight
c-082.summary: The stench of food waste comes from microbes breaking down protein into gases such as hydrogen sulfide. Squeezing out the water first slows microbial growth, reducing odor and weight.
c-082.principle: Sulfur amino acid breakdown: R-SH → H₂S. Microbial growth slows as water activity a_w drops.
c-082.example: Food waste is 70-80% water. Squeezing out just 20% of that water cuts the weight by roughly 15%, lowering disposal cost and odor together.
c-082.actionItem: Today, drain and squeeze your food waste in a strainer before throwing it out.

c-083.title: Shelf life is set by how reaction rates depend on temperature
c-083.summary: Spoilage reactions roughly double in speed for every 10°C rise. That is why the stated storage temperature must be kept for the date label to mean anything.
c-083.principle: Arrhenius equation: k = A e⁻E_a/RT. For typical spoilage reactions the rate rises about 2-3 times per 10°C.
c-083.example: Milk that lasts 7 days at 4°C may spoil in about 3-4 days at 14°C. Store it on an inner shelf rather than the door, where temperature swings more.
c-083.actionItem: Today, check that your refrigerator is between 0 and 4°C.

c-084.title: Washing soda for greasy grime
c-084.summary: Washing soda (sodium carbonate) cuts old kitchen grease better than baking soda because it is more alkaline.
c-084.principle: Fats (triglycerides) saponify in alkali: RCOOR' + OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + R'OH. Washing soda Na₂CO₃ has a pH of about 11.
c-084.example: Dissolve 1 tablespoon in 1L of hot water, soak 10 minutes, and wipe to loosen baked-on grease. It irritates skin, so wear gloves, and avoid aluminum and coated pans.
c-084.actionItem: Soak one range hood filter in washing soda solution today.

c-085.title: Fine dust from frying
c-085.summary: Frying and grilling raise indoor PM2.5 sharply, so turn on the hood and open a window while cooking.
c-085.principle: Oil heated beyond about 180°C thermally decomposes into particles and acrolein: C₃H₅(OH)₃ → CH₂=CHCHO + 2H₂O (glycerol dehydration)
c-085.example: Measurements show pan-frying mackerel can push indoor PM2.5 to hundreds of μg/m³, and running the hood cuts it considerably. Keep the hood on 10 minutes after cooking.
c-085.actionItem: Turn on the hood before you start cooking today and leave it on 10 minutes after.

c-086.title: Rinse your bike and car after the beach
c-086.summary: Sea salt corrodes metal quickly, so rinse your car and bike with fresh water after a beach trip.
c-086.principle: Sodium chloride solution acts as an electrolyte for iron corrosion cells: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻, O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
c-086.example: Iron corrodes several times faster in salty damp air than in dry air. Washing the underbody and chain with water within 24 hours of a coastal drive and oiling the chain greatly cuts rust.
c-086.actionItem: If you went to the coast, rinse your car underbody and bike chain with water today.

c-087.title: Washing produce: water first, baking soda second
c-087.summary: Running water is the basis, and a 12-minute baking soda soak has been reported to remove somewhat more surface pesticide.
c-087.principle: Some pesticides (such as thiabendazole) degrade more easily in mild alkali. A 1% NaHCO₃ solution has pH about 8.1.
c-087.example: In a study, apples soaked 12 minutes in 1% baking soda (10g per liter) lost more surface residue than with plain water. Rinse again under running water afterward for fruit you eat with the peel.
c-087.actionItem: Soak apples or grapes in 10g/L baking soda water today, then rinse.

c-088.title: Bird droppings and bug splatter are protein and need soaking first
c-088.summary: Droppings and insect fluids contain acids and proteins that bake onto paint as they dry. Soaking with a wet cloth first and then wiping gently limits paint damage.
c-088.principle: Dried proteins clump together and hydrogen-bond to the surface. Water and a mild alkaline cleaner (pH 8-9) break these bonds.
c-088.example: Droppings left a day or more can visibly etch paint within 1-2 days, so laying a wet microfiber towel on them for 5 minutes before wiping is safer.
c-088.actionItem: Today, if there is dried bird dropping on your car or window, lay a wet cloth on it for 5 minutes, then wipe it off.

c-089.title: Baking powder and baking soda are different ingredients
c-089.summary: Baking soda is just sodium bicarbonate and needs an acid to rise, while baking powder already contains acid and rises when it meets water. Swapping them can leave a bitter taste or a flat bake.
c-089.principle: NaHCO₃ + H⁺ → Na⁺ + H₂O + CO₂↑. One teaspoon of baking soda (about 5g) can release close to 1L of carbon dioxide.
c-089.example: If a recipe has 1/2 teaspoon of baking soda plus yogurt (an acid), the acid reacts the soda. Soda alone in a batter without acid leaves unreacted soda with a soapy, bitter taste.
c-089.actionItem: Today, check the labels on your baking soda and baking powder and keep them in separate, labeled containers.

c-090.title: Store apples and bananas apart
c-090.summary: Apples release ethylene, which ripens bananas faster, so keep different fruits apart.
c-090.principle: Ethylene CH₂=CH₂ is a plant hormone that activates cell-wall-degrading enzymes and speeds ripening. Its release surges as fruit ripens.
c-090.example: Unripe bananas in a bag with an apple ripen a day or two sooner, which you can use on purpose. To keep bananas longer, store apples separately to gain a day or two and reduce food waste.
c-090.actionItem: Put apples and bananas in separate spots or containers today.

c-091.title: Tannins in tea and coffee block iron absorption
c-091.summary: Tannins and polyphenols in tea and coffee bind iron ions into complexes that are hard to absorb. Leave at least 1-2 hours between them and iron supplements or iron-rich meals.
c-091.principle: Tannins chelate iron: Fe²⁺ + tannin → Fe-tannin complex. This complex is poorly absorbed in the gut.
c-091.example: Tea taken with a meal is reported to cut non-heme iron absorption by 40-60%. Waiting an hour after eating reduces the effect greatly.
c-091.actionItem: If you took iron or ate spinach or beans today, delay tea or coffee by an hour.

p-001.title: Preheat Your Thermos
p-001.summary: Rinsing a thermos with hot water first keeps your drink warm much longer.
p-001.principle: Heat escapes by conduction, convection and radiation; the vacuum layer blocks the first two and the silvered wall cuts radiation. Energy Q = mcΔT is first spent warming the flask wall.
p-001.example: Warming a 200g stainless wall (c ≈ 0.5J/g · K) from 20°C to 90°C takes about 7kJ. Without preheating, your drink supplies that heat and drops about 3-4°C right away.
p-001.actionItem: This morning, fill your thermos with boiling water for 3 minutes, pour it out, then add your drink.

p-002.title: Cool Hot Food Before the Fridge
p-002.summary: Putting hot soup straight into the fridge warms other food and costs extra electricity.
p-002.principle: A fridge must pump out the heat Q = mcΔT with its compressor. A shallow, wide dish has more surface area, so it cools faster via P = hAΔT.
p-002.example: Cooling 3L of soup from 80°C to 5°C removes about 3000 × 4.18 × 75 ≈ 940kJ. Letting it reach 40°C on the counter first takes nearly half of that load off the fridge.
p-002.actionItem: Today split hot food into shallow dishes, cool to 30-40°C, then refrigerate within 2 hours.

p-003.title: Bubble Wrap Window Insulation
p-003.summary: Sticking bubble wrap to a window traps still air that cuts heat loss sharply.
p-003.principle: Still air conducts only about 0.026W/m · K, 1/40 of glass (1.0). In Q = UAΔT the coefficient U falls.
p-003.example: A 2m² single pane with a 20°C indoor-outdoor gap and U ≈ 5.8 loses 232W. Bubble wrap lowering U to about 3.5 gives 140W, saving roughly 90W.
p-003.actionItem: Today spray water on a window and press bubble wrap, flat side to the glass.

p-004.title: Electric Blanket vs Central Heating
p-004.summary: When alone, warming just your body with an electric blanket beats heating a whole room.
p-004.principle: Heating energy E = Pt scales with the volume you heat. Warming only the small space under the covers needs far less heat.
p-004.example: A 50W electric blanket for 8 hours uses 0.4kWh. Heating a room with a 4kW heater for 8 hours can use up to 32kWh, dozens of times more.
p-004.actionItem: Tonight lower the thermostat by 1-2°C and use the blanket on low.

p-005.title: Rice Cooker Warm vs Freezing Portions
p-005.summary: Freezing leftover rice in portions uses less power than leaving the cooker on warm.
p-005.principle: Keeping warm must keep replacing wall losses P = UAΔT. Microwave reheating uses E = Pt only when needed.
p-005.example: Keep-warm of about 60W for 24 hours is 1.44kWh. Reheating one 200g bowl at 700W for 2 minutes is about 0.023kWh.
p-005.actionItem: Today wrap leftover rice in single portions, freeze them, and turn off keep-warm.

p-006.title: Phone Battery in the Cold
p-006.summary: A phone shutting off in freezing weather is because the battery chemistry slows down.
p-006.principle: Ion movement follows Arrhenius k = Ae⁻E_a/RT, dropping sharply as temperature falls while internal resistance rises and voltage sags.
p-006.example: A lithium-ion cell may deliver only about 70-80% of its capacity at 0°C and less at -10°C, so a phone showing 30% outdoors can suddenly die.
p-006.actionItem: When going out, keep your phone in an inner pocket; if it dies, warm it with your body before restarting.

p-007.title: Car Battery Winter Check
p-007.summary: A car fails to start in freezing weather because battery output drops and oil thickens.
p-007.principle: Power is P = VI; in the cold internal resistance r rises, so terminal voltage V = ε - Ir falls.
p-007.example: At a 400A cranking current, resistance rising from 0.01Ω to 0.02Ω raises the drop from 4V to 8V, leaving too little of a 12V battery.
p-007.actionItem: Today turn off lights and heater before cranking, and have a battery older than 3 years tested.

p-008.title: Walking on Ice
p-008.summary: On ice, short steps with the whole foot flat make the best use of friction.
p-008.principle: No slipping requires F ≤ µ N. On ice µ ≈ 0.05-0.1, about a tenth of dry asphalt (≈ 0.7).
p-008.example: The foot slips if the ratio of horizontal to vertical force, θ, exceeds µ. Halving your stride shrinks θ back into the safe range.
p-008.actionItem: On the next icy day halve your stride and keep your hands out of your pockets.

p-009.title: Leave the Microwave Center Empty
p-009.summary: Arranging food in a ring on the plate makes a microwave heat more evenly.
p-009.principle: Microwaves at 2.45GHz form standing waves with wavelength λ = c/f ≈ 12.2cm, creating hot and cold spots.
p-009.example: The plate center often gets less energy and stays cold. A ring layout plus one stir midway can cut temperature differences by 20°C or more.
p-009.actionItem: Today arrange food in a ring with the middle empty and stir halfway through.

p-010.title: Lid On When Boiling
p-010.summary: Just covering the pot noticeably lowers your gas bill.
p-010.principle: Evaporating water carries off latent heat L ≈ 2260J/g. A lid blocks steam and convection loss, so the same heat boils faster.
p-010.example: Heating 1L from 20°C to 100°C needs Q = 1000 × 4.18 × 80 ≈ 334kJ. A lid often cuts time and gas by about 20-30%.
p-010.actionItem: Today put the lid on from the start when boiling noodles or soup.

p-011.title: Full Freezer, Airy Fridge
p-011.summary: A full freezer holds its temperature when opened, while the fridge needs space for air to flow.
p-011.principle: Large heat capacity C = mc of ice and food stores cold, reducing ΔT = Q/C. The fridge compartment needs air circulation.
p-011.example: Opening the door for 10 s swaps about 100L of freezer air, so an empty freezer warms about 5°C, while a full one is buffered by its contents and recovers much faster.
p-011.actionItem: Today freeze a few water bottles and fill the empty spots in your freezer.

p-012.title: Reflector Behind the Radiator
p-012.summary: Foil on the wall behind a radiator sends heat back into the room.
p-012.principle: Radiated power is P = εσ A T⁴; shiny aluminum has low emissivity and high reflectance, bouncing infrared toward the room.
p-012.example: Part of a radiator's heat on an outside wall is absorbed by the wall. A reflector returns it, so the same heating warms the room faster with less wall loss.
p-012.actionItem: Today attach a heavy foil reflector behind a radiator on an exterior wall.

p-013.title: Hunt Standby Power
p-013.summary: Appliances that look off still draw electricity while plugged in.
p-013.principle: Energy is E = Pt. A 5W standby draw seems tiny but runs 24 hours a day, 8760 hours a year.
p-013.example: A combined 20W standby uses 0.02 × 8760 ≈ 175kWh, about 35,000 KRW a year at 200 KRW per kWh.
p-013.actionItem: Today group the TV, set-top box and chargers on a switched power strip and turn it off at bedtime.

p-014.title: Lower the Thermostat by 1°C
p-014.summary: Cutting room temperature by just 1°C noticeably reduces heating energy.
p-014.principle: Heat loss Q = UAΔT is proportional to the indoor-outdoor difference ΔT.
p-014.example: With 0°C outside, going from 22°C to 21°C reduces ΔT from 22 to 21, about 4.5%, and heating energy falls by roughly the same share.
p-014.actionItem: Today turn the thermostat down 1°C and put on a cardigan.

p-015.title: Curtain Length and Window Heat Loss
p-015.summary: Thick curtains reaching the floor stop cold air from circulating at the window.
p-015.principle: Air near cold glass is denser and sinks, creating convection. In Q = hAΔT a curtain lowers the convection coefficient h.
p-015.example: Closing thick curtains from frame to floor often cuts window heat loss 10-25%. A gap lets cold air spill out like a chimney.
p-015.actionItem: After sunset tonight draw the curtains fully and check the hem touches the floor.

p-016.title: Seal Door Drafts
p-016.summary: A 1mm gap around a door quietly eats your winter heating bill.
p-016.principle: Air leaking in must be warmed: P = ρ c V ΔT, with air ρ c ≈ 1.2kJ/m³ K.
p-016.example: A 20m³/h leak with ΔT=20°C costs P ≈ 1.2 × 20 × 20/3.6 ≈ 133W. Sealing half saves about 66W.
p-016.actionItem: Today apply weatherstrip tape to the door bottom and window edges.

p-017.title: Winter Tire Pressure
p-017.summary: Tire pressure falls along with the temperature.
p-017.principle: For an ideal gas at constant volume P/T = const. As absolute temperature T drops, pressure P drops in proportion.
p-017.example: A tire at 35psi at 20°C (293K) reads 35 × 263/293 ≈ 31.4psi at -10°C (263K), about 3.6psi lower.
p-017.actionItem: This morning check pressure on cold tires and fill to the recommended value.

p-018.title: Why Mittens Keep You Warmer
p-018.summary: Mittens with fingers together are warmer than gloves.
p-018.principle: Heat loss Q = hAΔT is proportional to exposed surface area A. Grouped fingers cut area and share warmth.
p-018.example: Compared to gloves wrapping five fingers separately, mittens expose roughly 20-30% less surface, so the same insulation loses that much less heat.
p-018.actionItem: On the coldest day wear mittens over thin gloves.

p-019.title: Layers Trap Air
p-019.summary: Several thin layers can be warmer than one thick garment.
p-019.principle: Still air between layers insulates. Total thermal resistance R = d_i/k_i grows with each layer.
p-019.example: A 5mm still-air layer adds R = 0.005/0.026 ≈ 0.19m²K/W. If you get hot, remove a layer to avoid sweat cooling.
p-019.actionItem: Today go out in three layers: fleece underlayer, shirt, windbreaker.

p-020.title: Indoor Laundry Drying
p-020.summary: Spacing clothes apart and ventilating makes indoor laundry dry far faster.
p-020.principle: Evaporation rate m ∝ A(p_s - p_a) scales with surface area and vapor-pressure difference.
p-020.example: If 500g of water evaporates from 1kg of wet laundry it absorbs about 500 × 2.26 ≈ 1130kJ. Spacing items can nearly halve drying time.
p-020.actionItem: Today hang laundry with gaps and run a fan on low.

p-021.title: Prevent Cracking in Hot Glass
p-021.summary: Pouring boiling water into a cold glass can shatter it.
p-021.principle: Uneven expansion creates thermal stress σ = EαΔT. Ordinary soda-lime glass tolerates it poorly.
p-021.example: With E ≈ 70 GPa, α ≈ 9 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ and ΔT=70°C, σ ≈ 44MPa, enough to cause surface failure.
p-021.actionItem: Today warm a cold glass with warm water first, then pour the hot drink.

p-022.title: Match Pot to Induction Hob
p-022.summary: An induction hob works best with a flat, well-sized pot base.
p-022.principle: Induction creates eddy currents so heat P = I²R is produced right in the pot base. The pot must be magnetic and well-contacted.
p-022.example: A pot much smaller than the coil receives less power and takes longer. Efficiency is about 85-90% versus about 40-50% for gas.
p-022.actionItem: Today hold a magnet to the bottom of your pots to check that it sticks.

p-023.title: Use Air-Fryer Convection
p-023.summary: Leave gaps between food in an air fryer so it crisps.
p-023.principle: Fast circulation of hot air is forced convection, where Q = hAΔT has a large h. Overlapping reduces the exposed area A.
p-023.example: Oven convection is about h ≈ 10W/m²K, fan convection about 30-50, 3 to 5 times faster. A single layer can save about 10 minutes.
p-023.actionItem: Today spread food in one layer in the air-fryer basket without overlap.

p-024.title: Clean the Dryer Lint Filter
p-024.summary: Emptying the lint filter shortens drying time.
p-024.principle: A clogged filter reduces airflow V and moisture removal m = VΔωρ.
p-024.example: A clogged filter can lengthen drying 20-30%. A cycle going from 80 to 100 minutes uses an extra 0.4kWh at 2kW.
p-024.actionItem: Today open the dryer and clear the lint filter.

p-025.title: Reduce Winter Static
p-025.summary: Winter door-handle zaps happen because dry air lets charge stay on you.
p-025.principle: Friction charge Q raises voltage like a capacitor V = Q/C; dry air slows discharge so it can reach thousands of volts.
p-025.example: A body with C ≈ 100 pF holding Q=0.3 µC reaches V = 3000V. Raising humidity above 40% lets charge leak away gradually.
p-025.actionItem: Today touch a key or the wall before grabbing a door handle to discharge.

p-026.title: Avoid Overloading a Power Strip
p-026.summary: Plugging several large heaters into one power strip risks overheating and fire.
p-026.principle: Power is P = VI, so at 220V I = P/V, and heating is P_heat = I²R, proportional to current squared.
p-026.example: A 1500W heater plus a 1000W kettle draws 2500/220 ≈ 11.4A, above a common 10A strip. A 10% rise in current raises heat by 21%.
p-026.actionItem: Today check your strip's rating (for example 10A) and plug heaters directly into a wall outlet.

p-027.title: Charge Between 20 and 80%
p-027.summary: Keeping a phone between 20% and 80% extends battery life.
p-027.principle: High charge voltage speeds electrolyte breakdown, and aging is temperature-sensitive as k ∝ e⁻E_a/RT.
p-027.example: Avoiding full charges and heat can add hundreds of cycles beyond the typical 500 before capacity falls to 80%.
p-027.actionItem: Today turn on your phone's optimized charging or 80% limit.

p-028.title: How Much an LED Swap Saves
p-028.summary: At the same brightness, an LED uses far less electricity.
p-028.principle: Compare luminous efficacy η = Φ/P (lm/W): incandescent about 13 lm/W, LED 100 lm/W or more.
p-028.example: An 800 lm bulb takes 60W as incandescent and 8W as LED. At 5 hours a day it saves 0.052 × 5 × 365 ≈ 95kWh a year.
p-028.actionItem: Today replace one bulb in your most-used room with an LED.

p-029.title: Why Metal Handles Feel Colder
p-029.summary: At the same temperature, metal feels much colder than wood.
p-029.principle: Contact heat flux depends on thermal effusivity e = √(kρ c); faster heat drain feels colder.
p-029.example: Metals have e ≈ 10,000-20,000 and wood e ≈ 400 (SI), tens of times apart. At 0°C iron feels far colder.
p-029.actionItem: On winter outings today grip metal handles with gloves or a cloth.

p-030.title: Preventing Frozen Pipes
p-030.summary: Below freezing, pipe water turns to ice, expands and can burst the pipe.
p-030.principle: Water expands about 9% when freezing. In a sealed pipe pressure spikes by ΔP = KΔV/V and the pipe fails.
p-030.example: With a bulk modulus K ≈ 2 GPa, theoretical pressure reaches hundreds of MPa. A slow trickle makes freezing less likely.
p-030.actionItem: If sub-zero is forecast today, leave a tap dripping and wrap the meter with insulation.

p-031.title: Heating Off or On When Out
p-031.summary: Keep heating on for short trips and lower it for long ones.
p-031.principle: Heat loss is P = UA(T_in-T_out), smaller at lower indoor temperature. Reheating costs CΔT.
p-031.example: Over 12 hours, dropping from 22°C to 17°C cuts losses about 25%, more than the reheat cost, a net gain. For 2-3 hours the gain is small.
p-031.actionItem: Today use away mode when out 6 hours or more, and leave heating alone for short errands.

p-032.title: Stopping Distance on Snow
p-032.summary: On snow, stopping distance grows to several times the dry-road value.
p-032.principle: Stopping distance is d = v²/(2µ g): proportional to speed squared, inversely to friction.
p-032.example: At 50km/h (13.9m/s) a dry road µ=0.7 gives d ≈ 14m, snow µ=0.2 gives d ≈ 49m. Slowing to 30km/h gives about 18m.
p-032.actionItem: On snowy roads today drive at half your usual speed and leave a larger gap.

p-033.title: Protect Your Back When Shoveling
p-033.summary: Keeping the load close and using your legs spares your back.
p-033.principle: Lever torque is τ = Fd; the farther the load from your spine, the larger the moment.
p-033.example: Holding 5kg of snow at arm's length (0.6m) gives τ ≈ 5 × 9.8 × 0.6 ≈ 29N · m; close in at 0.2m it is about 10N·m, one third.
p-033.actionItem: Today shovel light loads often, held close to your body, using legs rather than back.

p-034.title: Open Tight Jar Lids Easily
p-034.summary: A stubborn lid opens when a larger radius multiplies your torque.
p-034.principle: Torque is τ = Fr; for the same force a larger radius r gives proportionally more torque.
p-034.example: A 3cm lid (r=1.5cm) needing 3N·m takes F=200N. An opener with r=6cm needs only F=50N, one quarter.
p-034.actionItem: Today wrap a rubber glove or towel around a lid, or use a jar opener.

p-035.title: Before Standing on a Chair
p-035.summary: On a chair, your center of mass must stay above the base to avoid falling.
p-035.principle: A body is stable while the vertical through its center of mass stays within its base. The tilt limit is θ = b/h.
p-035.example: With a base half-width b=20cm and center of mass height h=100cm, a tilt of only θ=0.2 ≈ 11^° tips you over.
p-035.actionItem: Today use a stable step stool instead of a chair for high places.

p-036.title: Set Ladders at 75 Degrees
p-036.summary: Too steep and it tips back; too flat and it slides.
p-036.principle: Without wall friction, a ladder won't slip if θ ≥ 1/(2µ).
p-036.example: With floor µ=0.4, θ ≥ 1.25, so θ ≥ 51^°. About 75 degrees (base one quarter of the ladder's length from the wall) is the recommended safe setting.
p-036.actionItem: Today set a ladder's base out from the wall by a quarter of its length.

p-037.title: Bathroom Mirror Fog
p-037.summary: A mirror fogs after showers because vapor condenses below the dew point.
p-037.principle: Condensation happens when surface temperature falls below the dew point T_d. Approximately T_d ≈ T - (100-RH)/5.
p-037.example: At 30°C and 90% humidity T_d ≈ 28°C, so a 25°C mirror fogs. A fan lowering humidity to 60% gives T_d ≈ 14°C.
p-037.actionItem: Today run the bathroom fan during your shower and 10 minutes after.

p-038.title: Don't Drag Heavy Furniture
p-038.summary: Slip a cloth under heavy furniture rather than dragging it bare.
p-038.principle: Static friction is f = µ_s N. A cloth lowers µ and protects the floor.
p-038.example: A 50kg wardrobe with µ=0.5 needs f=0.5 × 50 × 9.8 ≈ 245N. Furniture sliders giving µ=0.2 cut it to 98N, 60% less.
p-038.actionItem: Today put felt pads or a towel under furniture legs before sliding.

p-039.title: Boil Only the Water You Need
p-039.summary: Boiling just what you drink saves power and time.
p-039.principle: Heat needed is Q = mcΔT, proportional to water mass m.
p-039.example: Heating 1L from 20°C to 100°C takes 334kJ, about 0.093kWh. One cup (250mL) takes 0.023kWh, a quarter.
p-039.actionItem: Today fill the kettle with only the amount you will use, checking the cup marks.

p-040.title: Leave Space Behind the Fridge
p-040.summary: A fridge pushed against the wall can't shed heat and uses more power.
p-040.principle: Compressor heat leaves through the rear coil by natural convection; in Q = hAΔT blocked airflow lowers h.
p-040.example: If blocked ventilation raises condenser temperature by 10°C, COP falls and consumption can rise about 10-15%. On 400kWh a year that is 40-60kWh.
p-040.actionItem: Today pull the fridge 5-10cm from the wall and dust the rear coil.

p-041.title: Reduce Washer Spin Shaking
p-041.summary: Unbalanced laundry makes a washing machine shake violently when spinning.
p-041.principle: A mass m off-center at radius r creates centrifugal force F = mω² r, proportional to angular speed squared.
p-041.example: At 1000 rpm (ω ≈ 105 rad/s) with 1kg unbalanced at r=0.2m, F ≈ 2200N. Balancing removes nearly all of it.
p-041.actionItem: Today when washing something bulky like a duvet, add small items and spread the load evenly.

p-042.title: Restore Vacuum Suction
p-042.summary: Emptying the bin and cleaning the filter brings suction back almost to new.
p-042.principle: Suction power is the product P = ΔP · Q of pressure difference and airflow. A clog sharply cuts airflow.
p-042.example: A half-clogged filter may reduce airflow 30-50%. The same motor delivers that much less dust-lifting power and cleaning takes longer.
p-042.actionItem: Today empty the vacuum bin and tap out or wash and dry the filter.

p-043.title: Latent Heat in Ice Packs
p-043.summary: The best way to keep things cold is the latent heat of melting ice.
p-043.principle: Melting ice absorbs Q = mL with L=334J/g while staying at 0°C.
p-043.example: Melting a 500g ice pack absorbs 500 × 334 ≈ 167kJ, 16 times the 10kJ it takes to warm the same amount of 0°C water by 5°C.
p-043.actionItem: Today bring an ice pack when grocery shopping and pick up frozen items last.

p-044.title: Snow Load on Roofs
p-044.summary: Wet snow is several times heavier than dry snow and can collapse roofs and greenhouses.
p-044.principle: Load is P = ρ g h; dry snow ρ ≈ 100kg/m³, wet snow ρ ≈ 400-500.
