p-044.example: 30cm of wet snow (ρ=400) gives 400 × 9.8 × 0.3 ≈ 1180Pa, four times dry snow (about 300Pa).
p-044.actionItem: If heavy snow falls today, safely clear snow from greenhouses and awnings.

p-045.title: Heat Pump vs Electric Heater
p-045.summary: Using an air conditioner for heating gives more heat from the same electricity.
p-045.principle: A heat pump moves heat, so COP = Q_h/W exceeds 1. An electric heater has COP=1.
p-045.example: At COP 3, 1kWh yields 3kWh of heat. Delivering 3kW for 5 hours takes 15kWh by resistance heater but 5kWh by heat pump, saving 10kWh.
p-045.actionItem: Today use your air conditioner's heating mode at 20°C instead of an electric heater.

p-046.title: Why Wet Gloves Feel Colder
p-046.summary: Wet gloves steal heat far faster than dry ones.
p-046.principle: Water conducts about 0.6W/m · K, around 23 times air (0.026), and evaporation adds more loss, enlarging Q = kAΔT/d.
p-046.example: At the same thickness a waterlogged glove loses several times more heat. Each gram evaporated takes another 2.26kJ.
p-046.actionItem: Today dry any gloves used in snow right away and carry a spare pair.

p-047.title: Icicles on the eaves signal heat leaking through the roof
p-047.summary: When snow melts from below and refreezes at the eaves, indoor heat is probably escaping through the roof.
p-047.principle: Heat loss is Q=UA ΔT. Poor insulation raises U, so the roof surface climbs above 0°C and melts the snow.
p-047.example: On a 100m² roof, cutting U from 0.5 to 0.25W/(m² K) at ΔT=20K drops the loss from 0.5 × 100 × 20=1,000W to 500W, half as much.
p-047.actionItem: Today, look for icicles on the eaves or balcony ceiling (do not stand under them) and, if there are many, check ceiling or attic insulation.

p-048.title: A Soap Film That Stops Foggy Glasses
p-048.summary: Glasses fog up because the lens is colder than the dew point of your breath. A thin soap film makes water spread into a clear layer instead of beading into droplets.
p-048.principle: Vapor condenses when the surface temperature T_s is below the dew point T_d. A surfactant lowers the contact angle so tiny droplets spread into a transparent film.
p-048.example: Breath at 34 C and 100% humidity has a dew point near 34 C, while a lens sits around 20 C, so it fogs at once. Spreading one drop of mild dish soap thinly over the lens and letting it dry makes water sheet across the surface and cuts fogging sharply.
p-048.actionItem: Today, spread one drop of mild dish soap over both sides of the lenses, let them air dry without wiping, and press the mask nose wire so breath does not leak upward.

p-049.title: Spotting Real Polarized Sunglasses
p-049.summary: Glare off water and wet roads is mostly horizontally polarized, so polarized lenses filter it out and ease eye strain. Some pairs are merely dark, so test them yourself.
p-049.principle: Light through a polarizer follows Malus's law I=I₀²θ, and reflection from water is almost fully polarized near Brewster's angle θ_B=(n) ≈ 53^°.
p-049.example: When the glare's polarization is 90^° to the lens axis, ² 90^°=0 and the glare is nearly blocked. You can verify a lens because two polarized lenses stacked at 90^° turn dark. Polarization is separate from UV protection, so also look for a UV400 label.
p-049.actionItem: Look at a phone screen through the lens and rotate it 90^° to see whether the screen goes dark, and check for the UV400 mark.

p-050.title: Why bridge roads freeze first
p-050.summary: Bridges lose heat from above and below, so they freeze before ordinary roads and often hide black ice.
p-050.principle: Ground roads receive heat from the soil, while a bridge has air underneath. Braking distance is d=(v² / 2µ g).
p-050.example: At 50km/h (v ≈ 13.9m/s), dry asphalt (µ ≈ 0.7) needs about 14m, but ice (µ ≈ 0.1) needs about 99m, nearly 7 times more.
p-050.actionItem: On nights and mornings below 3°C, slow down before bridges, tunnel mouths and shaded stretches.

p-051.title: Why a 2-3x Makeup Mirror Is Enough
p-051.summary: A higher magnification is not better. A short focal length forces you to press your face close and shows only a tiny area.
p-051.principle: Concave mirror 1f=1d_o+1d_i with magnification m=-(d_i / d_o). Inside the focal point you get an upright, enlarged virtual image.
p-051.example: With f=20cm and your face at d_o=10cm, d_i=-20cm and m=2 ×. A 10x mirror has f ≈ 5cm, so you must stay within 5cm and see only one eye at a time. Beyond the focal point the image flips upside down.
p-051.actionItem: Before buying, measure how far your face usually sits from the mirror and pick a model with a focal length about twice that distance (2-3x).

p-052.title: Cut Cooking Time and Energy with a Pressure Cooker
p-052.summary: A pressure cooker raises the boiling point of water to about 120 C, cutting cooking time to a third or less.
p-052.principle: Boiling point rises with pressure (Clausius-Clapeyron), and reaction rate roughly doubles per 10^°C, so 2^(120-100)/10=4 times faster.
p-052.example: At 1atm gauge (about 2atm absolute) water boils near 120 C. Braised short ribs that need 60 minutes in an open pot finish in about 20, saving roughly 1kWh on a 1.5kW induction hob. Never open the lid until the pressure has fully released.
p-052.actionItem: Cook a long-simmer dish tonight (boiled pork, beans, stews) in the pressure cooker and turn off the heat early so residual pressure finishes the job.

p-053.title: A 1% Door Gap Drops Soundproofing from 30dB to 20dB
p-053.summary: A thick door loses much of its soundproofing if it has even a small gap. A few dollars of weatherstrip cuts both noise and drafts.
p-053.principle: Composite transmission τ=( S_iτ_i / S_i) and transmission loss TL=-10₁₀τ.
p-053.example: A door rated 30dB (τ=0.001) with a gap equal to 1% of its area (τ ≈ 1) gives τ=0.99 × 0.001+0.01=0.011, so TL falls to about 19.6dB. Sealing the gap with weatherstrip (about 3 dollars) also reduces winter drafts and heating cost.
p-053.actionItem: Close the door and look for light leaking under and around it, then fit a silicone weatherstrip or a door sweep.

p-054.title: Moving the Wi-Fi Router Changes Your Speed
p-054.summary: Every doubling of distance weakens the signal fourfold (6dB), and each wall takes another 3-10dB. A router in an open central spot improves speed.
p-054.principle: Free-space path loss FSPL(dB)=20₁₀d+20₁₀f+32.44 (d in km, f in MHz).
p-054.example: At 2.4GHz, 10m costs about 60.0dB and 20m about 66.0dB, so doubling distance adds 6dB. A concrete wall removes another 5-10dB, which is why the far room is slow.
p-054.actionItem: Take the router out from behind the TV or a cabinet and put it on an open shelf 1-1.5m high near the center of the home, then compare speed in the far room.

p-055.title: Every 3dB Louder Halves Safe Earphone Time
p-055.summary: Each 3dB rise doubles sound energy and halves the time your ears can safely take it. Turning the volume down a little greatly extends safe listening.
p-055.principle: Sound level L=10₁₀(I / I₀) (I₀=10⁻¹² W/m²). Exposure guidance: 8 h at 85dB, halving the time for every 3dB.
p-055.example: 85dB gives 8 h, 88dB 4 h, 91dB 2 h, 94dB 1 h, and 100dB just 15 min. Raising volume to beat subway noise past 95dB makes even 30 minutes risky.
p-055.actionItem: Turn on your phone's headphone safety or volume limit setting today and cap the maximum at about 60%.

p-056.title: Hydroplaning in Spring Rain: Slow Down Just 20%
p-056.summary: At speed on wet road, water ahead of the tire cannot escape and forms a wedge that lifts the tire. Once it hydroplanes, steering and braking nearly vanish.
p-056.principle: Water's dynamic pressure q=12ρ v² approaching the contact pressure p lets a water film lift the tire. Critical speed v ≈ √(2p/ρ) (simple estimate).
p-056.example: With contact pressure of about 220kPa, v ≈ √(2 × 220000/1000) ≈ 21m/s, or about 76km/h. Worn grooves drain poorly and can lose grip at lower speeds, so on a 100km/h road drive at about 80km/h in rain.
p-056.actionItem: Check whether the tread wear indicators (TWI) have become level with the groove surface, and drive at 80% of normal speed in rain.

p-057.title: Do Not Trust the NRR Number on Earplugs
p-057.summary: The NRR printed on the pack is a lab best case, so real protection is much lower. Compare earplugs using a derated value for concerts and worksites.
p-057.principle: Real attenuation estimate NRRᵣₑₐₗ ≈ NRR-72dB (A-weighting correction, then 50% derating).
p-057.example: A foam plug labeled NRR 33 really gives (33-7)/2=13dB. At a 100dB concert that leaves 87dB, still a bit above the 85dB guideline. Proper insertion matters more than the label.
p-057.actionItem: Roll a foam plug thin, pull your ear up and back, insert it, and hold it with a finger for 30 seconds while it expands.

p-058.title: Wireless Charging: Coil Alignment Decides Efficiency
p-058.summary: Wireless charging loses more energy than a cable, and poor alignment adds heat and wasted power. Good alignment cuts both losses and battery wear.
p-058.principle: Inductive link efficiency depends on the coupling factor k: η=k²Q₁Q₂ ≤ ft(1+√(1+k²Q₁Q₂))². Misalignment sharply lowers k.
p-058.example: Charging a 5000 mAh, 3.85V phone (about 19.3Wh) needs 21.4Wh by cable at 90%, 27.5Wh wirelessly at 70%, and 38.5Wh when misaligned at 50%. Charging once daily, that is about 2kWh/year extra when aligned and about 6kWh/year when misaligned.
p-058.actionItem: Place the phone exactly on the pad's coil marking, and remove thick cases, cards and metal plates before charging.

p-059.title: Lift Off the Gas Early Before a Red Light
p-059.summary: Braking at a red light turns the car's kinetic energy into wasted heat. Lifting off early lets the car coast with fuel cut and saves fuel.
p-059.principle: Kinetic energy E_k=12mv², so the energy lost in braking scales with speed squared.
p-059.example: A 1,500kg car at 60km/h (16.7m/s) holds E_k ≈ 208kJ. Taking about 8.5MJ of useful energy per liter of gasoline, each stop represents about 25mL. Anticipating 10 lights saves tens to hundreds of milliliters a day.
p-059.actionItem: On today's drive, lift off the accelerator about 150m before a red light and coast, using the brake only lightly when needed.

p-060.title: Moving Water Without a Pump: the Siphon
p-060.summary: Changing aquarium water or emptying a rain barrel needs only a hose and a height difference. Once the hose is full, water keeps flowing downhill.
p-060.principle: If the outlet is Δh below the surface, the pressure difference ΔP=ρ gΔh drives flow, with ideal speed v=√(2gΔh).
p-060.example: For a 0.5m drop the ideal speed is 3.1m/s, but hose friction cuts it to about 1m/s. Through a 10mm hose that is Q ≈ 0.08L/s, moving 20L in about 4 minutes.
p-060.actionItem: Submerge the hose to fill it, plug one end, and place it into a bucket set lower. Never suck on the hose by mouth with chemical liquids.

p-061.title: On snowy days, UV comes from above and below
p-061.summary: Fresh snow reflects much ultraviolet light, so eyes and faces burn more easily on snowfields than you expect.
p-061.principle: Albedo is α=I_r/I₀, and total UV exposure is roughly I₀(1+α). Fresh snow has a UV albedo of about 0.8-0.9, grass about 0.03.
p-061.example: If direct UV is 1, you get about 1.03 over grass but about 1.8-1.9 over fresh snow, nearly double.
p-061.actionItem: When heading to snow, pack UV-blocking sunglasses or goggles and sunscreen.

p-062.title: Why Your Ears Plug Up When a Plane Descends
p-062.summary: Cabin pressure is like an altitude of about 2,400m, so air in your middle ear expands after takeoff and is squeezed on descent. Opening your ears early in the descent prevents pain.
p-062.example: Going from 101kPa on the ground to about 75kPa in cruise, the air in your ear expands by 101/75 ≈ 1.35, i.e. 35%. On descent it shrinks and pulls the eardrum inward. A stuffy nose from a cold makes it harder for the eustachian tube to open.
p-062.actionItem: When landing is announced, chew gum or repeatedly yawn and swallow, and stay awake.

p-063.title: Reading Binocular Numbers Like 8x42 for Brightness
p-063.summary: The binocular numbers are magnification times objective diameter. For dawn and dusk you need a large exit pupil, while a small light pair is fine for daytime.
p-063.principle: Exit pupil dₑₚ=(D / M) (mm), relative brightness ∝ dₑₚ².
p-063.example: An 8x42 gives 42/8=5.25mm with relative brightness about 27.6, while a 10x25 gives 2.5mm and about 6.3, so the 8x42 is over four times brighter in low light. Your pupil is 5-7mm in the dark, so for dawn birding aim for an exit pupil of 4mm or more.
p-063.actionItem: If you will use them at dawn or dusk, choose D/M ≥ 4mm; for daytime walks pick a light compact pair, and try them in person.

p-064.title: Wrap hot-water pipes to stop heat leaking
p-064.summary: Bare hot-water pipes between the boiler and the tap lose heat constantly. Insulation sleeves cut that loss sharply.
p-064.principle: Pipe heat loss scales as Q ∝ ΔT/R, and insulation raises the thermal resistance R. Doubling R halves the loss at the same ΔT.
p-064.example: Suppose 10m of bare pipe 25K above room temperature loses about 25W per metre: 250W. After insulation, about 60W remains, saving roughly 1.9kWh over 10 hours.
p-064.actionItem: Measure the bare hot-water pipe in the boiler room or under the sink and plan to wrap it with foam insulation.

p-065.title: Take Off the Roof Box This Spring
p-065.summary: Leaving the winter ski roof box on increases highway drag and wastes fuel.
p-065.principle: Drag power P=12ρ C_dAv³ (cubic in speed).
p-065.example: A car with C_dA=0.69m² at 100km/h (27.8m/s) needs about 8.9kW. A roof box that adds 20% to C_dA raises it to about 10.7kW, 1.8kW more, or roughly 0.8L extra per 100km.
p-065.actionItem: If your roof box and crossbars are empty, take them off today and store them in the garage.

p-066.title: Peel, don't pry: removing adhesive hooks
p-066.summary: Adhesive hooks resist a downward (shear) pull well but give way to a pull straight away from the wall (peel).
p-066.principle: In shear the whole bonded area shares the load, while in peeling the force concentrates on one edge line, so Fₚₑₑₗ Fₛₕₑₐᵣ.
p-066.example: For example, a hook holding 2 kgf in shear may let go at 0.2-0.5 kgf in peel. That is why a hook carries a downward load but fails when lifted outward.
p-066.actionItem: Wipe dust and moisture off the surface and press the hook for 1 minute or more. To remove it, stretch the strip slowly and parallel to the wall.

p-067.title: Use Noise Cancelling to Cut Volume by 6dB
p-067.summary: Noise cancelling generates sound in opposite phase to cancel noise. You need less volume on the subway, which protects your ears.
p-067.principle: Destructive interference: Aω t+A(ω t+π)=0. It works best on steady low-frequency noise (below about 1kHz).
p-067.example: In an 80dB subway, if cancelling removes about 20dB of low rumble you can listen at 6dB lower volume (e.g. 91dB down to 85dB), which raises safe listening time from 2 hours to 8 hours, four times longer.
p-067.actionItem: On the subway or bus, switch on noise cancelling and lower your volume by two or three steps.

p-068.title: Taking a Curve in Spring Rain: Your Real Speed Limit
p-068.summary: The top safe speed in a curve is set by tire friction and the curve radius. Wet road drops that limit sharply.
p-068.principle: Limit speed v=√(µ g r) (centripetal force equals friction).
p-068.example: On a 50m radius curve, dry road (µ=0.7) allows about 67km/h, wet road (0.4) about 50km/h and snow (0.2) about 36km/h. Posted advisory speeds assume dry road, so slow down more in rain.
p-068.actionItem: Slow down on the straight before entering a curve, and avoid hard braking or sharp steering inside it.

p-069.title: TV Size: Viewing Distance Beats Resolution
p-069.summary: The human eye resolves about one arcminute. From far away you cannot tell 4K from Full HD, so spend on screen size rather than resolution.
p-069.principle: Eye resolution θ ≈ 1' ≈ 2.9 × 10⁻⁴ rad; for pixel pitch p the farthest distance at which pixels are distinguishable is d=(p / θ).
p-069.example: A 55-inch 4K has a pixel pitch of about 0.32mm, so pixels are visible only inside about 1.1m. If your sofa is 3m away, even Full HD hides its pixels up to 75 inches, so look at size and picture quality (contrast, HDR) rather than paying a 4K premium.
p-069.actionItem: Measure the distance from your sofa to the TV spot with a tape and pick the screen size based on it.

p-070.title: Thick frost in the freezer makes it use more power
p-070.summary: Frost traps air between ice crystals, forming an insulating layer that blocks cold and keeps the compressor running longer.
p-070.principle: Thermal resistance is R=d/k, proportional to thickness d. Frost has k ≈ 0.2-0.5W/(m K), far below solid ice (about 2.2).
p-070.example: With k=0.3, a 5mm frost layer has R=0.005/0.3 ≈ 0.017m²K/W, five times that of 1mm, with cooling efficiency dropping accordingly.
p-070.actionItem: When frost exceeds 3-5mm, switch the unit off and defrost naturally. Never scrape with a knife or sharp tool.

p-071.title: 200 Liters of Rain: Free Water for the Spring Garden
p-071.summary: Spring rain collected from the roof can water a garden without tap water. Raising the barrel gives enough head to run a hose.
p-071.principle: Water pressure P=ρ g h, collection V=A × R (area times rainfall).
p-071.example: A 20mm rain on a 10m2 roof collects 10 × 20=200L. Raising the barrel 1m gives 9.8kPa (about 0.1bar) of head, enough to gravity-feed a low bed by hose.
p-071.actionItem: Put the rain barrel on a stand at least 50cm high and cover it with a lid and screen so mosquitoes cannot breed.

p-072.title: Microphone Feedback: Drop the Gain 3dB
p-072.summary: If a mic re-amplifies a speaker's sound you get a screeching feedback howl. Adjusting distance and volume easily stops it.
p-072.principle: The loop gain G=gₐₘₚ · gₚₐₜₕ ≥ 1 with matching phase causes oscillation.
p-072.example: Doubling the distance between mic and speaker adds 6dB of path loss, allowing more volume. Conversely, lowering the gain just 3dB halves the loop gain and the howl disappears.
p-072.actionItem: Do not place speakers in front of the mic, aim them at the audience, and turn the mic gain down by 3dB (one or two steps).

p-073.title: Judging UV Strength by Your Shadow
p-073.summary: If your shadow is shorter than you, the sun is higher than 45 degrees and UV is strong. By late March your noon shadow is already shorter than your height.
p-073.principle: UV dose scales with α for solar elevation α, and shadow length L=(h / α).
p-073.example: At 37 degrees north on the equinox (about March 20), noon elevation is 90^°-37^°=53^° and the shadow is 1/53^°=0.75 of your height. In early February (elevation about 38 degrees) it was 1.28 times.
p-073.actionItem: Check your shadow around noon today; if it is shorter than you, apply SPF 30+ sunscreen and wear a hat.

p-074.title: Section Speed Cameras: Speeding Saves Only 2 Minutes
p-074.summary: Section enforcement checks your average speed. The time gained by speeding is tiny while energy use and risk rise sharply.
p-074.principle: Average speed v=(Δs / Δt), drag power ∝ v³.
p-074.example: A 20km section takes 12 minutes at 100km/h and 10 at 120km/h, a gain of 2 minutes, but drag power rises 1.2³=1.73 times (+73%) and kinetic energy by 44%. Speeding early forces slowing later, so there is no real gain.
p-074.actionItem: In a section-control zone, set cruise control at the limit and hold a steady speed.

p-075.title: Judge Speakers by Sensitivity (dB), Not Watts
p-075.summary: A 3dB sensitivity difference equals a doubling of amplifier power for the same loudness. A big wattage number does not guarantee a louder speaker.
p-075.principle: Sound pressure SPL=S+10₁₀P-20₁₀d (S: 1W/1m sensitivity in dB).
p-075.example: To reach 85dB at 3m you need about 94.5dB at 1m. A 90dB-sensitivity speaker needs about 2.8W while an 84dB one needs about 11.2W, a fourfold difference.
p-075.actionItem: Check the sensitivity (dB at 1W/1m) in the spec sheet of the speaker you plan to buy and prefer the higher one.

p-076.title: Cut Fan Speed 20% and Power Drops by Half
p-076.summary: A fan's power use rises with the cube of its speed. If a slightly weaker breeze is fine, you can save a lot of electricity.
p-076.principle: Fan affinity laws: airflow Q ∝ N, power P ∝ N³.
p-076.example: At 80% speed, airflow is 80% but power is 0.8³=0.51, about half. A 40W fan drops to about 20W, saving roughly 4.7kWh a month at 8 hours a day.
p-076.actionItem: Today, set your fan or ventilator to medium instead of high and check whether it still feels comfortable.

p-077.title: One Nozzle Can Save 40% of Garden Water
p-077.summary: Narrowing the hose end speeds up the stream so it reaches farther, and a shut-off nozzle removes waste while you move.
p-077.example: A 15mm hose carrying 10L/min (0.167L/s) has a speed of about 0.94m/s. A 5mm nozzle raises it to about 8.5m/s, nine times faster, and needs about 36kPa. Shutting off the flow while moving can turn a 5-minute, 50L watering into about 30L.
p-077.actionItem: Fit a trigger shut-off nozzle on the hose end and water only at the base of plants.

p-078.title: Water Hammer: The Bang When You Shut a Faucet
p-078.summary: Closing quickly stops moving water abruptly and sends a shock wave through the pipes, causing a bang and possible damage.
p-078.principle: Joukowsky equation Δp=ρ c Δv (c: sound speed in the pipe).
p-078.example: With water at 2m/s in a copper pipe with c ≈ 1200m/s, an instant stop gives Δp ≈ 2.4MPa (24bar), six times the usual 3-4bar. If closing takes longer than 2L/c (about 17 ms for a 10m pipe) the shock drops sharply.
p-078.actionItem: Close lever faucets and washer valves slowly, and ask about a water hammer arrestor if the bang keeps happening.

p-079.title: When to Replace Running Shoes: Impact Force View
p-079.summary: As cushioning wears, your foot stops faster and knees and ankles take bigger forces. Check them every 500-800km.
p-079.principle: Impulse F Δt=Δp, so average force F=(mΔv / Δt).
p-079.example: Simplifying a 70kg runner as shedding 70N·s on landing, stopping in 0.035 s gives 2,000N, while worn cushioning that stops in 0.02 s gives 3,500N (about 5 times body weight), a 75% increase.
p-079.actionItem: Today, check whether the midsole of your running shoes is compressed and creased, and write down the distance since you last replaced them.

p-080.title: Night Driving: Do Not Outrun Your Low Beams
p-080.summary: Low beams light about 40m, yet stopping from 80km/h takes longer, so you are driving into unseen road.
p-080.principle: Stopping distance d=vt_r+(v² / 2µ g) ≤ visible distance.
p-080.example: At 80km/h (22.2m/s) with 1 s reaction and µ=0.7, you need 22.2+36=58m, beyond 40m. At 60km/h it is 16.7+20=37m, which is safe. Film or fog on the inside of the windshield scatters light and shortens your view further.
p-080.actionItem: Wipe the inside of your windshield and headlights before leaving, and stay at or below 60km/h on dark side roads.

p-081.title: Bike Helmet: Crush Thickness Is the Key
p-081.summary: A helmet lengthens the distance your head takes to stop, cutting the force. Certification and fit matter more than price or looks.
p-081.example: A 5kg head hitting at 6m/s carries E_k=90J. With no helmet and a 2mm stop, force is about 45kN; with 20mm of EPS foam it is about 4.5kN, one tenth. EPS loses its effect once crushed by an impact.
p-081.actionItem: Look for a CPSC, EN 1078 or other safety certification, fit it two fingers above the eyebrows, and adjust the straps into a Y under the ears.

p-082.title: Solar Garden Lights: Tilt 35 Degrees South for 25% More
p-082.summary: A solar panel collects most when perpendicular to sunlight. Tilting a garden light to match your latitude boosts charging.
p-082.principle: Energy received ∝ θ (θ: incidence angle). Best tilt ≈ latitude.
p-082.example: At 37 degrees north, with the equinox noon sun at 53 degrees, a flat panel gets 53^°=0.80, a wall-vertical panel 53^°=0.60, and a panel tilted 37 degrees gets 1.0. That is about 25% more than flat and 67% more than vertical.
p-082.actionItem: Face the garden light panel south, tilt it 35-40 degrees, and clear away shade and dust.

p-083.title: Desk Lamp 30cm Closer, a Quarter of the Power
p-083.summary: Light intensity falls with the square of distance. Putting the lamp near lets a weaker bulb give the same brightness.
p-083.example: Moving the lamp from 60cm to 30cm makes illuminance 4 times higher. Getting 500 lux at 60cm needs a 12W LED, but at 30cm 3W is enough, saving about 13kWh a year at 4 hours a day.
p-083.actionItem: Place the lamp about 30cm from your page, opposite your writing hand, and swap in a lower-wattage bulb.

p-084.title: Why Calls Drop in an Elevator
p-084.summary: A metal box is a Faraday cage that keeps electromagnetic waves out. Preparing before the signal drops protects important calls.
p-084.principle: Skin depth δ=1√(π fµσ) (the depth at which a wave decays inside a conductor).
p-084.example: In aluminum (σ=3.8 × 10⁷ S/m) a 1.8GHz wave has a skin depth of only about 1.9 micrometers, so even thin metal sheets block it. You rely on signal that leaks through door gaps and vents.
p-084.actionItem: Finish important calls before stepping in, turn on Wi-Fi calling, and download needed files before entering an underground garage.

p-085.title: Spring Cleaning: Wipe Dust, Do Not Sweep It
p-085.summary: How long dust stays airborne varies enormously with size. Sweeping lifts settled dust back into the air you breathe.
p-085.example: A 10 micrometer dust particle settles at about 6mm/s, falling 1m in about 3 minutes, while a 2.5 micrometer one falls at 1/16 that speed, 0.38mm/s, taking about 44 minutes. Small particles hang in the air long after cleaning.
p-085.actionItem: Clean today with a damp mop or wet cloth instead of sweeping, and ventilate with open windows for an hour afterward.

p-086.title: The Two-Second Following Distance Rule
p-086.summary: If both cars brake equally, the gap you need is just your reaction distance. Two seconds gives about 56m at 100km/h.
p-086.example: At 100km/h (27.8m/s) a 1.5 s reaction needs 41.7m, and the two-second rule gives 55.6m, a safe margin. In rain, extend it to 3-4 seconds.
p-086.actionItem: When the car ahead passes a sign or lamp post, count 'one, two' and make sure you do not reach that point before you finish counting.

p-087.title: Bigger wheels roll over curbs more easily
p-087.summary: A larger wheel climbs the same step at a gentler angle, so less force is needed.
p-087.principle: For a wheel of radius R over a step of height h, the horizontal force at the axle is F=mg √(2Rh-h²)R-h.
p-087.example: With mg=100N on the wheel and h=1cm, a 6cm wheel needs about 112N, a 10cm wheel about 75N and a 16cm wheel about 55N.
p-087.actionItem: When buying luggage or a stroller, check wheel diameter and material (rubber or polyurethane), and tilt the front wheels up at a curb.

p-088.title: Fast Charging: Higher Voltage Means Less Loss
p-088.summary: Heat lost in a cable grows with the square of current. Delivering the same power at higher voltage and lower current cuts the loss.
p-088.example: Delivering 18W at 5V takes 3.6A, wasting 2.6W (14%) in a 0.2 ohm cable, while at 9V it takes 2A and wastes only 0.8W (4.4%). Thin, long cables lose even more.
p-088.actionItem: Use a thick, short cable that supports the same standard as your charger (such as PD), and replace worn old cables.

p-089.title: Dry Laundry with Spring Sun and Breeze
p-089.summary: Evaporating water from wet clothes takes lots of energy, and sun and wind supply it for free.
p-089.principle: Latent heat Q=mL (L=2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg), evaporation rate E ∝ (a+bu)(e_s-e_a) (rising with wind u).
p-089.example: Evaporating 1kg of water takes 2.26MJ ≈ 0.63kWh. Spinning at 1,000 rpm or more and hanging in a 2m/s breeze dries far faster than indoors and saves the roughly 2-3kWh of one dryer cycle. On heavy pollen days, dry indoors instead.
p-089.actionItem: Shake out spin-dried laundry, space it so air can pass, and hang it in a sunny, breezy spot.

p-090.title: Stuck Wheel Nuts When Swapping Tires for Spring
p-090.summary: When changing from winter to regular tires, nuts will not budge because the torque is high. A longer wrench cuts the force you need.
p-090.example: Loosening a 110N·m wheel nut with a 0.3m wrench needs about 370N, while a 0.6m wrench needs about 183N, half as much. Do not add a pipe when tightening; use a torque wrench to hit the specified value.
p-090.actionItem: Before jacking up the car, loosen each nut a half turn while the tire is still on the ground, and always work on level ground.

p-091.title: Hiking Backpack: Keep Heavy Items Close to Your Back
p-091.summary: The farther a pack's load is from your body, the more rotational force your back and shoulders bear. Keep heavy items against your back and shift load to the hip belt.
p-091.principle: Torque τ=mgd (d: distance from the body axis to the load's center of mass).
p-091.example: A 6kg load 25cm away gives τ=6 × 9.8 × 0.25=14.7N·m, while 10cm gives 5.9N·m, about 60% less. Let the hip belt carry about 70% of the weight on your hips.
p-091.actionItem: Pack heavy items like the water bottle and lunch against your back at mid-height, then tighten the hip belt before setting off.

c-092.title: Chilling an onion first reduces tears when cutting
c-092.summary: Cutting an onion breaks cells so an enzyme makes a gas that irritates the eyes. Refrigerating the onion for 30 minutes slows that enzyme and reduces tears.
c-092.principle: Alliinase converts sulfoxides into an irritant: propanethial S-oxide (C₃H₆OS) stimulates eye nerves and triggers tears. Enzyme reaction rate falls as temperature drops.
c-092.example: An onion chilled to 4°C for 30 minutes forms the irritant at roughly half the rate or less compared with one at 25°C. Cut the root end last because it holds the most enzyme.
c-092.actionItem: Today, put the onion in the fridge 30 minutes before you cut it.

c-093.title: Wrinkles are hydrogen bonds that have reset in a new shape
c-093.summary: In fibers like cotton, water and heat free the hydrogen bonds between chains, and they set again in a new shape as the fabric cools. Steam and heat release them, and smoothing before it cools removes wrinkles.
c-093.principle: The -OH groups on cellulose chains hydrogen-bond to each other. Moisture and heat break these bonds, and they re-form in the flattened shape as it cools.
c-093.example: Suitable iron temperatures are about 200°C for cotton and below 110°C for synthetics. Hanging clothes in a steamy bathroom after a hot shower can relax light wrinkles on its own.
c-093.actionItem: Check the care label of the shirt you plan to wear today and steam it at the allowed temperature.

c-094.title: Wash fine dust off with a 30-second surfactant cleanse
c-094.summary: Fine dust clings to skin oil, so water alone barely moves it. A foaming cleanse removes oil and dust together.
c-094.principle: Surfactants have an oil-loving tail and a water-loving head; above the critical micelle concentration they trap sebum and dust inside micelles that rinse away. c>CMC;;micelle (sebum + dust trapped inside)
c-094.example: Rubbing a foaming cleanser for 30 seconds in 30-35°C water removes most surface dust. Skin surface pH is about 4.7-5.5, so a mildly acidic (pH 5-6) cleanser suits it.
c-094.actionItem: After going out today, build a good lather in lukewarm water and cleanse gently for 30 seconds (avoid hot water).

c-095.title: Dry cabin air on a flight calls for moisturizer and water
c-095.summary: Cabin relative humidity is usually 10-20%, desert-like, so skin and nasal membranes lose water quickly. Moisturizer and frequent sips of water help.
c-095.principle: Relative humidity RH = p_H₂Op^*_H₂O × 100%. Cabin air is heated outside air, so the saturation pressure is high while the actual vapor pressure is low, giving a low RH.
c-095.example: Normal indoor humidity is 40-60%, so water loss in a 10-20% cabin is 2-3 times faster. On a long flight, roughly 100-200mL of water each hour is a common guideline.
c-095.actionItem: On your next flight, carry moisturizer in a container of 100mL or less.

c-096.title: Blanch spring greens for just 30 seconds
c-096.summary: A brief blanch stops enzymes, keeps colour vivid and tames bitterness and grassy smell. Long boiling turns chlorophyll dull olive.
c-096.principle: Heat drives air out of the tissue and inactivates colour-degrading enzymes. With heat and acid, magnesium in chlorophyll is replaced by hydrogen ions, giving brownish pheophytin. Chl-Mg+2 H⁺ → Pheophytin+Mg²⁺
c-096.example: Blanching 100g of spinach for 30 s in 1L of boiling water with 10g (1%) salt, then chilling it, keeps it bright green; beyond 5 minutes it turns olive.
c-096.actionItem: Next time you buy spring greens, blanch them 30 seconds in 1% salted boiling water and cool them in cold water right away.

c-097.title: Firewood burns best when its moisture is below 20%
c-097.summary: Wet wood spends heat evaporating its water before it burns, giving lots of smoke and little warmth. Wood sheltered from rain and dried for six months or more works best.
c-097.principle: The heat of vaporization of water is ΔH_vap ≈ 2.26MJ/kg, which is subtracted from the wood's heat of combustion (about 18MJ/kg dry basis).
c-097.example: Green wood at 40% moisture delivers about 30% or more less usable heat than dry wood (15-20%) and makes more soot. Split a log to check that its center is dry.
c-097.actionItem: If you will use firewood outdoors, stack it somewhere dry and airy, away from rain.

c-098.title: Brew green tea in 70-80°C water for less bitterness
c-098.summary: Green tea catechins dissolve strongly at high temperatures, making it bitter and astringent, while the savory amino acid theanine comes out well even at lower temperatures. Water cooled to 70-80°C balances them.
c-098.principle: Solubility generally rises with temperature. The catechin epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) is extracted quickly above 80°C, increasing astringency.
c-098.example: Tea brewed in 90°C water for 3 minutes extracts noticeably more catechin than tea brewed at 70°C, tasting more bitter. Pouring boiled water into a cup first drops it by about 10°C.
c-098.actionItem: When brewing green tea today, pour the boiled water into a cup first to cool it, then steep for 2 minutes.

c-099.title: Glacial acetic acid is not vinegar; it is 99% acetic acid
c-099.summary: Vinegar is a 4-8% acetic acid solution, while glacial acetic acid is about 99% pure and can burn skin and eyes. For food use it must be labeled food grade and diluted heavily.
c-099.principle: Vinegar: CH₃COOH about 0.7 mol/L (4-5%). Glacial acetic acid is about 17 mol/L, more than 20 times stronger. Pure acetic acid freezes into ice-like crystals below 16.6°C, hence the name.
c-099.example: If a recipe uses 5% vinegar, using the same amount of 99% glacial acid adds about 20 times as much acid. Without a food-use dilution on the label, it is safer not to buy it.
c-099.actionItem: Today, check the acidity (%) and ingredients on your household vinegar label.

c-100.title: Alcohol becomes acetaldehyde in the liver, which causes hangovers
c-100.summary: The liver breaks alcohol into acetaldehyde, which causes headaches and nausea until it converts to acetic acid. Drinking water does not speed up the liver's breakdown.
c-100.principle: CH₃CH₂OH ―(ADH)→ CH₃CHO ―(ALDH)→ CH₃COOH. A typical adult liver clears only about 7g of pure alcohol per hour.
c-100.example: Processing a bottle of soju (about 360mL, roughly 50g alcohol) takes the liver over 7 hours. Water eases dehydration but does not speed up breakdown.
c-100.actionItem: If you are drinking today, have a glass of water alongside and set a limit beforehand.

c-101.title: A campfire must be put out completely with water
c-101.summary: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat, and removing any one puts it out. Pouring plenty of water over the embers and stirring until the ashes are cold prevents re-ignition.
c-101.principle: Of the three elements of combustion, water removes heat. Water's heat of vaporization ≈ 2.26MJ/kg absorbs a great deal of the embers' heat.
c-101.example: A lump of charcoal (about 100g) gives off several MJ, and 1L of water can absorb up to about 2.3MJ by evaporating. Keep pouring until holding the back of your hand near feels no heat.
c-101.actionItem: When you use a fire outdoors, fill a bucket of water beforehand for putting it out.

c-102.title: Sodium on the label x 2.54 = salt
c-102.summary: The sodium figure is the mass of sodium ions, not table salt (sodium chloride). Converting to salt makes your daily intake easier to grasp.
c-102.principle: Dividing the molar mass of NaCl, 58.44g/mol, by that of Na, 22.99g/mol, gives about 2.54, so multiply sodium by 2.54 to get salt. m_NaCl=m_Na × (58.44 / 22.99) ≈ 2.54m_Na
c-102.example: A pack of instant noodles with 1,800mg sodium equals about 4.6g of salt, nearly all of the WHO guideline of under 5g salt (2,000mg sodium) per day.
c-102.actionItem: Today, multiply the sodium mg of one packaged food at home by 2.54 to see its salt in grams.

c-103.title: Pasta can finish cooking on residual heat with the stove off
c-103.summary: After boiling noodles for 2-3 minutes, you can turn off the heat and cover the pot, and the starch keeps cooking. This reduces gas use.
c-103.principle: Starch gelatinization begins around 60-70°C and continues while the water stays above about 90°C. Reaction rate rises with temperature.
c-103.example: In a covered pot, the water drops only about 5-8°C in five minutes after the burner is off, so gelatinization continues. You can save 3-4 minutes of gas.
c-103.actionItem: When boiling pasta or noodles today, turn off the heat after two thirds of the package time and cover the pot.

c-104.title: Keep cut flowers fresh with sugar and a splash of vinegar
c-104.summary: Cut stems still respire and burn sugar. A little sugar and mild acidity feed them and cut the bacteria in the vase.
c-104.principle: Cut flowers use glucose for energy by respiration, and mildly acidic water (about pH 3.5-4) slows bacterial growth that clogs the stem's water channels. C₆H₁₂O₆+6 O₂ → 6 CO₂+6 H₂O
c-104.example: Mixing 10g of sugar (1%) and 5mL of vinegar into 1L of water gives about pH 3.7, and changing it every 2 days usually adds several days.
c-104.actionItem: Today, refresh the vase with 1L of clean water, 10g of sugar and 5mL of vinegar, and re-cut the stems at an angle.

c-105.title: Wipe sticker goo away with cooking oil
c-105.summary: Sticky residue left by a label will not wash off with water, but oil dissolves it. You rarely need a harsh solvent.
c-105.principle: Adhesive is a nonpolar polymer, so it resists polar water but mixes with nonpolar oil (like dissolves like). δ_oil ≈ δ_adhesive;;like dissolves like
c-105.example: Rub a few drops of cooking oil on the residue, wait 5 minutes, wipe, then remove the oil with dish soap; most glass and ceramic labels come clean.
c-105.actionItem: Today, dab oil on a sticky label mark on a jar or plate, wait 5 minutes and wipe it off (acetone can damage plastic).

c-106.title: Nuts go rancid because their unsaturated fats oxidize
c-106.summary: Unsaturated fatty acids in nuts and sesame oil oxidize on contact with air and develop a stale smell. Airtight storage in the freezer delays rancidity by months.
c-106.principle: Lipid autoxidation begins with RH + O₂ → ROOH and produces odorous aldehydes. The reaction rate roughly halves with each 10°C drop.
c-106.example: Walnuts at room temperature (25°C) start tasting rancid within weeks to a few months, but airtight at -18°C they keep 6-12 months. Discard nuts that taste bitter or stale.
c-106.actionItem: Today, put leftover nuts in a zip bag or airtight container and store them in the freezer.

c-107.title: Heat can ease the itch of a mosquito bite
c-107.summary: A mosquito's saliva triggers histamine release, causing swelling and itching. Brief heat of about 50°C denatures proteins in the saliva and quiets the itch signal.
c-107.principle: Histamine C₅H₉N₃ stimulates nerve endings, and heat unfolds the saliva proteins' structure to reduce the reaction (thermal denaturation).
c-107.example: Reports suggest about 10 seconds of 50°C heat relieves itching for several hours. To avoid burns, never hold a hot object on skin for long.
c-107.actionItem: On your next trip, pack an anti-itch or cooling gel for mosquito bites.

c-108.title: Potassium sorbate on a label is a mold-inhibiting preservative
c-108.summary: Potassium sorbate inhibits molds and yeasts in acidic foods and is used in cheese, drinks and bread. It is considered safe within regulatory limits, but sensitive people can check for it on labels.
c-108.principle: Sorbic acid (C₅H₇COOH, pK_a = 4.76) is more undissociated at low pH, and that form crosses cell membranes to do its work.
c-108.example: At pH 4.8 about 50% of sorbic acid is the active undissociated form, but at pH 6.8 only about 1% is. That is why it works better in acidic foods.
c-108.actionItem: Today, find the preservative listing on the ingredient labels of two foods you often eat.

c-109.title: Spent batteries belong in a collection bin, not general trash
c-109.summary: Batteries contain metals such as zinc, manganese and nickel that can leach into soil if landfilled. A battery collection bin lets those metals be recovered.
c-109.principle: Alkaline cell reaction: Zn + 2MnO₂ + H₂O → ZnO + 2MnOOH. Recovered, these metals become new raw material.
c-109.example: One AA battery weighs about 23g, and over 20% of that is metals like zinc and manganese. Collecting 100 batteries (about 2.3kg) allows a large share of that metal to be recycled.
c-109.actionItem: Today, gather your spent batteries in one container and drop them off at a local collection bin.

c-110.title: Hardened brown sugar softens with a slice of bread
c-110.summary: Brown sugar hardens as moisture leaves the molasses film and the crystals stick together. Sealing it with a slice of bread or damp paper towel returns moisture and softens it.
c-110.principle: Sugar is hygroscopic and draws in water vapor H₂O(g), so the molasses film on its surface softens again. Equilibrium is set between the vapor pressure in the air and at the sugar surface.
c-110.example: Sealing 500g of hardened brown sugar with one slice of bread usually softens it within a day. In a hurry, covering it with a damp paper towel and microwaving for 20 seconds loosens it.
c-110.actionItem: If you have hardened sugar today, seal it in an airtight container with a slice of bread.

c-111.title: Kelp releases more umami when steeped long in cold water
c-111.summary: Glutamic acid in kelp comes out slowly even in cold water, while hard boiling releases slime that clouds and thickens the broth. Steep in cold water 30 minutes or more, then remove just before boiling.
c-111.principle: Glutamic acid HOOC-CH₂CH₂-CH(NH₂)-COOH is water soluble, while slimy polysaccharides such as alginate dissolve heavily with long boiling.
c-111.example: Two 10cm strips of kelp in 1L of water for 30 minutes, removed as the water starts to boil (about 90°C), give plenty of umami. The removed kelp can be reused in braised dishes.
c-111.actionItem: When making broth this evening, soak kelp in cold water for 30 minutes before heating.

c-112.title: Urine color shows whether you are drinking enough
c-112.summary: Urine is yellow because of a pigment called urochrome, and it darkens when water intake is low. Pale yellow generally means you are drinking enough.
c-112.principle: In concentration c = (n / V), less water intake shrinks V, so the same amount of urochrome n looks more intense.
c-112.example: About 1.5L of urine a day in a pale straw color is generally adequate. Dark amber is a cue to drink more, but B vitamins or medications can change the color.
c-112.actionItem: Today, glance at your urine color once and drink a glass of water if it is dark.

c-113.title: Gasoline grades are octane ratings; use the one your car requires
c-113.summary: Octane rating measures how well fuel resists knocking, or self-igniting under compression. If your manual recommends a grade, paying for a higher one gives no benefit.
c-113.principle: Octane number compares knock resistance on a scale where isooctane (C₈H₁₈) is 100 and heptane is 0.
c-113.example: If the manual recommends 91 (regular) and you pump 94 (premium), you pay hundreds of won more per liter for almost no efficiency gain. Use premium only if the engine, such as a high-compression one, requires it.
c-113.actionItem: Today, check the recommended octane in your car manual or on the label inside the fuel door.

c-114.title: Cosmetic ingredient lists are in descending order of amount
c-114.summary: On cosmetic labels, ingredients above 1% are listed from most to least, and those under 1% may be in any order. The first few ingredients make up most of the product, so a headline ingredient near the end is present in small amounts.
c-114.principle: Most products list water (H₂O) first. When concentration w = m_ingredientmₜₒₜₐₗ × 100% is below 1%, any order is allowed.
c-114.example: If a toner lists water, glycerin, then butylene glycol, those three can make up over 90% of it. A promoted ingredient listed last is usually under 1%.
c-114.actionItem: Today, read the first five ingredients on one cosmetic you use.

c-115.title: Move camp food quickly through the 4-60°C danger zone
c-115.summary: Bacteria multiply fast between roughly 4 and 60°C, known as the danger zone. Keep meat and egg dishes below 4°C in a cooler and cook them thoroughly to the center.
c-115.principle: Bacterial count grows as N = N₀ × 2^(t/td) (일정 시간마다 2배씩 기하급수적 증식). E. coli can double about every 20 minutes near 37°C.
c-115.example: Food left out at 30°C in midsummer for two hours can see bacteria multiply by about 2⁶ = 64 times. Cook meat to a core temperature of 75°C or higher for at least a minute.
c-115.actionItem: On your next camping trip, fill the cooler with ice and bring a food thermometer.

c-116.title: Salting pasta water barely raises the boiling point
c-116.summary: Salt does not make the water much hotter. To save gas, use a lid and a lower flame instead.
c-116.principle: Dissolved particles raise the boiling point (boiling-point elevation), but the effect is tiny. ΔT_b=i K_b m=2 × 0.512 × 0.171 ≈ 0.17K
c-116.example: Adding 10g of salt to 1L of water raises the boiling point only about 0.17°C, so cooking time is unchanged and you just season the pasta.
c-116.actionItem: Today, salt noodle water only for taste, and once it boils, cover and turn the flame down.

c-117.title: Treat grass stains with alcohol first, then enzyme detergent
c-117.summary: Grass stain mixes oily chlorophyll with protein, so water alone fails. The right order lifts it.
c-117.principle: Chlorophyll dissolves in ethanol, and protease in enzyme detergent cuts protein stains into peptides. Hot water sets protein stains. protein stain+H₂O―( protease)→ peptides
c-117.example: Dabbing 70% ethanol on the stain for 5 minutes and then washing at 30-40°C with enzyme detergent fades most grass stains.
c-117.actionItem: Today, dab a grass stain with disinfectant ethanol for 5 minutes and wash at 30-40°C (test colourfastness on a hidden spot first).

c-118.title: Eat spinach with lemon to absorb more iron
c-118.summary: Plant (non-haem) iron is poorly absorbed, but vitamin C converts it to an absorbable form. Tannins in tea and coffee do the opposite.
c-118.principle: Non-haem iron is mostly Fe³⁺, but the gut absorbs Fe²⁺; vitamin C reduces ferric to ferrous iron and chelates it. Fe³⁺+ascorbate → Fe²⁺+dehydroascorbate
c-118.example: About 100mg of vitamin C (roughly one lemon) with a meal can raise non-haem iron absorption about 2-3 times.
c-118.actionItem: Today, squeeze lemon on a spinach or bean dish, and have tea or coffee an hour after the meal.

c-119.title: Chill drinks fast outdoors with salted ice
c-119.summary: Mixing salt into ice drops the temperature far below 0°C, so drinks cool in minutes. Handy at a picnic.
c-119.principle: Freezing-point depression means salty water freezes only below 0°C, so melting ice draws heat from its surroundings and the temperature plunges (eutectic -21°C). ΔT_f=i K_f m, K_f=1.86K kg mol⁻¹
c-119.example: Mixing ice and salt 3:1 by mass reaches roughly -15 to -20°C, and a can spun in it cools to about 5°C within minutes.
c-119.actionItem: At your next picnic, mix 3 parts ice with 1 part salt in the cooler and roll a can for 3-5 minutes (check it does not freeze and burst).

c-120.title: Brown meat is not automatically spoiled
c-120.summary: Meat colour reflects the state of iron in myoglobin, which does not always match freshness. Judge by date and smell too.
c-120.principle: Oxymyoglobin, bound to oxygen, is bright red; when its iron oxidizes it becomes brown metmyoglobin. Inside vacuum or tight packs there is little oxygen, so meat looks dark purple. Mb(Fe²⁺)+O₂ ⇌ MbO₂ (red),  Mb → metMb(Fe³⁺) (brown)
c-120.example: Ground beef turns bright red within 15-30 minutes in air and may brown after some days in the fridge, but colour alone is not proof of spoilage.
c-120.actionItem: When shopping for meat today, check the use-by date, the packaging, and any sour smell or sliminess, not only colour.

c-121.title: Let chopped garlic rest 10 minutes before cooking to form allicin
c-121.summary: Cutting or crushing garlic lets the enzyme alliinase convert alliin into allicin, the basis of garlic's antibacterial and health compounds. Heating immediately stops the enzyme so less allicin forms.
c-121.principle: Alliin ―(alliinase)→ allicin (C₆H₁₀OS₂). The enzyme denatures quickly above about 60-70°C.
c-121.example: Reports suggest that minced garlic rested 10 minutes keeps several times more allicin-derived compounds than garlic cooked right away. One or two cloves per serving is plenty.
c-121.actionItem: If you cook with garlic today, chop it and let it rest 10 minutes before heating.

c-122.title: Strain and shade frying oil to make it last
c-122.summary: Oil goes rancid when exposed to heat, light and oxygen, and smells bad. Storing it well avoids waste.
c-122.principle: Unsaturated fatty acids oxidize by a radical chain reaction, forming peroxides and aldehydes; heat and food particles speed it up. R · +O₂ → ROO · , ROO · +RH → ROOH+R ·
c-122.example: Use highly unsaturated oils within about 3 months of opening, and reuse strained frying oil only 2-3 times.
c-122.actionItem: Today, strain used frying oil through a coffee filter into a dark bottle and keep it cool; discard it if it smells like paint.

c-123.title: Stainless steel can rust if salty soup sits too long
c-123.summary: Stainless resists rust thanks to a thin chromium-oxide film, but chloride can break it and leave tiny pits and rust spots.
c-123.principle: With over 10.5% chromium a Cr₂O₃ film forms and self-heals in oxygen, but Cl⁻ locally destroys it and causes pitting corrosion. Cr₂O₃ (1-5nm film) + Cl⁻ → pitting
c-123.example: Grade 316, with about 2% molybdenum, resists salt better than 304 (about 18% Cr, 8% Ni). Salt water left for hours can cause pits.
c-123.actionItem: Today, wash any stainless pot that held soup or salty food right away and dry it fully.

c-124.title: Afternoon coffee still lingers at night
c-124.summary: Caffeine leaves the body slowly, so late coffee can disturb night sleep. Moving your last cup earlier helps.
c-124.principle: Caffeine has a half-life of about 5 hours (range 3-7 h) and declines by a fixed fraction per hour, like a first-order process. C(t)=C₀ ≤ ft(12)^t/t₁/2, t₁/2 ≈ 5 h
c-124.example: If you drink 150mg of caffeine at 3 pm, about 50mg (one third) remains 8 hours later at 11 pm. A daily total up to 400mg is the usual guideline.
c-124.actionItem: Today, set your last caffeinated drink at least 8 hours before bedtime and switch to decaf or barley tea afterwards.

c-125.title: At altitude water boils near 95°C, so cooking slows
c-125.summary: Air pressure falls with height, so water boils at a lower temperature. That is why instant noodles and rice come out undercooked.
c-125.principle: Lower air pressure lowers the boiling point (about 3.3°C per 1,000m). With the rule that rates double per 10°C, cooking time lengthens. ΔT_b ≈ -3.3 °CmathrmC per 1000m; (t' / t) ≈ 2^ΔT/10
c-125.example: At 1,500m water boils near 95°C, so the rate is 2⁻0.5 ≈ 0.7 of normal and cooking takes about 40% longer.
c-125.actionItem: If you are hiking today, plan 1.4 times the usual time for instant noodles and cook rice longer with a lid on.

c-126.title: Never preheat a non-stick pan empty on high heat
c-126.summary: PTFE (Teflon) coatings are stable to about 260°C but break down above that and give off harmful fumes. Preheating an empty pan on high is the most common home cause.
c-126.principle: PTFE is stable thanks to very strong C-F bonds, but above roughly 300°C it decomposes and releases fluorinated gases that are deadly to pet birds. -(CF₂-CF₂)_n-, E_C-F ≈ 485kJ mol⁻¹
c-126.example: An empty pan on high heat can pass 300°C within 2-5 minutes, while cooking with oil or food on medium heat usually stays under 200°C.
c-126.actionItem: Today, use non-stick pans on medium or lower heat with oil or food in them, never empty, and skip metal utensils.

c-127.title: Drinking undiluted vinegar dissolves tooth enamel
c-127.summary: Vinegar's pH is about 2.5, far below the pH 5.5 at which enamel begins to dissolve. If you drink it, dilute it well and rinse with water afterward.
c-127.principle: Enamel dissolution: Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂ + 14H⁺ → 10Ca²⁺ + 6H₂PO₄⁻ + 2H₂O. The lower pH = -[H⁺], the faster it dissolves.
c-127.example: Vinegar at pH 2.5 has 1000 times the hydrogen ion concentration of pH 5.5. Mix one tablespoon into at least 200mL of water, drink it through a straw, and brush 30 minutes later.
c-127.actionItem: If you drink vinegar or a sour drink today, rinse with water and wait 30 minutes before brushing.

c-128.title: Freeze bread, do not refrigerate it
c-128.summary: Bread goes hard not by drying but because starch recrystallizes, and that happens fastest in the fridge.
c-128.principle: Starch retrogradation, where amylose and amylopectin realign into crystals, is fastest at 0-5°C and nearly stops below -18°C. amylose/amylopectin recrystallization (retrogradation), fastest at 0-5 °CmathrmC
c-128.example: Room-temperature bread keeps 2-3 days and fridge bread stales faster, whereas bread at -18°C keeps about 3 months, and heating above 60°C melts the crystals and softens it.
c-128.actionItem: Today, slice leftover bread, freeze it in portions, and reheat in a toaster or steamer when needed.

c-129.title: Fix tomato stains in plastic containers with oil and sunlight
c-129.summary: The red pigment in tomato sauce mixes with oil and soaks into plastic. Oil and UV light work better than water.
c-129.principle: Lycopene is a nonpolar pigment that dissolves into plastic; its 11 conjugated double bonds absorb light and look red, and UV breaks them into colourless fragments. lycopene (11 conjugated C=C)―(h)→colourless fragments
c-129.example: Rub on a drop of oil, wash with dish soap, then leave the container in sunlight for 2-3 hours; most of the stain fades.
c-129.actionItem: Today, rub a drop of cooking oil on a stained plastic box, wash it with soap, and set it on a sunny windowsill for 2-3 hours (glass containers prevent it).

c-130.title: Oral rehydration uses salt and sugar together
c-130.summary: When glucose and sodium are absorbed together, water follows. It rehydrates better than plain water.
c-130.principle: The SGLT1 transporter in gut cells carries one glucose with two sodium ions, and water is drawn in by osmosis. SGLT1: 1 glucose+2 Na⁺ → water uptake
c-130.example: The WHO home recipe is 1L of boiled-and-cooled water with 6 level teaspoons (about 25g) of sugar and half a teaspoon (about 3g) of salt. Severe dehydration, infants or high fever need medical care.
c-130.actionItem: Today, stock a packet or two of commercial oral rehydration salts (ORS) in your medicine box.

c-131.title: Stinging pool eyes are chloramines, not chlorine itself
c-131.summary: Red eyes do not mean the pool is over-chlorinated; they come from chloramines formed when chlorine meets sweat and urine. A pre-swim shower is the best prevention.
c-131.principle: Chlorine becomes hypochlorous acid (HOCl) in water and disinfects; with ammonia-type nitrogen it forms irritating chloramines. At pH 7.5 about 50% is HOCl. Cl₂+H₂O ⇌ HOCl+H⁺+Cl⁻, HOCl ⇌ H⁺+OCl⁻ (pK_a ≈ 7.5)
c-131.example: Recommended pool values are pH 7.2-7.8 and free chlorine 1-3ppm. A 1-minute soap shower before swimming greatly cuts organic load.
c-131.actionItem: Before going swimming today, take a 1-minute soapy shower, and do not urinate in the pool.

c-132.title: Compute water hardness from the mineral-water label
c-132.summary: Bottled waters differ in hardness, which changes how coffee and tea taste and how much scale you get. The label numbers are enough to tell soft from hard.
c-132.principle: Hardness expresses calcium and magnesium ions as an equivalent mass of calcium carbonate. About 50-175mg/L is recommended for brewing coffee. H=2.497 [Ca]+4.118 [Mg] (mg L⁻¹ as CaCO₃)
c-132.example: Water with 80mg/L calcium and 26mg/L magnesium is 2.497 × 80+4.118 × 26 ≈ 307mg/L, very hard (above 180), and will scale a kettle quickly.
c-132.actionItem: Today, calculate the hardness of the bottled water you drink from the Ca and Mg numbers on its label.

c-133.title: Calories are heat of combustion: 4-4-9kcal per gram
c-133.summary: Food energy is defined by the heat released when food is burned. You can work out calories yourself from the grams on a label.
c-133.principle: Burning 1 mol of glucose releases 2,803kJ (about 15.6kJ/g, 3.7kcal/g). Atwater factors are 4kcal/g for carbohydrate and protein and 9kcal/g for fat. C₆H₁₂O₆+6 O₂ → 6 CO₂+6 H₂O, ΔH=-2803kJ mol⁻¹ ≈ 3.7kcal g⁻¹
c-133.example: A snack with 50g carbohydrate, 20g fat and 10g protein gives 50 × 4+20 × 9+10 × 4=420kcal.
c-133.actionItem: Today, use the nutrition label of one snack to calculate its kcal from the grams of carbs, fat and protein.

c-134.title: Drying laundry in sunlight also bleaches it
c-134.summary: Ultraviolet light breaks down leftover pigment stains in fabric, making whites look brighter. Small stains fade in sunlight even without percarbonate.
c-134.principle: Photo-oxidation: UV photons break the π bonds in pigments, which react with oxygen to form colorless products. Photon energy E = h must exceed the bond energy.
c-134.example: A stained white T-shirt hung wet in direct sun for 4-6 hours fades light stains noticeably. Colored clothes can fade by the same principle, so dry them inside out.
c-134.actionItem: Today, hang a stained white garment wet in a sunny spot to dry.

c-135.title: Soak superglued fingers in soapy water
c-135.summary: Superglue cures on skin moisture, but warm soapy water can loosen it slowly. Pulling apart tears skin.
c-135.principle: Cyanoacrylate polymerizes by chain reaction when moisture (OH⁻) triggers it, hardening in seconds to a minute. Soapy water and gentle rubbing soften and push off the bond. n CH₂=C(CN)COOR―( OH⁻)→ (moisture) ≤ ft[CH₂-C(CN)(COOR)]_n
c-135.example: Soaking in warm soapy water for 10-15 minutes and rolling with a thumb frees most fingers. If it sticks to eyes or lips, do not rub; get medical care.
c-135.actionItem: Today, ventilate when using superglue, and if fingers stick, soak them in warm soapy water for 15 minutes and roll them apart.

c-136.title: Adding acid reduces fishy smell
c-136.summary: The main culprit in fishy odor is trimethylamine, a basic compound. Sprinkling lemon juice or vinegar neutralizes it so less smell escapes.
c-136.principle: (CH₃)₃N + H⁺ → (CH₃)₃NH⁺. The ionized amine does not evaporate, so the odor falls.
c-136.example: A teaspoon (about 5mL) of lemon juice on a fish fillet for 5 minutes noticeably reduces the fishy smell. Soaking in milk for 20 minutes works on a similar principle, with proteins binding the odor compounds.
c-136.actionItem: When cooking fish today, first splash it with lemon juice or vinegar.

c-137.title: Oxygen partial pressure drops with altitude and makes you breathless
c-137.summary: The oxygen fraction in air is about 21% everywhere, but air pressure falls with altitude, so oxygen partial pressure drops. At 3000m you take in only about 70% as much as at sea level.
c-137.principle: Dalton's law: p_O₂ = x_O₂ × Pₜₒₜₐₗ. x_O₂ ≈ 0.21 stays constant while Pₜₒₜₐₗ falls.
c-137.example: At sea level (101kPa) oxygen partial pressure is about 21kPa, and at 3000m (about 70kPa) it is about 14.7kPa. Ascending slowly, within about 500m per day, lowers altitude sickness risk.
c-137.actionItem: If you plan a high-altitude trip, schedule a gradual ascent.

c-138.title: Discard cans that bulge or are badly dented
c-138.summary: A bulging can signals that microbes inside produced gas, possibly dangerous bacteria such as Clostridium botulinum. Do not open bulging cans; throw them away.
c-138.principle: Microbial fermentation gas: reactions such as C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ produce CO₂ and raise the pressure inside the can.
c-138.example: A normal can is near vacuum inside, so its lid is flat or slightly concave. If it bulges, hisses loudly or foams on opening, do not eat it.
c-138.actionItem: Today, check the cans in your pantry for bulging or rust.

c-139.title: Grease poured down a sink drain cools, hardens and clogs it
c-139.summary: Hot oil is liquid, but as it cools its saturated fats solidify on pipe walls and bind with debris. Wipe oil off with paper and put it in the trash, not the drain.
c-139.principle: Saturated fats melt around 30-60°C, and cooling oil goes through a liquid → solid phase change. With calcium ions it also forms fatty acid calcium salts (soap scum).
c-139.example: Pouring 200mL of frying oil down the drain can leave a 1-2mm hardened layer on pipe walls, and repeating it can clog the pipe. Wipe greasy dishes with paper towel before washing.
c-139.actionItem: Today, wipe greasy pans with paper towel before washing them.

c-140.title: Water bottles left in a hot car
c-140.summary: PET bottles left in a hot car can release more trace antimony and other compounds. A day or two is low risk, but water left for weeks is best avoided.
c-140.principle: Leaching rises with temperature: k = A e⁻E_a/RT (Arrhenius equation, larger T gives larger k)
c-140.example: A midsummer car interior can reach 60-70°C, making leaching several times faster than at 20°C.
c-140.actionItem: Do not drink PET-bottle water that has sat in your car; carry a stainless-steel tumbler for trips instead.

c-141.title: Why the R-32 refrigerant matters
c-141.summary: R-32 needs less charge than R-410A for the same cooling capacity and has roughly one third of the global warming potential (GWP). It is worth checking when you buy an air conditioner.
c-141.principle: R-32 is CH₂F₂; a large latent heat q = h_g - h_f means less refrigerant must circulate.
c-141.example: GWP is about 2088 for R-410A and about 675 for R-32. The charge is also about 20-30% smaller, giving slightly higher efficiency.
c-141.actionItem: When you buy or service an AC, read the label and note the refrigerant type (R-32 or R-410A).

c-142.title: Why soda goes flat
c-142.summary: Carbon dioxide dissolves best under pressure and in the cold, and escapes when the drink warms or the pressure drops. Keep it cold and recap quickly.
c-142.principle: Henry's law: C = k_H P_CO₂, where k_H falls as temperature rises.
c-142.example: Pressure in a sealed bottle is about 3-4atm, and CO₂ solubility at 25°C is roughly half that at 4°C.
c-142.actionItem: Recap the soda right after pouring and store it upright in the fridge today.

c-143.title: Baking soda in the fridge
c-143.summary: Baking soda is mildly basic, so it neutralises acidic odour molecules such as fatty acids. Its capacity is small, so replace it every 2-3 months.
c-143.example: About 100g (half a cup) in an open container is enough to tame mild odours in a small fridge.
c-143.actionItem: Put a cup of baking soda in a shallow dish on a fridge shelf and write a replacement date 3 months out.

c-144.title: Sweet potatoes taste sweetest when baked slowly through 70-75°C
c-144.summary: Beta-amylase in sweet potato breaks starch into sweet maltose, working best around 70-75°C and stopping above 90°C. The slower the bake, the longer it spends in the sweet zone.
c-144.principle: (C₆H₁₀O₅)_n + n/2 H₂O ―(β-amylase)→ n/2 C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Enzyme activity has an optimum temperature.
c-144.example: Baking at 150°C or below for 50 minutes or more keeps the interior in the 70-75°C range much longer than 5 minutes at 180°C, producing far more maltose. That is why roasted sweet potatoes are so sweet.
c-144.actionItem: When baking sweet potatoes today, roast them low and slow.

c-145.title: Eggs turn soft-boiled around 62-65°C because proteins denature
c-145.summary: Egg white and yolk proteins set at different temperatures. The white begins to set at about 62-65°C and the yolk at about 65-70°C, which separates soft-boiled from hard-boiled.
c-145.principle: Thermal denaturation unfolds the tertiary structure of proteins so they tangle together. Ovotransferrin denatures near 62°C and ovalbumin near 80°C.
c-145.example: Six minutes in boiling water gives a set white and runny yolk, while 10 minutes or more gives a hard-boiled egg. Because of Salmonella risk, older adults and pregnant people should eat them fully cooked.
c-145.actionItem: When boiling eggs today, set timers for 6 and 10 minutes and compare the results.

c-146.title: Water-soluble vitamins in excess leave in the urine
c-146.summary: Vitamin C and the B vitamins dissolve in water, so what exceeds your need is not stored but excreted in urine. Much of a high-dose supplement may simply be wasted.
c-146.principle: Water-soluble molecules are polar, dissolve readily in blood and urine, and are filtered by the kidneys. Fat-soluble vitamins, by contrast, accumulate in fat tissue.
c-146.example: The adult vitamin C recommendation is about 100mg a day, and taking 1000mg at once drops absorption below 50%, with much of the rest excreted. One fruit supplies about 50mg.
c-146.actionItem: If you take a vitamin supplement today, check that it plus your food stays within the recommended intake.

c-147.title: Sea salt and refined salt differ in NaCl share and minerals
c-147.summary: Refined salt is 99% or more sodium chloride (NaCl), while solar sea salt is about 80-90% NaCl mixed with magnesium, calcium and moisture. Either way sodium is similar, so eating less matters most.
c-147.principle: The sodium fraction is M_NaM_NaCl = (23 / 58.5) ≈ 0.39. For the same salt mass, the higher the NaCl share, the more sodium.
c-147.example: 5g of pure NaCl holds about 1.97g of sodium, while sea salt at 85% NaCl holds about 1.67g. WHO advises under 5g of salt a day.
c-147.actionItem: Today, check the sodium content (mg per 100g) on your salt's nutrition label.

c-148.title: Photochromic lenses explained
c-148.summary: Silver halide in photochromic lenses splits into silver specks under UV and darkens, then recombines when the light fades. In cars, glass blocks UV so they darken less.
c-148.principle: AgCl ―(h)→ Ag + Cl, and in the dark Ag + Cl → AgCl
c-148.example: In sunlight, transmission can fall from about 85% to the 20% range within a minute and recover over 5-15 minutes indoors.
c-148.actionItem: For sunny drives, carry regular UV-blocking sunglasses instead of relying on photochromic lenses.

c-149.title: Electric cars waste less energy than gasoline cars
c-149.summary: A gasoline engine turns only about 20-30% of fuel energy into motion and wastes the rest as heat. An electric car delivers about 80-90% of its electric energy to the wheels, so it needs less energy per distance.
c-149.principle: One liter of gasoline carries about 32MJ (≈ 8.9kWh), and at efficiency η = WₒᵤₜE_in of about 25% the useful work is roughly 2.2kWh.
c-149.example: A car that goes about 12km per liter of gasoline uses that 2.2kWh of useful work for 12km, while an electric car covers 12km on about 2kWh (roughly 6km per kWh). Counting power-plant losses narrows the gap.
c-149.actionItem: Today, walk or take transit for short trips to save fuel.

c-150.title: Cooking oil smoke points
c-150.summary: Past its smoke point, oil produces smoke and acrolein that irritate eyes and throat. High-heat cooking calls for oils with a high smoke point.
c-150.example: Smoke points are about 190°C for extra-virgin olive oil, about 240°C for canola and about 230°C for refined sunflower oil.
c-150.actionItem: Use a refined, high-smoke-point oil for stir-frying; if it smokes, lower the heat and ventilate.

c-151.title: Why iced tea turns cloudy
c-151.summary: When strong black tea cools, caffeine and tannins bind into particles and make it cloudy. Adding hot water clears it, and cold brewing avoids it.
c-151.principle: Caffeine + tannin (theaflavin) ⇌ complex: solubility drops at low temperature, so it precipitates.
c-151.example: Black tea brewed at 100°C and cooled to 4°C turns hazy within minutes; cold brew (4°C, 8 hours) is much clearer.
c-151.actionItem: Make today's iced tea by steeping a tea bag in 500mL cold water in the fridge for 8 hours.

c-152.title: Amygdalin in plum seeds is dangerous raw
c-152.summary: Unripe green plums and their seeds contain amygdalin, which can release hydrogen cyanide when broken down. Remove the pit or age plum syrup six months or more, strain it, and do not eat the seeds.
c-152.principle: C₂₀H₂₇NO₁₁ + 2H₂O ―(enzyme)→ C₆H₅CHO + HCN + 2C₆H₁₂O₆. Hydrogen cyanide forms when the enzyme contacts it.
c-152.example: The amygdalin in a single plum seed is tiny, but chewing many raw seeds could be dangerous. Layer pitted green plums with sugar at 1:1, age six months, then remove the fruit.
c-152.actionItem: If you make plum syrup today, do not eat the seeds and note on the calendar when to remove the fruit.

c-153.title: Spray cans can burst if left somewhere hot
c-153.summary: Aerosol cans hold compressed gas and a flammable propellant, so pressure rises with temperature. Left in a summer car or near a flame they can burst, so follow the label's storage limit of 50°C or lower.
c-153.principle: Gas pressure is proportional to temperature: (P₁ / T₁) = (P₂ / T₂) (T in kelvin). The vapor pressure of a liquefied propellant climbs steeply with temperature.
c-153.example: A can at 5atm at 20°C (293K) reaches about 5.7atm at 60°C (333K) by simple calculation, and far higher once the propellant's vapor pressure is added. A midsummer car interior can exceed 60°C.
c-153.actionItem: Today, gather the spray products at home and move them to a cool spot away from heat.

c-154.title: Why jelly will not set with fresh pineapple or kiwi
c-154.summary: Protein-digesting enzymes in raw pineapple and kiwi chop up gelatin. Heating them once or using canned fruit stops the enzymes so the jelly sets.
c-154.principle: Bromelain and actinidin hydrolyze peptide bonds: R-CO-NH-R' + H₂O → R-COOH + H₂N-R'. The enzymes denature above about 70 °CmathrmC.
c-154.example: 100mL of gelatin with raw pineapple stays liquid even after hours, but pineapple heated above 80°C for a minute, or canned pineapple, sets normally. The same enzymes are used to tenderize meat.
c-154.actionItem: When adding fresh fruit to jelly or pudding today, blanch pineapple or kiwi in boiling water for a minute first.

c-155.title: The musty smell of damp towels
c-155.summary: The smell of slow-drying laundry comes from fatty acids such as 4-methyl-3-hexenoic acid produced by Moraxella bacteria. Drying fast before they multiply is the key.
c-155.principle: Bacterial metabolism: skin lipids → C₇H₁₂O₂ (4-methyl-3-hexenoic acid) and other volatile fatty acids
c-155.example: If wet laundry stays damp for over 5 hours indoors, odour starts; a dryer at 60°C or above greatly reduces bacteria.
c-155.actionItem: Hang laundry right after washing and run a fan or dehumidifier so it dries within 5 hours.

c-156.title: What the pink bathroom slime is
c-156.summary: The pink slime is not mould but a red-pigmented film made by bacteria such as Serratia. Moisture and soap residue feed it, so drying is the best prevention.
c-156.principle: Bacterial growth N = N₀ × 2^(t/td) (일정 시간마다 2배씩 기하급수적 증식) (a doubling time t_d of 30 min gives hundreds of thousands of times in a day)
c-156.example: In a warm, damp bathroom at 25-35°C, counts can grow about 4,000-fold every 6 hours; drying stops growth.
c-156.actionItem: After showering, squeegee walls and floor and run the exhaust fan for 30 minutes.

c-157.title: Storing cut watermelon
c-157.summary: A cut watermelon loses water and sugar through its cut face and invites bacteria. Cover the cut surface and refrigerate it, and eat within two days.
c-157.principle: Evaporation scales with exposed area and temperature. At 4°C, bacterial growth is about 1/20 of that at 25°C.
c-157.example: At 30°C a cut melon can have tens of times more bacteria after 2 hours; in the fridge at 4°C it stays safe about 2 days.
c-157.actionItem: Keep leftover melon in large pieces with the rind on and wrap the cut face tightly before chilling.

c-158.title: Summer lunchboxes are safer with vinegared rice and cooled side dishes
c-158.summary: In acidic conditions (pH below 4.6) most food-poisoning bacteria struggle to grow. Adding a spoon of vinegar to the rice or packing cooled side dishes extends safety.
c-158.principle: With the weak-acid equilibrium CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺, a higher [H⁺] lowers pH and slows bacterial growth.
c-158.example: Adding 1 tablespoon (15mL) of vinegar to 2 cups of rice (about 300g) lowers its pH to around 5 and slows bacterial growth. Close the lunchbox only after the food has cooled fully, and pack an ice pack.
c-158.actionItem: For today's lunchbox, cool the food fully before closing it and add an ice pack.

c-159.title: Why tools rust on humid days
c-159.summary: Iron forms rust when water and oxygen are present, and it speeds up above about 60% humidity. A thin oil film or desiccant slows it.
c-159.principle: 4 Fe + 3 O₂ + 6 H₂O → 4 Fe(OH)₃, then Fe₂O₃ · xH₂O
c-159.example: At 60%+ relative humidity bare iron can rust within days, but below 40% it barely progresses.
c-159.actionItem: Wipe tools with a lightly oiled cloth and put silica gel in the toolbox.

c-160.title: Mothball safety
c-160.summary: Mothballs go straight from solid to gas (sublimation) to repel insects. The vapour is harmful to breathe, so ventilation and distance matter.
c-160.principle: Sublimation: C₁₀H₈(s) → C₁₀H₈(g); vapour pressure rises with temperature.
c-160.example: Naphthalene vapour pressure is about 11Pa at 25°C and roughly 4 times higher at 40°C. Keep it from touching clothes.
c-160.actionItem: Air clothes stored with mothballs on a balcony for 2-3 hours before wearing, and keep mothballs away from children.

c-161.title: Rubbing hands on stainless steel eases garlic and fish smells
c-161.summary: The sulfur compounds from garlic and onion are said to fade when you rub your hands on stainless steel. Soap helps by washing off and oxidizing the sulfur compounds.
c-161.principle: Sulfur compounds R-SH adsorb onto the oxide film (Cr₂O₃) on metal surfaces and become less volatile.
c-161.example: Many people find that rubbing hands on a stainless faucet for 30 seconds after mincing garlic reduces the smell, though scientific evidence for the effect size is limited. Lemon juice or vinegar can also be used.
c-161.actionItem: After mincing garlic today, rub your hands on a stainless sink for 30 seconds and then wash them with soap.

c-162.title: Why bread moulds fast in the rainy season
c-162.summary: Bread has a high water activity, so mould grows quickly above 70% humidity. Its threads reach deep inside, so cutting off only the visible spot is unsafe.
c-162.principle: Water activity a_w = (p / p₀) (bread about 0.95; mould grows above about 0.80)
c-162.example: On a humid day at 25°C bread moulds in 3-4 days, while frozen at -18°C it keeps for weeks.
c-162.actionItem: Freeze slices you cannot finish today, wrapped individually, and toast them straight from frozen.

c-163.title: Why rain is slightly acidic
c-163.summary: Rain is mildly acidic at about pH 5.6 because atmospheric CO2 dissolves in it; acid rain is below 5.6. It is harmless to skin at this level but slowly corrodes metal and stone.
c-163.example: [H⁺] ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ mol/L gives pH = -[H⁺] ≈ 5.6, versus 7 for pure water.
c-163.actionItem: After rain, wipe the water off your bicycle chain and add a drop of oil.

c-164.title: Cooled rice gains resistant starch, so less sugar is absorbed
c-164.summary: As rice cools, some of its starch turns into resistant starch that is hard to digest. Even after reheating, some remains, which may soften the blood sugar rise slightly.
c-164.principle: Starch retrogradation is the re-crystallization of gelatinized amylose as it cools. The amylase enzyme breaks these crystals down poorly.
c-164.example: Rice reheated after 12-24 hours in the fridge is reported to have several times more resistant starch than fresh rice, though the increase is only a few percent of total starch. Do not leave rice at room temperature; refrigerate it quickly.
c-164.actionItem: Today, refrigerate leftover rice within one hour.

c-165.title: Fabric softener and towel absorbency
c-165.summary: Fabric softener coats fibres with cationic surfactants, making them soft but less absorbent. For towels, use it less often or skip it.
c-165.principle: Cationic surfactant R₂N⁺(CH₃)₂ adsorbs onto negatively charged fibre -COO⁻ and forms a water-repelling film.
c-165.example: Softener can cut towel absorbency by about 20-30%. Use it in only 1 of every 3 towel loads.
c-165.actionItem: Wash today's towels without softener and shake them out well before drying.

c-166.title: Recycling an aluminum can takes only about 5% of the energy of making a new one
c-166.summary: Making aluminum from ore uses enormous electricity, but recycling it saves about 95%. Rinsing cans and sorting them properly boosts the benefit.
c-166.principle: Electrolysis of bauxite: 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. New aluminum takes about 14kWh per kg, while recycled aluminum takes about 0.7kWh.
c-166.example: Recycling one aluminum can (about 14g) saves roughly 0.2kWh. A hundred cans save about 20kWh, comparable to running an air conditioner for around five hours.
c-166.actionItem: Today, empty and rinse any cans you drank and put them in the aluminum recycling bin.

c-167.title: Cutting off the visible mold does not make moldy food safe
c-167.summary: Mold sends thread-like hyphae below what you can see, and some molds produce toxins. For soft foods like bread, fruit and jam, it is safest to discard the whole item if mold shows.
c-167.principle: Aflatoxin B₁ (C₁₇H₁₂O₆) is heat stable and decomposes only above about 270 °CmathrmC, so boiling or baking does not remove it.
c-167.example: For dense foods like hard cheese or carrots, guidelines say cutting at least 2.5cm around the moldy spot works, but soft, moist foods such as bread, jam and tofu must be discarded entirely.
c-167.actionItem: Today, check the bread and jam in your fridge for mold.

c-168.title: The smell of city gas is something deliberately added
c-168.summary: City gas (methane) is naturally odorless, so a small amount of rotten-egg-smelling thioether or mercaptan compounds is added to reveal leaks. If you smell it, do not use flames or electric switches; ventilate first.
