c-168.principle: Methane is explosive at roughly 5-15% in air: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Odorants added to odorless gas include compounds such as CH₃SH.
c-168.example: In an 8m³ space, 0.4-1.2m³ of leaked methane (5-15%) is within the explosive range. If you smell gas, close the valve, open windows, avoid touching light or fan switches, and report it from outside.
c-168.actionItem: Today, learn where your gas valve is and make a habit of closing it after use.

c-169.title: Optical brighteners in white-laundry detergent make whites look whiter
c-169.summary: Optical brighteners absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it as blue light, masking yellow tones so fabric looks whiter. It is a visual effect, not soil removal, and colored clothes do not need it.
c-169.principle: Fluorescence absorbs UV (about 350nm) and emits blue light (about 430nm); the emitted photon energy E = (hc / λ) is slightly lower.
c-169.example: A white T-shirt washed with brighteners can look about 5-10% brighter in sunlight because it emits extra blue light. For colored clothes, a regular detergent without them is enough.
c-169.actionItem: On laundry day, check the detergent labels for optical brighteners and use them only on whites.

c-170.title: Putting a wet phone in rice barely helps
c-170.summary: Rice absorbs moisture poorly, so it pulls water out of a phone at about the same rate as air drying. Power it off, do not charge it, and let it dry in a ventilated spot instead.
c-170.principle: Drying rate is proportional to the vapor pressure difference. Rice's desiccating power is far weaker than silica gel, and what matters is how long corrosion can proceed after a short circuit.
c-170.example: Silica gel can absorb up to about 40% of its weight in water, but rice absorbs far less. Keep the phone off for 24-48 hours or more before turning it on. If it fell in salt water, contact a service center first.
c-170.actionItem: If your phone gets wet, skip the rice and power it off and leave it somewhere ventilated.

c-171.title: For a burn, cool it under running water for 20 minutes first
c-171.summary: Immediately after a burn, running cool water (15-25°C) for 10-20 minutes draws out heat that spreads into deeper skin and limits damage. Do not use ice, toothpaste or soybean paste.
c-171.principle: Heat from a hot object transfers to tissue as q = mcΔT and denatures proteins. Running water carries heat away quickly.
c-171.example: Water at 60°C can cause a serious burn in 5 seconds. Twenty minutes of cool water reduces burn depth and pain, while very cold ice constricts blood vessels and can further harm tissue.
c-171.actionItem: Remember today: if you burn yourself in the kitchen, cool it under running water for 20 minutes right away.

c-172.title: What oxygen absorbers do in food packs
c-172.summary: The small sachet in seaweed or jerky packs contains iron powder that reacts with oxygen and removes it. Less oxygen slows fat oxidation and mould.
c-172.example: One sachet (about 2g iron) absorbs about 200mL of oxygen, nearly removing the 21% in a 1L pack.
c-172.actionItem: Do not eat the sachet; leave it in the pack until you open it.

c-173.title: Egg freshness float test
c-173.summary: An eggshell has tiny pores, so over time water and CO2 escape and the air cell grows. A fresh egg sinks and an old one floats.
c-173.principle: Buoyancy F_b = ρ_water V g; once the air cell lowers average density to ρ < ρ_water, it floats.
c-173.example: A fresh egg is about 1.09g/mL; after 3-4 weeks it drops to about 1.02g/mL and begins to float in plain water.
c-173.actionItem: Before cracking a doubtful egg, drop it in a bowl of water, and discard it if it floats.

c-174.title: Why honey crystallises
c-174.summary: When glucose in honey exceeds what the water can hold, it forms crystals. It is normal, not spoilage, and gentle warming reverses it.
c-174.principle: Glucose solubility: beyond saturation, C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → C₆H₁₂O₆(s)
c-174.example: Honey is about 31% glucose, 38% fructose and 17% water, and crystallises faster below 14°C; a 40°C water bath dissolves it.
c-174.actionItem: Soak the crystallised jar in water below 40°C instead of microwaving it.

c-175.title: Why oils and supplements come in brown bottles
c-175.summary: Light, especially UV and blue light, oxidises fats and vitamins and spoils them. Amber glass strongly blocks light below about 450nm.
c-175.principle: Photo-oxidation: RH + O₂ ―(h)→ ROO · (chain oxidation); photon energy E = hc/λ
c-175.example: Amber glass blocks over 90% of light near 400nm, whereas oil in clear bottles can turn rancid within weeks in sunlight.
c-175.actionItem: Store sesame and perilla oil in a dark cupboard, not on a sunny windowsill.

c-176.title: How instant cold packs get cold
c-176.summary: When ammonium nitrate or urea in the pack dissolves in water it absorbs heat and the temperature drops. Squeeze, shake and it works immediately.
c-176.example: One mole (80g) of ammonium nitrate absorbs 25.7kJ on dissolving, cooling 100mL of water by about 15-20°C below room temperature.
c-176.actionItem: Pack an instant cold pack for camping or sport, wrap it in a towel and use it for 15 minutes only.

c-177.title: Why lithium-ion batteries hate heat
c-177.summary: High temperature speeds electrolyte breakdown and SEI growth, permanently cutting capacity. Never leave a phone or power bank in a car in midsummer.
c-177.principle: Ageing rate k = A e⁻E_a/RT: roughly 2x faster for each 10°C rise (Arrhenius rule of thumb)
c-177.example: If a cell loses about 20% capacity in a year at 25°C, it may lose about 35-40% in the same time at 45°C.
c-177.actionItem: In summer, never leave battery devices in the car; carry them in your bag.

c-178.title: Why kimchi sours fast in summer
c-178.summary: Lactic acid bacteria in kimchi multiply faster when warm and make more lactic acid. Below 10°C it ripens slowly and tastes good longer.
c-178.principle: Lactic fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 CH₃CH(OH)COOH (pH falls, sourness rises)
c-178.example: At 20°C pH drops to about 4.2 in 3-4 days and the kimchi turns sour, whereas at 4°C it changes slowly over weeks.
c-178.actionItem: Portion only what you will eat into a small tub and keep the rest in the coldest part of the fridge.

c-179.title: Sunscreen is oily, so washing with water alone does not remove it
c-179.summary: Sunscreen's UV filters and oils barely dissolve in water, so water alone leaves them behind. Dissolving them with a cleansing oil or balm and finishing with a foaming cleanser removes them well.
c-179.principle: Like dissolves like: similar polarity mixes. Nonpolar oils dissolve in nonpolar cleansers, while water needs surfactant micelles to carry them away.
c-179.example: Water-resistant sunscreens are designed to retain 80% or more after immersion in water. Massaging with cleansing oil for 30 seconds, adding water to emulsify and rinsing is effective.
c-179.actionItem: If you wore sunscreen today, use an oil cleanser first and then a foaming cleanser.

c-180.title: The white crust from a leaking battery is alkaline; wear gloves to clean it
c-180.summary: The white powder from an aged alkaline battery is potassium carbonate, formed when leaked potassium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide in air. It irritates skin and eyes, so wear gloves and wipe it with a swab dampened with vinegar or lemon juice.
c-180.principle: 2KOH + CO₂ → K₂CO₃ + H₂O forms the white crystals, and a weak acid like vinegar neutralizes it: K₂CO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → 2CH₃COOK + H₂O + CO₂.
c-180.example: Leaked electrolyte is strongly alkaline at pH 13-14 and irritates bare skin. Wipe with a vinegar-dampened swab and finish with a dry cloth. Taking batteries out of devices you rarely use is safer.
c-180.actionItem: Today, remove the batteries from any remote or toy you do not use for long periods.

c-181.title: Why ice cubes are cloudy
c-181.summary: Dissolved air and impurities get pushed to the middle as water freezes, trapped as a white core. Boiled and cooled water is clearer but not fully transparent.
c-181.principle: Gas solubility C = k_H P: it drops to almost zero in ice, so bubbles get trapped
c-181.example: Ice made from boiled-and-cooled water has fewer bubbles and is visibly clearer; freezing from one side (directional freezing) gives clear ice.
c-181.actionItem: Fill an ice tray with boiled and cooled water and freeze it for today's drinks.

c-182.title: Storing hydrogen peroxide
c-182.summary: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes into oxygen and water when exposed to light, heat or metals. Keep it cool in a brown bottle; old bottles lose strength.
c-182.example: 3% hydrogen peroxide can lose much of its strength about 6 months after opening, and decomposes faster above 30°C.
c-182.actionItem: Write the opening date on your hydrogen peroxide bottle and keep it somewhere dark and cool.

p-092.title: Cross-ventilation in 10 minutes
p-092.summary: Opening two windows on opposite sides refreshes room air far faster than opening just one.
p-092.principle: Airflow follows Bernoulli's equation p+12ρ v²=const and the flow rate Q=Av. With an inlet and an outlet, the breeze passes through and the ventilation rate rises.
p-092.example: In a 75m³ room, a 1m/s breeze through a 0.5m² opening gives Q=0.5 × 1=0.5m³/s (1,800m³/h). In practice that is 5-10 air changes per hour, so 10 minutes is enough, versus only 1-2 with a single window.
p-092.actionItem: Today, open two windows (or a door and a window) on opposite sides for 10 minutes.

p-093.title: Bike tyre pressure and rolling resistance
p-093.summary: A soft tyre makes the same ride noticeably harder at the same speed.
p-093.principle: Rolling resistance is F_rr=C_rr mg. Low pressure widens the contact patch, increases deformation losses, and raises C_rr.
p-093.example: For a combined 80kg, raising C_rr from 0.005 to 0.010 doubles F_rr from about 3.9N to 7.8N, and at 20km/h (5.6m/s) the power goes from about 22W to 44W.
p-093.actionItem: Before riding, inflate your tyres to the pressure range printed on the sidewall (psi/bar).

p-094.title: Dust masks work by static electricity
p-094.summary: A KF/N95-type mask traps fine dust with static charge, not just tiny holes, so water or alcohol weakens it.
p-094.principle: Filter fibres carry permanent charge and attract particles via the Coulomb force F=k(q₁q₂ / r²). Water, alcohol or sweat removes that charge.
p-094.example: A KF94 mask filters at least 94% of 0.4μm particles, but after an alcohol spray efficiency can fall below 80%. One mask is typically good for about a day of use (roughly 8 hours).
p-094.actionItem: Do not wash or spray your mask; swap in a fresh one today if it is damp or misshapen.

p-095.title: Drip coffee and water-stream fluid dynamics
p-095.summary: A thin, slow pour extracts evenly, giving a richer cup from the same beans.
p-095.principle: A narrow spout raises the speed v=Q/A and creates turbulence that stirs the grounds evenly. Extraction depends on contact time and temperature.
p-095.example: The standard is 15g of coffee with 250mL of water at 92-96°C, poured in stages over 2.5-3 minutes. Dumping it all in 30 seconds cuts contact time to a fifth, giving a weak, sour cup.
p-095.actionItem: Brew this morning's coffee in three slow pours with a thin stream.

p-096.title: Lower screen brightness, lower power
p-096.summary: An LCD's backlight power is roughly proportional to brightness, so dimming saves electricity and eye strain.
p-096.principle: Backlight power scales as P ≈ kB with brightness B, so total power is P=P₀+kB.
p-096.example: If a 40W monitor spends 25W on the backlight at 100%, dropping to 50% saves 12.5W, about 31%. Over 8 h a day that is 0.0125 × 8 × 30 ≈ 3kWh per month.
p-096.actionItem: Today, set your monitor or TV brightness near 50%, matched to the room light.

p-097.title: Induction cookware needs a flat base
p-097.summary: Induction heats by currents inside the pan itself, so a warped base wastes energy.
p-097.principle: A changing magnetic field drives eddy currents in the pan base, which heat it by Joule heating P=I²R. A larger gap between pan and hob weakens the coupling.
p-097.example: Induction is about 85-90% efficient versus roughly 40-50% for gas. If the base lifts 2mm or more, efficiency visibly drops and boiling takes several extra minutes.
p-097.actionItem: Today, set your pan on a flat surface and check it does not rock or lift at the edges.

p-098.title: Keep heavy books near the shelf bracket
p-098.summary: The same weight farther from the bracket gives the shelf a larger turning moment, so it sags or pulls out.
p-098.principle: The moment on the bracket is M=Fd, proportional to the distance d.
p-098.example: A 5kg stack (about 49N) 5cm from the bracket gives M ≈ 2.5N m, but 25cm away gives about 12N m, five times more.
p-098.actionItem: When tidying shelves today, put heavy items close to the wall or bracket and light ones farther out.

p-099.title: Do not leave the fridge door open
p-099.summary: Opening the door lets cold air spill out and warm air in, so the compressor has to work again.
p-099.principle: Air moves by density-driven convection and the heat gain is Q=mcΔT. The air in a 300L fridge weighs about 0.36kg.
p-099.example: Holding the door open for 30 seconds can lift the interior from 4°C toward 10°C, and recooling takes 10-20 minutes of compressor run time. Needless openings 20 times a day can add about 2-4% to monthly use.
p-099.actionItem: Today, decide what you need before opening the fridge and close it within 10 seconds.

p-100.title: Noise drops 6dB when distance doubles
p-100.summary: Simply moving away from a noise source cuts the level a lot, the easiest hearing protection there is.
p-100.principle: Point-source intensity follows I ∝ 1/r² and sound level is L=10₁₀(I/I₀). Doubling the distance gives ΔL=-20₁₀2 ≈ -6dB.
p-100.example: A speaker at 90dB at 1m reads 84dB at 2m and 78dB at 4m. Guidelines allow roughly 8 hours at 85dB and 2 hours at 91dB, so distance lengthens your safe listening time.
p-100.actionItem: Today, at a concert or construction site, stand twice as far from the speaker or noise source.

p-101.title: Double the speed, four times the braking distance
p-101.summary: Slowing down a little shortens stopping distance a lot and lowers crash risk.
p-101.principle: Braking distance comes from 12mv²=µ mg d, so d=(v² / 2µ g), proportional to speed squared.
p-101.example: On dry road (µ ≈ 0.7), 50km/h (13.9m/s) needs about 14m and 100km/h (27.8m/s) about 56m, four times more. On wet road (µ ≈ 0.4), 100km/h needs about 98m.
p-101.actionItem: On a rainy day, drive 20% under the limit today and keep twice the usual gap to the car ahead.

p-102.title: Weigh yourself on a hard, flat floor
p-102.summary: On soft carpet or a tilted floor the load is not shared evenly by the scale's sensors, so readings drift.
p-102.principle: A scale sums its four corner sensors, W= F_i. A tilted or soft floor changes how the load splits among them.
p-102.example: A 70kg person gives mg ≈ 686N, about 171N per sensor. If one foot sinks into a soft surface, one sensor carries more and adds error.
p-102.actionItem: Pick a hard, flat spot such as bathroom tile for the scale and weigh yourself in the same place every time.

p-103.title: Suction hooks stick only after the air is pushed out
p-103.summary: A bathroom suction hook is held by outside air pressure, not by glue.
p-103.principle: The holding force is F=ΔP · A. Once the air inside is pushed out, the pressure difference with the roughly 101kPa outside presses the cup on.
p-103.example: A 5cm cup has A=π(0.025)² ≈ 1.96 × 10⁻³ m², so the theoretical limit is 101,000 × 1.96 × 10⁻³ ≈ 198N. Real hooks hold much less because air leaks in.
p-103.actionItem: Wipe water and dust off the tile or glass, press firmly to expel air, and never exceed the rated load printed on the hook.

p-104.title: Switch off lights and use window daylight
p-104.summary: On a clear spring day, light near a window is several times brighter than room lamps, so daytime lights are often unnecessary.
p-104.principle: Illuminance is E=Φ/A (in lux). Near a window on a clear day it is usually above 1,000 lx, while 300-500 lx suffices for office or reading work.
p-104.example: Turning off three 8W LED bulbs (24W) for 6 hours a day saves 0.024 × 6 × 30 ≈ 4.3kWh per month.
p-104.actionItem: Today, open the curtains, move your desk or reading spot toward the window and turn the lights off.

p-105.title: Compare a fan's airflow (CMM), not just its noise
p-105.summary: Two fans of the same diameter can move very different amounts of air, set by blade area and air speed.
p-105.principle: Airflow is Q=Av (in m³/min), and a fan of diameter D has area A=π D²/4.
p-105.example: A 0.3m fan (A ≈ 0.071m²) blowing at 3m/s on average moves Q ≈ 0.21m³/s ≈ 12.8m³/min, mixing the air of a 30m³ room in about 2 min 20 s.
p-105.actionItem: When buying a fan or circulator, compare airflow (CMM), noise (dB) and power (W) on the spec sheet together.

p-106.title: A finer window screen blocks insects but also airflow
p-106.summary: A higher mesh count makes smaller holes that keep out tiny insects, but it also shrinks the open area for air.
p-106.principle: Hole size is about 25.4/N-d mm (N: wires per inch, d: wire diameter) and open area is = ≤ ft((p-d / p))² with p=25.4/N.
p-106.example: With a 0.25mm wire, an 18-mesh screen has holes of about 1.16mm and about 68% open area, while 24-mesh has about 0.81mm holes and about 58% open area.
p-106.actionItem: Before replacing a screen, decide which insect size you need to block and how much ventilation you need, then pick the mesh count.

p-107.title: Charging wastes some electricity as heat
p-107.summary: The wall socket supplies more energy than the phone battery stores. The difference is lost as heat in the charger and battery.
p-107.example: A 5,000 mAh, 3.85V battery holds about 19.3Wh. At 85% charging efficiency you draw 19.3/0.85 ≈ 22.7Wh, or about 6.8kWh over 300 charges a year.
p-107.actionItem: Today, charge with a certified quality adapter and do it somewhere ventilated rather than under a blanket.

p-108.title: The more you tilt your head, the more load your neck bears
p-108.summary: The farther your head leans forward, the greater the leverage and the harder your neck muscles must work.
p-108.principle: A head weight W placed a distance d in front of the neck pivot creates a moment M=Wd that muscles must resist.
p-108.example: A head weighs about 5 kgf, and one model estimates neck load of about 12 kgf at 15° forward tilt and about 27 kgf at 60°.
p-108.actionItem: Today, raise your laptop or phone to eye level and lift your head to stretch your neck every 30 minutes.

p-109.title: A four-legged table wobbles because only three legs touch
p-109.summary: Three points define a plane, so if the fourth leg is not in that plane one leg always floats and the table rocks.
p-109.principle: Equilibrium requires F=W and M=0. Three-point support is always stable, but four points touch together only if they are coplanar.
p-109.example: If one leg is 1mm short, that leg floats and the other three share the load. A sheet of folded paper is usually 0.1-0.2mm thick, so you need several layers.
p-109.actionItem: Slip folded paper or an adjustable pad under the rocking leg, then press on the table to confirm it no longer wobbles.

p-110.title: When the shower flow weakens
p-110.summary: Limescale narrows the shower holes, and the flow drops dramatically.
p-110.principle: Flow through a narrow pipe follows Poiseuille's law Q=(π r⁴ΔP / 8η L), proportional to the fourth power of radius.
p-110.example: If the hole radius shrinks 20%, flow falls to 0.8⁴ ≈ 0.41, a 59% loss. Soaking the head in about 1:1 diluted vinegar for 30 minutes dissolves the scale.
p-110.actionItem: Today, unscrew your shower head, soak it in diluted vinegar for 30 minutes, then rinse.

p-111.title: A tent's hydrostatic head in mm is a water column height
p-111.summary: The waterproof rating of a rainy-season camping tent is the height of water column (in mm) its fabric can hold back.
p-111.principle: Hydrostatic pressure is P=ρ g h. A 1,000mm water column is about 9.8kPa.
p-111.example: A 1,500mm rating means the fabric holds 1000 × 9.8 × 1.5=14.7kPa. Heavy rain and a floor loaded by people favour higher values.
p-111.actionItem: Before rainy-season camping, check the tent label's rating (1,500mm or more is commonly advised for the fly) and the seam sealing.

p-112.title: Check a fridge door seal with a sheet of paper
p-112.summary: A loose rubber gasket lets warm air in, so the compressor runs longer.
p-112.principle: Heat entering through a gap is Q= m c_pΔT. A larger gap area raises both airflow and heat gain.
p-112.example: With an average 1mm gap around a 3m door perimeter, the gap area is 0.001 × 3=3 × 10⁻³ m², or 30cm², like a palm-sized hole left open.
p-112.actionItem: Close the door on a sheet of paper and tug it. If it slides out easily anywhere, clean or replace the gasket.

p-113.title: Electricity used by appliances ends up as heat in the room
p-113.summary: Almost all electrical energy finally becomes heat, warming the room and adding to the cooling load.
p-113.principle: Energy conservation gives Q=Pt. An appliance's power P becomes room heat almost one-for-one.
p-113.example: A 100W computer used for 4 hours releases 0.1 × 4=0.4kWh, about 1.44MJ, into the room, just like a 100W small heater.
p-113.actionItem: Today, switch off computers, lights and chargers you aren't using to cut heat sources in the room.

p-114.title: Compare energy labels by yearly kWh
p-114.summary: Don't stop at the grade: the label's yearly (or monthly) kWh tells you the real electricity use.
p-114.principle: Energy use is E=Pt in kWh. The yearly difference multiplied by years of use gives the total difference.
p-114.example: A 300kWh/year fridge versus a 450kWh/year one differs by 150kWh a year, 1,500kWh over 10 years.
p-114.actionItem: When buying an appliance, compare the label's efficiency grade together with its yearly kWh.

p-115.title: Choose an air purifier by CADR and room volume
p-115.summary: In yellow-dust season the purifier must match the room. What matters is how many times per hour it cleans the air.
p-115.principle: Air changes per hour are ACH=CADR/V, where CADR is the volume of cleaned air in m³/h.
p-115.example: A purifier with CADR 300m³/h in a 25m² × 2.4m = 60m³ room gives 300/60=5 air changes per hour.
p-115.actionItem: Today, multiply your room's floor area by ceiling height and check whether your purifier's CADR is at least about 5 times that volume.

p-116.title: Windshield fog is about the dew point
p-116.summary: When the glass is colder than the dew point of cabin air, water vapour condenses into fog.
p-116.principle: Relative humidity RH and temperature set the dew point T_d, via the Magnus formula T_d ≈ (243.12 γ / 17.62-γ), γ=+(17.62 T / 243.12+T).
p-116.example: At 22°C and 70% RH the dew point is about 16.3°C. Glass at 10°C will fog, and running the A/C (dehumidifying) together with warm air dries the glass surface.
p-116.actionItem: When your windshield fogs, press the A/C button today and switch to fresh-air mode to dehumidify.

p-117.title: Cut thick material near the scissors' pivot
p-117.summary: Scissors are levers, so cutting close to the pivot gives more cutting force for the same hand force.
p-117.principle: Lever balance gives F_cut d_c=F_hand d_h. The closer the cut is to the pivot, the smaller d_c and the larger F_cut.
p-117.example: With d_h=10cm from hand to pivot, cutting 3cm from the pivot turns a 50N hand force into 50 × 10/3 ≈ 167N. At the tip (10cm) it stays 50N.
p-117.actionItem: Today, when cutting thick packaging or cardboard, feed it deep into the blades near the pivot.

p-118.title: Climbing stairs is a good workout even in power terms
p-118.summary: Walking up a floor lifts your body, so it demands a surprisingly large power in a short time.
p-118.principle: Climbing power is P=(mgh / t), the gain in potential energy mgh divided by the time taken.
p-118.example: A 70kg person climbing one floor (3m) in 15 s produces P=70 × 9.8 × 3/15 ≈ 137W. One floor stores about 2.1kJ, or roughly 2kcal of metabolic energy at 25% muscle efficiency.
p-118.actionItem: Today, take the stairs for two floors instead of the elevator and hold the handrail for safety.

p-119.title: A travel adapter is about voltage and current, not just plug shape
p-119.summary: A matching plug doesn't mean a device works. Different mains voltages change the current and the safety.
p-119.principle: Power is P=VI, so at the same power a lower voltage means a larger current I=P/V.
p-119.example: A 1,500W device draws I ≈ 6.8A at 220V but I ≈ 13.6A at 110V, which can easily exceed an adapter's rating.
p-119.actionItem: Before travelling, check the destination voltage, your device's rated input (for example 100-240V) and the adapter's current limit.

p-120.title: Bend your knees and widen your stance on a braking bus
p-120.summary: When a bus brakes hard, inertia throws you forward. Posture and foot friction keep you upright.
p-120.principle: Inertial force is F=ma, and your feet won't slip only if µ ≥ a/g.
p-120.example: At a deceleration of a=3m/s² (about 0.3g), a 60kg rider feels about 180N forward and needs µ ≥ 0.31 between shoes and floor.
p-120.actionItem: Today, if you stand on a bus or subway, spread your feet along the direction of travel and hold a handrail.

p-121.title: A sharp knife takes less force
p-121.summary: A keen edge has a tiny contact area, so the same push gives far higher pressure and the food parts easily.
p-121.principle: Pressure is P=(F / A). A smaller edge area A gives larger P for the same F.
p-121.example: A 1cm edge 0.02mm wide has A=2 × 10⁻⁶ m², so 20N gives P=10MPa. Dulled to 0.2mm it drops to 1MPa, a tenth, forcing harder pushes that raise the risk of slipping and cutting yourself.
p-121.actionItem: Today, test your knife on a sheet of paper, and if it fails to slice cleanly, hone or sharpen it.

p-122.title: Don't toggle an inverter air conditioner on and off
p-122.summary: An inverter AC modulates compressor speed to hold the set temperature, so leaving it running is more efficient.
p-122.principle: The cooling coefficient of performance COP=(Q_c / W) rises at part load, because the heat exchangers are relatively larger and the temperature difference shrinks.
p-122.example: If a fixed-speed unit averages 480W (0.8kW at 60% duty) and an inverter about 300W, six hours a day is 2.88 versus 1.8kWh, saving about 32kWh over 30 days.
p-122.actionItem: Today, set your AC to 26-28°C and leave it running instead of switching it on and off.

p-123.title: Give the AC outdoor unit some shade
p-123.summary: The cooler the air around the outdoor unit, the less the compressor works for the same cooling.
p-123.principle: Ideal cooling performance is the Carnot COP_max=(T_c / T_h-T_c), which grows as the condensing temperature T_h falls.
p-123.example: With evaporator T_c=280K, T_h=318K gives 7.4 and 308K gives 10, about 35% higher. In real units, a 3-5°C cooler intake saves roughly 5-10% power.
p-123.actionItem: Today, put a shade above the outdoor unit, but never block airflow within 30cm in front or behind it.

p-124.title: Use a fan together with the air conditioner
p-124.summary: Moving air makes it feel 2-3°C cooler, so you can raise the AC setpoint.
p-124.principle: Convective heat loss from skin is Q=hA(T_s-T_a), and the heat-transfer coefficient h rises with air speed.
p-124.example: At skin 33°C, room 28°C and 1.8m², still air h ≈ 5 loses 45W, while a 1m/s breeze h ≈ 10 loses about 90W, so you feel cooler. Each 1°C higher setpoint cuts power roughly 5-10%.
p-124.actionItem: Today, raise your AC to 28°C and run a fan on low alongside it.

p-125.title: Chill a can fast with a wet paper towel
p-125.summary: Evaporating water takes heat with it, so a wet towel plus a breeze drops a drink's temperature by several degrees.
p-125.principle: Evaporation needs Q=mL_v of heat, with L_v ≈ 2.4kJ/g for water, and that heat comes from the drink.
p-125.example: Evaporating 10g of water absorbs about 24kJ, which would cool a 355mL drink by ΔT=24/(0.355 × 4.0) ≈ 17K ideally. In practice it is about 5-8°C in 10 minutes in a breeze.
p-125.actionItem: Today, wrap a lukewarm can in a wet paper towel and set it in front of a fan for 10 minutes.

p-126.title: Shading works best outside the glass
p-126.summary: Once sunlight passes through the glass, the heat is already inside, so exterior shades work far better.
p-126.principle: Solar heat entering a window is Q=SHGC × A × I. Shading lowers the effective SHGC.
p-126.example: For a 2m² window at 600W/m² solar, clear glass (SHGC 0.8) lets in 960W, an interior blind (0.5) 600W, and an exterior shade (0.15) about 180W, roughly 80% less.
p-126.actionItem: Today, look up exterior shading you can install, such as an awning, bamboo shade or roller screen.

p-127.title: A parked car heats up in minutes
p-127.summary: A car in the sun traps heat like a greenhouse, making even a short stay dangerous for children and pets.
p-127.principle: Glass passes shortwave sunlight and traps the longwave infrared that the warmed interior emits. Absorbed heat Q=α IA outweighs convective and conductive loss.
p-127.example: At 30°C outside, the cabin can reach about 50°C in 30 minutes and the dashboard over 70°C. Cracking a window barely reduces the rise.
p-127.actionItem: Today, check the back seat every time you leave your car, and never leave a child or pet inside.

p-128.title: Set your bike saddle so your knee stays slightly bent
p-128.summary: A saddle that is too low strains the knees, and one that is too high rocks the pelvis and can hurt the back and knees.
p-128.principle: A common rule of thumb is saddle height ≈ 0.883 × inseam. At the bottom of the pedal stroke the knee is bent 25-35°.
p-128.example: With an 80cm inseam, saddle height is 0.883 × 80 ≈ 70.6cm, measured from the pedal axis to the top of the saddle.
p-128.actionItem: Before riding today, measure the saddle height and check that your knee nearly straightens with your heel on the pedal at the bottom.

p-129.title: Lowering shower temperature by 2-4°C saves energy
p-129.summary: Even with the same hot-water volume, heating water to a higher temperature takes proportionally more energy.
p-129.principle: Heat to warm water is Q=mcΔT, with water's specific heat c=4.18kJ/(kg K).
p-129.example: Heating 40L from 15°C to 42°C takes 40 × 4.18 × 27 ≈ 4,514kJ (1.25kWh); to 38°C about 3,846kJ (1.07kWh). That is 0.19kWh per shower, about 68kWh a year.
p-129.actionItem: Today, try lowering your shower temperature by 2-4°C, or if you feel cold, shorten the shower first.

p-130.title: Slow down 10km/h on the highway
p-130.summary: Air drag grows with speed squared, so a small slowdown saves noticeable fuel.
p-130.principle: Drag force is F_d=12C_dρ A v² and drag power is P=12C_dρ A v³.
p-130.example: With C_dA=0.7m², 110km/h (30.6m/s) takes about 12.0kW and 100km/h about 9.0kW, 25% less. Energy per distance falls by (100/110)² ≈ 0.83, 17% less, and 100km takes only about 5 minutes longer.
p-130.actionItem: Today, drop 10km/h on the highway and cruise steadily, staying within the speed limit.

p-131.title: Check a life jacket's weight range and buoyancy (N)
p-131.summary: A swim ring is not a life jacket. A life jacket gives enough buoyancy to keep your face above water.
p-131.principle: Buoyancy is F_b=ρ V g. Displacing 1L of water gives about 9.8N.
p-131.example: A 50N-class jacket equals the buoyancy of about 5L of water (about 5.1 kgf). Children and adults need different amounts, so the weight range on the label must match.
p-131.actionItem: Before water play, check the weight range and certification mark on the jacket's label and fasten the straps firmly after putting it on.

p-132.title: Cycling behind another rider takes less effort
p-132.summary: A rider in front blocks the wind, so the slipstream lets you hold the same speed with far less power.
p-132.principle: Drag power is P=12C_dρ A v³. Riding behind lowers the effective C_d.
p-132.example: On the flat at 30km/h (8.3m/s) with C_dA=0.35m², P ≈ 0.5 × 0.35 × 1.2 × 8.3³ ≈ 120W; right behind another rider it drops 30-40% to about 75-85W.
p-132.actionItem: On a group ride today, keep a gap of 1-2m behind the rider ahead and never overlap their rear wheel.

p-133.title: Check certification and heat on fast chargers
p-133.summary: Higher charging power means more heat, so a certified charger and ventilation decide safety and battery life.
p-133.principle: Power is P=VI and conversion loss is P_loss=(1-η)P. At efficiency η=0.88, a 20W charger turns about 2.4W into heat.
p-133.example: A 5W charger sheds about 0.6W of heat, a 65W one about 7.8W. If heat cannot escape, such as under a duvet, the battery passes 35°C, charges slower, and ages faster.
p-133.actionItem: Today, check your charger for a safety certification mark and the right wattage for your device, and avoid charging under bedding.

p-134.title: If you'll idle more than 10 seconds, switch the engine off
p-134.summary: An idling engine keeps burning fuel without moving the car, and the waste grows with time.
p-134.principle: Fuel use is V_f= V_f t, and a car's idle fuel rate V_f is typically around 0.6-1L/h.
p-134.example: At V_f=0.8L/h, 5 minutes (300 s) of idling uses 0.8/3600 × 300 ≈ 0.067L; once a day for a year that is about 24L.
p-134.actionItem: When waiting in a car park or for someone, switch the engine off (cars with automatic stop-start can keep using it at lights).

p-135.title: A narrow heel can multiply pressure for the same body weight
p-135.summary: When weight is concentrated at one point, pressure rises and strains both your foot and the floor.
p-135.principle: Pressure is P=F/A. For the same force, a smaller contact area A means a higher pressure.
p-135.example: When 60 kgf (about 588N) rests on one foot, a heel with 1cm² contact gives about 5.9MPa, while a wide heel with 20cm² gives about 0.29MPa, a 20-fold difference.
p-135.actionItem: On a long walking day today, wear shoes with a wide contact area to ease strain on your feet and knees.

p-136.title: Floor-impact noise needs mass and absorption
p-136.summary: Heavy, thick materials block sound best, and mats or pads soften impacts.
p-136.principle: By the mass law, transmission loss is TL ≈ 20₁₀(mf)-47dB (m in kg/m², f in Hz), and doubling mass adds about 6dB.
p-136.example: A 10dB reduction sounds about half as loud. Felt pads under chair legs can cut scraping noise by roughly 5-10dB, and thick mats soften the thud of footsteps.
p-136.actionItem: Today, stick felt pads on your chair legs and lay a thick mat where you walk most.

p-137.title: Trekking poles ease your knees on descents
p-137.summary: Poles share part of the load with your arms and reduce knee stress downhill.
p-137.principle: On descents the knee takes roughly 3 times body weight in shock absorption, and when poles carry a support force F_s the knee force falls to F_k=3mg-F_s.
p-137.example: For 70kg, body weight is 686N and knee force about 2,060N. If poles take about 20%, that cuts roughly 410N.
p-137.actionItem: On today's hike, set your poles so your elbow is at 90 degrees and lengthen them for the descent.

p-138.title: Thaw frozen food in the fridge to reuse its cold
p-138.summary: Melting ice absorbs heat, so thawing in the fridge puts that cold to work cooling the compartment.
p-138.principle: Melting ice needs Q=mL_f, with L_f ≈ 334kJ/kg.
p-138.example: If 1kg of frozen meat is about 70% ice-forming water, thawing absorbs 0.7 × 334 ≈ 234kJ (about 0.065kWh), which the fridge no longer has to remove itself.
p-138.actionItem: Tonight, move tomorrow's ingredients from the freezer to the fridge the night before, and avoid thawing at room temperature for hygiene.

p-139.title: A tight clothesline loads its hooks far more
p-139.summary: Pulling a washing line taut reduces the sag, but the tension in the line and its anchors rises sharply.
p-139.principle: With weight W at the middle of a horizontal line making angle θ with the horizontal, tension is T=(W / 2θ).
p-139.example: For a 5kg load (about 49N), a sag angle of 30° gives T=49N, but 5° gives T ≈ 281N (about 29 kgf), roughly 6 times more.
p-139.actionItem: When you hang a line or rack today, don't pull it dead tight; leave a sag of about 5-10% of its length.

p-140.title: Judge heat by the heat index
p-140.summary: At the same air temperature, high humidity stops sweat from drying and feels far hotter and riskier.
p-140.principle: The heat index is a function of temperature and relative humidity, HI = f(T, RH); less evaporative cooling means a higher apparent temperature.
p-140.example: At 32°C and 40% humidity it feels like about 32°C, but at 70% humidity it feels like about 41°C, a heat-illness caution range.
p-140.actionItem: Before going out in the rainy season, check humidity as well as temperature and adjust your outdoor time.

p-141.title: The pitch of an ambulance siren tells you whether it's approaching
p-141.summary: A siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it recedes. That is the Doppler effect.
p-141.principle: For a source moving at v_s, the heard frequency is f'=f (v / v v_s) (- approaching, + receding).
p-141.example: A 1,000Hz siren on a vehicle moving at 20m/s sounds like 1000 × 343/323 ≈ 1,062Hz while approaching and 1000 × 343/363 ≈ 945Hz while receding.
p-141.actionItem: When a siren grows louder and higher today, check your surroundings and make way.

p-142.title: Choosing AC capacity by room size
p-142.summary: A bigger air conditioner is not better; efficiency is best when capacity matches the room's cooling load.
p-142.principle: Cooling load is Q ≈ q₀ A (about 150-200W/m²). An oversized unit cycles on and off more often.
p-142.example: A 15m² room needs roughly 2.3-3.0kW (about 8,000-10,000 BTU/h). Heavy oversizing causes short-cycling and lower efficiency.
p-142.actionItem: Before buying, note your room area, west-facing windows and floor level, then compare capacity with the seller.

p-143.title: Raising the AC setpoint by 1-2°C cuts the cooling load
p-143.summary: The smaller the inside-outside difference, the less heat enters through walls and windows, so the AC works less.
p-143.principle: Conducted heat is Q=UA ΔT, proportional to the temperature difference ΔT.
p-143.example: With 33°C outside, raising the room setting from 24°C to 26°C shrinks ΔT from 9K to 7K, reducing conducted heat gain by about 22%.
p-143.actionItem: Today, set your AC to 26°C and add a fan on low.

p-144.title: A flame wider than the pot bottom wastes gas
p-144.summary: A flame wider than the pot licks around the sides and heats only air. Keeping it under the base sends more heat into the pot.
p-144.principle: Heat delivered to the pot is Q=η E_fuel. The higher the efficiency η, the less fuel for the same heating.
p-144.example: Heating 1L of water from 20°C to 100°C takes 334kJ, so η=40% needs 835kJ of fuel while 50% needs 668kJ. With these assumed values you save 20%.
p-144.actionItem: When cooking today, turn the flame down until it stays under the edge of the pot base.

p-145.title: Umbrella water repellency and contact angle
p-145.summary: An umbrella sheds water because its surface has a high contact angle, and the coating can be restored.
p-145.principle: Young's equation: θ = γ_sv - γₛₗγ_lv. A contact angle θ > 90^° means hydrophobic.
p-145.example: A repellent umbrella fabric has a contact angle of about 110-120°, so droplets bead and roll off. Once wear drops it below about 70°, the fabric starts to wet.
p-145.actionItem: Dry your wet umbrella open in the shade, and apply a water-repellent spray if drops start soaking in.

p-146.title: Gauge lightning distance by thunder delay
p-146.summary: Count the seconds between a flash and its thunder to tell how close the lightning is.
p-146.principle: Sound travels at v ≈ 343m/s while light arrives almost instantly, so distance d = vt.
p-146.example: If thunder follows 9 seconds after the flash, d ≈ 343 × 9 ≈ 3.1km. Within about 10 s (3.4km) you are already in the strike zone.
p-146.actionItem: When you hear thunder in the rainy season, stop outdoor activity and move into a building or car.

p-147.title: Brake a bike with both brakes, favouring the front
p-147.summary: When you brake, weight shifts to the front wheel, which can then deliver more braking force.
p-147.principle: The load transferred to the front wheel is ΔN=(m a h / L) (h: centre-of-mass height, L: wheelbase).
p-147.example: With m=80kg, h=1.0m, L=1.0m and deceleration a=4m/s², ΔN=320N. The static loads of 314N front and 470N rear become 634N front and 150N rear.
p-147.actionItem: When riding today, squeeze both brakes smoothly rather than only the rear. Grabbing only the front hard can throw you over.

p-148.title: Check distance and emissivity on a non-contact thermometer
p-148.summary: An infrared thermometer reads temperature from emitted radiation, so surface condition and distance change the result.
p-148.principle: Radiated power is P=εσ T⁴. A shiny surface with low emissivity ε reads lower than the true value.
p-148.example: Skin has ε ≈ 0.98 and reads well, while shiny metal at 0.1-0.3 gives large errors. With a 12:1 distance ratio, at 1.2m the device averages a 10cm diameter spot.
p-148.actionItem: When buying one, check the intended distance and measuring site, and follow the distance in the manual (usually a few cm) when using it.

p-149.title: A small toaster oven uses less heat for small portions
p-149.summary: A large oven must heat much air and metal, so for one or two servings a small oven needs far less heat.
p-149.principle: Heat needed is Q= m c ΔT. The less mass to heat, the less energy.
p-149.example: Raising 5kg of trays and interior metal (c ≈ 0.45kJ/(kg K)) by 180K takes about 405kJ, but 1kg takes about 81kJ. Heating 60L of air adds only about 13kJ.
p-149.actionItem: Today, if you're baking only a small amount, use a toaster oven or air fryer instead of the big oven.

p-150.title: Turn off the heat a bit early and finish with residual heat
p-150.summary: Water and food in the pot store heat, so with the lid on, cooking continues without the flame.
p-150.principle: Stored heat is Q=mcΔT, and with a lid heat loss is small so the temperature falls slowly.
p-150.example: Turning off a 3kW burner 2 minutes early saves 3 × 120=360kJ of fuel heat. 1.5L of water in a lidded pot stays above 90°C for several minutes.
p-150.actionItem: Today, when cooking noodles, soup or steamed dishes, switch off 1-2 minutes early and keep the lid on to finish with residual heat.

p-151.title: Coil earphone cords in a figure eight to avoid tangles
p-151.summary: Winding a cord in one direction stores twist that tangles when released. A figure eight cancels the twist.
p-151.principle: Each full turn adds a twist angle θ=2π, and the torsional moment is τ=(GJ / L)θ.
p-151.example: Winding 1m of cord ten times in one direction stores 10 twists, but 5 turns one way and 5 the other (a figure eight) sum to 0 and leave almost no kink.
p-151.actionItem: Today, when tidying earphones or charging cables, fold them in a figure eight rather than wrapping them round your fingers.

p-152.title: Water stays in your ear because of surface tension
p-152.summary: A water drop in the narrow ear canal is trapped by the pressure that surface tension creates.
p-152.principle: The Laplace pressure is ΔP=(2γ / r), with γ ≈ 0.072N/m for water. The smaller the radius r, the larger the pressure.
p-152.example: For r=3mm, ΔP=2 × 0.072/0.003=48Pa, so gravity alone can hardly pull the drop out.
p-152.actionItem: After swimming, tilt your head, gently pull the earlobe and hop on one foot. Don't use cotton swabs, and see a doctor for pain or discharge.

p-153.title: Drive tent pegs in at an angle away from the line
p-153.summary: A peg that sits nearly perpendicular to the guy line lets the soil resist pull-out best.
p-153.principle: Line tension T splits into horizontal Tθ and vertical Tθ, and the vertical part lifts the peg.
p-153.example: With T=100N and a 45° line, you get 71N horizontal and 71N lifting. Driving the peg about 45-60° leaning away from the line lets the soil hold it.
p-153.actionItem: Today, when camping or picnicking, drive pegs in at a slant nearly perpendicular to the line and tension the line at about 45°.

p-154.title: Pick a cooler by wall thickness, lid seal and ice quantity
p-154.summary: How long a cooler stays cold depends on insulation thickness and how much ice it holds.
p-154.principle: Heat entering through the walls is Q=(kAΔT / d), and melting ice absorbs Q=mL_f with L_f ≈ 334kJ/kg.
p-154.example: At 10W of heat gain, 2kg of ice (668kJ) lasts 668,000/10 ≈ 18.6 hours; at 20W, about 9.3 hours.
p-154.actionItem: If you have an outing today, pack 2kg or more of ice and pre-chilled drinks with no gaps, and open the lid as little as possible.

p-155.title: Part of the AC's power in rainy season goes to condensing moisture
p-155.summary: On humid days an AC must not only cool the air but also turn water vapour into liquid.
p-155.principle: When vapour condenses, Q=mL_v of heat is released, with L_v ≈ 2,260kJ/kg for water.
p-155.example: In a 60m³ room (about 72kg of air), removing 2g of vapour per kg of air means handling 0.144 × 2,260 ≈ 325kJ (about 0.09kWh).
p-155.actionItem: On humid days today, use the AC's dry mode or 26-28°C on low fan and keep doors and windows closed so moisture stays out.

p-156.title: An electric kettle beats a gas hob for boiling water
p-156.summary: Because little heat escapes, an electric kettle uses less energy than a gas hob to boil the same water.
p-156.principle: Efficiency η = mcΔTE_in. Heating 1L of water from 20°C to 100°C needs 1 × 4.18 × 80 = 334kJ (≈ 0.093kWh).
p-156.example: A kettle at about 90% efficiency uses about 0.103kWh, while a gas burner at about 40% uses about 0.23kWh of energy.
p-156.actionItem: Measure only the water you need and boil it in an electric kettle.

p-157.title: Calculate the time to heat a single cup
p-157.summary: Guessing microwave time tends to run it too long and waste energy.
p-157.principle: Heating needs Q=mcΔT, and the time is t=Q/Pₒᵤₜₚᵤₜ.
p-157.example: Heating 250g of water from 20°C to 90°C needs 0.25 × 4.18 × 70 ≈ 73kJ, which at 700W output takes about 104 s (1 min 44 s).
p-157.actionItem: Today, start a drink at about 1 min 30 s and add 20 s at a time if needed.

p-158.title: When rain falls straight down, running keeps you drier
p-158.summary: Running in rain shortens the time rain hits your head and shoulders, but the rain on your front depends on distance.
p-158.principle: In vertical rain, the amount on the top surfaces is Wₜₒₚ ∝ t=L/v, inversely proportional to speed, while the front surface wetting depends only on distance L.
p-158.example: Covering 100m takes about 71 s walking (1.4m/s) but about 29 s running (3.5m/s), cutting the time top surfaces get wet by 59%. Wind changes the result.
p-158.actionItem: If it rains today, move briskly over short uncovered stretches only as far as is safe, and watch for slippery ground.

p-159.title: The 20-20-20 rule: look 6m away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes
p-159.summary: The longer you look at a near screen, the longer your eye's lens stays thickened and the more fatigue builds up.
p-159.principle: In the lens equation 1f=1d_o+1d_i, the closer the object, the greater the focusing power (dioptres) D=1/d_o needed.
p-159.example: A screen at 40cm needs about 2.5 D of accommodation, while an object at 6m needs only about 0.17 D, nearly 15 times less effort.
p-159.actionItem: Today, set a 20-minute timer and each time it rings, look at something at least 6m away for 20 seconds.

p-160.title: If caught in a rip current, swim parallel to the shore
p-160.summary: A rip current is a narrow, fast channel of water flowing out to sea, and swimming against it just exhausts you.
p-160.principle: By the continuity equation A₁v₁=A₂v₂, water squeezed through a narrow channel speeds up.
p-160.example: Rip currents can reach about 2m/s, faster than a person's swimming speed of about 1m/s, but they are usually only tens of metres wide, so moving 20-30m sideways gets you out.
p-160.actionItem: If you plan to swim at the sea today, stay where lifeguards are on duty. If caught, save your energy, swim parallel to the shore and wave for rescue.

p-161.title: Choose a parasol that is light outside and dark inside
p-161.summary: A white outer surface reflects sunlight while a dark inner surface absorbs light reflected from the ground.
p-161.principle: Radiation absorbed by a surface is q=(1-α)I, where α is reflectance.
p-161.example: At a noon irradiance of 800W/m², a white surface with α=0.7 absorbs 240W/m² while a black one with α=0.05 absorbs 760W/m² (assumed values).
p-161.actionItem: When buying a parasol, check the outer colour and a UV-protection label such as UPF 50+.

p-162.title: Why bigger fans are more efficient
p-162.summary: For the same airflow, a large-bladed fan at low speed uses far less energy.
p-162.principle: Air kinetic power P = (1 / 2)ρ A v³ = (ρ Q³ / 2A²) (Q = Av is the airflow).
p-162.example: At 0.5m³/s, a 30cm fan needs about 15W of ideal air power versus about 1W for a 60cm fan. Four times the area means 1/16 the power.
p-162.actionItem: When buying a fan, compare blade diameters and run a larger one on low.

p-163.title: A bike uses far less energy than a car for 5km
p-163.summary: Replacing a short car trip with a bike ride greatly cuts fuel and energy use.
p-163.principle: Work is W=Pt and then divided by efficiency. A litre of petrol holds about 9kWh of chemical energy.
p-163.example: A 5km ride (15km/h, 100W, 20 min) is 33Wh, or about 0.13kWh counting 25% muscle efficiency. A 12km/L car uses about 3.7kWh for 5km, a 28-fold difference.
p-163.actionItem: Today, walk or cycle for a trip under 5km.

p-164.title: Water a pot from below and capillary action does the rest
p-164.summary: Narrow gaps between soil grains pull water upward, so filling the saucer delivers water to the roots.
p-164.principle: Capillary rise is h=(2γθ / ρ g r). The smaller the pore radius r, the higher the rise.
p-164.actionItem: Today, pour water into a plant's saucer, wait 20 minutes and empty what's left. Standing water causes root rot and breeds mosquitoes.

p-165.title: Measure blood pressure with your arm at heart level
p-165.summary: If your arm hangs below the heart, the weight of blood (hydrostatic pressure) adds to the reading and makes it too high.
p-165.principle: The hydrostatic difference is ΔP=ρ g h. Blood density is about 1,060kg/m³ and 1kPa is about 7.5mmHg.
p-165.example: An arm 20cm below the heart adds ΔP=1060 × 9.8 × 0.2 ≈ 2.08kPa, about 15.6mmHg, to the reading.
p-165.actionItem: When measuring blood pressure, sit back in a chair and rest the cuffed arm on a desk so it is level with your heart.

p-166.title: Loose luggage becomes a projectile in a hard stop
p-166.summary: An unsecured item keeps moving forward by inertia when the car stops, turning into a large impact force.
p-166.principle: The force on luggage during deceleration is F=ma with a=v/Δt.
p-166.example: A 10kg bag at 50km/h (13.9m/s) stopped in 0.1 s has a ≈ 139m/s² and F ≈ 1,390N (about 140 kgf).
p-166.actionItem: Today, load luggage on the boot floor and secure it, and never leave heavy items on the rear shelf or seat.

p-167.title: An IPX rating describes the test conditions for water
p-167.summary: IPX4 means splash-proof and IPX7 means survives 30 minutes at 1m depth; a bigger digit is not always better for every use.
p-167.principle: Water pressure is P=ρ g h. At 1m depth it is about 9.8kPa.
p-167.example: IPX4 is tested against splashes from all directions and IPX7 against up to 30 minutes at 1m depth, and many makers do not cover seawater, soapy or hot water.
p-167.actionItem: Today, check the IPX rating of your earbuds or speaker, and if you use them in rain, make sure it is at least IPX4.

p-168.title: Dehumidifiers: compressor versus Peltier
p-168.summary: Use a compressor model for big rooms and a Peltier model only for small spaces such as closets.
p-168.principle: Coefficient of performance COP = (Q_c / W): about 3 for compressor units and about 0.5 for Peltier units.
p-168.example: Condensing 1kg of water takes about 2.26MJ (0.63kWh). A compressor unit uses about 0.2kWh and a Peltier unit about 1.3kWh.
p-168.actionItem: In the rainy season, match dehumidifier capacity to your room and use a compressor model for the living room.

p-169.title: Ventilate when the night air is cooler to flush out heat
p-169.summary: Heat built up during the day can be flushed out at night by opening windows when the outside air is cooler, at no energy cost.
p-169.principle: Heat removed by ventilation is Q= m c_pΔT.
p-169.example: With 28°C inside and 22°C outside, ventilating at 600m³/h (about 0.2kg/s of air) removes 0.2 × 1.005 × 6 ≈ 1.2kW of heat.
p-169.actionItem: If tonight turns cooler than your room, open windows for a cross draught and close them early in the morning.

p-170.title: A gurgling drain comes from air-pressure changes in the pipe
p-170.summary: When water drops down all at once, pressure in the pipe changes and sucks air through the trap, making that gurgle.
p-170.principle: A water column exerts P=ρ g h, so a suction ΔP pulls water by h=ΔP/(ρ g).
p-170.example: A suction of 100Pa corresponds to a water column of 100/(1000 × 9.8) ≈ 10mm. A trap seal 50mm or deeper usually holds.
p-170.actionItem: If a drain gurgles today, run water more slowly, and if it repeats, ask your building manager or a plumber to check.

p-171.title: A fan keeps mosquitoes away
p-171.summary: Mosquitoes are slow fliers, so they struggle to approach where a fan blows.
p-171.principle: Mosquito flight speed is about 1.5m/s or less, so when v_wind > v_mosq approach is hard, and wind also disperses the CO₂ plume.
p-171.example: A fan giving 3m/s is twice a mosquito's top speed. Aiming the breeze at your legs reduces bites.
p-171.actionItem: On a balcony or outdoors, point a fan at leg height.

p-172.title: Brace for crosswind when passing big vehicles or crossing bridges
p-172.summary: A sudden gust beside a truck or on a bridge can push your car sideways.
p-172.principle: Wind force on a car is F=12ρ C A v², proportional to the square of wind speed v.
p-172.example: With wind at 20m/s (72km/h), a side area of 2.5m² and C ≈ 0.8, F ≈ 0.5 × 1.2 × 0.8 × 2.5 × 400 ≈ 480N.
p-172.actionItem: If strong wind or rain is forecast today, hold the wheel with both hands and slow down at bridges and tunnel exits.

p-173.title: Choose cooling fabrics by contact-cooling value (Q-max)
p-173.summary: A cooling fabric feels cool because it draws heat from skin quickly at first touch, and Q-max measures that.
p-173.principle: Initial heat flux is q ∝ b ΔT√(t), and the larger the thermal effusivity b=√(kρ c), the cooler it feels.
p-173.example: At the same ΔT=5K, a fabric with Q-max 0.25W/cm² draws heat about 1.7 times faster than one with 0.15 (an illustration).
p-173.actionItem: When choosing summer clothes or bedding, check the label's Q-max (often 0.2 or above is labelled as cooling).

p-174.title: Work out an e-bike's range from battery Wh and consumption
p-174.summary: Dividing battery capacity (Wh) by energy per km (Wh/km) gives an estimate of range.
p-174.principle: Range is d=E/e, and since air drag scales as F ∝ v², higher speed raises e.
p-174.example: A 500Wh battery at 15Wh/km gives about 33km. Riding at 25km/h has (25/20)² ≈ 1.56 times the drag of 20km/h, so range shrinks.
p-174.actionItem: Today, hold your e-bike speed near 20km/h and check tyre pressure.

p-175.title: 100kg of unused cargo burns extra fuel over 100km
p-175.summary: A heavier car needs more energy for rolling resistance and acceleration, so carrying unused cargo wastes fuel.
p-175.principle: Rolling resistance is F_r=Cᵣᵣmg and the work is W=F_r d.
p-175.example: With Cᵣᵣ=0.01 and m=100kg, F_r ≈ 9.8N and W ≈ 0.27kWh over 100km. At 25% engine efficiency and 9kWh/L petrol that is about 0.12L, not counting acceleration energy.
p-175.actionItem: Today, take any unused items out of your boot.

p-176.title: Why wet bathroom floors are slippery
p-176.summary: A water film sharply lowers friction, so put an anti-slip mat in the bathroom.
p-176.principle: Static friction limit F ≤ µ N; you slip when µ is below what walking demands (about 0.3-0.4).
p-176.example: Dry tile has µ ≈ 0.6, wet smooth tile about 0.2, and a rubber mat about 0.6 even when wet.
p-176.actionItem: Lay an anti-slip mat on the bathroom floor and in the shower area.

p-177.title: UV passes through clouds
p-177.summary: Clouds dim visible light but let much UV through, so protect yourself even on overcast days.
p-177.principle: UV index UVI = 40 E_λ s(λ) dλ (erythemal action spectrum s). Thin cloud barely reduces UV.
p-177.example: Thin cloud transmits about 80-90% of UV. At a midday UV index of 8 in June, fair skin can burn in about 20 minutes.
p-177.actionItem: Check the UV index before going out, even on cloudy days, and apply sunscreen.

p-178.title: After driving through puddles, lightly dab the brakes to dry them
p-178.summary: Wet pads and discs lose friction, so braking is slower. A light press heats them and evaporates the water.
p-178.principle: Braking distance is d=(v² / 2µ g), and reduced brake friction makes d larger.
p-178.example: At 60km/h (16.7m/s), µ=0.4 gives about 35.5m, but if wetness cuts it to µ=0.25 it becomes about 56.7m, about 1.6 times longer (assumed values).
p-178.actionItem: Today, after crossing a deep puddle in rainy weather, gently press the brakes a few times when it is safe to check them.

p-179.title: Choose pots by base thickness and material
p-179.summary: A thick base with an aluminium or copper layer spreads heat evenly and reduces scorching.
p-179.principle: Fourier's law q = k(ΔT / d): stainless steel k ≈ 16, aluminium ≈ 237W/(m·K).
p-179.example: For a 3mm base and ΔT = 10K, stainless carries about 53kW/m² and aluminium about 790kW/m², roughly 15 times more heat.
p-179.actionItem: When buying a pot, check that its base is flat and thick, and magnetic if you use induction.

p-180.title: Warm a water tank in sunshine to cut hot-water use
p-180.summary: Sunlight delivers up to about 1kW per square metre, so water in a black container can be heated free of charge.
p-180.principle: Absorbed heat is Q=α I A t, and the temperature rise is ΔT=Q/(mc).
p-180.example: For a black 20L container (0.25m²) with I=700W/m² and absorptivity 0.9, about 0.9 × 700 × 0.25 ≈ 158W flows in. In 2 hours that is about 1.1MJ, warming the water by roughly 13°C.
p-180.actionItem: On a sunny day today, leave water in a black container or hose in the sun for 2-3 hours and use it for plants or washing the car.

p-181.title: Squeaky door: stick-slip friction
p-181.summary: A hinge squeaks because static friction exceeds kinetic friction, so it jerks as it slides.
p-181.principle: Stick-slip: F_s = µ_s N > F_k = µ_k N; lubrication lowers both µ values.
p-181.example: Dry metal with µ ≈ 0.5 drops to about 0.1 after lubrication, cutting friction about 80% and silencing the noise.
p-181.actionItem: Put one drop of silicone lubricant or oil on the hinge pin and wipe off the excess.

p-182.title: Noise adds up: two fans
p-182.summary: Two equal noise sources add only 3dB, not double the loudness, and quiet nights matter for sleep.
p-182.example: Two 40dB fans give 10₁₀(2 × 10⁴) ≈ 43dB. The WHO recommends bedroom night noise of about 30dB or less.
p-182.actionItem: Compare dB ratings on bedroom appliances and run only the quietest one while you sleep.

c-183.title: Drinking Only Plain Water After Heavy Sweating Can Dilute Blood Sodium
c-183.summary: After sweating for hours, gulping large amounts of plain water can dilute blood sodium and cause headache or nausea. Pair fluids with something salty.
c-183.principle: Sweat removes Na⁺ along with water. Refilling with plain water only enlarges the denominator in C_Na=n_NaV, so concentration falls and water moves into cells by osmosis. The normal range is about 135-145 mmol/L.
c-183.example: On a 3-hour summer hike you may lose about 2L of sweat, roughly 2g of sodium (about 5g of salt). Drinking 3L of plain water at once on top of that can push blood Na⁺ below 135 mmol/L.
c-183.actionItem: During long exercise or walks today, bring a salty snack (nuts, crackers) or a diluted sports drink with your water, and avoid drinking more than 500mL in one go.

c-184.title: Bleach Mixed in Hot Water Just Loses Its Disinfecting Power
c-184.summary: Mixing bleach into hot water breaks down the active ingredient quickly and mostly adds a harsh chlorine smell. Dilute it in cold or lukewarm water and use it right away.
c-184.principle: The active species HOCl from sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) is heat-sensitive and decomposes as 2HOCl → 2HCl+O₂. Each roughly 10°C rise typically speeds decomposition by 2x or more.
c-184.example: A small dose of household bleach (about 4-5% NaOCl) in 500mL of water stays effective for hours at 20°C, but in 60°C water a large share is gone within minutes and more irritating fumes escape.
c-184.actionItem: When disinfecting today, dilute bleach in cold water, use it right away, ventilate the room, and never mix it with acidic cleaners.

c-185.title: Heat Seaside Oysters and Clams to 85°C for 1 Minute to Stop Vibrio
c-185.summary: Cooking oysters and clams to 85°C or higher at the core for at least 1 minute greatly reduces Vibrio risk. Raw shellfish is especially risky for people with weak immunity.
c-185.principle: Heat denatures Vibrio proteins so the cells stop functioning. Counts fall as N=N₀ 10⁻t/D, and higher temperatures shorten D, the time for a 10-fold reduction.
c-185.example: Vibrio multiplies fast in 25-35°C seawater. Cooking 3-5 minutes after the shells open and holding the core at 85°C for 1 minute adds a good safety margin.
c-185.actionItem: If you eat seafood today, choose fully cooked shellfish over raw, and wash knives and boards that touched raw shellfish right away.

c-186.title: Lime or Lemon Juice on Skin Plus Sun Can Cause Blisters
c-186.summary: Citrus juice left on skin in sunlight can cause burn-like redness and blisters. If juice gets on you, wash with soap and stay out of the sun.
c-186.principle: Furocoumarins in citrus peel and juice absorb UVA (320-400nm) and bind skin DNA and proteins in a phototoxic reaction. Photon energy is E=h=(hc / λ), higher at shorter wavelength.
c-186.example: If you squeeze limes at an outdoor party and don't wash your hands before 1-2 hours in the sun, red marks and blisters in the shape of the juice can appear 24-72 hours later, with pigmentation lasting months.
c-186.actionItem: If you handle citrus today, wash your hands with soap and water right away, and cover any sun-exposed skin until you have washed.

c-187.title: For a Jellyfish Sting, Rinse With Seawater, Not Fresh Water
c-187.summary: Rinsing a jellyfish sting with fresh water can make leftover stingers fire. Rinse with seawater and remove tentacles with a tool, not bare hands.
c-187.principle: Jellyfish nematocysts fire in response to osmotic and chemical triggers. Fresh water has far lower osmotic pressure than seawater (about 35g/L salt); by =iMRT water can rush into the capsules and prompt discharge.
c-187.example: If stung at the beach, rinse with seawater for 30+ seconds, scrape tentacles off with a card edge, and for severe pain a soak in roughly 45°C water for about 20 minutes is commonly advised. First aid varies by species, so call emergency services for breathing trouble.
c-187.actionItem: If you go to the sea today, check jellyfish warnings and carry a bottle for seawater rinses and a credit card for scraping.

c-188.title: Why Swimsuits Sag After the Pool and How to Pick One
c-188.summary: Swimsuits go baggy after a few pool visits because chlorine breaks down stretch fibers. Choose chlorine-resistant fabric and rinse right after use.
c-188.principle: Spandex (polyurethane) chains are oxidized and cut by HOCl in pool disinfectant. Shorter chains mean less elasticity, and ordinary spandex degrades much faster than chlorine-resistant PBT-based swimwear fabric.
c-188.example: A regular nylon/spandex suit shows clear sagging after 30-50 pool sessions, while PBT blends last several times longer. Pool residual chlorine is typically 1-3mg/L.
c-188.actionItem: After swimming today, rinse your suit in cold water right away, don't wring it, and dry it in the shade.

c-189.title: Why Re-Frozen Ice Cream Turns Gritty
c-189.summary: When ice cream melts and refreezes, large coarse ice crystals form and make it gritty. After one thaw, it is better to eat it than to refreeze it.
c-189.principle: Small ice crystals have high surface energy, melt, and their water moves onto larger crystals that grow (Ostwald ripening). Solubility rises as radius r shrinks: (S_r / S_)=(2γ V_m / rRT).
c-189.example: Well-made ice cream has ice crystals under about 50μm and feels smooth, but after thawing and refreezing they can grow past 100μm and feel gritty. Freezer temperature swings cause the same effect.
c-189.actionItem: Today, keep ice cream at the back of the freezer instead of the door to limit temperature swings, and close the lid right after serving.

c-190.title: Never Leave Dry Ice in a Closed Car
c-190.summary: Dry ice does not melt but turns into gas, which can raise CO₂ in a closed car to dangerous levels. Transport it with windows open or in a ventilated space.
c-190.principle: Solid CO₂ sublimes: CO₂(s) → CO₂(g) (at -78.5°C). 1kg makes about 500L of gas, and CO₂ above 4% causes headache and dizziness, with higher levels being dangerous.
c-190.example: 2kg of dry ice releases about 1,000L of CO₂. If it fully evaporates in a car cabin of about 3,000L, the concentration could climb to about 25%, which is very dangerous.
c-190.actionItem: If you carry dry ice today, keep the space ventilated, handle it with gloves, and never put it in a sealed container.

c-191.title: Corn Loses Its Sweetness the Longer It Sits After Picking
c-191.summary: From the moment corn is picked, its sugars turn into starch and the sweetness fades. Boil it the day you buy it or refrigerate it to keep sweetness longer.
c-191.principle: Enzymes in the kernels convert sugars such as glucose into starch: n C₆H₁₂O₆ → (C₆H₁₀O₅)_n+n H₂O. Enzyme reactions slow in the cold, so refrigeration delays the change.
c-191.example: Fresh sweet corn left at room temperature for a day can convert about 40% of its sugar to starch, while at 0-4°C refrigeration the process is much slower. Keeping the husk on also reduces moisture loss.
c-191.actionItem: If you bought corn today, refrigerate it in its husk instead of leaving it out, and cook it within a day if you can.

c-192.title: Why Refrigerating Tomatoes Kills Their Flavor
c-192.summary: Chilling a ripe tomato dulls its aroma and makes the texture mealy. Keep ripe tomatoes at room temperature and eat them within a few days.
c-192.principle: Below about 12°C tomatoes suffer chilling injury, which lowers the activity of enzymes that make aroma compounds (such as cis-3-hexenal) and damages membranes. Enzyme rate depends on temperature via k=Ae⁻E_a/RT.
c-192.example: Just 3 days in a 5°C fridge can sharply cut a tomato's volatile aroma compounds. At room temperature, ripe tomatoes are best eaten within about 3-5 days.
c-192.actionItem: Today, store ripe tomatoes stem-side down in a cool spot, and if already chilled, take them out 30 minutes before eating.

c-193.title: How to Rescue Broken Mayonnaise
c-193.summary: Don't throw out mayonnaise whose oil and egg have separated. Whisk it little by little into a fresh egg yolk to bring it back; the fresh yolk's lecithin re-establishes the emulsion.
c-193.principle: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil dispersed in water, and lecithin in the yolk lowers the oil-water interfacial tension γ so droplets don't merge. If oil goes in too fast or temperatures are off, droplets coalesce and the phases separate.
c-193.example: About 200g of broken mayonnaise can be smoothed again by whisking it spoonful by spoonful into 1 new yolk and 1 teaspoon of water. One yolk can typically emulsify up to about 200mL of oil.
c-193.actionItem: If you make mayonnaise today, start adding oil drop by drop, then slowly speed up, use fresh eggs, and refrigerate it after making.

c-194.title: Menthol Cooling Products Don't Actually Lower Body Temperature
c-194.summary: Menthol cooling sprays and sheets only make you feel cool; they don't really lower body temperature. Water and shade come first for heat relief.
c-194.principle: Menthol activates the cold receptor TRPM8 in skin, sending your nerves a cold signal. Real heat transfer needs a temperature change, as in Q=mcΔT, and menthol itself removes almost no body heat.
c-194.example: A cooling product with about 1% menthol changes skin temperature by roughly 0.5°C at most, yet the cool feeling lasts tens of minutes. In heatwaves above 33°C, trusting the sensation alone is risky.
c-194.actionItem: On a hot day today, don't rely on cooling products alone; drink water and rest in the shade to actually lower your temperature.

c-195.title: For a Burning Mouth, Take a Sip of Milk Instead of Water
c-195.summary: When spicy food makes your mouth burn, water does little but milk or yogurt works better. Capsaicin clings to fats and proteins.
c-195.principle: Capsaicin (C₁₈H₂₇NO₃) is a fat-soluble molecule that barely dissolves in water. Milk fat dissolves it and casein protein binds it, helping lift it off receptors.
c-195.example: After spicy noodles, 200mL of water only rinses briefly, while a cup of milk (200mL, about 7g fat, about 6g protein) noticeably calms the burn within minutes.
c-195.actionItem: With spicy food today, have milk or plain yogurt alongside, and if your mouth is on fire, hold a sip in your mouth before swallowing.

c-196.title: The Charred Parts of Charcoal-Grilled Meat Contain Benzo[a]pyrene
c-196.summary: Blackened, charred bits of meat grilled over open charcoal can contain benzo[a]pyrene, a probable carcinogen. Trim charred parts and keep flames from touching the meat.
c-196.principle: When meat fat drips onto coals and pyrolyzes, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) form and rise in smoke to coat the meat. A key one is benzo[a]pyrene (C₂₀H₁₂).
c-196.example: Grilling fatty pork belly directly over flames raises benzo[a]pyrene in smoke and char. Wiping the grill often and using foil or a plate instead of a grate can cut PAHs substantially.
c-196.actionItem: If you grill meat today, use moderate heat away from dripping-fat flare-ups, and cut off any blackened parts before eating.

c-197.title: Use Graphite Powder, Not Oil, in a Key Lock
c-197.summary: For a sticky key lock, graphite powder (pencil lead dust) works better than ordinary oil. Oil attracts dust and makes the lock stickier over time.
c-197.principle: Graphite is a solid lubricant whose carbon layers slide over each other. It lowers the friction coefficient µ in F=µ N and, being dry, doesn't collect dust.
c-197.example: A puff or two of graphite powder in the keyhole reduces friction so the key turns smoothly. Ordinary oil mixes with dust and can gum up within months, clogging the lock.
c-197.actionItem: If a key is stiff today, puff a little graphite lubricant into the keyhole, or rub pencil lead onto the key's grooves and slide it in and out a few times.

c-198.title: Use Chain Oil, Not WD-40, on a Bicycle Chain
c-198.summary: WD-40 is mostly a solvent and cleaner and doesn't last as a bicycle chain lubricant. After cleaning, apply oil made for chains.
c-198.principle: WD-40 is volatile solvent with a thin oil film that evaporates or washes off fast. A lubricant's higher viscosity keeps a film between contact surfaces, cutting friction loss Pₗₒₛₛ=F_f v.
c-198.example: A clean, well-lubricated chain is about 98-99% efficient, while a dry, dirty one can lose 3 percentage points or more. At 150W of pedaling, 3% is about 4.5W lost.
c-198.actionItem: If your chain squeaks today, wipe it with a dry cloth, put one drop of chain oil on each link, then wipe off the excess.

c-199.title: When Aluminum Touches Stainless Steel, One Corrodes First
c-199.summary: When dissimilar metals touch in moisture, the more active one corrodes first. When bolting aluminum to stainless steel, put an insulating washer between them.
c-199.principle: Two metals with different potentials plus an electrolyte form a small cell, and aluminum dissolves at the anode: Al → Al³⁺+3e⁻. Standard potentials differ a lot: about -1.66V for Al versus roughly -0.44V or higher for stainless (Fe-based).
c-199.example: On a seaside terrace, using stainless screws directly in an aluminum railing can produce white powdery corrosion at the contact in months to a year, because the potential gap is large and seawater is a good electrolyte.
c-199.actionItem: Today, check places where different metals touch, and where water collects, separate them with an insulating washer or paint.

c-200.title: Don't Put Food in a Galvanized Bucket
c-200.summary: Putting acidic food (vinegar, pickled fruit, kimchi) in a zinc-galvanized bucket or sheet can leach zinc and cause vomiting and stomach pain. Use food-grade containers.
c-200.principle: The zinc coating dissolves in acid: Zn+2H⁺ → Zn²⁺+H₂. Acidic foods have pH 4 or lower, so the reaction is fast.
c-200.example: At a campsite, lemonade or pickles at about pH 3 left in a galvanized bucket for hours can pick up tens of mg/L of zinc, risking vomiting and nausea. The adult daily recommended intake is only about 8-11mg.
c-200.actionItem: When camping or cooking outdoors today, use only containers marked food-safe, and keep galvanized buckets for hauling water.

c-201.title: Check Imported Ceramic Cups for Lead Leaching From the Glaze
c-201.summary: Shiny imported ceramic cups can leach lead from the glaze into acidic drinks. Look for food-safe labels and test results, and don't leave acidic drinks in them long.
c-201.principle: Lead compounds in glaze dissolve in acid: PbO+2H⁺ → Pb²⁺+H₂O. Leaching rises with lower pH, such as vinegar or fruit juice, and with longer contact.
c-201.example: In the test of soaking in 4% acetic acid for 24 hours, Korea's limit for cups is 0.4mg/L of lead. Decorative ceramics without a test report may exceed this limit.
c-201.actionItem: Today, check imported ceramic cups for a food-safe mark and test report, and don't fill unverified decorative cups with acidic drinks such as juice or wine.

c-202.title: Perfume Left in a Car Changes Its Scent
c-202.summary: Perfume left in a hot car changes smell and loses its freshness. Store it in a cool, dark place.
c-202.principle: Light top-note molecules are highly volatile and evaporate faster as temperature rises. Vapor pressure grows exponentially with temperature, P=-ΔH_vapRT+C, and heat, light and oxygen oxidize fragrance components.
c-202.example: A parked car in midsummer can exceed 60°C inside, evaporating perfume several times faster than a 20°C room. After a few weeks, citrus top notes fade and the liquid can darken.
c-202.actionItem: Today, move perfume from the car or bathroom to a cool, dark drawer and close the cap tightly after use.

c-203.title: Ointments and Creams Left in a Summer Car Can Separate
c-203.summary: Ointments and creams left in a hot car can separate into water and oil and change, reducing effectiveness. Store medicines at the temperature on the label (usually 30°C or below).
c-203.principle: A cream is an emulsion of water and oil stabilized by emulsifiers. Heat lowers emulsifier performance and viscosity so droplets merge and phases separate. Reaction rates are temperature-sensitive, k=Ae⁻E_a/RT.
c-203.example: A parked car in midsummer can exceed 60°C, so a cream can thin out or release oil within hours. Once separated, a product may not return to its original state even when remixed.
c-203.actionItem: When you go out today, carry ointments, sunscreen and medicines in your bag rather than leaving them in the car.

c-204.title: Camping Alcohol Stoves: Methanol and Ethanol Are Not the Same
c-204.summary: For camping alcohol stoves, methanol is toxic and burns with a nearly invisible flame, so denatured ethanol is the safer choice. Check whether it's lit, and put the flame out before refueling.
c-204.principle: Ethanol burns as C₂H₅OH+3O₂ → 2CO₂+3H₂O and methanol as 2CH₃OH+3O₂ → 2CO₂+4H₂O. A methanol flame is almost transparent, and the body metabolizes it to formic acid, making it highly toxic.
c-204.example: Ethanol releases about 27kJ/g when burned versus about 20kJ/g for methanol, so ethanol gives more heat per gram. A small swallowed amount of methanol can cause blindness and poisoning.
c-204.actionItem: When using an alcohol stove today, check the fuel type, and refuel only after the flame is out and the stove has cooled.

c-205.title: Don't Keep Mower or Trimmer Gasoline Longer Than About Three Months
c-205.summary: Gasoline stored over about three months for a brush cutter or generator degrades, causing hard starts and clogged carburetors. Buy only what you need, or use fuel stabilizer for leftovers.
c-205.principle: Light fractions of gasoline evaporate and oxidation forms sticky gum that clogs fuel lines. Ethanol blends absorb water and can phase-separate. Oxidation proceeds as RH+O₂ → peroxides and other products.
c-205.example: In a sealed can, regular gasoline typically starts having problems after 3-6 months and ethanol blends after 1-3 months. A full, cool container lasts longer because less air contacts the fuel.
c-205.actionItem: If you won't use your brush cutter for long, empty the fuel or add stabilizer today, and keep leftover fuel in a sealed, cool place.

c-206.title: If You Put Gasoline in a Diesel Car, Don't Start the Engine
c-206.summary: If you mistakenly put gasoline in a diesel car, don't start it and call a tow. The fuel pump and injectors can be damaged.
c-206.principle: Diesel engines use compression ignition (air compressed to high heat self-ignites the fuel), but gasoline resists ignition and has low viscosity, so it doesn't lubricate. Diesel compression ratio is about ε=15 20.
c-206.example: Gasoline mixing in weakens lubrication of the high-pressure pump and can cause metal wear, with repairs costing millions of KRW (thousands of USD). Draining the tank without starting the engine usually prevents damage.
c-206.actionItem: When refueling today, check the pump handle color and fuel type, and if you filled the wrong fuel, don't turn the key and call a repair shop.

c-207.title: AdBlue Diesel Exhaust Fluid Degrades in Summer Heat
c-207.summary: If kept hot for long, the urea in diesel exhaust fluid breaks down, its concentration drops, and it smells of ammonia. Store it in a cool shaded place and don't use old fluid.
c-207.principle: The fluid (32.5% urea solution) hydrolyzes to ammonia, (NH₂)₂CO+H₂O → 2NH₃+CO₂, and in the SCR unit reduces nitrogen oxides, 4NH₃+4NO+O₂ → 4N₂+6H₂O.
c-207.example: Stored at 25°C or below it typically lasts about a year, but above 30°C that shrinks to a few months, and in a 50°C car trunk quality can fall within weeks. The concentration drifts from the 32.5% spec.
c-207.actionItem: Today, keep exhaust fluid in a cool spot out of direct sun, and check any bottle left long in the trunk before using it.

c-208.title: Judge Engine Oil by Oxidation and Additive Depletion, Not Just Mileage
c-208.summary: When to change engine oil depends on time, short trips and hot weather as well as mileage. Use the maker's interval as a baseline and shorten it under severe conditions.
