c-208.principle: Engine oil oxidizes at high temperature, thickening and forming sludge, while additives such as detergents and dispersants are used up and trap acids and soot less well. Oxidation follows k=Ae⁻E_a/RT, roughly doubling for each 10°C rise.
c-208.example: If the maker recommends 10,000km or 1 year, severe use such as only short trips or driving in heatwaves calls for a change at about 5,000-7,500km or 6 months. Even at 5,000km a year, change it after a year.
c-208.actionItem: Today, check the service sticker or manual for the change interval and compare it to your last oil-change date.

c-209.title: Is Filling Tires With Nitrogen Worth It?
c-209.summary: Nitrogen-filled tires lose pressure a bit more slowly, but the effect is small. What matters most is checking pressure once a month, not the gas type.
c-209.principle: Rubber lets oxygen through about 3-4 times faster than nitrogen. Air is about 78% N₂ and 21% O₂, so nitrogen fill reduces O₂ permeation and slows the pressure drop. At fixed volume, pressure follows P=(nRT / V), proportional to moles and temperature.
c-209.example: Air-filled tires typically lose about 1-2psi (about 7-14kPa) a month, and nitrogen only somewhat less. A 10°C drop in air temperature reduces pressure by about 1psi in both nitrogen and air.
c-209.actionItem: Today, check tire pressure when the tires are cold and set it to the spec printed on the door-jamb label.

c-210.title: A Lunchbox Left at Room Temperature Keeps Its Toxins Even if Reheated
c-210.summary: Lunchboxes or rice rolls left out in summer can carry toxins that reheating or boiling won't remove once they start to spoil. If in doubt, throw it out.
c-210.principle: Enterotoxins made by Staphylococcus aureus growing at room temperature are heat-stable, and most remain even after 30+ minutes at 100°C. The bacteria die but the toxin protein structure isn't easily destroyed, so symptoms still occur.
c-210.example: Bacteria multiply fast at 20-37°C and can make toxin within hours, with vomiting and stomach pain starting 1-6 hours after eating. Food left out more than 2 hours (1 hour above 30°C) after cooking is risky.
c-210.actionItem: Today, pack lunch in a cooler bag with an ice pack, and throw away food left at room temperature more than 2 hours after cooking.

c-211.title: Don't Wash Dishes With Detergent in a Stream or the Sea
c-211.summary: Washing dishes with detergent in a stream or at the beach pollutes water, can kill fish and cause algal blooms. Wash up only in designated campground areas.
c-211.principle: Surfactants in detergent damage aquatic organisms' gill membranes, and phosphates add nutrients that cause algal blooms and eutrophication. When algae die, decomposition uses oxygen and lowers dissolved oxygen (DO).
c-211.example: Even one drop of ordinary dish detergent (about 0.05mL) can affect aquatic life in tens of liters of water. When stream dissolved oxygen falls below 5mg/L, fish struggle to survive.
c-211.actionItem: Outdoors today, carry food scraps out with you and wash dishes at the campground's designated greywater point.

c-212.title: Mosquitoes Follow Your Breath and Sweat Odor
c-212.summary: Mosquitoes follow the carbon dioxide you exhale and the lactic acid smell in sweat to find where to bite. Wiping sweat and applying repellent lowers your chance of bites.
c-212.principle: Receptors on mosquito antennae track concentration gradients, moving toward higher CO₂ and lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃). Exhaled air is about 4% CO₂, about 100 times the roughly 0.04% in ambient air.
c-212.example: A person exhales about 1kg of CO₂ a day, and after exercise sweat lactic acid rises, so mosquitoes can find you from tens of meters away. DEET 10-30% products typically protect for several hours.
c-212.actionItem: Before going outdoors today, wipe off sweat, apply repellent to exposed skin and clothing, and empty any standing water.

c-213.title: Sewer Smell From a Floor Drain Rises When the Trap Seal Dries Out
c-213.summary: If a drain smells like sewage, its trap water seal has probably dried out. Pour a jug of water down to refill the seal and block the odor.
c-213.principle: Water held in the trap's U-bend (the seal) blocks sewer gas. When it evaporates, hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) made by microbes in the sewage can rise. Seal depth is commonly about 50mm.
c-213.example: An unused bathroom floor drain's seal can dry within 1-2 weeks, letting odor through. Pouring about 500mL of water refills it, and in summer evaporation is faster so it dries more often.
c-213.actionItem: Today, pour a jug of water into unused bathroom or balcony drains to refill the seal, and repeat once a month.

c-214.title: Why Air Conditioners Smell Sour
c-214.summary: A sour smell from an air conditioner comes from bacteria and mold growing in condensed water and dust inside. Drying the inside with fan mode before turning off helps.
c-214.principle: Water condenses on the cooling fins as H₂O(g) → H₂O(l), and microbes grow in dust and organic matter, producing volatile metabolites (fatty acids, alcohols, etc.) that smell sour.
c-214.example: Turning off right after cooling leaves internal humidity above 80%, so bacteria grow easily. Running fan mode for 10-30 minutes before shutting off dries most of the interior and cuts the smell sharply.
c-214.actionItem: Today, run the AC in fan mode for 15 minutes before turning it off, and remove the filter to dust it off and let it dry.

c-215.title: White Film on Chocolate Isn't Mold
c-215.summary: The white film on chocolate is usually not mold but fat bloom, cocoa butter that melted and resolidified. The texture gets slightly coarse but it is safe to eat.
c-215.principle: Cocoa butter has several crystal forms (polymorphs). The stable form V converts to the more stable form VI with temperature changes and rises to the surface, appearing white. Form V melts at about 34°C.
c-215.example: Stored above 28°C or with frequent temperature swings, bloom can appear in days to weeks. The best chocolate storage is about 15-18°C at 50% relative humidity or lower.
c-215.actionItem: Today, keep chocolate in a cool spot out of direct sun, and when taking it from the fridge, leave it in its wrapper at room temperature to prevent condensation.

c-216.title: Mackerel and Tuna Left at Room Temperature Form Histamine
c-216.summary: Red-fleshed fish such as mackerel and tuna can form histamine if left out, causing facial flushing, headache and hives. Cooking doesn't remove it, so keep fish fresh and cold.
c-216.principle: Bacterial histidine decarboxylase converts the fish's histidine to histamine: C₆H₉N₃O₂ → C₅H₉N₃+CO₂. Histamine is heat-stable and hardly destroyed by cooking.
c-216.example: Histamine can form within hours at 25°C but far more slowly at 4°C. Food limits are typically 200mg/kg or less, and eating 100mg or more may cause symptoms.
c-216.actionItem: Today, refrigerate or freeze red-fleshed fish as soon as you bring it home, and don't eat fish left at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

c-217.title: Why Old Tents and Rain Gear Turn Sticky
c-217.summary: The waterproof coating inside an old tent or rain jacket becomes sticky and peels because polyurethane hydrolyzes in moisture and heat. Storing it fully dry slows this down.
c-217.principle: Ester bonds in polyurethane (PU) coating react with water and break, R-COO-R'+H₂O → R-COOH+R'-OH, shortening the chains so the coating turns tacky. Hot, humid conditions speed it up.
c-217.example: PU-coated tents typically begin to hydrolyze after 3-5 years. Folded damp and stored above 30°C, they can turn sticky within a single season.
c-217.actionItem: Today, dry tents and rain gear completely, then store them unfolded in a cool place, and if already sticky, consider replacing rather than recoating.

c-218.title: Why Laundry Capsules Stay as Clumps
c-218.summary: Laundry capsules stay clumped when the water is cold, too little, or the load is too full. Put the capsule in the bottom of the drum first, then add clothes on top.
c-218.principle: The PVA (polyvinyl alcohol) film around a capsule dissolves in water, and the dissolving rate depends strongly on temperature, slowing at low temperature as with k=Ae⁻E_a/RT, so it doesn't dissolve well in cold water.
c-218.example: PVA film dissolves in about 1-3 minutes in 40°C water but can take over 10 minutes in cold water at 15°C or below. A drum stuffed with laundry presses the capsule against fabric so water can't reach it.
c-218.actionItem: Today, don't touch capsules with wet hands, put them in the drum first and clothes over them, and use liquid detergent for cold-water cycles.

c-219.title: Camping Glow Sticks Shine Through a Chemical Reaction
c-219.summary: A camping glow stick lights up when you bend it and two liquids inside mix in a chemical reaction. It shines without electricity or heat, brighter and shorter when warm, dimmer and longer when cold.
c-219.principle: Hydrogen peroxide and an oxalate ester inside the tube react to form a high-energy intermediate, which excites a fluorescent dye so it emits light (chemiluminescence). The rate is temperature-sensitive, k=Ae⁻E_a/RT.
c-219.example: A glow stick typically lasts 6-12 hours at 20°C, but at 40°C it is much brighter and can fade in 1-2 hours, while in a freezer it dims and brightens again when warmed. It gives off almost no heat, so fire risk is low.
c-219.actionItem: For night camping or a power outage today, tuck one or two glow sticks into your bag, and keep any leaked liquid off your skin.

c-220.title: Fireworks Colors Come From Metal Elements' Flame Emission
c-220.summary: Firework colors come from metal elements mixed into the powder. Strontium gives red, copper gives blue, and barium gives green.
c-220.principle: The flame's heat excites electrons in metal atoms, and when they fall back to lower energy levels they emit light of energy E=h=(hc / λ). Each element has different levels, so each has its own color.
c-220.example: Sr gives red at about 650nm, Ba green at about 520nm, Cu blue at about 450nm and Na yellow at about 589nm. Blue is hardest to make because copper compounds break down easily above about 1,200°C.
c-220.actionItem: If you watch fireworks today, try to guess the metal from each color, and keep your distance from the debris and smoke.

c-221.title: Disinfecting Water With a Clear PET Bottle and Sunshine
c-221.summary: Filling a clear PET bottle with clear water and leaving it in sunshine for 6 hours is an emergency method (SODIS) to reduce pathogens. Cloudy water must be filtered first, and it is not a perfect drinking-water treatment.
c-221.principle: UVA (320-400nm) and heat damage the DNA and proteins of pathogens and inactivate them. The effect scales with UV dose H=I t (intensity times time), and a water temperature above 50°C greatly increases it.
c-221.example: On a sunny day a 1-2L clear PET bottle left 6 hours reduces most bacteria, and under cloudy skies it needs two days. Effectiveness drops when turbidity exceeds 30 NTU.
c-221.actionItem: If you try it as an emergency test today, use only clear water and lay the bottle in sun for 6 hours, but normally prefer boiled or treated water.

c-222.title: Plastic Wrap Comes in PVC and PE, and They Differ
c-222.summary: Cling wrap comes in PVC and PE (polyethylene), and each has different safe limits for microwave use and contact with fatty foods. Check the material and heat rating on the pack.
c-222.principle: PVC wrap contains plasticizers for flexibility, which can migrate into food when it touches fatty food or is heated. PE wrap needs no plasticizer and its heat rating of about 110°C differs from PVC's (some labeled products list 130°C or more).
c-222.example: When microwaving, fatty food can exceed 100°C so wrap touching it can melt or let plasticizer migrate. Keep 2-3cm of space between wrap and food.
c-222.actionItem: Today, check the material and heat rating before using wrap, and in the microwave keep it lifted off the food.

c-223.title: When Hot Oil Touches a Styrofoam Instant-Noodle Container
c-223.summary: Putting hot, oily food in a polystyrene (Styrofoam) container can soften it and let a little styrene leach out. Follow the container's heat rating.
c-223.principle: Polystyrene softens near its glass transition at about 100°C and dissolves readily in oil, so styrene monomer (C₈H₈) can migrate into food. Migration rises with temperature and contact time.
c-223.example: Instant-noodle broth at about 90°C is below polystyrene's softening point and generally acceptable, but cooking oil above 100°C or very oily food can melt the container. Use disposable containers only once.
c-223.actionItem: Today, move hot, oily food from a Styrofoam container into a heat-resistant glass or ceramic bowl.

c-224.title: Biodegradable Plastic Bags Don't Rot at Home
c-224.summary: Most biodegradable bags break down only at the high temperatures of composting facilities and barely rot in a home garden or trash can. Follow local disposal labels.
c-224.principle: PLA (polylactic acid) hydrolyzes with water, (C₃H₄O₂)_n+n H₂O → n C₃H₆O₃ (lactic acid). The reaction speeds up above the glass transition of about 58°C, so it needs industrial composting conditions (about 58°C and humid).
c-224.example: In an industrial composter (58°C, moist), PLA breaks down in about 90-180 days, but in a 20°C home it can take years or barely degrade. It doesn't break down well in the sea either.
c-224.actionItem: If you get a biodegradable-labeled bag today, sort it as general waste and, if you can, bring a reusable shopping bag instead.

c-225.title: Why Garden Hoses Crack and Crumble in the Sun
c-225.summary: A garden hose left outside gets stiffer and cracks over the years because UV in sunlight breaks polymer chains. When not in use, coil it in the shade.
c-225.principle: UV photon energy E=(hc / λ) breaks C-Cl and C-H bonds in polymers such as PVC, forming radicals that react with oxygen and cut the chains. Shorter chains make the material brittle.
c-225.example: A hose with UV stabilizer lasts 3-5 years, whereas one left in constant sun can lose plasticizer and crack within 1-2 years. Midday in midsummer, when UV index is highest, is the most damaging.
c-225.actionItem: After using the hose today, drain it and coil it in shade or inside a hose reel box away from sunlight.

c-226.title: Why Rubber Bands and Rubber Gloves Crack
c-226.summary: Rubber bands and gloves suddenly crack and snap because ozone in the air attacks the rubber's double bonds. Rubber stored stretched cracks faster.
c-226.principle: Ozone adds across the C=C double bonds of natural rubber (polyisoprene), C=C+O₃ → ozonide, and the bond breaks. Cracks run perpendicular to the stretch on the surface of stretched rubber.
c-226.example: Ambient ozone is typically 0.02-0.06ppm, yet even that can crack stretched rubber in weeks to months. Storing it in a cool place extends its life considerably.
c-226.actionItem: Today, store rubber bands and gloves unstretched in a sealed bag in a cool, dark drawer.

c-227.title: Why White Sneakers Turn Yellow
c-227.summary: White sneakers yellow even in storage because polyurethane in the sole oxidizes with light and oxygen and phenolic antioxidants change. Store them in a cool, dark place.
c-227.principle: Aromatic parts of polyurethane oxidize under UV and oxygen to form yellow chromophores, and phenolic antioxidants react with nitrogen oxides to become yellow quinone-type compounds. Photo-oxidation grows with UV dose.
c-227.example: Left on a bright windowsill they can yellow noticeably within weeks to months, several times faster than in a dark shoe cabinet. The yellow forms in a thin surface layer, which oxygen bleach can partly reduce.
c-227.actionItem: Today, keep white sneakers in a dark, ventilated shoe cabinet instead of a sunny windowsill, and store them in a cotton bag rather than plastic.

c-228.title: Why New Jeans Bleed Color the First Time You Wash Them
c-228.summary: New jeans bleed blue in the first wash because indigo dye sits only on the fiber surface as particles. Wash them inside out, alone, in cold water the first time.
c-228.principle: Indigo is insoluble in water: it's dyed in a reduced soluble form, then oxidizes in air so insoluble particles cling to the fiber surface. It doesn't chemically bond to the fiber, so friction and water wash it off.
c-228.example: A new pair of jeans (about 600g) can shed about 1-2g of dye in the first wash, turning white clothes blue if washed together. In cold water (30°C or below) less dye comes out.
c-228.actionItem: Today, wash new jeans alone inside out in cold water the first time, don't mix them with whites, and dry them in the shade.

c-229.title: Wet cement is alkaline and can burn your skin
c-229.summary: Wet cement and concrete are strongly alkaline, and skin left in contact can suffer chemical burns before it hurts.
c-229.principle: Calcium compounds in cement react with water to form Ca(OH)₂ (pH about 12.5), and alkali hydrolyzes skin proteins and fats. CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂
c-229.example: Kneeling on wet concrete for 1-2 hours has caused painless second-degree burns in reported cases. A pH of 12.5 means roughly 300,000 times more [OH⁻] than neutral water.
c-229.actionItem: If cement touches skin, brush off dry powder first, then rinse under running water for 15+ minutes; wear waterproof gloves and long trousers for any job today.

c-230.title: Be careful with heat and gas from drain openers
c-230.summary: Lye-based drain openers heat up as they dissolve, and they release hydrogen gas if they touch aluminum.
c-230.principle: NaOH releases about 44.5kJ/mol when dissolving, and reacts with aluminum to form hydrogen. 2Al + 2NaOH + 6H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄] + 3H₂
c-230.example: Dissolving 100g NaOH (2.5 mol) releases about 111kJ, enough to warm 1L of water by about 26°C. In a narrow pipe it can get much hotter locally and spatter.
c-230.actionItem: If you use a drain opener today, ventilate, wear goggles and gloves, and never mix it with other cleaners or put it in aluminum containers.

c-231.title: Epoxy only cures if you mix the ratio exactly
c-231.summary: Epoxy hardens fully only when resin and hardener meet in the stated ratio; otherwise it stays tacky.
c-231.principle: Epoxide groups react with amine active hydrogens in equivalent amounts to build a network. Hardener mass is m_hardener = AHEWEEW × m_resin.
c-231.example: With 5mL resin and 5mL hardener (1:1), a ratio error of 20% or more often leaves a sticky, soft result. Full cure usually takes about 24 hours.
c-231.actionItem: If you use epoxy today, measure to the label ratio, mix for at least 2 minutes while scraping the bottom, and apply a thin layer.

c-232.title: A fish tank stabilizes as ammonia turns into nitrate
c-232.summary: A new tank builds up ammonia and nitrite until nitrifying bacteria establish, which is dangerous for fish.
c-232.principle: Nitrifying bacteria convert toxic ammonia to nitrite, then to less toxic nitrate. NH₄⁺ + 1.5 O₂ → NO₂⁻ + 2H⁺ + H₂O, NO₂⁻ + 0.5 O₂ → NO₃⁻
c-232.example: A new tank usually needs 4-6 weeks to cycle, and it is safest to add fish only once ammonia and nitrite read 0ppm. Keep nitrate under 40ppm with a 20-30% water change weekly.
c-232.actionItem: Test ammonia, nitrite and nitrate with a test kit today, and when changing water rinse the filter media in removed tank water, not in tap water.

c-233.title: Never pour water on a grease fire; cover it with a lid
c-233.summary: Water on burning oil sends flaming oil and steam flying in every direction.
c-233.principle: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat, so a lid cuts off oxygen. Water sinks under the oil, flashes to steam, and expands about 1,700 times. H₂O(l) → H₂O(g)
c-233.example: One cup (200mL) of water hitting oil above 300°C instantly makes about 340L of steam, which can throw burning oil up to the ceiling.
c-233.actionItem: Today, keep a lid that fits your pan within reach of the stove, and remember the order: turn off the heat, then cover the pan.

c-234.title: Why recirculation-only on a long drive makes you sleepy
c-234.summary: Running recirculation mode for a long time lets carbon dioxide build up in the car, which can bring drowsiness and weaker focus.
c-234.principle: In a sealed cabin, exhaled CO2 cannot escape, so its concentration rises with time. ΔC ≈ (G / V) t (G: generation rate, V: cabin volume)
c-234.example: Outdoor air holds about 420ppm CO2, but a car with several people on recirculation for 30-60 minutes has been measured above 2,000ppm. Drowsiness is commonly reported above about 1,000ppm.
c-234.actionItem: On today's drive, switch to fresh-air mode or crack a window for a minute every 20-30 minutes.

c-235.title: Let the first morning tap water run for a moment
c-235.summary: Water that sat in the pipes overnight can pick up metal ions, so run the tap briefly before using it.
c-235.principle: Copper and lead in pipes and fittings slowly oxidize into the water. Pb → Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ The longer it stagnates, the higher the concentration.
c-235.example: After 6+ hours of standing, run the tap 30-60 seconds until the water turns cold. At 6L/min, a minute is about 6L, which can go to plants or cleaning so it is not wasted.
c-235.actionItem: Tomorrow morning, run the tap 30-60 seconds before filling a cup, and collect that water for plants or mopping.

c-236.title: Alkaline water is quickly neutralized in your stomach
c-236.summary: Stomach acid neutralizes alkaline water almost immediately, so it cannot change your body's pH and is rarely worth a premium price.
c-236.principle: Gastric juice is about 0.01-0.1 M HCl (pH 1.5-3.5), and the OH⁻ in alkaline water reacts with it at once. HCl + OH⁻ → H₂O + Cl⁻
c-236.example: One liter of pH 9 water has only 10⁻⁵ mol of OH⁻, enough to neutralize about 1% of 100mL of pH 2 stomach acid (10⁻³ mol H+). Blood pH is held at 7.35-7.45 by breathing and the kidneys.
c-236.actionItem: Before buying alkaline water, check for unsupported health claims; today, plain tap or filtered water is enough to hydrate.

c-237.title: Storing batteries in the fridge gains you almost nothing
c-237.summary: Modern alkaline batteries self-discharge very slowly even at room temperature, so refrigeration helps little and risks condensation.
c-237.principle: Self-discharge is chemical, so it speeds up with temperature according to the Arrhenius equation. k = A e⁻E_a/RT Cooling slows it, but alkaline cells are already very slow.
c-237.example: Alkaline batteries lose only about 2-3% per year at 20°C, giving a shelf life of 5-10 years. A fridge saves around 1% a year, and water droplets after removal can corrode the terminals.
c-237.actionItem: Today, keep batteries in a cool, dry drawer grouped by type, and never mix new and old cells in one device.

c-238.title: Camping charcoal: briquettes, white and black charcoal differ
c-238.summary: Charcoal types differ in how fast they light, how much smoke they make and how long the heat lasts, so match the type to the job.
c-238.principle: The higher the carbonization, the less volatile matter and the more carbon, giving less smoke and longer burning. C + O₂ → CO₂ (ΔH ≈ -394kJ/mol); with too little oxygen, 2C + O₂ → 2CO.
c-238.example: One kg of charcoal gives about 29MJ (about 8kWh). White charcoal baked near 1,000°C burns long and clean but is hard to light; black charcoal lights easily but smokes more; briquettes leave more ash because of binders.
c-238.actionItem: If you buy camping charcoal today, pick by purpose, and never burn charcoal inside a tent or closed space (carbon monoxide poisoning).

c-239.title: Why eat carbs right after exercise
c-239.summary: In the first hour or two after exercise, muscles take up sugar best, so carbohydrates then refill glycogen quickly.
c-239.principle: Glycogen emptied by exercise is rebuilt with insulin and muscle glucose transporters. (Glucose)_n + Glucose → (Glucose)ₙ₊₁
c-239.example: Muscles store about 400g of glycogen. For a typical exerciser, a banana (about 27g carbs) and a glass of milk after a hard workout is enough; if you rest a day or more, exact timing matters little.
c-239.actionItem: If you work out today, eat carbs with some protein within an hour afterward, such as a banana, a bowl of rice, or milk.

c-240.title: The bright color of dried apricots comes from sulfites
c-240.summary: Bright orange dried apricots are protected from browning by sulfites, while brown ones are usually unsulfured, and people with asthma should be careful.
c-240.principle: SO₂ dissolves in water to form bisulfite, which inhibits browning enzymes and oxidation. SO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HSO₃⁻ + H⁺
c-240.example: Sulfured dried apricots can contain several hundred to about 2,000mg/kg of SO₂, and many countries require a label at 10mg/kg or more. Sulfite-sensitive asthma patients can have breathing trouble.
c-240.actionItem: When buying dried fruit today, read the ingredient list for sulfites (sulphur dioxide), and choose brown unsulfured ones if you are sensitive.

c-241.title: Low-sodium salt is rich in potassium: caution with kidney disease
c-241.summary: Low-sodium salt swaps part of the sodium for potassium, so people with kidney disease or potassium-affecting medicines must talk to a doctor first.
c-241.principle: Part of the NaCl is replaced by KCl, cutting sodium but raising potassium. By mass, Na is 39.3% of NaCl and K is 52.4% of KCl.
c-241.example: Five g of a 70% sodium / 30% potassium blend has about 1.4g sodium (30% less than the 2.0g in 5g of regular salt) and about 0.79g potassium. With reduced kidney function, potassium can build up and risk dangerous heart rhythms.
c-241.actionItem: Before buying low-sodium salt today, check the KCl share on the label, and ask your doctor first if you have kidney disease or take related medicines.

c-242.title: 14K and 18K gold are not pure gold
c-242.summary: The karat number shows gold content: 18K is 75% gold and 14K about 58%, with other metals making up the rest.
c-242.principle: Purity is expressed in 24ths. purity = (K / 24) Alloying makes gold harder and changes its color, while 24K pure gold is soft at about 99.9%.
c-242.example: A 10g 18K ring holds 7.5g of pure gold, and a 14K one about 5.8g. Hallmarks are usually 750 for 18K and 585 for 14K.
c-242.actionItem: When buying gold today, check the hallmark (750, 585, etc.) and weight, and calculate the pure gold content yourself.

c-243.title: Coffee beans degas after roasting, then oxidize
c-243.summary: Beans release carbon dioxide right after roasting and then oxidize, so aim to drink them within about 1-4 weeks of the roast date.
c-243.principle: The CO₂ made during roasting slowly escapes, while aroma compounds and oils react with oxygen and go stale. RH + O₂ → ROOH
c-243.example: One gram of beans releases several mL of CO2 after roasting, and grinding multiplies surface area so aroma fades within minutes to hours. Opened beans at room temperature noticeably lose flavor in about 2-4 weeks.
c-243.actionItem: When buying beans today, choose a bag with a roast date, grind just before brewing, and store airtight in a cool dark place (the fridge risks moisture).

c-244.title: Why the oil-repellent coating on a phone screen wears off
c-244.summary: A phone's anti-fingerprint coating is only a few to tens of nanometers thick, so it gradually wears away with wiping and abrasion.
c-244.principle: A fluoropolymer film lowers surface energy so oil beads up instead of spreading. The contact angle follows θ = γ_SV - γ_SLγ_LV, and as the film wears, θ drops.
c-244.example: The coating is roughly a few to tens of nm thick, about one ten-thousandth of a hair's width (around 80,000nm). Sand and keys in a pocket plus repeated alcohol cleaning wear it down visibly within months to 2 years.
c-244.actionItem: From today, wipe the screen with a dry microfiber cloth, and avoid alcohol-heavy wipes or rough cloths.

c-245.title: Take dry-cleaned clothes out of the plastic and air them
c-245.summary: Freshly dry-cleaned clothes can retain solvent, so remove the plastic and ventilate before wearing or storing them.
c-245.principle: The cleaning solvent perchloroethylene boils at 121°C and has a vapor pressure of about 1.9kPa at 20°C, so it evaporates slowly. C₂Cl₄(l) → C₂Cl₄(g) Plastic traps the vapor.
c-245.example: Leaving garments in plastic inside the closet traps vapor and raises odor and exposure. Hanging them in a breezy place for several hours to a day lets most escape. Some cleaners use hydrocarbon solvents instead.
c-245.actionItem: Take clothes out of the plastic as soon as you bring them home from the cleaner, and hang them for several hours on a balcony or in a ventilated spot.

c-246.title: A condensing boiler recovers heat from the water vapor in exhaust
c-246.summary: A condensing boiler condenses the water vapor in its exhaust and uses that latent heat for heating, instead of throwing it away.
c-246.principle: Burning natural gas makes water, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, and condensing that vapor releases latent heat of about 2.26MJ/kg. To recover it, the return water should be below about 55°C.
c-246.example: Burning 1m³ of gas makes about 1.6kg of water, adding roughly 3.6MJ (about 10% of the total heat). That is why it can save about 10-15% energy versus a conventional boiler.
c-246.actionItem: If you use a condensing boiler today, lower the heating setpoint so return water stays below 55°C and condensation works well.

c-247.title: A candle burns vaporized wax, not melted wax
c-247.summary: A candle flame burns wax vapor drawn up the wick, not the liquid wax itself.
c-247.principle: Melted wax climbs the wick by capillary action, vaporizes in the heat, and the vapor reacts with oxygen. C₂₅H₅₂ + 38 O₂ → 25 CO₂ + 26 H₂O
c-247.example: An ordinary candle burns about 7g of wax per hour and gives off roughly 80W of heat. A wick that is too long burns incompletely and makes more soot.
c-247.actionItem: Before lighting a candle today, trim the wick to about 5mm to cut soot, and never leave a lit candle unattended.

c-248.title: Boiling pasta in less water cuts energy use
c-248.summary: Pasta needs only about 1L of water per 100g, so switching from a habit of boiling 3L cuts the heat needed a lot.
c-248.principle: Heating water takes Q = mcΔT, and pasta starch absorbs water and gelatinizes from about 60-70°C, so a huge pot is unnecessary.
c-248.example: Raising 1L of water from 20°C to 100°C takes about 334kJ (0.093kWh), so cutting from 3L to 1L saves about 0.19kWh each time. Using a lid saves even more.
c-248.actionItem: When cooking pasta today, use only about 1L of water per 100g, put a lid on while heating, and stir often so it doesn't stick.

c-249.title: Ventilate first when a fluorescent lamp breaks
c-249.summary: Fluorescent lamps contain a little mercury, so when one breaks, move people and pets out and ventilate before cleaning up.
c-249.principle: Mercury is a metal that evaporates even at room temperature. Hg(l) → Hg(g) Its vapor pressure at 20°C is about 0.16Pa, and the vapor builds up in a closed room.
c-249.example: One compact fluorescent lamp (CFL) usually holds a few mg of mercury. After a break, ventilate for 5-10+ minutes, and collect the pieces with stiff paper and tape instead of a vacuum, then seal them for a collection bin.
c-249.actionItem: Today, find any spent fluorescent tubes at home, put them in their original box, and learn where the nearest lamp collection bin is.

c-250.title: Use less water for new-crop rice than for old rice
c-250.summary: New-crop rice holds more moisture, so use about 90% of your usual water or the rice turns mushy.
c-250.principle: The older rice gets, the drier it is and the more water it absorbs. Cooking water is roughly m_water = m_rice × r, with r about 1.1 for new rice and 1.2 for old.
c-250.example: For 2 cups (about 360mL) of rice you might use about 400mL of water, but with new rice use about 360mL, roughly 40mL less. New rice is about 15-16% moisture, old rice 13-14%.
c-250.actionItem: When cooking new-crop rice today, use about 90% of your usual water, and cut back more next time if it is mushy.

c-251.title: Mix pancake batter briefly in cold water for crispness
c-251.summary: Korean-style jeon batter turns crisp when mixed briefly with cold water, which limits chewy gluten.
c-251.principle: Glutenin and gliadin in flour form a gluten network when wet and agitated. glutenin + gliadin + H₂O ―(mixing)→ gluten Cold water slows this down.
c-251.example: Stir 1 cup (about 120g) of flour with 1 cup of cold water for only about 10 strokes; small lumps are fine. Replacing about 20% of the flour with starch dilutes gluten for extra crispness.
c-251.actionItem: If you make savory pancakes today, mix with ice-cold water for only 10-15 seconds, and don't keep stirring the batter for 10+ minutes.

c-252.title: Bracken fiddleheads need blanching and soaking to cut toxins
c-252.summary: Raw bracken contains a carcinogen called ptaquiloside, so always boil and soak it, and still avoid eating it very often.
c-252.principle: Ptaquiloside breaks down with heat and alkali. ptaquiloside ―(Δ, OH⁻)→ pterosin B (non-toxic)
c-252.example: Boil for 5-10 minutes, then soak in cold water for about a day; adding about 5g (0.5%) baking soda per 1L of water helps breakdown. It does not guarantee zero, so don't eat it often or in large amounts.
c-252.actionItem: If you cook bracken today, boil it thoroughly, soak it in cold water, and only then prepare the dish.

c-253.title: Why taro makes your hands itch, and the fix
c-253.summary: Taro skin and juice contain needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals that sting and itch bare hands.
c-253.principle: Calcium oxalate crystals (raphides) pierce skin to cause itching, and they partly dissolve or lose effect in acid or heat. CaC₂O₄ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Ca²⁺ + H₂C₂O₄
c-253.example: The crystals are tens to hundreds of micrometers long (0.02-0.2mm), sharp enough to pierce the outer skin layer. For itching, rinsing in warm water with a little vinegar can help, and boiling greatly reduces the acrid taste.
c-253.actionItem: When preparing taro today, wear rubber gloves and peel it under running water.

c-254.title: Pine needles help songpyeon keep a bit longer as a natural preservative
c-254.summary: The terpenes in the pine needles under songpyeon have a mild antibacterial effect, but they are not a preservative, so storage still matters.
c-254.principle: Terpenes like alpha-pinene (C₁₀H₁₆) disturb bacterial cell membranes and slow growth. The effect is weak and extends keeping time only by hours to about a day.
c-254.example: Songpyeon usually lasts about a day at cool room temperature; in the fridge the rice cake hardens (retrogradation); frozen it keeps about 1 month. Relying on the pine needles alone at summer room temperature can lead to spoilage.
c-254.actionItem: Today, cool leftover songpyeon, wrap each one in plastic wrap and freeze it, then steam to reheat before eating.

c-255.title: Red ginseng is steamed, so its saponin structure has changed
c-255.summary: Red ginseng is fresh ginseng steamed and dried, and steaming strips sugars off ginseng saponins (ginsenosides), creating compounds found only in red ginseng.
c-255.principle: Steam heat and moisture hydrolyze the sugar chains of ginsenosides. Rb₁ ―(steam, H)→⁺ Rg₃ + 2 glucose
c-255.example: Red ginseng is made by steaming fresh ginseng at about 95-100°C for hours and then drying, which produces compounds such as Rg3, Rg5 and Rk1. Health benefits cannot be assumed, and ginsenoside content varies by product.
c-255.actionItem: When buying a red ginseng product today, compare the root age (such as 6-year) and the labeled ginsenoside content (Rg1+Rb1+Rg3 total).

c-256.title: The white powder on grape skin is not pesticide
c-256.summary: The dusty white coating on grapes is natural wax (bloom) the fruit makes itself, and it is also a sign of freshness.
c-256.principle: Bloom is hydrophobic wax crystals such as oleanolic acid (C₃₀H₄₈O₃), a natural waterproof layer that slows water loss and blocks mold and rain.
c-256.example: The bloom layer is only a few micrometers thick or less and rubs off easily with a finger. An even bloom suggests the grapes were handled little since harvest, which helps judge freshness.
c-256.actionItem: Today, rinse grapes under running water for 30 seconds just before eating, and don't wash them in advance.

c-257.title: Autumn leaves turn red because the leaf makes new pigment
c-257.summary: Yellow leaves reveal pigment that was already there, while red leaves make new anthocyanin in autumn.
c-257.principle: As days shorten and cool, chlorophyll (C₅₅H₇₂O₅N₄Mg) breaks down, exposing yellow carotenoids, and as sugar accumulates, anthocyanin is newly synthesized, turning leaves red.
c-257.example: Reds are most vivid with sunny days that build sugar and mornings dropping to 5-10°C. In a rainy, warm autumn, colors are duller.
c-257.actionItem: If you plan a foliage trip today, check the foliage forecast map for 1-2 weeks after morning lows start hovering around 5°C.

c-258.title: Don't pick up ginkgo fruit with bare hands
c-258.summary: The pulp of ginkgo fruit can cause a rash like poison ivy on bare skin, and the smell comes from butyric acid.
c-258.principle: Ginkgolic acids (alkylphenols) in the pulp cause contact dermatitis, and the foul odor is butyric acid. CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH
c-258.example: Pulp juice on skin can lead to red rash and itching hours to a day later. Butyric acid is the same family of smell as rancid butter or vomit.
c-258.actionItem: On today's autumn walk, don't pick up fallen ginkgo fruit, and if you must, wear disposable gloves and handle it inside a bag.

c-259.title: Boiling or drying doesn't remove poisonous mushroom toxins
c-259.summary: Toxins of poisonous mushrooms survive boiling, drying and the silver spoon test, so never eat wild mushrooms that an expert hasn't identified.
c-259.principle: The amatoxin (alpha-amanitin) of death caps is a heat-stable cyclic peptide that blocks RNA polymerase II and damages liver and kidney cells. amatoxin + RNA polymerase II → inactive complex
c-259.example: The lethal dose is about 0.1mg/kg, so a single death cap (about 50g) can be fatal to an adult. Symptoms appear only after 6-24 hours, making it easy to get help too late.
c-259.actionItem: If you meet wild mushrooms on a hike today, don't pick them, and if you ate some and have vomiting or diarrhea, go to the ER at once and bring the mushroom.

c-260.title: Why you shouldn't burn autumn leaves and trash
c-260.summary: Burning leaves and trash outdoors burns incompletely and releases fine dust and harmful compounds, and burning plastic or PVC can make dioxins.
c-260.principle: Open burning with limited oxygen is incomplete combustion, giving PAHs and carbon monoxide. 2C + O₂ → 2CO PVC (C₂H₃Cl)_n can form hydrogen chloride and dioxin-type compounds when burned.
c-260.example: About 57% of PVC's mass is chlorine, so 1kg holds about 570g of chlorine. Open burning of crop residue can emit roughly 5-15g of fine particles per kg.
c-260.actionItem: Today, don't burn leaves; compost them or put them out following your local collection rules.

c-261.title: The white powder from humidifiers is tap-water minerals
c-261.summary: The white dust that settles around an ultrasonic humidifier is the calcium and magnesium minerals dissolved in your tap water.
c-261.principle: An ultrasonic humidifier sprays fine droplets without boiling, so dissolved salts stay behind as solid particles when the droplets dry. Boiling lets some hardness settle out. Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O
c-261.example: With about 80mg/L of minerals in tap water and 2.4L sprayed over an 8-hour night, roughly 190mg of particles can spread into the air. These are small enough to reach the airways.
c-261.actionItem: Today, empty, rinse and refill the humidifier tank daily, and where possible use distilled water or a heated or evaporative model.

c-262.title: Why old books turn yellow
c-262.summary: Old books yellow and crumble because acids and lignin in the paper oxidize and break down.
c-262.principle: Lignin in acidic paper oxidizes with light and oxygen and turns yellow, and acid hydrolyzes cellulose to weaken the paper. (C₆H₁₀O₅)_n + nH₂O ―(H⁺)→ nC₆H₁₂O₆
c-262.example: Lignin-rich paper like newsprint (about 25% lignin) yellows in months, while acid-free books can last centuries. Higher humidity and temperature speed the reactions up.
c-262.actionItem: Today, shelve valued books away from direct sunlight in a cool dry spot, and don't tuck newspaper clippings between pages.

c-263.title: Black rot at the base of tomatoes comes from calcium
c-263.summary: The black rot at the bottom of tomatoes (blossom-end rot) is usually less about missing calcium in the soil and more about calcium not reaching the fruit.
c-263.principle: Calcium ions travel with the water stream driven by transpiration, and the fruit tip, which transpires little, gets it last. Slow flow means less supply. J = C × V (C: calcium concentration, V: water flow)
c-263.example: Uneven watering interrupts calcium movement and triggers symptoms; steady watering of about 25mm (1 inch) of water per week is commonly advised. Managing water works better than adding lots of calcium to the soil.
c-263.actionItem: Today, water tomatoes at a steady interval before the soil dries out instead of in irregular bursts, and add mulch.

c-264.title: Charcoal-fire ash is free potassium for the garden, with cautions
c-264.summary: Wood ash is an alkaline fertilizer supplying potassium and calcium, but it harms acid-loving plants, and ash from additive-laden briquettes or painted wood must not be used.
c-264.principle: The K₂CO₃ in ash dissolves into potassium and hydroxide ions, raising soil pH. K₂CO₃ + H₂O ⇌ 2K⁺ + HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻
c-264.example: Wood ash has a pH of 10-13 and about 3-10% potassium (as K2O). A common limit is about 100g per m² per year (a couple of handfuls), and avoid blueberries and potatoes.
c-264.actionItem: If you have fully cooled, pure wood ash today, sift it, test your soil pH, and spread a thin layer only on neutral to alkaline beds.

c-265.title: If your compost smells bad, add carbon
c-265.summary: If compost smells of ammonia or rot, it has too much nitrogen, so mix in carbon materials such as dry leaves.
c-265.principle: Microbes work best at a carbon to nitrogen ratio of about 30:1. C/N = (m_C / m_N) ≈ 30 Excess nitrogen escapes as ammonia smell via NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O.
c-265.example: Food scraps have a C/N of about 15-20, dry leaves 50-80 and sawdust about 400. Mixing 2-3 parts by volume of browns like dry leaves with 1 part food scraps greatly cuts the smell.
c-265.actionItem: If your compost bin smells today, add a bag of dry leaves or shredded cardboard, and mix well to aerate it.

c-266.title: Undercooked kidney beans carry lectin toxicity
c-266.summary: Raw kidney beans, or beans only warmed to about 80°C, can cause vomiting and diarrhea from lectins, so they must be boiled hard.
c-266.principle: Kidney bean lectin (phytohaemagglutinin) is a protein that only denatures with sufficient heat at 100°C. active lectin ―(100°CmathrmC)→, ≥ 10 min denatured lectin At about 80°C, toxicity can actually rise severalfold.
c-266.example: As few as 4-5 raw red kidney beans can cause nausea and vomiting within 1-3 hours, and low-temperature 80°C cooking has been reported to raise toxicity about 5 times above raw beans. Canned beans are already cooked.
c-266.actionItem: If you cook dried kidney beans today, soak 5+ hours, discard the water, boil vigorously for at least 10 minutes, then simmer.

c-267.title: Don't screw the plum syrup jar lid on tight
c-267.summary: Plum syrup ferments with yeast and gives off carbon dioxide, so a tightly sealed jar can build pressure and burst.
c-267.principle: Yeast breaks sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂
c-267.example: Fermenting just 10g of glucose (about 0.056 mol) releases about 2.7L of CO2, so pressure can rise fast in a 3L jar. It happens more when sugar is undissolved or the weather is warm.
c-267.actionItem: Today, set the plum syrup jar lid loosely or cover with cloth, and if it foams, open the lid once a day to vent gas.

c-268.title: Why washing curry stains with soap turns them red
c-268.summary: Curry's yellow pigment (curcumin) turns red in alkali, so scrubbing with alkaline soap makes the stain redder and darker.
c-268.principle: Curcumin is a pH indicator: yellow in acidic to neutral conditions and reddish-brown above about pH 8.6. HCur ⇌ H⁺ + Cur⁻ (yellow ⇌ red)
c-268.example: Bar soap solution has a pH of 9-10, beyond that color change. A neutral dish detergent (about pH 7) doesn't shift the color, and drying in sunlight photodegrades curcumin so it fades.
c-268.actionItem: If you get a curry stain today, rinse with cold water, dab with neutral dish detergent, skip the soap, and dry it in the sun.

c-269.title: Why hard-boiled yolks get a greenish ring
c-269.summary: The green ring on overcooked hard-boiled yolks is harmless iron sulfide, and shorter cooking prevents it.
c-269.principle: Hydrogen sulfide released from sulfur amino acids in the white reacts with iron in the yolk to form iron sulfide. Fe²⁺ + H₂S → FeS + 2H⁺
c-269.example: A large egg is fully hard-boiled about 10-12 minutes after the water starts boiling, and past about 15 minutes a green ring easily forms. Chilling in cold water for 5 minutes right away stops the reaction.
c-269.actionItem: When boiling eggs today, cook only 10-12 minutes after boiling starts, then cool immediately in cold water for 5 minutes.

c-270.title: Swallowing a button battery can burn within 2 hours
c-270.summary: A swallowed coin-shaped button battery can cause severe burns in the esophagus within 2 hours, so go to the ER immediately even without symptoms.
c-270.principle: When the battery touches saliva in the esophagus, current flows and electrolyzes water, producing hydroxide at the negative side and a strongly alkaline burn. 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻
c-270.example: A 20mm, 3V lithium button cell (CR2032) easily lodges in a child's esophagus, and tissue pH can reach 12-13. Damage starts within 2 hours, and you must not induce vomiting or wait it out.
c-270.actionItem: Today, check that the battery compartments of remotes, key fobs and toys are screwed shut, and keep spare cells out of children's reach.

c-271.title: Limit tuna and swordfish to 1-2 times a week because of mercury
c-271.summary: Large predatory fish like tuna and swordfish concentrate methylmercury, so it is wise to limit them to about 1-2 servings a week.
c-271.principle: Microbes convert mercury into methylmercury, which accumulates up the food chain. Hg²⁺ ―(microbes)→ CH₃Hg⁺ The EFSA tolerable weekly intake is 1.3 μg per kg of body weight.
c-271.example: For a 60kg person the weekly limit is 78 μg. A 100g portion of swordfish at 1.0ppm holds about 100 μg and can exceed it in one meal, while 100g of light tuna at about 0.1ppm has about 10 μg. Pregnant people and children should be stricter.
c-271.actionItem: Today, keep tuna, swordfish and shark to about 100g per serving, and plan no more than 1-2 servings of such large fish this week.

c-272.title: Shrimp and crab turn red when cooked
c-272.summary: Shrimp and crab turn red because heat changes their proteins and releases trapped red pigment, which is a good sign they are cooked.
c-272.principle: Alive, astaxanthin is bound to protein (crustacyanin) and looks blue-gray; heat denatures the protein and frees red astaxanthin. astaxanthin-protein (blue-gray) ―(Δ)→ astaxanthin (red) + denatured protein
c-272.example: Shrimp is done at an internal temperature of 63°C (145°F), turning opaque and pink, and 2-3 minutes in boiling water is enough. Cooking longer makes the flesh rubbery.
c-272.actionItem: When boiling shrimp today, lift them out as soon as they turn opaque pink and curl into a C shape, so they don't turn tough.

c-273.title: Old brake fluid weakens braking
c-273.summary: Brake fluid absorbs moisture from the air, lowering its boiling point, and it can boil during hard braking such as long downhills and weaken braking.
c-273.principle: Glycol-based brake fluid is hygroscopic, so water lowers its boiling point and vapor forms; vapor compresses and cannot transmit braking force. (P₂ / P₁) = -ΔH_vapR ≤ ft((1 / T₂) - (1 / T₁))
c-273.example: DOT 4 fluid has a dry boiling point of at least 230°C, but with absorbed water it can fall to 155°C, a drop of about 75°C. It typically absorbs about 2-3% water a year, so replacement every 2 years or 40,000km is advised.
c-273.actionItem: Today, check your service record for the last brake fluid change, and if it was over 2 years ago, book a brake fluid check at a shop.

c-274.title: The pink of ham gift sets comes from nitrite curing
c-274.summary: Ham stays pink after cooking because of color made by nitrite, and it is wise not to eat much processed meat.
c-274.principle: In acid, nitrite becomes nitric oxide (NO), which binds the iron of the meat pigment myoglobin and makes pink nitrosomyoglobin. NO + Mb(Fe²⁺) → Mb(Fe²⁺)-NO
c-274.example: Korea's residual nitrite limit in meat products is 70mg/kg or less. The WHO classifies processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen, estimating about 18% higher colorectal cancer risk for 50g eaten daily.
c-274.actionItem: Refrigerate any ham gift set you receive today, and eat it in portions of about 50g with vegetables.

p-183.title: Why dry beach sand is scorching at noon while wet sand stays cool
p-183.summary: Dry sand heats up fast enough to burn bare soles at midday, while water-soaked sand stays far cooler.
p-183.principle: For the same absorbed heat Q, the temperature rise is ΔT=(Q / mc). Dry sand has c ≈ 0.8kJ/(kg · K) while water has 4.18kJ/(kg · K), so water warms much less, and evaporating water also carries heat away.
p-183.example: If 1kg of sand and 1kg of water each absorb 50kJ, the sand rises about 62 °CmathrmC and the water about 12 °CmathrmC. That is why midday dry sand can reach 50-60°C while sand washed by waves stays around 30°C.
p-183.actionItem: At midday, wear sandals across the dry beach and walk on the wet sand near the waterline.

p-184.title: Seawater holds you up better than fresh water
p-184.summary: The same person floats a little higher in the sea than in a pool or river.
p-184.principle: Buoyancy equals the weight of displaced fluid: F_b=ρ g V. Seawater has ρ ≈ 1025kg/m³ versus 1000kg/m³ for fresh water, about 2.5% more.
p-184.example: A 70kg person must displace 70L of fresh water to float fully, but only 70/1.025 ≈ 68.3L of seawater, about 1.7L less submerged volume. In the much saltier Dead Sea (about 1240kg/m³) floating is far easier.
p-184.actionItem: Practice a relaxed back float in shallow sea water with lungs comfortably full, and keep your life jacket on when it is required.

p-185.title: Keep snorkel tubes short, never longer than about 30cm above water
p-185.summary: A long snorkel tube makes breathing sharply harder because of water pressure, and it traps exhaled air.
p-185.principle: Water pressure rises as ΔP=ρ g h, about 0.1atm (9.8kPa) per metre of depth. Your chest must work against it to inhale, and a longer tube adds dead space where exhaled air stays.
p-185.example: With the tube top at the surface, 30cm of depth gives ΔP ≈ 2.9kPa, but at 1m it is about 9.8kPa, close to the limit of human inspiratory pressure, so breathing becomes nearly impossible. A tube 18mm wide and 30cm long holds about 75mL of dead space.
p-185.actionItem: Check your snorkel length today and never use a longer tube or a hose added to the end.

p-186.title: A pool floor looks shallower than it really is
p-186.summary: The bottom of the water looks only about three quarters as deep as it really is, so the water is deeper than it appears.
p-186.principle: Light bends when it leaves water for air, so apparent depth is d'=(d / n). Water has n ≈ 1.33, so d' ≈ 0.75 d.
p-186.example: A pool floor 2.0m down appears at 2.0/1.33 ≈ 1.5m when viewed from above. A 3m depth appears as about 2.3m, a 0.7m difference.
p-186.actionItem: Read the depth markings on the pool wall before getting in, and never dive head-first into a section whose depth you do not know.

p-187.title: Why you suddenly hit a cold layer of water in the sea
p-187.summary: Summer seas and lakes form a warm upper layer over cold water, so a few steps deeper can suddenly feel much colder.
p-187.principle: Sun-warmed surface water has lower density ρ(T) and floats, while cold water sinks, forming a stable layer (the thermocline). A stable layer resists mixing, so temperature changes sharply at the boundary.
p-187.example: Water density is about 997.0kg/m³ at 25°C and 999.1kg/m³ at 15°C, only 0.2% apart, yet enough to keep layers separate. A 5-10°C drop within a few metres is common in lakes and seas, and offshore wind that pushes surface water away can pull cold water up to the beach.
p-187.actionItem: Before going deep, lower your legs in slowly to feel the temperature change, and on cold-water days do not swim far out in one go.

p-188.title: Diving entry speed: from 3m you hit the water at about 28km/h
p-188.summary: Jumping from 3m means hitting the water at roughly 28km/h, so entering without checking the depth is dangerous.
p-188.principle: Ignoring air drag, energy conservation gives the speed after falling a height h: v=√(2gh).
p-188.example: For h=3m, v=√(2 × 9.8 × 3) ≈ 7.7m/s ≈ 27.6km/h. From 10m it is about 14m/s (around 50km/h): more than 3 times the height gives about 1.8 times the speed.
p-188.actionItem: Check the depth sign before any jump or dive, and never go in head-first where the depth is unknown.

p-189.title: Shop for summer clothes by reflectivity, not just colour
p-189.summary: How cool a summer garment feels depends on how much sunlight it reflects and how well it breathes, not just on the colour name.
p-189.principle: Absorbed energy is q=(1-α) I, where α is the albedo (reflectance) and I the solar irradiance. Light colours reflect more visible light, so they absorb less.
p-189.example: At I=1000W/m², white clothing with α=0.7 absorbs about 300W/m², while black with α=0.1 absorbs about 900W/m², a threefold difference. Some dark fabrics block UV better, so also check the UPF rating.
p-189.actionItem: When buying summer clothes, choose light colours with a breathable weave and check the UPF label.

p-190.title: A clear bottle of water or a glass fishbowl can start a fire
p-190.summary: A round clear bottle or bowl of water can focus sunlight like a lens and ignite flammable material.
p-190.principle: A convex lens obeys (1 / f)=(1 / u)+(1 / v), and light from a very distant object such as the sun (u →) focuses at v=f. A water-filled sphere has focal length f ≈ (nD / 4(n-1)).
p-190.example: A bottle with diameter D=8cm gives f ≈ 1.33 × 8/(4 × 0.33) ≈ 8cm. At 1000W/m², a cross-section of about 50cm² collects about 5W, squeezed into a spot of a few mm², hot enough to scorch paper or fabric.
p-190.actionItem: Move water bottles, fishbowls and glass ornaments out of sunny windowsills, balconies and cars, or cover them with opaque cloth.

p-191.title: Choose a watermelon by the sound of a knock
p-191.summary: A ripe watermelon tends to give a low, resonant sound, so knocking is a useful clue, but combine it with weight and appearance.
p-191.principle: An object's natural frequency is f ∝ √(k/m). As the flesh ripens its stiffness k drops, lowering the pitch, while an unripe melon sounds higher and harder.
p-191.example: With the same mass, if stiffness falls 36% to 0.64k, the frequency becomes √(0.64)=0.8 times, a 20% drop. Among melons of similar size, also pick the heavier one and one with a yellow ground spot.
p-191.actionItem: When buying a watermelon, knock to listen for a low, resonant note and pick the heavier one among equal sizes.

p-192.title: Inflate pool tubes and beach balls to only about 80%
p-192.summary: Under hot sun the air inside expands, so a fully inflated tube or beach ball can burst; 80% full is safer.
p-192.principle: For an ideal gas PV=nRT, at constant pressure V ∝ T (Charles's law), and at fixed volume P ∝ T. Use absolute temperature in kelvin.
p-192.example: Rising from 25°C (298K) to 50°C (323K) multiplies volume by 323/298 ≈ 1.084, an 8.4% increase. A tube filled to 95% already exceeds its limit, and in a 60°C car trunk (333K) the growth is about 12%.
p-192.actionItem: Inflate tubes and beach balls to only 80-90% and do not leave them in a hot car or direct sun for long.

p-193.title: Why raindrops do not hurt: terminal velocity of about 9m/s
p-193.summary: Even drops from several kilometres up stop speeding up at around 30km/h because of air drag, so rain does not hurt, but hail is fast and dangerous.
p-193.principle: Speed levels off when gravity equals drag: mg=12ρ v²C_dA gives terminal velocity v_t=√((2mg / ρ C_dA)).
p-193.example: A 5mm raindrop falls at about 9m/s (32km/h) and a 2mm drop at about 6.5m/s. In a vacuum a 1km fall would reach about 140m/s. A 2cm hailstone falls at about 20m/s (72km/h), enough to dent a car.
p-193.actionItem: On days when hail is forecast, check the forecast and park your car under cover.

p-194.title: Aim the air conditioner's airflow upward
p-194.summary: When cooling, send the airflow upward so cold air sinks and the whole room cools evenly.
p-194.principle: Ideal-gas density is ρ=(PM / RT), higher at lower temperature. Cold air is heavier and sinks while warm air rises, driving natural convection.
p-194.example: At 1atm, air at 18°C (291K) is about 1.21kg/m³ and at 28°C (301K) about 1.17kg/m³, so cold air is about 3.4% denser. Aiming upward avoids a direct blast on people, so a setpoint 1-2°C higher can still feel comfortable, saving energy.
p-194.actionItem: When cooling today, set the louvres upward or horizontal, and downward when heating.

p-195.title: Watching waves from a breakwater: double the wave height, four times the energy
p-195.summary: Doubling the wave height quadruples a wave's energy, so watching waves from a breakwater or rocks is far more dangerous than it looks.
p-195.principle: For regular waves, the energy per unit area is E=(1 / 8)ρ g H², proportional to the square of the wave height H.
p-195.example: With ρ=1025kg/m³, a 1m wave carries about 1.26kJ/m² and a 2m wave about 5.0kJ/m², four times as much. Overtopping waves can sweep a person off in one hit.
p-195.actionItem: On rough-sea days, stay off breakwaters and rocks, and check the marine forecast for wave height before you go.

p-196.title: Phone overheating in midsummer: take the case off to protect battery life
p-196.summary: Heat quickly shortens battery life, so in midsummer remove the case and avoid direct sun to let heat escape.
p-196.principle: Conductive thermal resistance is R=(L / kA), and with heat output P the temperature difference is ΔT=PR. A thick insulating case raises R and traps heat.
p-196.example: A 2mm silicone case with k ≈ 0.2W/(m · K) over 70cm² gives R ≈ 1.4K/W. At 3W, as with navigation, the phone runs about 4°C hotter. Lithium-ion cells age faster above 35°C, roughly doubling their ageing rate for every 10°C rise.
p-196.actionItem: When using navigation or charging in the sun, take the case off and keep the phone in shade or somewhere ventilated.

p-197.title: A flying disc flies farther and straighter with spin
p-197.summary: Snapping your wrist to put spin on a disc keeps it steady and sends it farther, and throwing is a light whole-body exercise too.
p-197.principle: With no external torque, angular momentum L=Iω is conserved. A spinning disc resists changes in its orientation, a gyroscopic effect that stabilises its attitude.
p-197.example: A disc thrown with about 5-8 revolutions per second flies steadily for 30-40m, while one thrown flat with no spin flips or drops within a few metres. At the same speed, doubling the spin doubles L, so twice the torque is needed to upset it.
p-197.actionItem: Spend 10 minutes at a park throwing a disc with a wrist snap, and loosen your shoulders and wrists first.

p-198.title: Microwaved water may not look like it is boiling, then suddenly erupts
p-198.summary: Heating water in a smooth cup for too long can push it past boiling without bubbles, then it erupts violently when disturbed and can scald.
p-198.principle: Bubbles need nucleation sites such as scratches or particles. A smooth cup and clean water have none, so water can superheat above 100°C. A jolt or added powder makes it flash to vapour at once.
p-198.example: Heating 250mL from 20°C to 100°C needs Q=0.25 × 4.18 × 80 ≈ 84kJ, about 105 s in an 800W microwave. Heating longer can leave some water above 100°C, so even a spoonful of powder can make it foam over.
p-198.actionItem: When heating water, add a wooden stick or microwave-safe stirrer, let it rest 30 seconds before taking it out, and keep your face away from the cup.

p-199.title: Preheat the pan until water drops roll like beads
p-199.summary: Preheat a stainless pan only until water drops roll around like beads: food sticks less, and extra heating wastes gas.
p-199.principle: Above about 200°C a vapour film forms under a water drop, so it floats and skitters instead of boiling away (the Leidenfrost effect). That is a good signal to add oil.
p-199.example: Heating a 1.2kg stainless pan (specific heat about 0.5kJ/(kg·K)) from 20°C to 200°C takes Q=1.2 × 0.5 × 180 ≈ 108kJ (about 0.03kWh). If a drop hisses and vanishes at once, the pan is still around 150-190°C.
p-199.actionItem: Flick a drop of water onto the pan; when it rolls like a bead, add the oil and lower the heat.

p-200.title: Use anchors on drywall to spread the load
p-200.summary: Drywall is weak and a bare screw pulls out easily, so use an anchor that opens behind the board to spread the load over a wider area.
p-200.principle: Bearing pressure is p=(F / A). The larger the contact area A, the lower the pressure on the board for the same load. Expansion and toggle anchors open behind the wall to enlarge the area.
p-200.example: A 10kg frame (F ≈ 98N) held by a screw with about 1cm² of bearing gives about 0.98MPa, but a toggle anchor with 8cm² gives about 0.12MPa, one eighth. Each anchor has its own rated load, so check the package.
p-200.actionItem: Hang heavy items on a stud, or pick an anchor whose rated load comfortably exceeds the item's weight.

p-201.title: Bulb colour temperature: 3000K for the living room, 5000K for the study
p-201.summary: The higher a bulb's colour temperature, the bluer and cooler its light. Choose a low K for relaxing spaces and a high K for study and work.
p-201.principle: A hot blackbody emits most strongly at λₘₐₓ=(b / T) (Wien's law), b=2.898 × 10⁻³ m · K. Higher temperature shifts toward blue, and a bulb's colour temperature is named by comparison with that blackbody colour.
p-201.example: A 3000K blackbody peaks near 966nm, 5000K near 580nm and 6500K near 446nm, so higher feels bluer. Living rooms typically use 2700-3000K (warm white) and study rooms 4000-5000K (daylight).
p-201.actionItem: When buying bulbs, check the K rating on the box and pick about 3000K for the living room and about 5000K for the study.

p-202.title: Check LED flicker with your phone's slow-motion mode
p-202.summary: LED lights can flicker invisibly, and cheap ones flicker more deeply, which can tire your eyes. Slow-motion video shows it easily.
p-202.principle: A rectified-AC LED varies at twice the mains frequency: 120Hz on 60Hz grids and 100Hz on 50Hz grids. The period is T=(1 / f), about 8.3 ms at 120Hz.
p-202.example: Shooting a lamp in 240 fps slow motion gives a frame gap of about 4.2 ms, so about 2 frames fit in each cycle and bands or brightness steps show up. Deeply flickering products can cause eye strain or headaches in some people.
p-202.actionItem: Film your home lights in slow motion, and if you see bands, consider swapping in a flicker-free product.

p-203.title: Use engine braking downhill to avoid overheated brakes
p-203.summary: On a long downhill, using only the brakes builds up heat and loses stopping power, so use engine braking in a low gear as well, which can also save fuel.
p-203.principle: The potential energy mgh lost, minus the change in kinetic energy (1 / 2)mv², becomes heat in the brake pads. If they overheat, friction collapses in what is called brake fade.
p-203.example: A 1500kg car descending 500m turns about 1500 × 9.8 × 500 ≈ 7.4MJ (about 2kWh) into heat. Stopping from 100km/h (27.8m/s) alone is about 580kJ. Using a low gear lets engine drag share that load.
p-203.actionItem: Before a long descent begins, shift down to a low gear so you only need to brake occasionally.

p-204.title: Swinging your arms while walking saves energy
p-204.summary: Walking with natural arm swing costs less energy than holding the arms still, and keeps your body steadier.
p-204.principle: An arm swinging from the shoulder is a pendulum with natural period T=2π√(L/g). When the swing resonates with your stride, effort drops, and the swinging arms cancel the torso twist created by the legs.
p-204.example: With an effective arm length L ≈ 0.35m, T ≈ 1.2 s, close to a stride period of about 1.1 s. Studies find that preventing arm swing raises walking energy cost by about 10%.
p-204.actionItem: On today's walk, relax your shoulders and let your arms swing naturally for 10 minutes.

p-205.title: Why singing sounds great in the shower: reverberation
p-205.summary: Tile and glass in a bathroom absorb almost no sound, so it lingers and makes singing sound full, but on a video call that echo is a nuisance.
p-205.principle: Reverberation time follows Sabine's formula T=(0.161V / A), where V is room volume (m³) and A the total absorption (m²), the sum of each surface area times its absorption coefficient.
p-205.example: With a volume of 7.2m³, about 23m² of surface and a tile absorption coefficient near 0.02, A ≈ 0.46m² and T ≈ 2.5 s. A carpeted, curtained living room is around 0.4-0.6 s, so sound dies away far faster.
p-205.actionItem: If you need to take a call or record in the bathroom, hang towels or a mat to cut the echo, or move to a room with soft furnishings.

p-206.title: Keep the AC drain hose sloping downhill all the way
p-206.summary: AC condensate flows only by gravity, so the drain hose must slope down its whole length, or sags and kinks can block it and leak water indoors.
p-206.principle: Condensate flows from high to low under gravity, so the hose needs a fall of at least 1cm per metre (slope 1/100 or more). Pooled water leads to grime, clogs and leaks.
p-206.example: On humid days an air conditioner makes roughly 1L of condensate per hour. A 5m hose must end at least 5cm lower than it starts. A leak soaking the wall and floor can be costly to repair.
p-206.actionItem: Check that the drain hose runs downhill to the very end, has no kinks or sags, and that its end is not submerged.

p-207.title: It is hard to tell where sound comes from underwater
p-207.summary: Sound travels so fast in water that the time difference between your ears disappears, making it hard to tell which way a boat or person is coming from.
p-207.principle: Sound travels at about 343m/s in air and about 1500m/s in water. We judge direction from the arrival-time difference between the ears, Δt=(dθ / v), which becomes tiny when v is large.
p-207.example: With ears d ≈ 0.2m apart, the maximum time difference is about 0.58 ms in air but about 0.13 ms underwater, 4.4 times smaller. The brain struggles to resolve it, so you cannot tell where a motor is.
p-207.actionItem: When swimming, stay inside the buoyed area and lift your head regularly to look for boats with your eyes.

p-208.title: A water gun shoots farthest at 45 degrees
p-208.summary: When air drag is small, a water jet fired at 45 degrees goes the farthest. Try it when you compete for distance at the water park.
p-208.principle: For a projectile launched and landing at the same height, the range is R=(v²2θ / g), largest when 2θ is maximal, at θ=45^°. In practice air drag can lower the best angle slightly.
p-208.example: A jet at 10m/s reaches R=10²/9.8 ≈ 10.2m at 45 degrees. At 30 or 60 degrees, 60°Capprox0.866 gives about 8.8m, 86% as far.
p-208.actionItem: When using a water gun, vary the angle to find the farthest throw, but never aim at anyone's face or eyes.

p-209.title: Why a ball curves: spin and the Magnus force
p-209.summary: A spinning ball curves sideways in flight because the spin makes air pressure differ on its two sides.
p-209.principle: A spinning ball moving through air feels a force perpendicular to both its velocity v and spin axis ω: F=S(ω × v) (the Magnus force). Air moves faster on one side, creating a pressure difference.
p-209.example: A football free kick at 108km/h (30m/s) spinning about 8 times per second can bend sideways about 3-4m over 25m. With no spin it flies almost straight.
p-209.actionItem: Next time you kick a ball in a park, put side spin on it with the inside of your foot and watch how the curve changes.

p-210.title: The beach horizon is only about 4.7km away
p-210.summary: From an eye height of 1.7m the sea horizon is only about 4.7km away, so the open sea you see from the beach is closer than it looks.
p-210.principle: Because the Earth is round, the distance to the horizon from eye height h (m) is d ≈ 3.57√(h) km. This value already includes the correction for atmospheric refraction.
p-210.example: At 1.7m eye height, d ≈ 3.57 × √(1.7) ≈ 4.65km, and from a 10m high building it is about 11.3km. A ship in the distance loses its hull first, and only its mast remains visible.
p-210.actionItem: At the beach, watch a distant ship and notice how its hull disappears below the horizon while only the mast remains.

p-211.title: Press the RCD test button monthly during the rainy season
p-211.summary: Leakage risk rises in humid rainy-season weather, so check monthly that your residual-current breaker works by pressing its test button.
p-211.principle: An RCD senses the difference between current going in and coming out, I<sub>Δ</sub> = |Iᵢₙ - Iₒᵤₜ|, and typically cuts power within about 0.03 s once it reaches its rated sensitivity, often 30mA. The test button creates that imbalance on purpose.
p-211.example: A 30mA leakage current can be dangerous to a person who touches a live part, so it must trip immediately at that level. When you press the test button the lever should drop and the power should cut off.
p-211.actionItem: Save any open work, press the RCD test button to check that it trips, and call an electrician if it does not.

p-212.title: Check an AC remote's infrared with your phone camera
p-212.summary: If your air conditioner ignores the remote, use a phone camera to see whether the remote is sending a signal and avoid an unnecessary repair visit.
p-212.principle: A remote's infrared LED sends signals at about 940nm, invisible to the eye, with photon energy E=(hc / λ) ≈ 1240 eV · nm940 nm ≈ 1.32 eV. A camera's CMOS sensor detects this light and shows it as a bright glow on screen.
p-212.example: Point the remote at the camera lens and press a button: a faint violet or white flicker on screen means the remote works. If nothing shows, replace the batteries (usually two AAA) or check the remote first. Some front cameras have weaker infrared filters and show it better.
p-212.actionItem: Open your phone's front camera, press a remote button and check whether you can see a light.

p-213.title: Why your weight changes when an elevator starts and stops
p-213.summary: You feel heavier as an elevator starts up and lighter as it stops, but your mass has not changed: the floor's push on you has.
p-213.principle: In an elevator accelerating upward at a, the floor pushes you with normal force N=m(g+a). A scale reads this value, so apparent weight changes.
p-213.example: For a 70kg person with an upward acceleration of 1m/s², N=70 × (9.8+1) ≈ 756N, so a scale reads about 77kg. When the rising elevator stops with a downward acceleration of 1m/s², it feels like about 63kg.
p-213.actionItem: As an elevator starts and stops, bend your knees slightly and hold the handrail to stay balanced.

p-214.title: The right-hand side of a typhoon's path is more dangerous
p-214.summary: In the Northern Hemisphere a typhoon's winds are stronger to the right of its track, so areas to the right of the path should brace for greater damage.
p-214.principle: A typhoon has counter-clockwise rotating wind vᵣₒₜ and the storm's own forward speed v_move. On the right of the track they add and on the left they subtract: v_wind=vᵣₒₜ ± v_move.
p-214.example: With 40m/s rotating wind and an 8m/s forward speed, the right side sees about 48m/s and the left about 32m/s, and since wind pressure scales with speed squared, the ratio is (48/32)²=2.25. The right side is called the dangerous semicircle.
p-214.actionItem: During a typhoon, check the forecast track, and if you are to the right of it, cancel or postpone outings and coastal trips.

p-215.title: Double the typhoon wind speed, four times the wind load
p-215.summary: When wind speed doubles, the force on windows and signs quadruples, so you cannot judge a typhoon by the feel of an ordinary breeze.
p-215.principle: Wind force on an area A is F=(1 / 2)ρ v²A (assuming a drag coefficient near 1), proportional to speed squared. Air density is ρ ≈ 1.225kg/m³.
p-215.example: On a 1m² window, 20m/s wind gives F ≈ 245N and 40m/s about 980N (about 100 kgf), four times as much. Large glass panes carry far more.
p-215.actionItem: Before a typhoon, check that your window latches are locked, and during it keep away from the windows.

p-216.title: If windows rattle in strong wind, fit gap cushioning
p-216.summary: A rattling window means the wind is matching its natural frequency, so cushioning the gaps cuts both noise and draughts.
p-216.principle: A window sash's natural frequency is f=(1 / 2π)√((k / m)). When gust frequency is close to f the sash resonates and shakes hard. Cushioning adds damping and changes the stiffness k to avoid resonance.
p-216.example: An 8kg sash held with k=80kN/m has f=(1 / 2π)√(80000/8) ≈ 15.9Hz. If cushioning doubles k, it rises to about 22.5Hz and damping increases, so rattling eases. Sealing the gaps also cuts winter draughts and saves heating energy.
p-216.actionItem: Stick 5-10mm weatherstrip cushioning along the window frame gaps and see whether the rattling quietens.

p-217.title: Why a camping tarp flaps and lifts in the wind
p-217.summary: Fast wind sweeping over a tarp lowers pressure and lifts the fabric, so how you anchor it decides safety on windy days.
p-217.principle: By Bernoulli's principle, pressure drops where fluid speed is high, and the pressure difference between the two sides is about ΔP ≈ (1 / 2)ρ v². That difference is the lift on the cloth.
p-217.example: At 10m/s, ΔP ≈ (1 / 2) × 1.225 × 10² ≈ 61Pa, so a 4m by 4m (16m²) tarp can see up to about 980N (roughly 100 kgf). At 20m/s it is four times that.
p-217.actionItem: When buying a tarp check the number of eyelets and how well they are reinforced, and when pitching face the low edge into the wind and drive stakes in deep at an angle.

p-218.title: Run the AC fan for 10 minutes before switching it off
p-218.summary: Running the AC in fan mode for about 10 minutes before turning it off dries the inside and reduces mould odour, at almost no electricity cost.
p-218.principle: After cooling, condensed droplets remain on the evaporator coil. Evaporation rate scales with the vapour pressure deficit (p_s-p), so blowing humid air away dries it faster.
p-218.example: Fan mode draws about 40W, so 10 minutes uses only 40 × (10 / 60) ≈ 6.7Wh. Leftover moisture lets mould and bacteria grow, causing odour and leading to cleaning costs and reduced performance.
p-218.actionItem: Today, before switching the AC off, run fan or dry mode for 10 minutes, or enable the auto-dry function if it has one.

p-219.title: Keep your seatbelt fastened in-flight, whenever seated
p-219.summary: Turbulence strikes without warning, so keeping your seatbelt on whenever you are seated is the surest way to prevent injury.
p-219.principle: By Newton's second law F=ma, when the plane accelerates sharply vertically, your body feels the same acceleration. With a vertical acceleration of ± 1g, your apparent weight becomes zero or doubles.
p-219.example: A 70kg person feels a force change of about 0.5 × 70 × 9.8 ≈ 343N even in moderate ± 0.5g turbulence. In severe turbulence above 1g, an unbelted person can be lifted from the seat and hit the ceiling.
p-219.actionItem: While seated in flight, keep your seatbelt fastened snugly low across your hips.

p-220.title: A car submerged in water cannot have its door opened
p-220.summary: A submerged car's doors will not open against water pressure, so escape quickly through a window rather than the door.
p-220.principle: The force of water on a door is the average-depth pressure times the area: F=ρ g(h / 2)A. Until water levels inside and out equalise, you must push against this force.
p-220.example: With a door 1.0m wide and water 0.5m deep (area 0.5m²), F=1000 × 9.8 × 0.25 × 0.5 ≈ 1225N, about 125 kgf. Power windows may stop working soon. You must act as soon as the car starts to sink, before it fills.
p-220.actionItem: Keep an emergency window-breaker within reach in your car, and never drive into a flooded road.

p-221.title: Unplug appliances when thunder rolls
p-221.summary: Lightning can induce a momentary extremely high voltage (a surge) on wires that can wreck TVs and computers, so unplug before the storm arrives.
p-221.principle: When lightning current changes rapidly, it induces a voltage V=-M(dI / dt) in nearby wire loops (M is mutual inductance). The faster the change, the more kilovolts appear.
p-221.example: With M=1 µ H and dI/dt=6 × 10⁹ A/s, V ≈ 6kV, beyond the roughly 1.5-2.5kV that household 220V appliances can withstand. But do not approach plugs to pull them while lightning is right overhead.
p-221.actionItem: Before the storm arrives, unplug your TV, computer and router or use a surge-protector strip, and do not touch cables or devices during thunder.

p-222.title: Bring balcony plant pots indoors before a typhoon
p-222.summary: A plant pot blown or knocked off by a typhoon can be deadly for someone below, so bring balcony pots and objects inside beforehand.
p-222.principle: A body falling from height h carries energy mgh, and without air drag its speed is v=√(2gh). Danger grows with weight and height.
p-222.example: A 5kg pot falling from about 30m (10th floor) reaches v ≈ 24m/s (about 87km/h) with energy of about 5 × 9.8 × 30 ≈ 1470J, similar to a roughly 3.8kg object travelling at about 100km/h.
p-222.actionItem: When a typhoon is forecast, bring pots from the balcony rail, drying racks and small furniture indoors and lock the windows.

p-223.title: Seasickness is milder in a low, central part of the ship
p-223.summary: The middle, lower decks of a ship move the least, so seasickness is milder there. Choose a cabin or seat in that area.
p-223.principle: A ship rocks about a point near its centre, so the size of motion at a location scales with its distance from the rotation centre (s ≈ rθ). Motion that your eyes see clashing with what the inner-ear vestibular system senses causes seasickness.
p-223.example: For a ± 2^° (0.035 rad) rocking, the bow 40m from the centre moves about ± 1.4m, while a spot 5m from the centre moves only about ± 0.17m, an 8-fold difference. Higher decks also sway more.
p-223.actionItem: When booking a ship, choose a cabin low and amidships, and once aboard look at the horizon.

p-224.title: Shooting stars appear after your eyes adapt to the dark for 20 minutes
