p-224.summary: Coming from a bright place, your eyes need about 20-30 minutes to adapt to the dark, and until then faint meteors are hard to see.
p-224.principle: In the dark, rod cells become more sensitive as their photopigment regenerates, and the visual threshold light level drops steeply over time. Full rod adaptation takes about 20-30 minutes, and light from a phone screen undoes it.
p-224.example: Once dark-adapted, sensitivity to light is roughly 10,000 times higher or more than in the light. The Perseid meteor shower peaks around 12-13 August each year, and under dark skies with little moonlight or city glow dozens can be seen per hour.
p-224.actionItem: When you go out to watch a meteor shower, stay in the darkest spot you can, keep off your phone for 20 minutes and gaze broadly at the sky.

p-225.title: Why the screen is unreadable outdoors at midday: luminance and reflected light
p-225.summary: A screen is unreadable in bright outdoors not because it is dim but because sunlight reflected off its surface overwhelms the light it emits.
p-225.principle: Contrast ratio is CR=(L+L_a / L_a), where L is the screen luminance (nit) and L_a=(RE / π) is the luminance of ambient light reflected by the surface (R reflectance, E illuminance). Strong reflection pushes the contrast ratio toward 1.
p-225.example: In direct sun with E=100,000 lx and reflectance R=2%, L_a ≈ 637 nit. An 800 nit screen gives CR ≈ (800+637)/637 ≈ 2.3:1, nearly unreadable, whereas in a 300 lx room L_a ≈ 1.9 nit and CR is in the hundreds.
p-225.actionItem: On bright days, set screen brightness to maximum or auto, and shade the screen with your body or hand.

p-226.title: Why your map compass app points the wrong way while travelling
p-226.summary: A phone compass reads the weak Earth's magnetic field, so nearby magnets or metal easily throw its direction off.
p-226.principle: Earth's field is only about 50 µT (in Korea), so when interfering magnetic fields B_int from nearby magnetic objects are added, the heading error is θ ≈ B_intBₑₐᵣₜₕ.
p-226.example: Even an extra 10 µT from a magnetic case or car mount gives an error of (10/50) ≈ 11^°. Korea also has a magnetic declination of about 8°, so the gap between magnetic and true north must be considered.
p-226.actionItem: If your map app shows an odd heading, move the phone in a figure-8 to recalibrate the compass and keep it away from magnets and metal.

p-227.title: Every 100m you climb, the air gets about 0.65 degrees cooler
p-227.summary: A high mountain is much cooler than the lowlands on the same day, so dressing for the valley heat leaves you cold on top.
p-227.principle: Air temperature falls with altitude at an average lapse rate ≈ 6.5 °CmathrmC/km. For an altitude difference Δz the temperature changes by ΔT=-Δz.
p-227.example: If it is 30°C at a 100m start, the summit of Jirisan's Cheonwangbong (1915m) is 30-0.65 × 18.15 ≈ 18.2 °CmathrmC. Wind makes it feel colder still.
p-227.actionItem: Before a mountain trip, check the forecast temperature at summit height and pack a light windproof layer.

p-228.title: Tropical nights: heat the walls stored by day comes out at night
p-228.summary: Tropical nights feel hot because heat stored in walls and floors by day is released at night, so block the sun by day and ventilate at night.
p-228.principle: A thermal-mass material such as concrete stores Q=mcΔT of heat as its temperature rises and releases it when the room cools. Greater mass and specific heat mean more storage.
p-228.example: A 20cm thick, 10m² concrete wall (about 4800kg, specific heat about 0.88kJ/(kg·K)) that warms by 5°C stores Q ≈ 4800 × 0.88 × 5 ≈ 21MJ (about 5.9kWh). That heat leaks into the room slowly all night.
p-228.actionItem: By day, close curtains or blinds on sunny windows, and when it gets cooler outside than inside at night, open windows to ventilate, then set the AC to 26-27°C.

p-229.title: A lukewarm shower 1-2 hours before bed
p-229.summary: A warm shower 1-2 hours before bed helps the body shed heat, creating the temperature drop that favors falling asleep.
p-229.principle: Warm water widens peripheral blood vessels, so heat leaves through the skin and core temperature falls: q = hA(T_s - T_a).
p-229.example: A 10-minute shower at about 40°C taken 1-2 hours before bed is reported in studies to shorten time to fall asleep by roughly 10 minutes on average.
p-229.actionItem: Tonight, take a 10-minute shower at about 40°C, 1-2 hours before you go to bed.

p-230.title: A plunger works on the pull, not just the push
p-230.summary: A plunger works best when the cup is sealed under water and pulled sharply, which jerks the clog loose.
p-230.principle: The pressure difference across the cup creates the force: F = ΔP · A. Water, not air, transmits that pressure fully.
p-230.example: With a cup area of 0.01m² and ΔP = 5kPa, about 50N (roughly 5 kgf) acts on the clog.
p-230.actionItem: Today, cover the plunger cup with water, seal it, then press gently and pull sharply 10 times (never combine with drain chemicals).

p-231.title: Finer screw threads drive in with less force
p-231.summary: The tighter the thread spacing (pitch), the more force a screw multiplies, so fine threads suit hard wood.
p-231.principle: The ideal mechanical advantage of a screw is MA = (2π r / p) (r: driver radius, p: pitch).
p-231.example: With r = 2mm, a 1.0mm pitch gives MA ≈ 12.6 and a 0.5mm pitch gives MA ≈ 25, half the force (ignoring friction).
p-231.actionItem: Today, pick a finer-pitch screw for hardwood and drill a pilot hole first.

p-232.title: Resistance bands change resistance with stretch length
p-232.summary: A resistance band pulls back roughly in proportion to how far it is stretched, so a consistent stretch length keeps your workout intensity consistent.
p-232.principle: Hooke's law: F = kx (an approximation, since rubber becomes nonlinear at large stretch).
p-232.example: A band with k = 100N/m gives about 30N at 0.3m of stretch and about 60N at 0.6m.
p-232.actionItem: In today's band workout, mark your hand spacing so you stretch to the same length each time.

p-233.title: A sudden cool breeze before a shower means take shelter
p-233.summary: A sudden chilly gust just before a storm is a thunderstorm's cold downdraft, warning that lightning and strong winds are near.
p-233.principle: Cold air is denser, so it sinks and spreads out: ρ = (P / R_s T).
p-233.example: At 1atm, air density is about 1.165kg/m³ at 30°C and 1.204kg/m³ at 20°C, about 3% heavier, and gusts can reach 60-90km/h.
p-233.actionItem: If you feel a sudden cool wind outdoors and hear thunder, move into a building or a car right away.

p-234.title: Car AC: outside air first, recirculate once cool
p-234.summary: Vent the hot cabin with open windows first, then switch to recirculation once it cools to cut the cooling load.
p-234.principle: Cooling load scales with airflow and temperature difference: Q = m c_p ΔT.
p-234.example: With m = 0.1kg/s and c_p = 1.005kJ/(kg · K), cooling outside air from 35°C to 22°C takes about 1.3kW, while recirculated 25°C air takes about 0.3kW.
p-234.actionItem: Today, open the windows for 1 minute after getting in, then switch to recirculation once cool (refresh with outside air now and then on long drives).

p-235.title: Steady night shots with the 1/focal-length rule
p-235.summary: When shooting handheld, keeping shutter time shorter than the reciprocal of focal length greatly reduces hand-shake blur.
p-235.principle: Rule of thumb: t ≤ (1 / f) (seconds, with f the full-frame equivalent focal length in mm).
p-235.example: A 50mm lens stays safe at about 1/50 s or faster and a 200mm lens at 1/200 s or faster; in dim light, raise ISO or brace yourself.
p-235.actionItem: Tonight, brace your elbows against your body or a wall and use a 2-second timer for a night shot.

p-236.title: A campfire burns better with logs stacked upright
p-236.summary: Leaning logs upright in a teepee draws air in from below through the chimney effect, so the fire catches well.
p-236.principle: Draft pressure from a hot gas column: ΔP ≈ ρ g h (ΔT / T).
p-236.example: With h = 0.5m, flame-side gas at 600K and air at 300K, ΔP ≈ 1.2 × 9.8 × 0.5 × (300 / 600) ≈ 3Pa.
p-236.actionItem: At your next campfire, lean small logs into a teepee, keep water nearby, and never light one where fires are banned.

p-237.title: Melting ice does not make the glass overflow
p-237.summary: Floating ice barely changes the water level as it melts, so a brim-full glass does not overflow.
p-237.principle: Floating ice displaces its own weight of water: V_d = (m / ρ_w), and the meltwater also occupies (m / ρ_w).
p-237.example: 90g of ice displaces 90mL of water (only about 8cm³ of its roughly 98cm³ sticks out), and melts into 90mL, so the level stays put.
p-237.actionItem: Today, fill a glass to the brim with ice and water and watch the level as it melts (do not press the ice down).

p-238.title: Check that your extinguisher gauge is in the green
p-238.summary: A stored-pressure extinguisher is ready to use only when its gauge needle sits in the green zone (normal 0.7-0.98MPa).
p-238.principle: Pressure is force per unit area: P = (F / A). If gas leaks, the vessel pressure drops and the spray weakens.
p-238.example: The normal 0.7-0.98MPa is about 7-9.8bar (7 to 10 times atmospheric); a needle in red or near zero means it needs replacing or refilling.
p-238.actionItem: Today, check that the gauge on your home or car extinguisher is in the green, and look at the safety pin and hose too.

p-239.title: A seesaw balances when the heavier rider sits nearer the pivot
p-239.summary: Riders of different weights can balance a seesaw if the heavier one sits closer to the pivot.
p-239.principle: Torque balance: m₁ d₁ = m₂ d₂.
p-239.example: A 30kg child 2m from the pivot balances a 60kg child 1m away, since 30 × 2 = 60 × 1.
p-239.actionItem: At the playground today, try shifting seat positions to find the balance point, and get off one at a time safely.

p-240.title: Why bridges and roads have gaps at their joints
p-240.summary: Metal and concrete expand when hot, so bridges and roads leave expansion gaps at their joints.
p-240.principle: Linear expansion: ΔL = α L ΔT.
p-240.example: A 100m steel span (α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K) going from -10°C to 40°C lengthens by ΔL ≈ 0.06m, about 60mm.
p-240.actionItem: Today, look for the expansion joints when you cross a bridge or walkway, and never wedge stones or trash into them.

p-241.title: Flashlight batteries: series is brighter, parallel lasts longer
p-241.summary: Batteries in series add voltage for a brighter light; in parallel, voltage stays the same and capacity adds up, but the total energy is identical.
p-241.principle: Series: V = V₁ + V₂. Parallel: Q = Q₁ + Q₂. Energy E = VQ.
p-241.example: Two 1.5V, 2500 mAh cells give 3V at 2.5 Ah in series or 1.5V at 5 Ah in parallel, both about 7.5Wh.
p-241.actionItem: Today, replace flashlight batteries all at once with the same type and charge level, and never mix old and new.

p-242.title: A windscreen cuts wind noise in beach videos
p-242.summary: A furry windscreen over the mic breaks up turbulence and cuts wind noise a lot.
p-242.principle: Turbulence onset is governed by the Reynolds number: Re = (ρ v D / µ).
p-242.example: At 5m/s wind and a 1cm mic, Re ≈ 3,300, and a furry cover reduces wind noise by roughly 10-20dB.
p-242.actionItem: Today at the beach, fit a furry windscreen on your mic and point it away from the wind.

p-243.title: Why touchscreens misbehave with wet hands
p-243.summary: Water droplets conduct and smear across the screen, changing capacitance at several electrodes and causing phantom touches.
p-243.principle: Capacitance: C = (ε A / d) (relative permittivity of water about 80, air about 1).
p-243.example: A droplet can produce a capacitance change similar to a fingertip, so many wet-screen glitches are not real defects.
p-243.actionItem: If your screen acts up today, dry your hands and screen with a cloth before assuming it needs repair.

p-244.title: Shield a camp stove from wind, but never wrap the gas canister
p-244.summary: A windscreen cuts heat loss from the stove and pot, but wrapping the gas canister can overheat it and is dangerous.
p-244.principle: Convective heat loss: q = hAΔT (h rises with wind).
p-244.example: For a pot area of 0.05m² and ΔT = 80K, raising h from 10 to 30W/(m² · K) increases loss from 40W to 120W (illustrative).
p-244.actionItem: When cooking outdoors today, set the windscreen around the pot and burner only, keep the canister outside it, and never use a stove inside a tent.

p-245.title: Why fog forms on clear autumn dawns
p-245.summary: On clear, calm nights the ground cools by radiation until the air reaches its dew point, and fog forms.
p-245.principle: Dew point approximation: T_d ≈ T - 100 - RH5 (°C, RH in %).
p-245.example: With 20°C and 70% humidity in the afternoon, T_d ≈ 14°C, so if the night cools to 12°C the air saturates and fog forms.
p-245.actionItem: If you drive in fog this morning, use low beams and fog lights and leave a larger gap than usual.

p-246.title: Choose bike gears by cadence, not by muscle
p-246.summary: At the same power, a gear that lets you spin the pedals at 70-90 rpm eases the load on your knees.
p-246.principle: Power is torque times angular speed: P = τ ω, ω = 2π · rpm60.
p-246.example: To produce about 210W you need roughly 33N·m of torque at 60 rpm but only about 22N·m at 90 rpm.
p-246.actionItem: On today's ride, shift gears to keep your cadence at 70-90 rpm.

p-247.title: Tidal flats open about 50 minutes later each day
p-247.summary: The Moon takes about 50 minutes extra each day to come around again, so tide times slip later by about 50 minutes daily.
p-247.principle: The lunar day is Tₗᵤₙₐᵣ ≈ 24 h 50 min and there are two tides per lunar day, so tides come about 12 h 25 min apart.
p-247.example: If low tide is at 10:00 today, it is about 10:50 tomorrow and, six days later, 6 × 50 = 300 min later, around 15:00.
p-247.actionItem: Before you go to a tidal flat, check the tide table and set the time you will be back out before the tide returns.

p-248.title: A vacuum sealer lets air pressure do the squeezing
p-248.summary: A vacuum sealer removes air from the bag so outside atmospheric pressure presses the packaging tight against the food.
p-248.principle: Squeezing force: F = ΔP · A (atmospheric pressure P₀ ≈ 101kPa).
p-248.example: On a 0.03m² bag with an 80kPa pressure difference, about 2.4kN (roughly 240 kgf) is spread over the whole surface.
p-248.actionItem: Today, vacuum-pack dry goods or freezer portions, but still refrigerate or freeze perishable food.

p-249.title: A steamer cooks fast with condensation heat
p-249.summary: Steam condenses on food and releases a lot of latent heat, delivering heat faster than boiling water would.
p-249.principle: Heat released on condensation: Q = mL (L ≈ 2260kJ/kg).
p-249.example: Condensing 50g of steam releases about 113kJ, roughly 6.8 times the 16.7kJ released by 50g of 100°C water cooling to 20°C.
p-249.actionItem: When steaming today, keep the lid on, and lift it away from your face to avoid steam burns.

p-250.title: You can estimate temperature from cricket chirps
p-250.summary: Crickets chirp faster when it is warmer, so counting chirps gives a rough temperature.
p-250.principle: Dolbear's law: T_F ≈ 40 + N₆₀4 (N₆₀: chirps per minute).
p-250.example: 100 chirps per minute gives about 65°F (about 18°C) and 160 gives about 80°F (about 27°C), a rough estimate that varies by species.
p-250.actionItem: This evening, count cricket chirps for 15 seconds, multiply by 4, and estimate the temperature with the formula.

p-251.title: Why sunsets are red
p-251.summary: When the Sun is low, light travels a long path through air, blue is scattered away first, and the red is what remains.
p-251.example: Blue (450nm) scatters (700/450)⁴ ≈ 5.9 times more strongly than red (700nm), so it drops out first.
p-251.actionItem: Watch the sky colors at sunset today, but never look at the Sun directly or aim a camera or binoculars at it.

p-252.title: A full Moon looks like a coin held far away
p-252.summary: The full Moon is smaller than it feels, small enough that a grain of rice at arm's length covers it.
p-252.example: A 24mm coin about 2.7m away has the same angular size, and at an arm's length of about 60cm an object roughly 5mm wide covers the Moon.
p-252.actionItem: When the full Moon rises today, stretch out your arm and cover it with a single grain of rice.

p-253.title: Holiday traffic jams start with one brake tap
p-253.summary: On a dense road, one car braking stacks up the reaction delays behind it and a jam wave spreads backward.
p-253.principle: Stopping distance: d = v t_r + (v² / 2a); a jam wave typically travels backward at about 15-20km/h.
p-253.example: At 100km/h (about 27.8m/s), a 1-second reaction covers 27.8m before braking even starts, and keeping a 3-second gap with smooth driving can save roughly 5-10% fuel.
p-253.actionItem: On today's drive, keep a 2-3 second gap and lift off the throttle early to brake less.

p-254.title: Keep at least 15m clear of a brush cutter
p-254.summary: A brush cutter blade tip moves so fast that stones fly like bullets, so keep everyone beyond 15m of the work area.
p-254.principle: Blade tip speed: v = ω r; thrown range: R = (v² 2θ / g).
p-254.example: With a 0.115m blade radius at 6,500 rpm (ω ≈ 681 rad/s), v ≈ 78m/s, about 280km/h.
p-254.actionItem: Before mowing with a brush cutter today, confirm no people or cars are within 15m and wear eye and face protection.

p-255.title: Check the sleeping bag's comfort rating and the mat's R-value
p-255.summary: At night more heat is lost into the ground than into the air, so check both the bag's comfort rating and the mat's R-value.
p-255.principle: Thermal resistance: R = (L / k) (thickness L, conductivity k).
p-255.example: A 2cm foam mat with k = 0.035W/(m · K) has R ≈ 0.57m² K/W (about 3.2 in US R-value units), and an R-value of 3 or more is a common guideline for autumn camping.
p-255.actionItem: When choosing camping gear today, check that the bag's comfort rating is at or below the expected low and the mat's R-value is 3 or more.

p-256.title: A phone barometer can read changes in height
p-256.summary: Many phones have a pressure sensor, so pressure changes can estimate how far you have climbed or descended.
p-256.principle: ΔP ≈ -ρ g Δh; near sea level, about 1hPa drop = about 8m of rise.
p-256.example: With ρ = 1.2kg/m³, each 8m is 1.2 × 9.8 × 8 ≈ 94Pa ≈ 0.94hPa, so a 30-story building (about 90m) is roughly 11hPa lower at the top.
p-256.actionItem: Today, open a barometer app and compare the reading on the ground floor and an upper floor (measure quickly, since weather also shifts pressure).

p-257.title: Anchor bookcases and refrigerators for earthquakes
p-257.summary: Tall, narrow furniture tips over in a small shake, so anchoring it to the wall keeps it safe.
p-257.principle: Tipping condition: mg (b / 2) < m a h_c, i.e. a > g (b / 2 h_c) (b: width, h_c: height of center of mass).
p-257.example: A 1.8m tall bookcase (h_c = 0.9m) that is 0.3m deep tips at a > 0.3/1.8g ≈ 0.17g.
p-257.actionItem: Today, secure tall furniture to a wall stud with L-brackets and put heavy items on lower shelves.

p-258.title: Why a guitar drifts out of tune with big temperature swings
p-258.summary: When temperature changes, string tension changes and the pitch shifts, so retune before playing.
p-258.principle: String frequency: f = (1 / 2L)√((T / µ)), so f ∝ √(T).
p-258.example: A 1% drop in tension lowers frequency by about 0.5%, so a 440Hz note falls about 2.2Hz (about 9 cents), which can be noticeable.
p-258.actionItem: Before playing today, retune with a tuner (and once more after the guitar settles).

p-259.title: Lean into the curve on a running track
p-259.summary: Leaning inward through a curve lets friction supply the centripetal force so you turn without slipping.
p-259.example: Running 14.4km/h (4m/s) around a 20m radius curve gives θ ≈ 16/196 ≈ 0.082, about a 4.7° lean.
p-259.actionItem: On a curve today, slow down early and lean slightly inward from the ankles as you turn.

p-260.title: Lingering contrails signal moist air aloft
p-260.summary: If a contrail does not vanish quickly and spreads, the high air is moist enough to be supersaturated with respect to ice.
p-260.principle: Relative humidity over ice: RH_i = (e / e_i) × 100%; a contrail persists when RH_i > 100%.
p-260.example: At about -40°C, saturation vapor pressure over ice is only about 68% of that over water, so 70% humidity relative to water already gives RH_i > 100%.
p-260.actionItem: Today, watch how long contrails last in the sky, and treat a long, spreading one only as a rough hint of moist upper air, not a forecast.

p-261.title: A chopstick in a rice jar can lift the whole jar
p-261.summary: Pack rice into a jar and push in a chopstick and the grains grip it so tightly that the whole jar lifts.
p-261.principle: Pressure between grains squeezes the chopstick and creates friction: f = µ N.
p-261.example: As an illustration, a side force N = 50N with µ = 0.4 gives about 20N of friction, enough to lift roughly 1kg (about 9.8N) of jar and rice.
p-261.actionItem: Today, fill a narrow jar with rice, pack it down, push a chopstick in deeply and lift, doing it over a table so nothing breaks.

p-262.title: Pick the heavier fruit when sizes match
p-262.summary: Between equal-sized fruits, the heavier one is usually juicier and less dried out.
p-262.example: Of two oranges of similar volume at 220g (ρ ≈ 1.10g/cm³) and 190g (ρ ≈ 0.95g/cm³), the heavier one is typically juicier.
p-262.actionItem: When buying fruit today, hold similar-sized ones in each hand to compare weight, and check for bruises too.

p-263.title: Walking on an airport moving walkway adds the speeds
p-263.summary: Walking on a moving walkway adds your walking speed to the belt speed, so you get far ahead.
p-263.principle: Relative velocity addition: v = v₁ + v₂.
p-263.example: A 0.75m/s walkway plus a 1.4m/s walk gives 2.15m/s; over 200m that is about 93 s instead of 267 s standing, nearly 3 minutes faster.
p-263.actionItem: When you walk on a moving walkway today, keep to one side, hold the handrail, and keep luggage close.

p-264.title: Bike reflector stickers send light back to its source
p-264.summary: Retroreflective stickers return a car's headlight beam toward where it came from, making a bike stand out on dark roads.
p-264.principle: A corner cube uses three mutually perpendicular mirrors to send light back antiparallel: rₒᵤₜ = -r_in.
p-264.example: Reflective gear is often visible from about 150m away, while dark clothing is often noticed only within 30-50m.
p-264.actionItem: Today, stick reflectors on your bike's wheels, frame and pedals, and use front and rear lights as well.

p-265.title: Do not blend hot soup right away
p-265.summary: Blending hot soup in a sealed blender lets steam expand and blow the lid off, which can cause burns.
p-265.principle: Ideal gas law: PV = nRT. One gram of water turning to steam occupies about 1.7L at 100°C and 1atm.
p-265.example: With n = (1 / 18) ≈ 0.056 mol, V = (nRT / P) ≈ 1.7L, about 1,700 times the liquid volume.
p-265.actionItem: Today, let hot soup cool 10 minutes or more, fill the jar no more than half, vent the lid and cover it with a towel while blending.

p-266.title: Why day and night are nearly equal at the autumn equinox
p-266.summary: At the autumn equinox the Sun is directly over the equator, so day and night are close to 12 hours everywhere on Earth.
p-266.principle: Axial tilt 23.4^°; solar declination δ ≈ 23.44^° ! ≤ ft[(360^° / 365)(d - 81)].
p-266.example: Declination is +23.4° at the June solstice (about June 21), 0° at the autumn equinox (about September 22), and -23.4° at the December solstice (about December 21).
p-266.actionItem: Today, look up sunrise and sunset times and calculate whether the day is about 12 hours long.

p-267.title: Bleed boiler and radiator air at the change of season
p-267.summary: Trapped air in a heating loop blocks water flow, leaving the top of a radiator cold; bleeding it gives more warmth for the same fuel.
p-267.principle: Heat delivered scales with circulation flow: Q = m c ΔT.
p-267.example: A 1kW radiator needs about 1L/min of water at ΔT = 15K, and the air-filled part gives off no heat.
p-267.actionItem: With the heating off and cooled, open the air valve on a radiator that is cold at the top to bleed it, then check boiler pressure as the manual says.

p-268.title: On a slope, park with wheels turned against the curb
p-268.summary: When parking on a slope, besides the handbrake and gear, turn the wheels so the curb stops the car if it rolls.
p-268.principle: Force along the slope: F = mgθ; friction: f = µ N.
p-268.example: A 1,500kg car on a 10% grade (θ ≈ 5.7^°) is pulled downhill with about 1.46kN (roughly 150 kgf).
p-268.actionItem: Today, park facing downhill with wheels turned toward the curb, or uphill by a curb with wheels turned away, and set the handbrake and P (or first gear).

p-269.title: Near scenery rushes past a train window faster
p-269.summary: At the same speed, nearby objects sweep across your view much faster, while distant mountains seem to crawl.
p-269.example: At 100km/h (27.8m/s), a tree 20m away sweeps at ω ≈ 1.39 rad/s ≈ 80^°/s, while a mountain 5km away sweeps at about 0.3^°/s.
p-269.actionItem: If you feel queasy while traveling today, look at distant mountains or the sky instead of nearby scenery.

p-270.title: Tug of war is won by foot friction, not body weight
p-270.summary: In tug of war the rope pulls equally on both sides, and the result is decided by the maximum friction the ground can give your feet.
p-270.principle: Static friction: f ≤ µ N (N = mg); rope tension is the same on both sides (action-reaction).
p-270.example: For a 70kg person, µ = 0.8 on dry ground allows up to about 550N, but µ = 0.4 on slippery ground only about 270N.
p-270.actionItem: If you play tug of war today, wear grippy shoes and lean back low, but never wrap the rope around your arm.

p-271.title: Halving a cut of meat cooks it about 4 times faster
p-271.summary: Cutting meat to half the thickness cuts the time for heat to reach the center to about a quarter, saving fuel too.
p-271.principle: Heat diffusion time: t ∝ (L² / α) (L: thickness, α: thermal diffusivity).
p-271.example: If a 6cm thick piece takes about 60 min, a 3cm piece takes roughly 60 × ≤ ft((3 / 6))² = 15 min.
p-271.actionItem: Today, slice big pieces of meat thinner before cooking, and check with a thermometer that the center reaches about 75°C or more.

p-272.title: Hit with a baseball bat's sweet spot to avoid stinging hands
p-272.summary: A bat has a center of percussion, the sweet spot, where hitting the ball sends almost no shock into your hands.
p-272.principle: Distance of the center of percussion from the pivot: q = (I / m d) (I: moment of inertia about the pivot, d: pivot-to-center-of-mass distance).
p-272.example: For a uniform 0.84m rod held at the end, q = (2 / 3) L ≈ 0.56m; real bats are end-heavy, so the spot shifts slightly.
p-272.actionItem: In today's batting practice, aim to meet the ball with the middle sweet spot of the bat, not the tip.

p-273.title: Wrapping a rope three times around a post cuts the force needed
p-273.summary: A few turns of rope around a post raise friction so much that a tiny force can hold a heavy load.
p-273.example: With µ = 0.3 and 3 turns (= 6π ≈ 18.85 rad), e⁵.65 ≈ 285, so a 1,000N load is held with about 3.5N (ideal value).
p-273.actionItem: When securing a load today, take 2-3 turns around a post, but never wrap rope around your hand or body or use it for life-critical loads.

p-274.title: Warm honey or syrup flows far more easily
p-274.summary: As honey or syrup warms, its viscosity drops sharply, leaving less stuck in the jar.
p-274.principle: Temperature dependence of viscosity (Arrhenius type): η = A e^E/(RT).
p-274.example: Honey at about 10Pa·s at 20°C thins to roughly 1-2Pa·s at 40°C, 5 to 10 times runnier.
p-274.actionItem: Today, stand a closed honey jar in about 40°C warm water for 5 minutes before use, and avoid boiling water or the microwave.

c-275.title: White Powder on Dried Persimmons Is Sugar Crystals, Not Mold
c-275.summary: The pale bloom on dried persimmons is usually crystallized sugar (glucose and fructose), not mold. Fuzzy green or black spots are mold, so discard those.
c-275.principle: As the fruit dries, water leaves and sugar concentration rises. Once it passes the saturation solubility, sugar crystallizes out: C > Cₛₐₜ(T), where C=m_sugarV_water grows because the denominator shrinks.
c-275.example: A fresh persimmon is about 80% water and about 15% sugar, but a dried one falls to roughly 25-30% water and 60% or more sugar by weight. That concentration is what forms the white surface bloom.
c-275.actionItem: When buying dried persimmons today, pick ones with an even, firm, dry bloom and avoid any with fuzzy green spots or sticky patches.

c-276.title: The Burning Smell When You First Turn On a Heater Is Burning Dust
c-276.summary: The musty burnt smell when you first switch on a heater after summer is often dust that settled on it being thermally decomposed. It usually fades in minutes with ventilation, but if it persists, get it checked.
c-276.principle: Organic matter in dust (fibers, skin flakes) pyrolyzes when heated, releasing volatiles and char. This starts at roughly T ≈ 150~250 °CmathrmC, and heating element surfaces run much hotter than that.
c-276.example: An electric heater element commonly reaches 300-800°C at the surface, so dust burns easily. A 1-2kW heater can smell for the first 30 minutes, and after cleaning the smell nearly disappears.
c-276.actionItem: Before turning your heater on today, unplug it, vacuum the intake and floor dust, then open a window and run it for 10 minutes. If the burning smell persists or smoke appears, switch it off and have it inspected.

c-277.title: Salting Napa Cabbage Wilts It and Lets Kimchi Flavor Soak In
c-277.summary: Salting cabbage draws out water by osmosis, so it wilts, takes up seasoning well, and stays crunchy. Under-salted cabbage makes bland, soggy kimchi.
c-277.principle: Cell membranes are semipermeable, so when the outside salt concentration is higher, water moves out of the cells. Osmotic pressure is = iCRT, and calcium cross-links pectin, keeping the tissue firm.
c-277.example: Salting one napa cabbage (about 2.5kg) with about 200g of salt (roughly 8%) for 4-6 hours cuts its weight by 20-25%, releasing about 0.5-0.6kg of water. A final salt level around 2% is about right.
c-277.actionItem: If you make kimchi today, turn the cabbage once while brining, and rinse and drain it when the stem bends without snapping.

c-278.title: Astringent Persimmons Stop Being Astringent When Soluble Tannins Turn Insoluble
c-278.summary: A persimmon's puckery taste comes from water-soluble tannins, and it fades once they become insoluble. Drying or deastringency treatments rely on exactly this.
c-278.principle: Soluble tannins bind proteins in saliva and on the tongue, giving the dry feeling. As the fruit ripens, dries or is sealed, acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) forms and polymerizes tannins into insoluble clumps that no longer dissolve in saliva.
c-278.example: An astringent persimmon holds roughly 1% soluble tannin, which dries your mouth, but sealed at about 20-25°C for 3-5 days most of it becomes insoluble and the puckery taste nearly vanishes.
c-278.actionItem: If you have astringent persimmons today, seal them in a container or bag with an apple or banana for 2-3 days, or peel and sun-dry them. Taste a small piece before eating to check.

c-279.title: Grapefruit Juice Can Change How Some Medicines Work
c-279.summary: Grapefruit can block the breakdown of some drugs, raising their levels in the blood. If you take any medication, ask a pharmacist whether grapefruit interacts with it.
c-279.principle: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit inhibit the intestinal drug-metabolizing enzyme CYP3A4. With less breakdown, more drug is absorbed, so AUC=₀^ C(t) dt rises and side-effect risk increases.
c-279.example: For some statins, one glass (about 250mL) of grapefruit juice can multiply blood exposure (AUC) several-fold, and the effect can last more than a day. The size of the effect varies a lot between drugs.
c-279.actionItem: Today, check the leaflet of any medicine you take or ask a pharmacist whether grapefruit is a concern, and if so, avoid the juice and fresh fruit. Do not stop a medicine on your own.

c-280.title: Why Liquids Must Be in 100mL Containers in Cabin Baggage
c-280.summary: On international flights, liquids and gels in carry-on bags must be in containers of 100mL or less, packed in a clear zip bag. The limit is meant to keep any single container below a dangerous quantity.
c-280.principle: The rule limits container size because liquid explosives are only dangerous above a certain quantity. The carried total is Vₜₒₜₐₗ= V_i with each V_i ≤ 100mL, usually capped at one 1L bag.
c-280.example: Ten 100mL containers in one 1L bag give a maximum total of about 1L. A 200mL bottle, even half empty, is often rejected because the container capacity is what counts.
c-280.actionItem: If you are preparing for a trip today, decant shampoo, lotion and liquid medicine into 100mL or smaller bottles, put them in one clear zip bag, and keep it at the top of your bag. Check the airline and country rules again before departure.

c-281.title: Choose Fermented Seafood by Aging and Amino-Acid Flavor, Not Just Saltiness
c-281.summary: The savory depth of jeotgal comes from amino acids released as proteins break down during aging. Check that it is not just salty and that the production and aging details are clear.
c-281.principle: Protease enzymes in the fish gut hydrolyze protein into peptides and amino acids: protein + n H₂O → n amino acids. Glutamic acid in particular gives the savory umami taste.
c-281.example: Salted shrimp usually has a salt level around 20%, and after 3-6 months of aging its amino nitrogen rises and the flavor deepens. At the same salt level, a short-aged product tastes fishy and merely salty.
c-281.actionItem: When buying jeotgal today, check the production date, ingredients and salt level on the label, and if you can taste, pick the one that leaves sweetness and richness after the saltiness.

c-282.title: Check Gas Connections With Soapy Water Bubbles, Not by Smell Alone
c-282.summary: To check a suspected gas leak at a connection, brush on soapy water and watch for bubbles. Never use a flame or lighter to check, as it risks an explosion.
c-282.principle: Leaking gas pushes up the soap film formed by surfactant and makes bubbles. For a bubble, ΔP = (4γ / r), so even a small leak shows up as a visible bubble.
c-282.example: Brush a mix of about 1mL dish soap in 100mL of water onto a stove hose connection, and bubbles that keep growing or forming mean a leak. Natural gas is lighter than air and rises, while LPG is heavier and settles low.
c-282.actionItem: Today, with the gas valve closed, brush soapy water on hose connections and look for bubbles. If bubbles keep growing, shut the valve, ventilate and have a professional inspect it.

c-283.title: Chestnuts Stored Cold Get Sweeter as Starch Turns Into Sugar
c-283.summary: Fresh chestnuts kept in the fridge at 0-4°C for a few weeks turn starch into sugar and taste sweeter. At room temperature they spoil fast, so refrigeration is the thrifty choice.
c-283.principle: In the cold, amylase and other enzymes break starch into maltose and glucose: (C₆H₁₀O₅)_n + n H₂O → n C₆H₁₂O₆. Plants build up sugars to protect against freezing through osmotic protection.
c-283.example: Freshly harvested chestnuts hold about 5-8% sugar, but after 4-8 weeks at 0-2°C the sugar content can rise about 1.5-2 times, giving a clearly sweeter taste. At room temperature, worms and mold appear within about two weeks.
c-283.actionItem: Today, wrap whole chestnuts in paper towels, put them in a zip bag in the fridge (about 1-4°C), and steam or roast them within 1-2 weeks.

c-284.title: Whether Home Canning Is Safe Depends on the pH 4.6 Threshold
c-284.summary: In home canning, you must separate high-acid foods at pH 4.6 or below from low-acid foods above it. Boiling-water heating alone can leave a botulism toxin risk in low-acid foods.
c-284.principle: Botulinum spores can produce toxin in sealed, oxygen-free conditions when pH is above 4.6. Acidity is pH=-₁₀[H⁺], and pH 4.6 corresponds to [H⁺] ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.
c-284.example: Jam and fruit preserves have a pH around 3-4, so boiling-water processing is relatively safe, but vegetables, meat and beans sit at pH 5-7 and need pressure heating at about 116-121°C. Boiling water cannot exceed 100°C.
c-284.actionItem: If you do home canning today, check whether the ingredient is acidic (fruit or vinegar pickle), and for low-acid foods refrigerate or freeze instead of canning at home. If a lid bulges or there are bubbles or an off smell, do not eat it and throw it away.

c-285.title: Chocolate Can Be Poisonous to Dogs
c-285.summary: The theobromine in chocolate is broken down slowly by dogs and can cause poisoning. The higher the cocoa content, the greater the risk, so if a dog ate some, note the type and amount and call a vet.
c-285.principle: Theobromine (C₇H₈N₄O₂) has a half-life of about 17 hours in dogs versus about 6-10 hours in humans, so it accumulates. Risk is gauged by dose per body weight D=m_theobrominem_body.
c-285.example: Dark chocolate (70% cocoa) holds about 5-8mg/g of theobromine, so a 10kg dog eating about 50g (roughly half a standard bar) takes in about 250-400mg (about 25-40mg/kg), a range with risk of severe signs. Milk chocolate has less.
c-285.actionItem: Today, store chocolate and cocoa products high up or in a sealed cupboard where a dog cannot reach. If one ate any, do not wait: note the type, amount and time, and call a vet right away.

c-286.title: Airplane Food Tastes Bland Because of Cabin Pressure and Dryness
c-286.summary: Cabin air is low in pressure and very dry, which dulls smell and taste so food seems bland. That is why airline meals are deliberately seasoned strongly.
c-286.principle: Cabin pressure equals about 2,000-2,400m of altitude (about 0.75-0.8atm) and relative humidity is 10-20%. Under low pressure and dryness, smell and taste receptors become much less sensitive, with sweet and salty perception reported to drop about 30%. The pressure ratio is P_cabinP₀ ≈ 0.8.
c-286.example: A food that tastes normal on the ground can seem 20-30% less sweet and salty at cruising altitude, so airline meals use extra salt and spices. A similar reason is given for why tomato juice tastes especially good in flight.
c-286.actionItem: If you fly today, sip water often so your mouth does not dry out, and instead of adding more salt to bland food, choose strongly flavored dishes or a tangy drink.

c-287.title: Choose Baking Flour by Protein Content: Bread, All-Purpose or Cake
c-287.summary: The difference among bread, all-purpose and cake flour is protein content. Bread flour for bread, low-protein cake flour for cakes and cookies gives the right texture.
c-287.principle: Wheat proteins gliadin and glutenin form a gluten network with water: gliadin+glutenin+H₂O → gluten. The more protein, the tougher and more elastic the network.
c-287.example: Bread flour has about 11-13% protein for chewy loaves and bagels, all-purpose about 9-10% for noodles and pancakes, and cake flour about 7-9% for tender cakes and cookies. A 100g portion of cake flour has about 8g of protein.
c-287.actionItem: When buying flour today, read the protein figure on the nutrition label and pick bread, all-purpose or cake flour to match what you plan to bake.

c-288.title: Mixing New and Old Batteries Greatly Raises the Risk of Leaks
c-288.summary: Mixing new and used batteries, or different types, can over-discharge the weak cell and make it leak. Replace all batteries in a device together with the same type and age.
c-288.principle: In series, the same current flows, and when the weak cell's voltage falls to near 0V, the others drive it in reverse. Hydrogen forms by reactions such as 2 H₂O+2e⁻ → H₂+2 OH⁻, raising internal pressure and causing leaks.
c-288.example: With three fresh 1.5V cells in series (4.5V) and one nearly drained to 0V, the other two keep pushing about 3V and force that cell into reverse charging. Leaked potassium hydroxide is strongly alkaline (pH about 14) and corrodes skin and devices.
c-288.actionItem: Today, check the batteries in your remote, clock or toys, and when replacing them, swap all of a device's batteries for the same brand and fresh ones. Do not touch leaked white powder with bare hands.

c-289.title: Boil Bone Broth in One Big Batch and Portion It Out
c-289.summary: Long simmering turns bone collagen into gelatin for a rich broth that sets like jelly when cooled. Boiling one big batch and freezing portions saves gas and time.
c-289.principle: Heating unwinds collagen into gelatin, and on cooling it shifts from sol to gel. The hydrolysis is collagen―(Δ, H₂O)→gelatin, and it typically sets below about 35°C.
c-289.example: Simmering 1kg of ox bones in about 6L of water for 6-8 hours gives roughly 4-5L of broth. Instead of lighting the stove each time, one boil portioned into fifteen 300mL servings cuts gas use a lot.
c-289.actionItem: If you make bone broth today, cool it fully, divide it into single-serving bags or containers and freeze them, then thaw and heat only what you need.

c-290.title: White Powder on Potting Soil May Be Mineral Salts, Not Mold
c-290.summary: A white crust on potting soil or the pot rim may be leftover mineral salts from fertilizer or tap water rather than mold. Flushing with plenty of water reduces it.
c-290.principle: When water evaporates from the surface, dissolved salts are left behind and precipitate. Concentration C=mₛₐₗₜV_water rises as V_water falls, and past saturation crystals form, such as the hard-water component CaCO₃.
c-290.example: If tap water has hardness of about 100mg/L (as CaCO3), evaporating 1L leaves about 100mg of calcium carbonate. Even 200mL per week builds a visible white layer on the surface within a few months.
c-290.actionItem: If you see white powder today, scrape off the top 1-2cm of soil and cover with fresh soil, then slowly water with about the pot's volume so it drains out fully.

c-291.title: Xylitol Gum Is Dangerous if Your Dog Eats It
c-291.summary: Xylitol, safe for people, is very dangerous to dogs and even small amounts can cause low blood sugar and liver damage. Keep sugar-free gum, candy and some peanut butters out of a dog's reach.
c-291.principle: A dog's pancreas mistakes xylitol for glucose and releases insulin sharply, so blood sugar plunges. The risk of xylitol (C₅H₁₂O₅) is gauged by dose per weight D=mm_body.
c-291.example: A 10kg dog can drop in blood sugar from only about 0.1g/kg (about 1g) of xylitol, and above about 0.5g/kg (about 5g) liver damage becomes likely. One piece of sugar-free gum typically holds about 0.2-1g, so a few pieces reach the danger range.
c-291.actionItem: Today, move sugar-free gum and candy out of bags, pockets and drawers to where your dog cannot reach. If a dog ate some, bring the ingredient label and call a vet right away.

c-292.title: Why Alkaline Hot Spring Water Feels Slippery
c-292.summary: The slippery feel of alkaline hot springs comes from skin oils turning soap-like. If your skin is sensitive, do not soak too long and moisturize afterward.
c-292.principle: Alkali (pH above about 8.5) saponifies skin oils (triglycerides) into soap and glycerol: fat + 3 OH⁻ → 3 fatty acid salt (soap)+glycerol. That soap emulsifies on the surface and feels slick.
c-292.example: Soaking 20 minutes at about 40°C in an alkaline spring of pH 9-10 loosens dead skin and sebum, leaving it smooth. At pH 10, [OH⁻] is 1,000 times higher than at neutral pH 7.
c-292.actionItem: If you visit a hot spring or take a bath today, keep alkaline springs to about 10-20 minutes at a time, then pat dry and apply moisturizer right away.

c-293.title: 'Extra Virgin' on Olive Oil Means Acidity of 0.8% or Less
c-293.summary: Extra virgin is a grade for pressed olive oil with free fatty acidity of 0.8% or less that also passes sensory tests. Lower acidity does not always mean better taste, so also check harvest and bottling dates.
c-293.principle: Acidity is the share of free fatty acids (as oleic acid) in oil: acidity (%)=m_free FAm_oil × 100. Fresher olives have less triglyceride breakdown and so lower acidity, and polyphenols slow oxidation.
c-293.example: Oil at 0.8% or lower is extra virgin, and 2% or lower is virgin. In a 1L bottle, extra virgin holds about 8g or less of free fatty acids. Oil is sensitive to light and heat, so dark bottles are better.
c-293.actionItem: When buying olive oil today, check the 'extra virgin' label plus the harvest year and bottling date, choose a dark bottle over a clear one, and store it somewhere cool.

c-294.title: Cover the Terminals of 9V Batteries With Tape Before Storing
c-294.summary: On a 9V battery both terminals sit close together on the same face, so touching metal can short them and cause heating. Cover the terminals with tape or keep each in its own packaging when putting it in a drawer.
c-294.principle: When the terminals touch metal like keys or coins and short, resistance is tiny, a large current I=(V / R) flows, and Joule heat P=I²R is produced. For example with R=0.5Ω, I=18A.
c-294.example: A 9V battery with about 1.5Ω internal resistance shorted could in theory reach I ≈ 6A and about 54W of heat, getting hot within minutes. Alkaline cells are usually lower than that, but burn and fire risks remain.
c-294.actionItem: Today, cover the terminals of spare 9V batteries in your drawer with clear tape or put them back in the original packaging or a plastic case. Do not store them loose with coins or keys.

c-295.title: Keep Tofu Longer by Submerging It in Water and Changing It Daily
c-295.summary: Opened tofu submerged in clean water in the fridge, with the water changed daily, stays fresh 2-3 days longer. If it smells sour or turns slimy, throw it out.
c-295.principle: Tofu is a soy-protein gel with about 85% water, so bacteria grow easily. Submerging reduces surface contact with air and changes surface water activity a_w=(p / p₀), and changing the water rinses away grown bacteria and byproducts.
c-295.example: At 4°C, opened tofu soaked in water and changed daily often lasts 3-5 days, while left dry it tends to turn slimy in 1-2 days. Saving one block (300g, about 2,000 KRW, roughly USD 1.50) from the bin is a real saving.
c-295.actionItem: Today, put leftover tofu in a sealed container with enough clean water (bottled or boiled and cooled) to cover it, refrigerate, and change the water once a day starting tomorrow.

c-296.title: Wash Down Jackets With Neutral Detergent and Dry Them Completely
c-296.summary: Strong alkaline detergent strips the natural oils from down feathers and reduces their loft. Washing with neutral detergent and drying all the way through prevents odor and mold.
c-296.principle: Feather oils (lipids) are saponified and washed away under alkaline conditions: oil+3 OH⁻ → soap+glycerol. Without the oils, feathers clump and the insulating air layer gets thinner.
c-296.example: A typical laundry powder solution is pH about 10-11 and alkaline, while neutral detergent is about pH 7-8. If even 100g of moisture remains in a 500g, 800-fill-power jacket, a musty smell and mold can develop after drying.
c-296.actionItem: If you wash a jacket today, use a neutral (wool or down) detergent, rinse well, then dry fully in a low-heat dryer with 2-3 tennis balls or in the shade for several days until dry through.

c-297.title: Take Calcium and Iron Supplements at Different Times
c-297.summary: Calcium and iron supplements can interfere with each other's absorption when taken together. If you take both, space them at least 2 hours apart.
c-297.principle: Divalent cations such as Ca²⁺ and Fe²⁺ compete for the same absorption transporters (such as DMT1) in the small intestine. A high level of one lowers absorption of the other, and calcium above about 500mg can noticeably reduce iron uptake.
c-297.example: Taking 600mg of calcium together with 18mg of iron has been reported to cut iron absorption by about 40-50%. A common routine is iron on an empty stomach with vitamin C and calcium with a meal.
c-297.actionItem: If you take both today, split them: iron in the morning or on an empty stomach and calcium with dinner. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist first.

c-298.title: Lighters Have Rules for Carrying Onto Planes
c-298.summary: Lighter rules differ by country and airline, but generally only one per person is allowed on your body and it often cannot go in checked luggage. Torch (turbo) types are mostly banned. Check before you go.
c-298.principle: Lighter fuel butane (C₄H₁₀) is a pressurized liquid and highly flammable, burning as 2 C₄H₁₀+13 O₂ → 8 CO₂+10 H₂O. When cabin pressure drops, the pressure difference ΔP across the container grows.
c-298.example: Butane has a vapor pressure of about 2atm at 20°C. In a cabin (about 0.8atm) the difference from outside is larger than on the ground, so some lighters may leak fuel or give a bigger flame. A typical disposable lighter holds a few grams of butane.
c-298.actionItem: If you are traveling today, check the lighter rules of your airline and destination country, and leave the lighter at home if you do not need it. If you carry one, keep a single lighter in a pocket so you can show it at security.

c-299.title: Brewed and Acid-Hydrolyzed Soy Sauce Are Made by Different Reactions
c-299.summary: Brewed soy sauce is fermented and aged with microbes from soybeans and wheat, while acid-hydrolyzed sauce breaks soy protein quickly with hydrochloric acid. The label wording and ingredients tell them apart.
c-299.principle: Both hydrolyze protein into amino acids but with different catalysts. Fermentation is protein―(enzymes)→, monthsamino acids, and acid hydrolysis is protein―(HCl)→, Δamino acids, done in hours to days.
c-299.example: Brewed soy sauce usually ages 6 months to several years, while acid-hydrolyzed sauce can be made in days, so it is cheaper but has a flatter aroma. Blended sauces on the market mix both, with the ratio on the label.
c-299.actionItem: When buying soy sauce today, check the ingredients for whether it is 100% brewed or a blend with acid-hydrolyzed sauce, and match it to use: brewed for soups and braises, blended for stir-fries and stews.

c-300.title: In Extreme Cold, Diesel's Paraffin Wax Solidifies and the Engine Won't Start
c-300.summary: Paraffin wax in diesel crystallizes in freezing temperatures and clogs the fuel filter so the engine will not start. When a cold snap is forecast, use winter-grade diesel and keep the tank well filled.
c-300.principle: Diesel's n-paraffins (for example C₂₀H₄₂) precipitate as crystals below the cloud point T_cp. When T<T_cp, wax crystals grow, and at the lower cold filter plugging point the filter blocks.
c-300.example: Summer-grade diesel has a cloud point around 0°C, while winter grade is adjusted down to about -15 to -20°C. On a -10°C morning, leftover summer-grade diesel raises the risk of a failed start.
c-300.actionItem: If a cold wave is forecast today, check that your car has winter-grade diesel and keep the tank more than half full. If it will not start, do not keep cranking, and call a garage or roadside assistance.

c-301.title: A Few Grains of Rice in the Salt Shaker Keep It From Clumping
c-301.summary: When salt clumps from moisture, a few grains of rice help because the rice absorbs moisture first so salt cakes less. It is not perfect, so airtight storage comes first.
c-301.principle: Sodium chloride is deliquescent above about 75% relative humidity, absorbing moisture from the air and dissolving. This critical humidity is RH_c ≈ 75%, and above it the grains stick together into lumps.
c-301.example: In humid weather above 80% humidity, an open salt shaker can cake within a day or two. Adding about 10-20 rice grains absorbs some moisture per 100g of salt and slows clumping.
c-301.actionItem: Today, put 10-20 grains of rice in your salt shaker, close the lid tightly, and keep it somewhere cool and dry rather than beside the stove.

c-302.title: Do Not Use Enzyme Detergent on Wool and Silk
c-302.summary: Wool and silk are protein fibers, so detergent containing protein-digesting enzymes damages them. Use a neutral wool and silk detergent.
c-302.principle: Protease in enzyme detergent hydrolyzes the peptide bonds of proteins: R-CO-NH-R'+H₂O → R-COOH+H₂N-R'. Wool keratin and silk fibroin are proteins too, so the same reaction weakens them.
c-302.example: Protease enzymes work best at 30-50°C, which covers typical wash temperatures. Soaking a wool sweater in enzyme detergent at 30°C for just one hour can thin the fibers, dull the sheen or even make holes.
c-302.actionItem: Today, check the care label on your wool or silk clothes, and if a detergent lists 'enzyme (protease)', skip it and gently hand wash in cold water with a neutral wool and silk detergent.

c-303.title: Follow the Storage Temperature on Probiotic Products
c-303.summary: Probiotics are live bacteria that are sensitive to heat and moisture, so follow the storage instructions. If it says refrigerate, do not leave it in a car or a summer delivery box.
c-303.principle: Live bacteria die faster as temperature rises, following N(t)=N₀ e⁻kt with k larger at higher temperatures. Spore-forming strains (such as Bacillus) and coated or freeze-dried products are relatively stable at room temperature.
c-303.example: A refrigerate-labeled product kept at 25-30°C can lose a noticeable share of live cells within weeks, and faster above 40°C inside a car. Guaranteed counts usually refer to live cells at the expiry date rather than at manufacture.
c-303.actionItem: Today, check the label of any probiotic you have for 'refrigerate' or 'room temperature', keep refrigerated ones in the fridge, and do not leave them in a summer car or on a windowsill. If you have a health condition, talk to your doctor.

c-304.title: Ask for Medicine by Its Generic Name at Pharmacies Abroad
c-304.summary: The same medicine has different brand names in each country, so at an overseas pharmacy the generic (English) ingredient name is the most accurate. For example, acetaminophen is also called paracetamol abroad.
c-304.principle: Drug generic names (INN) are standardized internationally while brand names vary by maker. The same compound C₈H₉NO₂ is called acetaminophen (US, Korea) or paracetamol (Europe, much of Asia).
c-304.example: A 500mg acetaminophen product is sold as Tylenol, Panadol, Paracetamol and others depending on the country, but the ingredient is the same. An adult's usual daily maximum is kept at or below 4g (eight 500mg tablets).
c-304.actionItem: Today, as part of trip prep, note down or save in your phone the English generic names of medicines you take. At the pharmacy, mention symptoms, current medicines and allergies, and carry a doctor's letter for prescription drugs.

c-305.title: The Difference Between Black, Green and Oolong Tea Is Leaf Oxidation
c-305.summary: Black, oolong and green tea come from the same tea plant but differ in oxidation (fermentation), changing taste and color. Green tea prevents oxidation, while black tea is fully oxidized.
c-305.principle: Polyphenol oxidase (PPO) in tea leaves reacts catechins with oxygen into theaflavins and others: catechin+O₂―(PPO)→theaflavin. Green tea is heated first to deactivate the enzyme and stop oxidation.
c-305.example: Green tea has about 0% oxidation, oolong about 10-80%, and black tea nearly 100%. Green tea is usually brewed with about 70-80°C water for 1-2 minutes and black tea with about 90-95°C water for 3-5 minutes.
c-305.actionItem: When buying tea today, check the pack for unoxidized (green), partly oxidized (oolong) or fully oxidized (black), and brew with the matching water temperature and time.

c-306.title: Keep Your Fuel Tank More Than Half Full in Winter
c-306.summary: In winter, an empty fuel tank lets water vapor in the air condense into the fuel, and it can freeze in the lines below zero. Keeping the tank more than half full reduces this.
c-306.principle: Water vapor in the empty space condenses on the cold tank wall. Condensation occurs when temperature falls below the dew point T_d, and the more air in the tank, the more vapor can condense. Water freezes at 0°CmathrmC or below and blocks fuel flow.
c-306.example: An empty 50L tank holds about 50L of humid air, so at 80% relative humidity and 10°C, a few grams of water can condense in theory. A full tank has less air and so less water, cutting the chance that fuel lines freeze on a -10°C morning and block starting.
c-306.actionItem: Today, check the fuel level of your car or heating tank and top up if it is under half. Keeping it above half is an easier winter habit than waiting to fill up completely.

c-307.title: If Coffee Tastes Bitter, Shorten Extraction Instead of Adding More Beans
c-307.summary: If coffee tastes bitter, coarsen the grind or shorten extraction instead of adding more beans. Over-extraction causes bitterness, so you can fix taste without wasting beans.
c-307.principle: Extraction yield is yield (%)=m_dissolved solidsm_coffee × 100, with 18-22% typically ideal. Beyond that, bitter compounds such as chlorogenic acid lactones and phenylindanes are extracted heavily.
c-307.example: With 20g of coffee, going past 22% yield dissolves more than 4.4g and tastes bitter and harsh. Targeting 20% from the same 20g dissolves about 4g, tasting sweet and balanced. At about 1,000 KRW (roughly USD 0.70) per 20g of beans, cutting waste adds up.
c-307.actionItem: If your coffee is bitter today, do not add more beans. Grind one step coarser or cut brew time by 20-30 seconds, and keep water at 90-94°C.

c-308.title: Yeast Dies in Water Hotter Than About 55°C
c-308.summary: Yeast for bread dough dies in water that is too hot, so the dough will not rise. Keep water lukewarm to the touch, around 30-38°C.
c-308.principle: Yeast (Saccharomyces) dies quickly above about 55°C where its proteins denature. Activity peaks around 28-35°C, and fermentation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH+2 CO₂ makes carbon dioxide that lifts the dough.
c-308.example: With 7g of yeast in 500g of flour, 35°C water lets the dough roughly double within an hour, but 60°C water kills most of the yeast and the dough barely rises. It also saves a packet of yeast (about 500 KRW, roughly USD 0.35).
c-308.actionItem: If you bake bread today, check the water temperature with a thermometer or your inner wrist so it is lukewarm at 30-38°C, not hot, and mix salt and yeast apart so they do not touch directly.

c-309.title: Stacking Cold Medicines Can Double Up on Acetaminophen
c-309.summary: Taking a combination cold medicine, a pain reliever and Tylenol separately can duplicate acetaminophen and exceed the daily maximum. Add up the acetaminophen (paracetamol) content across the labels.
c-309.principle: Acetaminophen is mostly metabolized in the liver, but at an overdose the toxic metabolite NAPQI builds up, depleting glutathione and damaging liver cells. Add up the daily total Dₜₒₜₐₗ= D_i and keep it at or below 4g for adults (often advised at 3g or less).
c-309.example: Four 500mg Tylenol tablets (2g) plus three sachets of a combination cold medicine with 325mg each (about 1g) already reach 3g a day. You must tally so that one more Tylenol dose does not push you over 4g.
c-309.actionItem: If you are taking cold medicine today, check every product label for acetaminophen content, write down the daily total, and stay within the limit. If unsure, ask a pharmacist.

c-310.title: Solid Shampoo and Conditioner Bars Avoid the Liquid Limit When Traveling
c-310.summary: Solid shampoo and conditioner bars are not liquids or gels, so they escape the 100mL cabin limit and lighten your travel bag. Many airlines and countries do not treat solid soaps as liquids.
c-310.principle: They are made by solidifying surfactants (such as sodium cocoyl isethionate) without water, so they contain almost none. The liquid rule limits volume to V ≤ 100mL, so solids are not covered, though the final call rests with the security officer.
c-310.example: A 250mL liquid shampoo cannot go in the cabin because of its container size, while one shampoo bar (about 50g) typically lasts about 50-80 washes and weighs about a fifth of a liquid bottle. This fits a long trip.
c-310.actionItem: If you travel today, pack solid shampoo and conditioner bars in a draining tin, and dry them completely before packing rather than putting them in wet. Rules differ by airline and country, so check before departure.

c-311.title: Check Fat Makeup and Trans Fat Labeling on Butter and Margarine
c-311.summary: Butter and margarine differ in fat type, so compare saturated and trans fat on the nutrition label. Margarine is not automatically better or worse, as it varies by product.
c-311.principle: Adding hydrogen to the unsaturated fatty acids of vegetable oil firms it up, and some double bonds turn into trans isomers: C=C+H₂―(Ni)→C-C. This partial hydrogenation can create trans fat.
c-311.example: Butter is about 80% fat, mostly saturated (about 50%), with a small amount of natural trans fat. Older margarines made with partially hydrogenated oil were high in trans fat, but most current products are under 0.5g per serving and often lower in saturated fat.
c-311.actionItem: When buying butter or margarine today, compare saturated and trans fat per serving on the nutrition label and check whether the ingredients list 'partially hydrogenated oil'.

c-312.title: Read What Fuel Additive Ingredients Do Before Believing the Ads
c-312.summary: For fuel additives, look at which ingredient does what rather than at the advertising claims. Detergent-dispersants clean deposits but do not guarantee a big fuel economy gain.
c-312.principle: Detergent-dispersant surfactant molecules, which have two kinds of ends, surround deposits (carbon) and disperse them in the fuel. Fuel economy is measured as η=distancefuel, and in a clean engine the gain is very small.
c-312.example: Many products call for a few mL per liter, yet fuel economy gains average about 1-2% and are often limited. For a car at 12km/L, 2% gives 12.24km/L, and a 5,000 KRW (roughly USD 3.50) bottle of additive may not be recovered in fuel savings.
c-312.actionItem: If you plan to buy a fuel additive today, check the ingredient description (detergent-dispersant, cetane improver and so on) and the fuel and vehicle types, and see whether advertised economy gains come with conditions.

c-313.title: Feed Leather Shoes With Cream Rather Than Just Polishing Them
c-313.summary: Leather shoes need cream to replenish oils, not just a shine, to stop them drying and cracking. They last longer, saving the cost of new shoes.
c-313.principle: Lipids fill the spaces between collagen fibers and keep leather supple. When these lipids evaporate or wash out, fibers rub together and the leather dries and cracks. Cream refills those gaps with oils and waxes.
c-313.example: If a pair of leather shoes costs about 150,000 KRW (roughly USD 105), caring for them with cream once a month can stretch their life from 2-3 years to 5 or more. Per year, that roughly halves the cost of the shoes. One tin of shoe cream (about 5,000 KRW, roughly USD 3.50) covers dozens of pairs.
c-313.actionItem: Today, wipe the dust off your leather shoes with a dry cloth, apply a thin layer of shoe cream, and after 5 minutes buff with a soft brush or cloth.

c-314.title: Green Vegetables Turn Yellowish When You Add Vinegar
c-314.summary: When blanching green vegetables like spinach or broccoli, adding acid such as vinegar or lemon juice turns the bright green into dull olive. Add acid at the end or just before eating.
c-314.principle: H⁺ from the acid replaces the central Mg²⁺ of chlorophyll, forming pheophytin: chlorophyll+2 H⁺ → pheophytin+Mg²⁺. Pheophytin is yellow-brown, so the color dulls.
c-314.example: Boiling 100g of spinach in water with a tablespoon (15mL) of vinegar lowers the pH from about 7 to around 4, and color starts shifting within 5 minutes. By contrast, blanching briefly in boiling water with a little salt keeps the green longer.
c-314.actionItem: If you blanch greens today, blanch uncovered in boiling water for just 1-2 minutes, rinse in cold water, and sprinkle vinegar or lemon juice just before eating.

c-315.title: Use Retinol at Night and Wear Sunscreen in the Daytime
c-315.summary: Retinol breaks down in light and can make skin more sensitive to the sun, so use it at night and always wear sunscreen by day. If you are pregnant or have a skin condition, talk to a professional first.
c-315.principle: Retinol degrades under UV: retinol―(h)→degradation products. Also, the stratum corneum thins and new skin comes up, so the same UV dose can cause redness more easily.
c-315.example: It is common to start at a low retinol strength (0.1-0.3%) two or three times a week and use SPF 30 or higher sunscreen by day at about 2mg/cm². SPF 30 blocks about 97% of UVB.
c-315.actionItem: Tonight, use retinol after washing your face, and tomorrow morning put on SPF 30 or higher sunscreen. If stinging or redness is strong, cut back and consult a doctor.

c-316.title: Why Retort Instant Rice Keeps at Room Temperature
c-316.summary: Instant rice lasts at room temperature because it is sealed and then sterilized at high heat and pressure, killing nearly all microbes. It can be stored unrefrigerated until opened, making it good emergency travel food.
c-316.principle: Retort sterilization applies pressure at about 120°C to kill even heat-resistant bacterial spores. The sterilization time is calculated from F=D_T (N₀ / N), and the oxygen-free seal stops aerobic bacteria from growing.
c-316.example: One pack of instant rice (210g) is sterilized at about 120°C for roughly 20-30 minutes and typically keeps 6-12 months at room temperature. It can sit unrefrigerated before opening, but after opening it should be eaten right away or refrigerated.
c-316.actionItem: When packing travel bags today, include instant rice as emergency food, and throw away any pack with a bulging lid or a leak. Heat in the microwave as directed on the container.

c-317.title: Sugar Substitutes Like Allulose and Erythritol Each Differ in Sweetness and Properties
c-317.summary: Substitutes such as allulose, erythritol and xylitol differ in sweetness, calories and digestive effects, so choose by use. Too much can cause stomach upset, so start small.
c-317.principle: Sugar alcohols and rare sugars differ in molecular structure, so absorption and calories differ. Erythritol (C₄H₁₀O₄), for example, is mostly absorbed and excreted in urine, giving near-zero calories, and it absorbs heat on dissolving (ΔHₛₒₗ>0), creating a cooling feel.
c-317.example: Sugar has about 4kcal per gram, while erythritol has about 0-0.2kcal/g and allulose about 0.4kcal/g. With sugar as 1, sweetness is about 0.7 for both erythritol and allulose. Quantities must be adjusted when replacing sugar.
c-317.actionItem: When buying a sugar substitute today, check the type (allulose, erythritol and so on) and the calories per serving on the label, and start with around 10g a day to see how your body reacts.

c-318.title: Black Water in Heating Pipes Is Sludge From Oxidized Iron
c-318.summary: If water drained from heating pipes is black, it may be sludge (magnetite) from oxidized iron, and as it builds up, heat transfer worsens. Consider a boiler technician's flush and a corrosion inhibitor check.
c-318.principle: In hot water with almost no oxygen, iron slowly oxidizes: 3 Fe+4 H₂O → Fe₃O₄+4 H₂. The magnetite (Fe₃O₄) that forms is a black powder that builds up and raises thermal resistance.
c-318.example: A 1mm layer of sludge in pipes and radiators can cut heat transfer by a few percent, making the boiler run longer and raising fuel cost by about 5-10%. A flush usually costs several hundred thousand KRW (a few hundred USD), but savings and longer equipment life can repay it.
c-318.actionItem: Today, check when your heating pipes were last flushed, and if it has been several years, ask a boiler technician for an inspection. Do not dismantle the pipes or touch drained water yourself.

c-319.title: Freezer Burn Is Where Moisture Left an Air-Exposed Surface
c-319.summary: The white, dry patches on meat or vegetables kept long in the freezer are freezer burn. It is not harmful to eat but is tough and loses flavor, and squeezing out air and sealing prevents it.
c-319.principle: In the freezer, surface ice sublimates straight to vapor without going through liquid, so moisture leaves: H₂O(s) → H₂O(g). The dried surface meets air, so fats oxidize and give off-flavors.
c-319.example: Unwrapped meat in a -18°C freezer loses a few percent of surface moisture within weeks and dries white. Pressing air out with vacuum or zip bags keeps quality for 3-6 months or more and reduces thrown-away food (a few thousand KRW a month or more).
c-319.actionItem: Today, pack meat and vegetables for the freezer in single portions in zip bags, squeeze out as much air as you can, seal and write the date. For parts that already have freezer burn, trim them off or use them in soups and stews.

c-320.title: Dissolve Curry and Sauce Powder in Cold Water First to Avoid Lumps
c-320.summary: Adding curry or sauce powder straight into hot liquid cooks only the outside and forms lumps. Dissolve it first in cold or lukewarm water, or turn off the heat and mix it in a little at a time.
c-320.principle: When starch granules meet hot water, their surface gelatinizes first into a sticky gel film that keeps water from reaching the powder inside. Gelatinization starts around 60-70°C and happens first at the surface where T>T_gel.
c-320.example: Dumping 100g of curry powder into 90°C broth forms lumps several millimeters across as the surface gelatinizes, but dissolving it first in 200mL of 20-30°C water spreads the particles evenly with almost no lumps.
c-320.actionItem: If you make curry or sauce today, dissolve the powder in cold water first and strain it, or turn off the heat and add it a little at a time while stirring, then bring it back to a gentle simmer.

c-321.title: AHA and BHA exfoliants depend on pH and concentration
c-321.summary: What decides both results and irritation is the product's pH and acid concentration, not just the ingredient name. Even a mild acid can sting if the pH is low.
c-321.principle: Acids ionize according to pH = pK_a + [A⁻][HA], and only the un-ionized free acid (HA) acts on skin. The lower the pH is below pK_a, the larger the free-acid share.
c-321.example: A 10% glycolic acid product (pK_a about 3.83) is 50% free acid at pH 3.83 but about 87% at pH 3.0, so it irritates more. Salicylic acid (pK_a about 2.97) is typically formulated near pH 3-4.
c-321.actionItem: If you use an exfoliant today, check its acid type, concentration and pH, start with 2 times a week or fewer, and apply sunscreen the next day.

c-322.title: Durian is banned from many hotels because of its smell
c-322.summary: Durian is banned in hotels and on transit not because it is toxic, but because its smell is overwhelming even in tiny amounts.
c-322.principle: Esters (RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H₂O) and sulfur compounds (thiols, R-SH) have odor thresholds in the ppb range, so trace amounts are detectable.
c-322.example: 1ppb is one part per billion by volume, which equals only about 0.03mL of vapor in a 30m³ room. That is why the smell lingers in a whole room and in the AC filter.
c-322.actionItem: Before a Southeast Asia trip, check your lodging's durian rule, and eat durian at the shop or outdoors.

c-323.title: Moisturizer ingredients do different jobs: ceramides, glycerin, oils
c-323.summary: A good moisturizer pairs an ingredient that draws in water, one that fills gaps, and one that blocks evaporation.
c-323.principle: Humectants (glycerin) attract water, emollients (ceramides) fill gaps between skin cells, and occlusives (petrolatum) block evaporation. Water movement follows J = -D(ΔC / Δx).
c-323.example: Glycerin is typically used at 5-10%, and petrolatum is known to cut transepidermal water loss by more than 90%. A product with all three lasts longer in dry winter air than a single-ingredient one.
c-323.actionItem: Today, check the ingredient list for glycerin, ceramides and an oil or petrolatum, and apply within 3 minutes after showering.

c-324.title: Check your fireplace or stove chimney for creosote every year
c-324.summary: Tar from wood smoke condenses on chimney walls, and the buildup can cause a chimney fire, so inspect it every year.
c-324.principle: Tar and soot vapors from incomplete combustion condense on cool chimney walls as creosote. Oxygen-starved burning, C_xH_y + O₂ → C + CO + H₂O, produces more unburned material.
c-324.example: NFPA 211 in the US advises cleaning when deposits reach about 3mm (1/8 inch). Wet wood above 20% moisture lowers the burn temperature and speeds up buildup.
c-324.actionItem: Today, check that your firewood is dried to 20% moisture or less, and book a professional chimney inspection and sweep.

c-325.title: Butter absorbs odors when stored next to strong-smelling foods
c-325.summary: Butter is about 80% fat, which dissolves and soaks up odor molecules from foods like kimchi or fish.
c-325.principle: Fat is nonpolar, so it dissolves the nonpolar volatile molecules that carry odors. The partition coefficient is K = C_fatC_water, and K = 3 means a 1,000 times higher concentration in fat.
c-325.example: A 200g block of butter holds about 160g of fat. Left uncovered next to kimchi for a few days, it picks up the smell and may end up thrown away.
c-325.actionItem: Today, put your butter in its wrapper inside a sealed container and keep it away from strong-smelling foods.

c-326.title: Why glasses turn cloudy in the dishwasher
c-326.summary: Cloudiness can be a mineral film or actual etching of the glass surface. A vinegar soak tells you which.
c-326.principle: Soft water and alkaline detergent at high temperature dissolve the silicate network of glass and etch the surface. SiO₂ + 2OH⁻ → SiO₃²⁻ + H₂O
c-326.example: Etching is permanent, but a hard-water lime film vanishes after 5 minutes in white vinegar. Using less detergent and an eco cycle around 55°C reduces etching.
c-326.actionItem: Today, soak a cloudy glass in white vinegar for 5 minutes to see if it is film, and use only the recommended detergent dose.

c-327.title: Replace mascara every 3 to 6 months
c-327.summary: Mascara goes right next to the eyes and gets air pumped in with every use, so bacteria build up; replace it within 3-6 months of opening.
c-327.principle: After opening, preservatives gradually deplete and bacteria multiply exponentially, doubling at regular intervals. Each time the wand is inserted and removed, air and microbes enter, accelerating drying and contamination.
c-327.example: Under ideal conditions where bacteria double every 20 minutes, a single bacterium multiplies over 260,000 times (2¹⁸) in just 6 hours. If your eyes feel itchy or red, suspect an expired mascara first.
c-327.actionItem: Today, write the opening date on your mascara tube, and replace it with a new one if it is older than 3 months.

c-328.title: Rice abroad tastes different because of its amylose content
c-328.summary: Rice abroad can come out fluffy and separate or sticky because the amylose-to-amylopectin ratio differs.
c-328.principle: More amylose (linear) keeps grains separate and firm, while more amylopectin (branched) makes rice sticky. amylose % = m_amylosem_amylose+m_amylopectin × 100
c-328.example: Korean and Japanese short-grain rice has roughly 17-20% amylose, long-grain indica about 22-28%, and glutinous rice nearly 0%. Long-grain rice usually needs 1.5-2 times its volume of water.
c-328.actionItem: Today, check whether your rice package says short, medium or long grain, and cook it with the water ratio printed on the package.

c-329.title: Check mouthwash for alcohol-free formulas and CPC
c-329.summary: Pick a mouthwash by its antibacterial ingredient (CPC) and whether it has alcohol, which can dry out your mouth.
c-329.principle: CPC (cetylpyridinium chloride) is a cationic surfactant that sticks to negatively charged bacterial membranes and disrupts them. The attraction follows F = k(q₁ q₂ / r²).
c-329.example: CPC products are usually 0.05-0.07%, so one 20mL rinse contains about 10-14mg. Some products contain 20% ethanol or more, so people prone to dry mouth may prefer alcohol-free.
c-329.actionItem: Today, check the label for CPC and ethanol, then rinse for 30 seconds and spit it out rather than swallowing.

c-330.title: Window caulk smell is acetic acid released during curing
c-330.summary: The vinegar smell of caulk is acetic acid released as the silicone cures, and it fades once curing is done.
c-330.principle: Acetoxy silicone reacts with moisture in the air, releasing acetic acid as it crosslinks. R-Si(OCOCH₃)₃ + 3H₂O → R-Si(OH)₃ + 3CH₃COOH
c-330.example: The surface skins over in about 10-30 minutes, and a 3mm bead takes about 24 hours to cure fully. Acetic acid can corrode metal and marble, so use neutral-cure silicone there.
c-330.actionItem: If you apply caulk today, keep a window open to ventilate for 24 hours, and choose neutral-cure silicone for metal or stone.

c-331.title: Olive oil turning cloudy and solid in the fridge isn't spoiled
c-331.summary: Olive oil that goes cloudy and solid in the fridge is not spoiled; its fat has crystallized, and it clears again at room temperature.
c-331.principle: Even unsaturated fatty acids crystallize below their melting point. The melting temperature follows T_m = (ΔH / ΔS), and olive oil starts to cloud below about 5-10°C.
c-331.example: At 4°C in the fridge it turns cloudy, but 30-60 minutes at 20-25°C clears it. For oxidation, a dark, cool room-temperature spot is better than the fridge.
c-331.actionItem: Today, let cloudy olive oil sit at room temperature for 30 minutes instead of microwaving it, and store it in a dark cupboard from now on.

c-332.title: Make caramel by melting sugar without stirring
c-332.summary: You avoid stirring when making caramel to stop sugar crystals from re-forming in a chain reaction.
c-332.principle: One stray sugar crystal can seed crystallization of the whole syrup. Above 160°C, hydrolysis and dehydration cause browning. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆
c-332.example: Boiling 200g sugar with 50mL water reaches a golden caramel at about 170-180°C after 5-10 minutes. Caramel at that temperature can cause serious burns if it splatters.
c-332.actionItem: If you make caramel today, swirl the pan instead of stirring and wash crystals off the pot wall with a wet brush.

c-333.title: Red skin under metal jewelry may be nickel allergy
c-333.summary: If skin turns red and itchy under earrings or a watch buckle, nickel in the metal may be the cause. A dermatologist can confirm it.
c-333.principle: Nickel in the metal is oxidized by sweat and dissolves as ions. Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ These ions can bind skin proteins and trigger contact dermatitis.
c-333.example: The EU limits nickel release from items in prolonged skin contact to 0.5 µg/cm² per week. Roughly 1 in 10 people are reported to be nickel-sensitive.
