c-333.actionItem: Today, check for a nickel-free label on any jewelry that keeps itching, and see a dermatologist if symptoms continue.

c-334.title: Wasabi's heat only appears when grated and fades fast
c-334.summary: Real wasabi's heat is created when its cells are crushed by grating, and it is volatile, so it fades quickly.
c-334.principle: When cells break, the enzyme myrosinase splits the glycoside sinigrin into pungent allyl isothiocyanate. C₁₀H₁₆KNO₉S₂ + H₂O → C₄H₅NS + C₆H₁₂O₆ + KHSO₄
c-334.example: The heat is strongest within minutes of grating and drops sharply in 15-30 minutes. Many tube wasabi products are mainly horseradish.
c-334.actionItem: If you use fresh wasabi today, grate it right before eating and keep it covered, and check the ingredients on tube products.

c-335.title: More dish soap foam doesn't mean better cleaning
c-335.summary: Lots of foam and good grease removal are separate things; foam can come from stabilizers.
c-335.principle: Surfactants form micelles above the critical micelle concentration (CMC) and wrap around grease. Surface tension falls until the CMC and stays almost constant after that.
c-335.example: The CMC of SDS is about 8.2 mM, or about 2.4g per liter. Adding more soap beyond that does not boost cleaning much and only makes rinsing harder.
c-335.actionItem: Today, use only a pea-sized amount of dish soap and judge by whether grease is gone, not by how much foam there is.

c-336.title: Heat-generating thermal underwear warms by adsorbing sweat vapor
c-336.summary: Heat-generating underwear feels warm because water vapor from your body releases heat when it sticks to the fibers; the effect is modest and short-lived.
c-336.principle: When water vapor attaches to fibers, heat is released much like condensation. Q = m L, and water's condensation heat L is about 2.26MJ/kg.
c-336.example: Adsorbing 10g of moisture releases up to about 23kJ, but it stops once the fibers saturate. If you sweat heavily and the fabric gets wet, it draws heat away and you feel colder.
c-336.actionItem: Today, wear a thin layer over thermal underwear, and remove a layer when you start to sweat so the fabric stays dry.

c-337.title: Remove labels and caps from PET bottles so they can be recycled
c-337.summary: PET bottles become good recycled material only if you remove the label and rinse them, so they do not mix with other plastics.
c-337.principle: Recycling separates sinking PET from floating PP and PE by density, ρ = (m / V), then melts it. PET melts near 250°C, PP near 165°C and PE around 110-130°C.
c-337.example: PET has a density of about 1.38g/cm³ while PP and PE are about 0.9g/cm³, so they separate in water. If a 2g cap is mixed with a 20g bottle, contaminants reach about 10%.
c-337.actionItem: Today, empty and rinse your PET bottle, peel off the label, and put it in the clear-PET collection bin.

c-338.title: Meringue won't whip with even a drop of grease
c-338.summary: The most common reason meringue won't rise is a trace of fat on the bowl or in the whites.
c-338.principle: Egg white proteins unfold at the air-water boundary and form a film that holds the bubbles. Fat takes up that spot first and blocks film formation. The pressure difference across a bubble film is ΔP = (4γ / r).
c-338.example: Three egg whites (about 100g) are roughly 90% water and 10% protein, while yolk is about 30% fat, so even a drop sharply cuts the volume. Plastic bowls often hold traces of oil.
c-338.actionItem: If you make meringue today, wipe a glass or steel bowl with vinegar or lemon juice and separate each white into a small bowl first.

c-339.title: Do a patch test two days before covering gray hair
c-339.summary: Hair dye allergy can appear suddenly, so patch-test behind the ear or on the inner arm 48 hours before dyeing.
c-339.principle: Oxidative dyes such as para-phenylenediamine (PPD) form reactive intermediates with hydrogen peroxide that bind skin proteins and can cause allergy. C₆H₄(NH₂)₂ ―(H₂O₂)→ reactive intermediates
c-339.example: The EU limits PPD on the head to 2% after mixing. Apply a small amount no bigger than a coin and watch for 48 hours; if there is redness, itching or swelling, do not dye.
c-339.actionItem: If you plan to dye soon, do the patch test two days ahead with a small amount behind the ear, and skip dyeing if any reaction appears, seeking care if it is severe.

c-340.title: Proof on a foreign liquor bottle is twice the ABV
c-340.summary: On US bottles, proof is twice the alcohol by volume (ABV), so 80 proof means 40%.
c-340.principle: The US system is proof = 2 × ABV. The old British proof used a different basis, where 100 proof was about 57.15%, so check by country.
c-340.example: A 45mL (1.5 oz) pour of 80 proof whiskey holds 45 × 0.40 = 18mL ethanol, about 14.2g, which is one US standard drink. The same pour at 100 proof (50%) holds about 17.8g.
c-340.actionItem: Today, divide any foreign bottle's proof by 2 to get the ABV, and keep track of how much you drink.

c-341.title: Water filters: activated carbon and reverse osmosis remove different things
c-341.summary: Activated carbon mostly removes organics such as chlorine and odor, while reverse osmosis mostly removes dissolved ions. Decide what you need to remove before buying.
c-341.principle: Carbon adsorbs onto its surface, while reverse osmosis applies pressure above the osmotic pressure π = iMRT so only water passes through the semipermeable membrane.
c-341.example: The osmotic pressure of 500mg/L NaCl (about 8.6 mmol/L) at 25°C is about 0.42atm. Home RO units usually apply 3-4bar and remove most ions.
c-341.actionItem: Today, check when your water filter is due for replacement, and verify its claims through an official certification mark.

c-342.title: Camping lantern mantles glow because of rare-earth oxides
c-342.summary: A gas lantern's bright light is not the flame but a rare-earth oxide mantle heated by it.
c-342.principle: When the oxide mantle is heated to about 2,000K, it radiates strongly toward visible wavelengths. The peak wavelength follows λ_ T = 2898µm · K.
c-342.example: At 2,000K, λ_ is about 1.45μm. Yttrium and cerium mantles emit much more visible light than a bare flame from the same fuel. Older mantles used radioactive thorium oxide.
c-342.actionItem: Today, burn a new mantle off outdoors for its first use, do not touch the ash, and look for a thorium-free label.

c-343.title: Paper cups aren't recycled as ordinary paper because of their polyethylene lining
c-343.summary: Paper cups have a plastic film for waterproofing, so putting them in the regular paper bin makes recycling difficult.
c-343.principle: The polyethylene (PE) inside a paper cup does not dissolve in water and floats at ρ ≈ 0.92g/cm³, so it is hard to separate from fiber during pulping.
c-343.example: One paper cup weighs about 10g and the PE coating is roughly 5% of that. Without a dedicated process, that coating can ruin the quality of a whole paper batch.
c-343.actionItem: Today, bring your own tumbler, and if you do use a paper cup, check your local sorting rule and collect it separately.

c-344.title: Cream whips firm only when it is cold
c-344.summary: Cream whips into stiff peaks only when very cold; lukewarm cream will not rise no matter how long you whisk.
c-344.principle: When cold, fat inside the globules is crystallized, so whipping makes the globules partly clump into a network that traps air bubbles. Melted fat cannot build that network.
c-344.example: Whipping 200mL of cream with 35% or more fat at 4°C roughly doubles the volume in 3-5 minutes. Above 20°C it barely rises, and overwhipping splits it into butter and buttermilk.
c-344.actionItem: Today, chill the cream and bowl for 10+ minutes before whipping, and stop as soon as stiff peaks form.

c-345.title: Don't hold whitening toothpaste peroxide in your mouth for long
c-345.summary: Peroxide in whitening toothpaste or strips can irritate gums, so use it only for the stated time.
c-345.principle: Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes and breaks down stain molecules while releasing oxygen. 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ That same reactivity can irritate mucous membranes.
c-345.example: The EU limits hydrogen peroxide in ordinary toothpaste to 0.1% and requires dental supervision for 0.1-6% whitening products. Holding it longer than directed increases gum irritation and sensitivity.
c-345.actionItem: Today, use any whitening product only for the time on the label, and stop and consult a dentist if your gums sting.

c-346.title: Don't drink melted snow without treating it
c-346.summary: Snow looks clean but collects airborne pollutants and microbes, so melted snow should be boiled before drinking.
c-346.principle: Snow crystals trap dust and fine particles as they form and fall. Boiling kills microbes but does not remove heavy metals or chemicals. The water yield depends on snow density, V_water ≈ V_snow10.
c-346.example: Melting 10L of fresh snow gives about 1L of water, and the usual rule is to boil for at least 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000m). Avoid snow near roads or that is discolored.
c-346.actionItem: Today, in an emergency, collect only clean fresh snow, start with a little water in the pot, melt and boil it, and otherwise carry bottled water.

c-347.title: Lactose-free milk is milk with the lactose broken down in advance
c-347.summary: Lactose-free milk has its lactose pre-digested, so it suits lactose intolerance, but its milk proteins remain, so it is not suitable for milk allergy.
c-347.principle: The enzyme lactase hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O ―(lactase)→ C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆
c-347.example: Regular milk has about 4.7-5g of lactose per 100mL, so 200mL holds about 9.5g. The EU lactose-free standard is 0.01g per 100g or less, and the released sugars make it taste slightly sweeter.
c-347.actionItem: Today, if lactose upsets your stomach, choose a lactose-free product, but avoid both regular and lactose-free milk if you have a milk allergy.

c-348.title: Turn on the hood when cooking on a gas stove because it releases nitrogen dioxide
c-348.summary: A gas flame produces nitrogen dioxide that can degrade air in a small kitchen, so run the hood while cooking.
c-348.principle: In a hot flame, nitrogen and oxygen from air react (N₂ + O₂ → 2NO) and then oxidize further. 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂
c-348.example: Measurements in small unventilated kitchens have reported nitrogen dioxide above the WHO 1-hour guideline of 200 µg/m³. A hood that vents outdoors lowers it substantially.
c-348.actionItem: Today, switch the hood on before you start cooking and keep it running about 10 minutes after turning off the flame.

c-349.title: Leftover cooking oil can be turned into laundry soap
c-349.summary: Instead of pouring leftover cooking oil down the drain, you can collect it and react it with lye to make soap.
c-349.principle: Saponification turns triglycerides and NaOH into soap and glycerol. C₃H₅(OOCR)₃ + 3NaOH → C₃H₅(OH)₃ + 3RCOONa
c-349.example: Soybean oil needs about 0.135g NaOH per gram of oil, so 500g of oil needs about 68g. Lye is strongly caustic, so goggles and gloves are essential, and the soap cures for about 4 weeks.
c-349.actionItem: Today, strain leftover oil through a coffee filter into a sealed bottle, and never pour it down the drain.

c-350.title: One drop of water makes melted chocolate seize up
c-350.summary: A little water in melted chocolate can suddenly turn it from smooth to a stiff, grainy lump.
c-350.principle: Sugar and cocoa particles absorb water and form sticky syrup films that glue the particles together, sharply raising viscosity. This is called seizing.
c-350.example: Just a few grams of water, about 1-2% of 200g of chocolate, is enough to seize it. Adding much more water, to roughly 20% or beyond, can make it smooth again as a thin ganache.
c-350.actionItem: Today, when melting chocolate, dry the bowl and spatula and keep steam and water from the double boiler out of the bowl.

c-351.title: Wash cutting boards right after use and dry them completely
c-351.summary: Bacteria need moisture to multiply, so washing your cutting board right away and drying it completely is the key.
c-351.principle: Water activity, which shows how available water is, is a_w = (p / p₀), and many pathogens grow fast at a_w of about 0.9 or higher.
c-351.example: The surface of raw meat has an a_w of about 0.99, which suits bacterial growth. Standing the board up to dry with airflow reduces surface moisture and limits growth.
c-351.actionItem: Today, wash your board with hot water and detergent right after use and stand it up to dry fully, keeping raw-meat and vegetable boards separate.

c-352.title: Boiling Christmas-market Glühwein drives off the aroma
c-352.summary: Mulled wine should be heated only until it steams, not boiled, so more of its aroma and alcohol stays.
c-352.principle: Ethanol boils at about 78°C, lower than water, so it evaporates first when heated. The vapor pressure of a mixture follows P = x_EtOH P^°_EtOH (Raoult's law).
c-352.example: A 750mL bottle of 12% wine contains about 90mL of ethanol. It is usually served at 60-70°C, and boiling above 78°C expels alcohol and aroma compounds quickly.
c-352.actionItem: Today, warm mulled wine on low heat below 70°C and remove the spices before it boils.

c-353.title: The ABC marking on a fire extinguisher shows fire types
c-353.summary: The A, B and C on an extinguisher show which fires it can fight, and an ABC dry-powder unit is the usual home choice.
c-353.principle: In Korean and US labeling, A is ordinary combustibles, B is flammable liquids and C is electrical fires. Monoammonium phosphate decomposes on heating and suppresses the combustion chain reaction. NH₄H₂PO₄ → NH₃ + H₃PO₄
c-353.example: A 3.3kg home powder extinguisher usually discharges in about 10-20 seconds, so know how to use it beforehand. In Europe the classes differ, for example C means gas fires, so check local standards.
c-353.actionItem: Today, check that your extinguisher's pressure gauge is in the green range and keep it within easy reach.

c-354.title: Reusable hand warmers use sodium acetate's heat of crystallization
c-354.summary: Reusable hand warmers use the heat released when a supersaturated solution crystallizes all at once, and boiling them in water resets them.
c-354.principle: Sodium acetate trihydrate melts at about 58°C, and when the supercooled liquid crystallizes it releases heat of fusion. Q = m ΔH_fus, with ΔH_fus about 265J/g.
c-354.example: A 100g pack releases about 26kJ as it crystallizes, and its surface rises to around 50°C. Leaving the same pack in boiling water for about 10 minutes turns it clear again.
c-354.actionItem: Today, boil a used warmer in water until every crystal dissolves, cool it slowly, and avoid holding it on bare skin for long.

c-355.title: Blocking oxygen keeps opened wine good for about four more days
c-355.summary: Oxygen is the main reason opened wine goes off, so re-corking and refrigerating it usually buys 3-5 more days.
c-355.principle: Oxygen and acetic acid bacteria convert ethanol to acetic acid via acetaldehyde. CH₃CH₂OH + O₂ → CH₃COOH + H₂O The rate follows k = Ae⁻E_a/RT, roughly halving for each 10°C drop.
c-355.example: Re-corked and refrigerated, red and white both usually last 3-5 days, while left open at room temperature they decline in 1-2 days. If little remains, move it to a smaller bottle to cut the air inside.
c-355.actionItem: Today, cork leftover wine and refrigerate it right away, and take red out 20 minutes before drinking.

c-356.title: White crystals at the bottom of a wine bottle are tartrate deposits
c-356.summary: White granules at the bottom of a bottle or on the cork are tartrate crystals, not spoilage, and are harmless.
c-356.principle: Potassium hydrogen tartrate (KHT) becomes less soluble at low temperature and precipitates. KHC₄H₄O₆(s) ⇌ K⁺ + HC₄H₄O₆⁻ with Kₛₚ = [K⁺][HC₄H₄O₆⁻].
c-356.example: Wine usually contains 1.5-4g/L tartaric acid, and crystals form slowly in cold storage such as a fridge. The same substance is the cream of tartar used in baking.
c-356.actionItem: Today, if you see crystals, do not throw the wine out; stand the bottle upright and pour slowly, leaving the sediment behind.

c-357.title: Don't put aroma oil or detergent into a humidifier
c-357.summary: Only clean water belongs in a humidifier tank. Oils or detergents turn into fine particles that you then breathe in.
c-357.principle: An ultrasonic humidifier atomizes water into fine droplets, carrying dissolved substances into the air with it. The mass of non-volatile material released is m = C × V_mist.
c-357.example: At a mist output of about 300mL per hour, a 1% additive means roughly 3mL of oil or detergent aerosolized every hour. Tap-water minerals (assuming 150mg/L) also become about 45mg of white dust per hour.
c-357.actionItem: Today, change the humidifier water daily, use a dedicated diffuser for aromas, and wash the tank weekly.

c-358.title: E10 at foreign pumps is gasoline blended with ethanol
c-358.summary: E10 is gasoline with about 10% ethanol; most gasoline cars can use it, but it has slightly less energy.
c-358.principle: Ethanol has about 21MJ/L of energy by volume, lower than gasoline's roughly 32MJ/L. E_E10 = 0.9E_gas + 0.1E_EtOH, and octane rises slightly.
c-358.example: E10 delivers about 30.9MJ/L, around 3% less than gasoline, so a car that does 14km/L would do about 13.6km/L. Check the fuel-cap label to confirm your car suits E10.
c-358.actionItem: Today, when you pick up a rental car, check the fuel-cap label (gasoline, diesel, E10-compatible) and do not mix up diesel and gasoline.

c-359.title: Smoke detectors differ: photoelectric versus ionization
c-359.summary: Different smoke detector types respond best to different fires, with photoelectric stronger on slow smoldering fires.
c-359.principle: An ionization alarm uses americium-241 to ionize air and sounds when smoke particles reduce the current, while a photoelectric alarm senses light scattered by smoke particles.
c-359.example: Ionization responds faster to small particles (about 0.01-0.3μm) from flaming fires, and photoelectric to larger particles (about 0.3-10μm) from smoldering fires. An ionization unit holds about 30-40 kBq of americium.
c-359.actionItem: Today, press the test button on your detector, and replace it if the manufacture date on the back is over 10 years old.

c-360.title: Only short trips in a diesel car clog the particulate filter
c-360.summary: If you only drive a diesel car on short trips, exhaust never gets hot enough and soot builds up in the diesel particulate filter (DPF).
c-360.principle: Soot in a DPF has to be burned off in regeneration. C + O₂ → CO₂ happens at about 350-450°C with a catalyst, and active regeneration at about 600°C.
c-360.example: On short trips the exhaust stays below 200°C and regeneration never happens. That is why you occasionally need a drive of 20-30 minutes or more at highway speed to burn the filter clean.
c-360.actionItem: This week, drive 20-30 minutes or more at a steady highway speed, and have it checked at a garage if a warning light is on.

c-361.title: A little baking soda tenderizes tough meat
c-361.summary: A very small amount of baking soda raises the pH of tough meat so it holds more water and turns tender.
c-361.principle: Muscle proteins hold water worst near their isoelectric point (pH about 5-5.5). Raising meat pH (about 5.5-5.7) with baking soda adds negative charge so proteins repel each other and hold more water. NaHCO₃ ⇌ Na⁺ + HCO₃⁻
c-361.example: Toss 450g of sliced meat with about 2.5g (0.5%) of baking soda for 15 minutes, then rinse. Too much gives a soapy taste and mushy texture.
c-361.actionItem: Today, if stir-fry meat is tough, coat it with 0.5% or less baking soda for only 15 minutes, rinse well, and then cook.

c-362.title: Milk sometimes curdles in hot coffee
c-362.summary: Milk curdling in coffee is proteins clumping because of acidity and heat, and fresh milk is usually harmless.
c-362.principle: The isoelectric point of milk casein is about pH 4.6, so as pH approaches it the charge drops and the proteins clump together. Heat speeds up this aggregation.
c-362.example: Milk is about pH 6.7 and coffee about 4.8-5.1. Older milk already has a lower pH and curdles more easily, so if it smells sour, discard it rather than drink it.
c-362.actionItem: Today, pour milk into the cup first or use warmed milk for your coffee, and throw it out if it smells sour.

c-363.title: Inhaling helium from balloon gas is dangerous
c-363.summary: Inhaling helium changes your voice, but it displaces oxygen and can cause suffocation, so it is dangerous.
c-363.principle: The oxygen partial pressure in breathing gas is P_O₂ = F_O₂ × P. Pure helium has F_O₂ = 0, so it pushes oxygen out of the lungs. Sound speed, v = √((γ RT / M)), is much higher in helium, which raises the voice.
c-363.example: Air is 20.9% oxygen while 100% helium has 0%. Sound speed in helium is about 1,007m/s, roughly 3 times that in air (about 343m/s), and breathing directly from a pressurized tank can injure the lungs.
c-363.actionItem: Today, when inflating balloons, do not inhale the helium, and ventilate in a closed room.

c-364.title: Don't send high-speed film through airport X-rays
c-364.summary: Airport X-rays can fog film, so for high-speed film it is safer to ask for a hand inspection.
c-364.principle: When silver halide crystals absorb light or X-ray photons, they form a latent image of silver atoms. AgBr + h → Ag + Br Exposure accumulates.
c-364.example: Film rated ISO 800 or higher can fog after several scans, and X-rays for checked baggage are stronger. Because exposure adds up, keep the number of scans on a trip low.
c-364.actionItem: Today, put your film in a clear bag, ask for a hand inspection at security, and do not pack it in checked luggage.

c-365.title: Judge perfume lasting power and price by EDP or EDT strength
c-365.summary: With perfume, the fragrance concentration (%) tells you more about lasting power and price than the name does.
c-365.principle: The higher the fragrance concentration, the slower the evaporation and the longer it lasts. Eau de parfum (EDP) is about 15-20%, eau de toilette (EDT) about 5-15% and eau de cologne (EDC) about 2-4%.
c-365.example: In a 50mL bottle, 15% EDP holds about 7.5mL of fragrance oil and 8% EDT about 4mL, so EDP usually costs more. EDT typically lasts about 3-4 hours and EDP about 5-8 hours.
c-365.actionItem: Before buying perfume, spray it on your inner forearm and check how it smells after 4 hours.

c-366.title: The aerogel in insoles and gloves is mostly air held in silica
c-366.summary: Aerogel in cold-weather gear is a silica structure that is mostly air, so even a thin layer blocks heat well.
c-366.principle: Nano-sized pores smaller than the mean free path of air molecules (about 68nm) block heat transfer. λ = k_B T√(2) π d² P and heat flow is Q = (kA ΔT / L).
c-366.example: Silica aerogel has a thermal conductivity of about 0.015-0.02W/m·K, lower than still air (about 0.026). For an area of 0.02m², a thickness of 3mm and a 20K difference with k = 0.02, heat loss is about 2.7W.
c-366.actionItem: Today, check the actual aerogel content and thickness of your insoles and gloves, and keep them dry because wetness reduces insulation.

p-275.title: Store kimchi in a shaded balcony inside a styrofoam box
p-275.summary: Styrofoam barely conducts heat and shade blocks radiant heat from the sun. Together they keep stored kimchi cold and steady for longer.
p-275.principle: Conductive heat loss is q=(kAΔT / L). Polystyrene foam has k ≈ 0.035W/(m · K), lower than wood (about 0.12). Direct sunlight heats a container surface by radiation, so shade is needed too.
p-275.example: For a box with 3cm walls and 1m² area and a 10 °CmathrmC inside-outside difference, q=0.035 × 1 × 10/0.03 ≈ 12W. A wooden box of the same thickness leaks about 40W, over 3 times more.
p-275.actionItem: Today, put the kimchi container in a foam box on the shaded side of the balcony and fill gaps with newspaper before closing the lid.

p-276.title: Clear leaves from drains before the water overflows
p-276.summary: Leaves covering a drain cut the flow it can carry, so the same rain can back up and flood. One minute of cleaning before rain is the cheapest prevention.
p-276.principle: Flow rate is Q=Av, so when the effective open area A shrinks, drainage falls in proportion. Leaves plug the grate openings and cut A sharply.
p-276.example: A drain 10cm in diameter has an area of about 79cm². If leaves cover half of it, A ≈ 39cm², and at the same flow speed drainage drops to about 50%.
p-276.actionItem: Today, remove leaves from the balcony, rooftop or doorstep drain cover with gloved hands or tongs.

p-277.title: Ten minutes of morning daylight is tens of times brighter than indoor lights
p-277.summary: Even an overcast morning outdoors is much brighter than indoor lighting, and bright light helps set the body's daily rhythm. A short morning outing is the easiest lighting habit.
p-277.principle: Illuminance is the light reaching a surface per area, E=(Φ / A), measured in lux (lm/m²). Outdoors on a clear day it is about 10,000100,000 lux; typical indoor light is 100500 lux.
p-277.example: A clear morning outdoors at about 10,000 lux is roughly 20 times an office at 500 lux and about 70 times a living room at 150 lux. Even overcast days are usually above 1,000 lux, brighter than indoors.
p-277.actionItem: This morning, spend 10 minutes walking outdoors rather than just looking through a window. Never stare directly at the sun.

p-278.title: On autumn hikes the sun sets earlier than the table says because of mountain shade
p-278.summary: Sunset tables assume a flat horizon, so a ridge to the west hides the sun much earlier. In the mountains the real sunset is when the sun reaches the ridgeline.
p-278.principle: If the western ridge blocks the sun up to an elevation h, the real sunset is when the sun drops to that height, about Δt ≈ (h / ω) earlier. At mid-latitudes in autumn the sun's descent rate is roughly ω ≈ 12^°/h.
p-278.example: With a 10^° ridge to the west, Δt ≈ 10^°/12°Cmathrm/h ≈ 50 min earlier shade. Adding the dusk that follows, your safe descent margin shrinks by more than an hour.
p-278.actionItem: Today, set your planned finish time for a hike 1.5 to 2 hours before the tabulated sunset and pack a headlamp.

p-279.title: Check both the fill power and the fill weight of a down jacket
p-279.summary: Fill power measures how well down fluffs up to trap air. A higher number means the same warmth with less weight, but total warmth also depends on how much fill is used.
p-279.principle: Fill power is FP=V (in³)m (oz), the volume per unit weight of down. Warmth depends on the thickness of trapped still air (k ≈ 0.026W/(m · K)), so the weight needed to fill a given volume is m ∝ 1FP.
p-279.example: To fill the same thickness, fill power 600 needs 100g and fill power 800 needs 600/800 × 100=75g. For the same warmth that is about 25% lighter.
p-279.actionItem: Today, when shopping for a puffer jacket, compare both the fill power and the fill weight (g) on the label.

p-280.title: A solar calculator works even under indoor lights
p-280.summary: A calculator uses only a few microwatts, so weak indoor light is enough. What matters is whether each photon's energy clears the threshold, not how bright the light is.
p-280.principle: Photon energy is E=h=(hc / λ) ≈ 1240 eV · nmλ. If it exceeds the semiconductor band gap, electrons are freed and current flows; dimmer light only reduces the current.
p-280.example: A 550nm visible photon carries E ≈ 2.25 eV, above the roughly 1.7 eV band gap of amorphous silicon. A 500 lux room is about 1/200 of clear-day sunlight (about 100,000 lux) but still enough for a calculator using a few µW.
p-280.actionItem: Today, turn on a solar calculator under room light and cover its panel with your hand to watch the display fade.

p-281.title: Dark mode saves battery on OLED phones
p-281.summary: Each OLED pixel makes its own light, so black pixels use almost no power. The more dark background on screen, the less display power is used.
p-281.principle: Display power is the sum over pixels P=_i P_i, and a black pixel has P_i ≈ 0. An LCD with an always-on backlight draws nearly the same power whatever is shown, so dark mode does little there.
p-281.example: Assume display power is 1.0W on a white background and 0.5W on black. Over 3 hours that saves 0.5W × 3 h=1.5Wh, about 10% of a 15Wh battery.
p-281.actionItem: Today, if your phone has an OLED screen, turn on dark mode in settings. On an LCD phone, lower the brightness instead.

p-282.title: Drive in fog with low beams and fog lights
p-282.summary: In fog, high beams bounce off water droplets back at you and make visibility worse. Low beams and fog lights, aimed low, give a clearer view.
p-282.principle: Fog droplets (about 120µm across) are comparable to light's wavelength, so Mie scattering sends light strongly in all directions, including back toward the driver. Light fades as I=I₀e⁻β x, and high-beam light near eye level is reflected back as glare.
p-282.example: In Korea, when visibility is within 50m, the speed limit must be cut by at least 50%, so a 100km/h road becomes 50km/h or less.
p-282.actionItem: From today, on foggy days switch on low beams and fog lights, turn off the high beams and leave a larger gap to the car ahead.

p-283.title: Place your reading lamp on the side opposite your writing hand
p-283.summary: Because light travels in straight lines, your hand and pen cast a shadow over the words. A lamp on the opposite side throws that shadow behind your hand so your eyes strain less.
p-283.principle: For a point source at height H, an object of height h at horizontal distance d casts a shadow extending s=(dh / H-h) behind it. A lamp on the same side as your writing hand puts that shadow over the text.
p-283.example: With a lamp height H=40cm, hand height h=3cm and distance d=30cm, the shadow is s=(30 × 3 / 37) ≈ 2.4cm. Reading light of 300500 lux is typical.
p-283.actionItem: Today, if you are right-handed, put the desk lamp at the front left; if left-handed, at the front right.

p-284.title: Zigzag up steep slopes
p-284.summary: For the same height gained the work is the same, but taking a slanted path lowers the force per step so you tire less. The trade-off is a longer walk.
p-284.principle: On a slope the work is W=mgh regardless of path, but the force along the slope is F=mgθ=mg(h / L), which falls as the path length L grows.
p-284.example: A 70kg person climbing 100m does W ≈ 69kJ. A straight 30^° climb needs F ≈ 343N over 200m; a 15^° zigzag needs F ≈ 178N over about 386m.
p-284.actionItem: Today, on a steep stretch, follow the marked trail's switchbacks and do not cut straight across them.

p-285.title: Winter tires stay soft below 7°C
p-285.summary: Rubber hardens in the cold and loses grip, but winter tires use a compound that stays supple at low temperatures. Even without snow, they help when temperatures hover near 7°C.
p-285.principle: Rubber stays elastic above its glass transition temperature T_g and stiffens near it. Friction is F=µ N and stopping distance is d=(v² / 2µ g), so a lower µ lengthens it.
p-285.example: At 80km/h (22.2m/s), µ=0.8 gives about 31m, while a cold-hardened tire with µ=0.6 needs about 42m. The values are illustrative assumptions.
p-285.actionItem: Today, check the forecast to see whether daily lows will stay near 7°C and schedule your winter tire swap.

p-286.title: A hallway motion light senses infrared from body heat
p-286.summary: A motion light turns on when it detects changes in the infrared radiation your body gives off as you move. Lighting only when needed cuts hallway lighting energy sharply.
p-286.principle: Peak radiation wavelength follows Wien's law λ_=(b / T) with b ≈ 2898µm · K. For skin at about 33 °CmathrmC (306K), λ_ ≈ 9.5µm, and a PIR sensor watches changes in this infrared.
p-286.example: A 10W hallway LED left on for 24 hours uses 240Wh. With a sensor that lights it 2 hours a day and uses 0.5W standby, the total is 20+12=32Wh, about 87% less.
p-286.actionItem: Today, swap a hallway or entrance light for a motion-sensing one, or set its on-time to 1 to 2 minutes.

p-287.title: Close the door of unused rooms to shrink the volume you heat
p-287.summary: Less air and wall area to warm means less heat for the same temperature. Do not seal a room completely, though, since condensation can form; keep a minimum temperature.
p-287.principle: Heat to warm air is Q=mcΔT with m=ρ V, so it scales with the volume V being heated. Air has ρ ≈ 1.2kg/m³ and c ≈ 1005J/(kg · K).
p-287.example: Raising the air in an empty 25m³ room by 5 °CmathrmC takes Q=1.2 × 25 × 1005 × 5 ≈ 151kJ ≈ 0.04kWh. Adding the walls, furniture and continuous leakage, the real figure is several times larger.
p-287.actionItem: Today, close the door of an unused room and lower its heating valve to the minimum rather than shutting it off fully.

p-288.title: Glare from oncoming headlights: look toward the right lane edge
p-288.summary: The farther your gaze is from a light source, the less scattered light inside your eye veils your vision. Looking at the right lane edge cuts the glare and still shows the road.
p-288.principle: Veiling luminance from scattered light in the eye is approximately L_v ≈ (10E / θ²), where E is the illuminance at the eye (lux) and θ is the angle between the source and your gaze (^°).
p-288.example: A gaze 5^° from the source gives L_v ∝ 1/25, and 10^° gives 1/100, so veiling luminance drops to 1/4. Your pupil also constricts in bright light, which helps further.
p-288.actionItem: Tonight, if you meet oncoming high beams, do not close your eyes; fix your gaze on the right lane line and slow down.

p-289.title: Why a lit screen in a dark room tires your eyes
p-289.summary: In a dark room your pupils are wide while the screen is very bright, so your eyes keep adjusting to the brightness gap. Softly lighting the surroundings narrows the gap and eases strain.
p-289.principle: Pupil area is A=(π d² / 4) with diameter varying from about 28mm, and retinal illuminance scales as E_r ∝ L A. A large luminance ratio between screen and surroundings forces constant re-adaptation.
p-289.example: Going from a 2mm to an 8mm pupil multiplies the area by 16. With surroundings at 0.5 cd/m² and a screen at 200 cd/m², the ratio is 400:1, far above the commonly advised 3:110:1.
p-289.actionItem: Tonight, when using a screen, turn on a bias light behind it or a small desk lamp to softly light the room.

p-290.title: The platform safety line exists because of train wind
p-290.summary: A fast train speeds up the air beside it and lowers its pressure, which can pull a person toward the train. Standing behind the safety line is the surest precaution.
p-290.principle: By Bernoulli's principle, p+12ρ v²=const, faster air speed v means lower pressure p. The pressure drop is Δp=12ρ v².
p-290.example: If air beside the train flows at 10m/s, Δp=0.5 × 1.2 × 10²=60Pa, giving a force of about F ≈ 36N (about 3.7 kgf) on a body side area of 0.6m². Turbulence makes the real value fluctuate.
p-290.actionItem: Today, when a train approaches the platform, take one more step back behind the safety line.

p-291.title: Dark baking pans bake faster
p-291.summary: A dark pan absorbs more of the oven's radiant heat, while a shiny silver pan reflects most of it. The same recipe browns the bottom sooner in a dark pan.
p-291.principle: A surface absorbs radiant energy in proportion to its absorptivity (equal to emissivity) ε, and emitted power is P=εσ AT⁴. A black surface has ε ≈ 0.95 and polished aluminum about 0.1.
p-291.example: In the same radiant environment, a black pan absorbs about 0.95/0.1 ≈ 9 times as much radiant heat as a polished silver one. That is why recipes often suggest lowering the oven by about 1015 °CmathrmC for dark pans.
p-291.actionItem: Today, when baking in a dark pan, lower the oven by 1015 °CmathrmC and check the browning early.

p-292.title: An electric blanket's thermostat is a bimetal strip
p-292.summary: A thin strip made of two bonded metals bends when heated and opens or closes an electrical contact. That makes a simple thermostat that cuts power at a set temperature.
p-292.principle: Linear expansion is ΔL=α LΔT. Because the two metals differ in expansion coefficient by Δα, the strip bends, and its tip moves δ=(3ΔαΔT L² / 4t) (t: total thickness).
p-292.example: With L=50mm, t=1mm, Δα=7 × 10⁻⁶ /K and ΔT=40K, the tip moves δ ≈ 0.5mm, enough to separate the contact.
p-292.actionItem: Today, use an electric blanket laid flat, never folded or bunched up, and set it to a low level for sleeping.

p-293.title: A heat source near the boiler thermostat fools your heating
p-293.summary: The thermostat only measures the temperature where it hangs to switch the boiler on and off. A heater or sun beside it leaves the rest of the home colder than set, while a cold wall beside it causes overheating.
p-293.principle: A thermostat runs only when the temperature at its sensor, Tₛₑₙₛₒᵣ, is below the setpoint Tₛₑₜ. So with room average Tᵣₒₒₘ=Tₛₑₙₛₒᵣ+ε, the placement error ε is the heating error.
p-293.example: If a nearby heat source makes the sensor read 23 °CmathrmC while the room averages 20 °CmathrmC, the boiler shuts off even at a 22 °CmathrmC setpoint and the room is 2 °CmathrmC cold. In the opposite case, 2 °CmathrmC of overheating raises heating cost about 14% (a rule of thumb of about 7% per 1°C).
p-293.actionItem: Today, move electric heaters, TVs and other heat sources or furniture away from the thermostat.

p-294.title: Reversing polarity on one speaker makes the bass vanish
p-294.summary: If one speaker's + and − are swapped, the two speakers play in opposite phase and the long-wavelength bass cancels out. If the sound is thin with odd imaging, check polarity first.
p-294.principle: Two waves that differ in phase by π interfere destructively and their sum shrinks. When the wavelength λ=(v / f) is much longer than the speaker spacing, cancellation is nearly complete almost everywhere.
p-294.example: At 100Hz, λ=343/100=3.4m, longer than a 2m speaker spacing, so the level drops sharply near the center. At 5kHz, λ ≈ 6.9cm, so moving a few cm swings the level up and down; the net effect is bass missing.
p-294.actionItem: Today, check that both speakers connect + (red) to the + terminal and − (black) to the − terminal in the same way.

p-295.title: Knee push-ups shorten the body's lever
p-295.summary: Resting on your knees shortens the lever, so your arms carry less load. If standard push-ups are hard, starting with knee push-ups in good form is fine.
p-295.principle: Treating the body as a lever, torque balance F_hand L=mg d gives the hand force F_hand=mg(d / L). Moving the pivot from the toes to the knees changes L and d and lowers the load fraction.
p-295.example: Studies report hand loads of about 64% of body weight in standard push-ups and about 49% in knee push-ups. For 70kg, that is about 45kg versus 34kg, roughly 23% lighter.
p-295.actionItem: Today, try 2 sets of 8 knee push-ups, keeping head, hips and knees in a straight line. Stop if anything hurts.

p-296.title: Find south with an analog watch and the sun
p-296.summary: Point the hour hand at the sun, and the halfway direction between the hour hand and 12 o'clock is roughly south. It is a rough no-compass method for the Northern Hemisphere.
p-296.principle: The sun moves ω_=15^° per hour while the hour hand moves ω_h=30^° per hour. The ratio (ω_ / ω_h)=12 is why the bisector points south.
p-296.example: At 4 p.m., point the hour hand (at 120^° from 12) at the sun, and the halfway direction, 2 o'clock, is south. Korea's standard meridian (135^° E) differs from Seoul (about 127^° E), so solar time is off by about 30 minutes and the error is around ± 15^°.
p-296.actionItem: Today, on a sunny day outdoors, estimate south with an analog watch and compare with your phone's compass.

p-297.title: A higher dioptre magnifier has a shorter focal length
p-297.summary: Magnifier power is the reciprocal of focal length, so a bigger number means a shorter focus and more magnification. The stronger the lens, the narrower the view and the closer it must be held to the eye and object.
p-297.principle: Lens power is D=(1 / f) (f in m, D in dioptres), and angular magnification for the eye's 25cm near point is M ≈ 25 cmf=(D / 4).
p-297.example: 5 D means f=20cm and about 1.25 ×; 10 D means f=10cm and about 2.5 ×; 20 D means f=5cm and about 5 ×.
p-297.actionItem: Today, when choosing a magnifier, pick the power for your use, and never leave it in sunlight, since it can focus the sun and start a fire.

p-298.title: Heat-recovery ventilation takes back the heat that leaves
p-298.summary: This device passes heat from the outgoing indoor air to the incoming cold air. You change the air while keeping much of the heating.
p-298.principle: Recovery efficiency is η=T_supply-TₒᵤₜT_in-Tₒᵤₜ, and ventilation heat loss is P=ρ c V ΔT (ρ c ≈ 1200J/(m³ · K)).
p-298.example: With 22 °CmathrmC indoors, 0 °CmathrmC outdoors and 150m³/h of airflow, the loss is 1200 × (150 / 3600) × 22 ≈ 1100W. At η=70% it falls to about 330W and the supply air arrives at about 15.4 °CmathrmC.
p-298.actionItem: Today, if you have a heat-recovery ventilator, clean its filter at the interval in its manual.

p-299.title: A floor rug adds one more layer of thermal resistance
p-299.summary: A rug adds an insulating layer between the floor and your feet. On a heated floor, though, a thick rug also blocks heat into the room, so choose a thin one.
p-299.principle: For layers in series, thermal resistance is R=(L_i / k_i) and heat flux is q=(ΔT / R). Adding a layer raises R and lowers q.
p-299.example: A rug 1cm thick with k ≈ 0.05W/(m · K) has R=0.2m²K/W. If the floor has R=0.5 and ΔT=10 °CmathrmC, flux drops from 20 to 14.3W/m², about 29% less.
p-299.actionItem: Today, lay a rug where you often sit or stand on a cold floor, and pick a thin one if the room has floor heating.

p-300.title: If a door sags, tighten the top hinge screws first
p-300.summary: The door's weight pulls on the top hinge and presses on the bottom one, so the top screws loosen first. Tightening only the top hinge screws often fixes the sag.
p-300.principle: A door at rest is in torque balance, τ=0. With weight W acting at the door's center ((w / 2) from the hinges) and hinge spacing h, the horizontal force is F=(W w/2 / h).
p-300.example: For a 20kg door (W ≈ 196N), 0.9m wide with hinges 1.6m apart, F=(196 × 0.45 / 1.6) ≈ 55N pulls on the top hinge and pushes on the bottom.
p-300.actionItem: Today, with the door open, tighten the top hinge screws with a Phillips screwdriver; fill any stripped hole with toothpicks and wood glue, then retighten.

p-301.title: When rising from a chair, lean your torso forward first
p-301.summary: Seated, your center of mass is behind your feet, so leaning forward to bring it over your feet makes standing easier and steadier.
p-301.principle: To stand, the vertical projection of the center of mass (COM) must fall inside the support area your feet make. If the COM is a horizontal distance x from the feet, gravity's torque is τ=mg x.
p-301.example: When the seated COM is about 15cm behind the feet, leaning the torso forward about 30^° moves the COM about 10cm forward and removes most of x (rough values).
p-301.actionItem: Today, when standing from a chair, lean your nose toward your toes, pull your feet close to the chair, then rise. If dizziness keeps happening, talk to a professional.

p-302.title: On winter nights, Polaris's altitude equals your latitude
p-302.summary: Polaris sits near the north celestial pole, so its height above the horizon almost equals the observer's latitude. One star lets you estimate your latitude.
p-302.principle: The altitude of the north celestial pole equals the observer's latitude , and Polaris is about 0.7^° from the pole, so h_Polaris ≈.
p-302.example: In Seoul (about 37.5^° N) Polaris is about 37.5^° above the horizon, and in Jeju (about 33.5^° N) about 33.5^°. An outstretched fist is about 10^°, so Seoul's Polaris is about 3.75 fists high.
p-302.actionItem: Tonight, if the sky is clear, find Polaris using the Big Dipper or the W of Cassiopeia and measure its height with your fist.

p-303.title: Why anti-reflective eyeglass coatings look bluish
p-303.summary: An anti-reflective coating is a very thin film that makes reflected light waves cancel each other. It is tuned to the middle green wavelengths, so some blue and red remain and tint the reflection.
p-303.principle: If the film thickness is d=(λ / 4n), reflections from its top and bottom surfaces differ by a path of (λ / 2) and cancel. The ideal film index is n_c=√(n_s).
p-303.example: A MgF₂ film (n=1.38) at λ=550nm needs d=(550 / 4 × 1.38) ≈ 100nm. Uncoated glass reflects about 4% per surface; coating cuts it to under 1%.
p-303.actionItem: Today, clean your lenses with a lens cleaner and a microfiber cloth, and avoid dry rubbing or hot water.

p-304.title: A thin charging cable charges slower
p-304.summary: A thin wire has higher resistance, so voltage drops across the cable and some power leaks away as heat. With the same charger, a thicker cable carries more current.
p-304.principle: Voltage drop is V=IR and wire resistance is R=(ρ L / A). Power lost as heat in the cable is P=I²R.
p-304.example: For 2A charging over a 2m round-trip of copper (ρ=1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ωm), a 0.08mm² (28 AWG) wire has R ≈ 0.42Ω, dropping 0.84V and losing 1.7W. A 0.2mm² (24 AWG) wire has 0.17Ω, 0.34V and 0.7W.
p-304.actionItem: Today, replace a slow or hot thin cable with a thicker one that states its rated current.

p-305.title: A top-opening kimchi fridge spills less cold air when opened
p-305.summary: Cold air is denser and sinks, pooling at the bottom. A top-loading lid keeps that cold air in the tub, so less escapes when you open it.
p-305.principle: Air density is ρ=(p / R_sT), larger at lower temperature. The buoyant force from density difference is Δρ g V, so cold air settles stably below.
p-305.example: Air at 4 °CmathrmC is about 1.27kg/m³ and at 25 °CmathrmC about 1.18kg/m³, about 7% heavier. A side-door fridge lets this heavy cold air spill out of the open door.
p-305.actionItem: Today, decide what to take out of the kimchi fridge in advance and open the lid once, briefly.

p-306.title: Lay a wooden chopstick across a pot that boils over
p-306.summary: A bubble touching the chopstick often bursts, which can delay boil-over. It is not a complete fix, so lowering the heat and watching the pot remains the basic rule.
p-306.principle: The pressure difference across a bubble film layer is the Laplace relation Δp=(2γ / r) (γ: surface tension, r: radius of curvature). A film touching rough wood thins and pops more easily.
p-306.example: For water at 100 °CmathrmC, γ ≈ 0.059N/m, a 1mm radius bubble gives Δp=(2 × 0.059 / 0.001) ≈ 118Pa. Starchy noodle or pasta water makes the bubble films tougher.
p-306.actionItem: Today, when boiling noodles, rest a dry wooden chopstick across the pot rim and use medium-low heat. Keep the chopstick away from the flame.

p-307.title: Each extra 1m/s of wind lowers the felt temperature by about 1°C
p-307.summary: Wind strips away the warm air layer near your skin, so the same air temperature feels colder. In winter, check the wind as well as the temperature when choosing clothes.
p-307.principle: Forced-convection heat loss is q=h(v) A (T_skin-T_air), and h grows with wind speed v. The wind chill index is T_wc=13.12+0.6215T-11.37v⁰.16+0.3965Tv⁰.16 (v in km/h).
p-307.example: At an air temperature of 0 °CmathrmC, a wind of 1.4m/s (5km/h) feels like about -1.6 °CmathrmC and 5m/s (18km/h) about -4.9 °CmathrmC, a drop of about 3.3 °CmathrmC for about 3.6m/s more wind.
p-307.actionItem: Today, on a windy day, cover exposed skin with a windproof outer layer and a neck gaiter.

p-308.title: A halo around the moon can signal coming rain
p-308.summary: A lunar halo is a ring made when ice crystals in high clouds bend moonlight. These clouds often appear as a front approaches, so rain becomes more likely, though not certain.
p-308.principle: For a hexagonal ice prism, the minimum deviation is D_=2 ≤ ft(n30°Cright)-60^°. With ice n ≈ 1.31, D_ ≈ 22^°, giving a 22^° ring around the moon.
p-308.example: With n=1.31, (0.655) ≈ 40.9^°, so D_ ≈ 2 × 40.9-60 ≈ 21.8^°. An outstretched open hand spans about 20^°, so the ring is about a hand-span from the moon.
p-308.actionItem: Tonight, if you see a moon halo, check tomorrow's forecast and bring an umbrella.

p-309.title: The 9H on a tempered-glass film is pencil hardness
p-309.summary: 9H means the hardest pencil leaves no mark; it is not Mohs hardness 9. Dust in your pocket can be harder and still scratch it.
p-309.principle: A surface scratches when a particle is harder than it, H_particle>H_surface. The pencil hardness scale and the Mohs scale are different scales.
p-309.example: Quartz, the main component of sand, has Mohs hardness 7, harder than glass (about 5.56). A 9H film can still be scratched by sand dust if its Mohs hardness is below 7.
p-309.actionItem: Today, keep your phone in a different pocket from keys and coins and shake sand dust out of your pockets.

p-310.title: In winter, open south-facing curtains by day to catch the sun
p-310.summary: Even with the winter sun low, a south-facing window takes it almost head-on and gains a lot of heat. Opening curtains by day and closing them at dusk is free heating.
p-310.principle: Solar heat gain through a window is Q=A I SHGCθ (I: solar intensity, SHGC: solar heat gain coefficient, θ: incidence angle). A south-facing vertical window in winter has a small incidence angle and transmits a lot.
p-310.example: For a 2m² window, noon solar intensity on a vertical surface I ≈ 500W/m² on a clear day and SHGC=0.6, the gain is 600W. Assuming a 400W average over 4 hours, that is about 1.6kWh of heat (an assumed value).
p-310.actionItem: Today, on a clear day, open the curtains and blinds on south-facing windows and close them before sunset to cut night heat loss.

p-311.title: An entrance vestibule door is a draft-buffer space
p-311.summary: The small space between the front door and the inner door acts as a buffer that keeps cold air from rushing straight into the home. The key is not to open both doors at once.
p-311.principle: Air exchange through an open door happens by convection, and the heat loss is Q=ρ cVΔT (V: volume of air exchanged). An inner door limits the exchanged volume to about the vestibule.
p-311.example: If a 3m³ vestibule exchanges air across a 20 °CmathrmC difference, Q=1.2 × 1005 × 3 × 20 ≈ 72kJ ≈ 0.02kWh. Without an inner door, the upper bound with a 60m³ living room affected is about 0.4kWh.
p-311.actionItem: Today, when coming home, close the front door before opening the inner door, and when leaving, close the inner door before opening the front door.

p-312.title: If only the top of the oven food burns, blame the rack position
p-312.summary: The closer to the top heater, the sharply stronger the radiant heat, so the top burns first. Lowering the rack one level cooks top and bottom more evenly.
p-312.principle: In the point-source approximation, radiant intensity is I=(P / 4π r²), inversely proportional to distance squared. A real heater is an extended source so the change is gentler, but it still grows as you get closer.
p-312.example: In the simple model, a rack 5cm from the heater gets (10/5)²=4 times the radiation of one 10cm away. With a real flat heater it is more like 2 to 3 times.
p-312.actionItem: Today, if the top browns first, lower the rack one level and, if needed, loosely tent the top with foil.

p-313.title: Wearing two pairs of socks reduces blisters
p-313.summary: Blisters come from friction as skin drags against the sock; with two layers the rubbing happens between the sock layers so skin is pulled less. If your shoes become tight, it backfires, so leave some room.
p-313.principle: Friction is F=µ N and the shear stress on skin is τ=(F / A). If the friction coefficient between layers is lower than between skin and sock, slip occurs between the layers and skin stress drops.
p-313.example: Assume N ≈ 700N on one foot while walking over A ≈ 100cm². With µ=0.5, τ ≈ 35kPa; with µ=0.3 between layers, τ ≈ 21kPa, about 40% less (assumed values).
p-313.actionItem: Today, if you have a long walk, put a second layer over a thin moisture-wicking sock and check that your shoes are not tight.

p-314.title: Why snow photos come out gray and dark
p-314.summary: A camera's auto exposure sets the scene average to middle gray, so white snow is rendered gray. Raising exposure makes snow come out white.
p-314.principle: Auto exposure aims the average reflectance at 18% gray. If snow has reflectance ρ, the needed correction is ΔEV=₂(ρ / 0.18).
p-314.example: For snow with ρ ≈ 0.8, ΔEV=₂(0.8 / 0.18) ≈ 2.1. That is why photographers usually apply +1+2 EV correction.
p-314.actionItem: Today, when photographing snow, tap the snow on the screen and raise the brightness slider by +1+2.

p-315.title: Choose a compact umbrella with vents for wind
p-315.summary: When wind pushes hard on the canopy, a vent that lets air escape reduces the pressure difference and the chance of flipping. No umbrella should be used in a strong gale.
p-315.principle: Drag is F_D=12ρ C_DAv², proportional to wind speed squared. If a vented design reduces the pressure difference and so lowers C_D, the force falls by the same fraction.
p-315.example: At 15m/s with a 100cm diameter (A ≈ 0.79m²) and C_D=1.2, F_D ≈ 127N (about 13 kgf). If C_D drops to 0.9, the force is about 95N, 25% less (assumed values).
p-315.actionItem: Today, when picking an umbrella, look for a double canopy or vent design and fiberglass ribs.

p-316.title: A 1kW electric heater heats exactly 1kW
p-316.summary: An electric heater turns almost all the electricity it uses into heat. So the electricity needed for a given amount of heat is just power times time.
p-316.principle: Resistive heating is 100% efficient, and energy used is E=Pt. A heat pump (air-conditioner heating) has a coefficient of performance COP=(Q / W) of about 3, making the same heat with 13 of the electricity.
p-316.example: A 1kW heater run for 3 hours uses 3kWh; assuming 200 KRW/kWh, that is 600 KRW (about USD 0.45). A heat pump with COP=3 needs 1kWh, about 200 KRW, for the same heat.
p-316.actionItem: Today, when using a heater, check its rated power (W) and set a timer so it runs only as long as needed.

p-317.title: A lap blanket stands in for 1 to 2°C of heating
p-317.summary: Felt warmth rises as less heat leaves your body, so one lap blanket gives the effect of raising the room by 1 to 2°C. You can stay warm with the heating set a little lower.
p-317.principle: Heat loss is q=T_skin-T_airR_clo+R_air, and for seated activity, 1 clo of clothing (0.155m²K/W) lowers the comfort temperature by about 5.5 °CmathrmC.
p-317.example: A lap blanket of about 0.3 clo lowers the comfort temperature by about 1.7 °CmathrmC. As a rule of thumb, each 1 °CmathrmC lower heating setting cuts heating cost about 7%, so 1.5 °CmathrmC is about 10%.
p-317.actionItem: Today, lower your living room heating setpoint by 1°C and keep a lap blanket on the sofa.

p-318.title: Foil sparks in a microwave start at sharp points
p-318.summary: At a sharp metal tip the electric field concentrates and breaks down the air, throwing sparks. Do not put foil, gold-rimmed dishes or metal decorations in.
p-318.principle: At a tip with small radius of curvature, the field grows as E ≈ (V / r). Air breaks down at about E_b ≈ 3 MV/m, producing corona and spark discharge.
p-318.example: Assume an induced voltage V=300V at a foil edge with tip radius r=0.1mm: E=30010⁻⁴=3 MV/m, right at breakdown (assumed values). A large flat sheet is less prone than its edges but still dangerous.
p-318.actionItem: Today, keep metal containers, foil and gold-rimmed dishes out of the microwave. If sparks fly, stop it at once and take the food out after it cools.

p-319.title: Why sitting by a cold window feels colder than the room
p-319.summary: Your body loses heat by radiation to cold surfaces around you as well as to the air. A window has a cold surface, so it feels colder even with the same air temperature.
p-319.principle: Net radiative loss is q=εσ ≤ ft(T_skin⁴-T_s⁴) ≈ h_r ≤ ft(T_skin-T_s), with h_r ≈ 5W/(m² · K) near room temperature.
p-319.example: With a clothing surface at 28 °CmathrmC and a window surface at 8 °CmathrmC, q ≈ 5 × 20=100W/m², versus 50W/m² for a wall at 18 °CmathrmC. Over 0.5m² facing it, that is about 25W more (assumed values).
p-319.actionItem: Today, if the window seat feels cold, move the chair about 1m back or hang a curtain or insulating film.

p-320.title: Pitch a winter camping tent mid-ridge rather than in the valley
p-320.summary: On clear, calm nights cold air sinks and pools in valleys and hollows. A ridge top is windy, so a sheltered flat spot partway up is better.
p-320.principle: Cold air is dense and flows downhill with buoyancy acceleration a ≈ g(ΔT / T), forming cold-air pools. Temperature normally falls about 0.65 °CmathrmC/100m with height, but a night-time inversion reverses this.
p-320.example: With ΔT=5K and T=278K, a ≈ 9.8 × (5 / 278) ≈ 0.18m/s². On a clear, calm winter night the valley floor can be several °CmathrmC colder than mid-slope.
p-320.actionItem: Today, if you plan to camp, stay within the designated campsite, avoid hollows and choose a flat spot with less wind.

p-321.title: Radiant and convection heaters work differently
p-321.summary: A radiant heater warms people and objects directly and feels warm at once, while a convection heater warms the air and slowly heats the whole room. Pick by how you will use it.
p-321.principle: Radiation transfers heat to surfaces without heating the air, q=εσ(T_h⁴-T_s⁴)A, while convection moves heat by circulating warmed air, q=hA ΔT.
p-321.example: A 1kW radiant unit warms skin 1m away right after switching on, but a convection unit needs Q=mcΔT ≈ 0.18MJ just to raise a 30m³ room (about 36kg of air) by 5°C, and much longer once walls and furniture soak up heat.
p-321.actionItem: If you plan to buy a heater today, decide the use first: radiant for one spot such as a desk, convection for a whole room.

p-322.title: In winter, heat the seat instead of the air in an EV
p-322.summary: An EV cabin heater draws a lot from the battery, so warming your body directly with seat and wheel heaters and lowering the cabin setting protects range.
p-322.principle: Direct contact heating needs far less heat. Heating cabin air takes Q=mcΔT plus constant make-up for losses through the body and glass.
p-322.example: Cutting a cabin heater from about 3kW to half and using a 60W seat heater saves about 1.4kWh per hour, which is roughly 8km of range at 6km/kWh.
p-322.actionItem: On your next drive, switch on the seat and wheel heaters first and lower the cabin setting by 1-2°C.

p-323.title: Winter car heat is waste engine heat, so it is nearly free
p-323.summary: A combustion car's heater uses engine waste heat carried by the coolant, so running it costs almost no extra fuel. The A/C compressor is what burns fuel.
p-323.principle: About 60% of fuel energy leaves as waste heat (Q_waste ≈ 0.6 Q_fuel), and the heater core redirects part of it into the cabin. The A/C compressor draws extra work W from the engine.
p-323.example: Cabin heating takes roughly 2-4kW, a small part of the engine's waste heat while cruising, whereas the A/C compressor takes about 1-3kW of extra engine power.
p-323.actionItem: If the windows are not fogging, keep the A/C button off on your winter drive today and use heat only.

p-324.title: Do not shake a ketchup bottle, whack it upside down
p-324.summary: Ketchup holds still like a solid, then suddenly thins when forced. Hold the bottle upside down and give it one sharp whack to apply a burst of stress.
p-324.principle: Ketchup is a shear-thinning non-Newtonian fluid: as shear rate γ rises, apparent viscosity η=τ/γ falls, and it flows once stress exceeds the yield stress.
p-324.example: At rest its viscosity is on the order of 50Pa·s or more, and under strong shear it can drop by a factor of tens, though it is still far thicker than water (about 0.001Pa·s).
p-324.actionItem: Today, hold a ketchup bottle upside down and give the neck area one firm whack with your palm.

p-325.title: Set the treadmill to 1% incline to match outdoors
p-325.summary: A treadmill has no air resistance, so the same speed feels easier than outside. A 1% incline roughly makes up for the difference.
p-325.principle: The work lost to air drag is replaced by gravitational potential energy: P=mgvθ ≈ mgv × (grade).
p-325.example: A 70kg runner at 10km/h (about 2.78m/s) adds 70 × 9.81 × 2.78 × 0.01 ≈ 19W at a 1% grade.
p-325.actionItem: If you use a treadmill today, set the incline to 1% before you start.

p-326.title: Press your lens against the window for bus and train shots
p-326.summary: Reflections of the bright interior on a window drop sharply when the lens is close to the glass. Cupping a hand or using a hood around the lens helps further.
p-326.principle: A glass surface reflects about 4% by Fresnel reflection (R= ≤ ft((n-1 / n+1))², n ≈ 1.5), and a lens close to the glass cuts the angle at which reflected light can enter.
p-326.example: Two glass surfaces reflect about 4% each, so roughly 8% of interior light shows up in the window, and the share is much more visible when it is dark outside.
p-326.actionItem: When shooting out the window today, rest the lens lightly on the glass and shade it with a hand, but do not press hard on a vibrating part.

p-327.title: Match earphones to your phone by impedance (ohms)
p-327.summary: A low-impedance earphone plays louder from a low-voltage device such as a smartphone. A high-impedance model delivers less power at the same voltage.
p-327.principle: Power delivered is P=(V² / R), so at the same voltage V a larger impedance R gives smaller P.
p-327.example: At 0.5V (rms), a 16Ω earphone gets about 15.6mW and a 300Ω earphone about 0.83mW, roughly 19 times less.
p-327.actionItem: Check the impedance on an earphone spec sheet today and choose 16-32Ω if you will plug it straight into a phone.

p-328.title: 1kWh is 3.6MJ, about 860kcal
p-328.summary: The kWh on your power bill, the kcal on food labels and the joule in science are all units of energy and convert exactly.
p-328.example: A 2,000kcal day is about 8.4MJ, or 2.3kWh, an average of about 97W. One kWh runs a 100W bulb for 10 hours.
p-328.actionItem: Check this month's usage in kWh on your electricity bill or app today.

p-329.title: Each time you open the oven door, it loses about 25°C
p-329.summary: Opening the oven door lets hot air out and cold air in, so the temperature drops noticeably and takes energy to recover.
p-329.principle: An open door lets air exchange by convection driven by the temperature difference, and recovery needs heat Q=CΔT again. The walls store heat, so the drop varies by oven.
p-329.example: A 180°C oven is commonly reported to drop roughly 20-30°C after one opening, and recovery takes minutes, lengthening cooking time and using more electricity.
p-329.actionItem: While baking today, keep the door shut and check progress through the window with the oven light.

p-330.title: Tell raw from boiled eggs by spinning them
p-330.summary: Spin an egg on a table: a boiled egg spins smoothly for a long time, while a raw egg wobbles and stops quickly.
p-330.principle: A boiled egg is one rigid body, so it spins steadily with L=Iω. In a raw egg the liquid moves separately from the shell, dissipating energy, and after you stop the shell the liquid keeps turning and the egg creeps around again.
p-330.example: For an egg of about 60g, a boiled one spins steadily for several seconds while a raw one usually stops noticeably sooner. If you stop it briefly and let go, only the raw egg moves again.
p-330.actionItem: Spin two eggs from the fridge on a table today and see which one turns smoothly.

p-331.title: Cough into your sleeve or elbow, since droplets travel meters
p-331.summary: Coughs and sneezes make fast airflow that carries droplets several meters. Covering with the inside of your elbow or a sleeve greatly shortens how far they spread.
p-331.principle: The jet leaving the mouth carries momentum p=mv and spreads forward, slowing gradually as it diffuses into the air.
p-331.example: A cough's initial airflow is reported at around 10m/s, and small particles can hang in the air and reach several meters.
p-331.actionItem: If you cough today, cover your mouth and nose with the inside of your elbow or a sleeve instead of your hand.

p-332.title: Pick ski goggle lens colors for the weather
p-332.summary: On sunny days, use darker lenses to cut glare; on overcast or snowy days, yellow or orange lenses bring out snow contours.
p-332.principle: Lenses differ in transmittance by wavelength, and brightness follows visible light transmission VLT=I/I₀. Yellow and orange filter blue light and raise contrast in flat light.
p-332.example: Common choices are dark gray or mirrored lenses with VLT of about 10-20% for sun, and yellow or rose lenses with VLT of about 40-60% for cloud.
p-332.actionItem: When packing ski goggles today, check the forecast and choose the lens color, or bring a spare lens.

p-333.title: Keep speakers at least 20cm from the wall
p-333.summary: Speakers pushed against a wall bloat the bass and cancel some notes, making the sound dull and muddy.
p-333.principle: Near a wall, boundary effects boost bass (about 3-6dB), and sound drops at the frequency f=(c / 4d) where the wall reflection arrives out of phase with the direct sound.
p-333.example: At 20cm from the wall the dip falls near f=(343 / 4 × 0.2) ≈ 430Hz, and at 50cm near 170Hz, changing the bass balance. Results vary with the room.
p-333.actionItem: Today, move your speakers at least 20cm from the wall and replay the same track.

p-334.title: A car inverter draws high current at 12V
p-334.summary: Plugging a power-hungry device such as a laptop charger into a car inverter pulls a large current on the 12V side and can blow the socket fuse.
p-334.principle: Power is P=VI, so at the same power a lower voltage means a larger current, I=P/V.
p-334.example: A 150W device needs 150/12=12.5A in theory, and with 90% inverter efficiency about 13.9A, close to the limit of a common 10-15A socket fuse.
p-334.actionItem: Today, check your car socket's fuse rating in amps and divide your device's wattage by 12V.

p-335.title: Oven preheat is a fixed cost, so bake in one batch
p-335.summary: The energy to preheat an oven is the same no matter how much you bake. Cooking several things at once means fewer preheats.
p-335.principle: Preheating heat depends on the oven's heat capacity and temperature rise, Q=C_ovenΔT, not on the amount of food.
p-335.example: Preheating an electric oven to 180°C takes about 0.3-0.4kWh, so baking in one session instead of two saves about 70 KRW (roughly 0.05 USD).
p-335.actionItem: If you use the oven today, gather everything and bake it together on two racks.

p-336.title: Find wall studs by knocking
p-336.summary: Knock on drywall: a hollow spot sounds low and drummy, while over a stud (frame) it sounds solid and higher.
p-336.principle: The knocked panel vibrates at a resonant frequency f ∝ √(k/m), and over a stud the stiffness k is larger, so the sound is higher and shorter.
p-336.example: Studs are usually 400-600mm apart, so knocking every 10cm or so along the wall shows the sound changing at regular intervals.
p-336.actionItem: Before driving a nail today, knock to find the stud and check that no wires or pipes run there.

p-337.title: You survive an 80°C sauna but not 80°C water
p-337.summary: Air conducts heat poorly, so an 80°C sauna is tolerable, but water at the same temperature scalds at once.
p-337.principle: Heat flow to skin scales with thermal conductivity and heat capacity. Water conducts about 0.6W/m K, roughly 25 times air (0.026), and holds far more heat per volume.
p-337.example: Water conducts about 25 times better than air and holds about 3,500 times more heat per volume, so water above 60°C can scald within seconds.
p-337.actionItem: Before a shower or bath today, test the water on your inner forearm first.

p-338.title: Walk on a frozen lake only when the ice is 10cm or thicker
p-338.summary: Ice strength grows with the square of thickness, but thin ice is dangerous. Check the thickness and follow local guidance.
p-338.principle: The load an ice sheet supports scales as P ∝ h², so doubling thickness h roughly quadruples capacity.
p-338.example: As a rule of thumb, 5cm barely holds one person on foot and 10cm or more is needed for groups, and going from 5cm to 10cm raises capacity about 4 times.
p-338.actionItem: Before stepping onto ice today, confirm local advice and the thickness, and stay off if in doubt.

p-339.title: Judge lanterns by lumens, and run time by watt-hours
p-339.summary: Compare lantern brightness in lumens (lm) and run time as battery capacity (Wh) divided by power draw.
p-339.principle: Efficacy is η=lm/W, and run time is t=(E / P).
p-339.example: 300 lm at 100 lm/W is 3W. A 3.7V 5,000 mAh battery (about 18.5Wh) runs it about 6 hours in theory.
p-339.actionItem: Check the lumens and battery Wh (or mAh times V) on your lantern today and calculate its run time.

p-340.title: The earliest sunset is not on the winter solstice
p-340.summary: The earliest sunset comes in early December, about two weeks before the solstice (around December 21), the shortest day. The latest sunrise comes in early January.
p-340.principle: The time the sun crosses due south shifts by the equation of time E, so the extremes of sunset and sunrise fall on different dates than the solstice.
p-340.example: In Seoul the earliest sunset is about 17:16 in early December and about 17:20 near the solstice, roughly 4 minutes later, although total daylight is shortest at the solstice.
p-340.actionItem: Check today's sunset time and watch whether it starts getting later by mid-December.

p-341.title: A kitchen scale wastes less food than measuring cups
p-341.summary: Flour scooped in a cup varies widely with how packed it is, while a scale measures in grams and wastes less.
p-341.principle: Mass is m=ρ V, but powders change density ρ by 20% or more as they pack, so the same volume gives a different mass.
p-341.example: One cup of flour (about 240mL) can weigh roughly 100-150g depending on how it is scooped, a difference of nearly 50% that turns dough stiff or sticky.
p-341.actionItem: If you bake today, weigh ingredients in grams on a scale instead of using cups.

p-342.title: A smartphone in a glass cup sounds louder
p-342.summary: Placing a phone in an empty glass focuses the sound forward and makes it ring inside the cup, so it sounds louder by a few dB.
p-342.principle: A tube closed at one end resonates near f=(c / 4L), and the cup gathers sound in one direction, increasing directivity.
p-342.example: A 10cm deep cup strengthens sound near f=(343 / 4 × 0.1) ≈ 860Hz, for roughly 3-6dB (2-4 times the sound power), varying by device.
p-342.actionItem: Today, place a phone speaker-side into a cup and compare the loudness.

p-343.title: Low-temperature burns can occur at 44°C within hours
p-343.summary: Even mild heat from an electric blanket or heat pack can damage deep skin if it stays in one spot too long, and it is easy to miss because it hurts little.
p-343.principle: Skin damage builds up from conduction with temperature and contact time together, so even a low temperature harms if the contact is long.
p-343.example: Contact at about 44°C for roughly 6 hours or more is known to cause burns, and a heat pack near 60°C is dangerous in far shorter times.
p-343.actionItem: Today, keep heat packs and electric blankets over clothing or fabric rather than on bare skin, and turn them off before you fall asleep.

p-344.title: Avalanches are most likely on slopes of 30-45°
p-344.summary: Snowy slopes release most often at 30-45°. Gentler slopes hold the snow, and steeper ones shed it before it builds up.
p-344.principle: A slab slides when the shear stress at the weak layer, τ=ρ g hθθ, exceeds frictional resistance, and τ rises with slope angle θ to a maximum at 45°.
p-344.example: A 1m layer of 300kg/m³ snow on a 38° slope gives τ ≈ 300 × 9.81 × 1 × 0.485 ≈ 1.4kPa, and when that exceeds the layer's strength it releases.
p-344.actionItem: If you head into snowy mountains today, check the avalanche forecast and slope angles first, and avoid slopes steeper than 30°.

p-345.title: Hang a weight on a light tripod
p-345.summary: A light tripod topples in wind easily. Hanging a bag low and centered lowers the center of gravity and makes it much steadier.
p-345.principle: It tips when the force at height exceeds the restoring torque: the tipping force is F=(mgr / h), so the lower the center of mass h, the larger the force needed.
p-345.example: For a 1.5kg tripod (center 1.2m high, leg radius 0.4m), hanging a 3kg bag at 0.3m lowers the center to 0.6m and raises the tipping force from about 4.9N to about 14.7N, about 3 times.
p-345.actionItem: When you use a tripod today, hang a bag from the hook under the center column so it hangs low without touching the ground.

p-346.title: One person is a 100W heater
p-346.summary: A person gives off about 100W of heat even at rest, so a room full of people warms up quickly without heating.
p-346.principle: Food energy ends up as heat, and basal metabolic output is about P=E/t ≈ 80-120W.
p-346.example: A 2,000kcal day is 8.37MJ86400 s ≈ 97W. A room of 20 people gives about 2kW, equal to one small electric heater.
p-346.actionItem: If people gather in a room today, lower the heating setting by 1-2°C.

p-347.title: Dry a wet pot bottom before putting it on the burner
p-347.summary: Water on the bottom of a pot evaporates on the flame and steals a lot of heat, wasting time and gas, and spattering drops can be hazardous.
p-347.principle: Evaporation needs latent heat Q=mL, and water's latent heat of vaporization is L ≈ 2.26kJ/g.
p-347.example: 10g of water on the base takes Q=10 × 2.26=22.6kJ, about 11 seconds of heat from an effective 2kW burner.
p-347.actionItem: Before you put a pot on the burner today, wipe its base dry with a cloth.

p-348.title: Why one bad tree bulb turns off the whole string
p-348.summary: On a string of bulbs wired in series, one break leaves no path for current, so the entire string goes dark.
p-348.principle: Series current is the same through every part, I=(V / R₁+R₂+ · s). One open point makes resistance infinite, so I=0.
p-348.example: Fifty 2.4V bulbs in series share about 120V. Remove one and the other 49 get zero current.
p-348.actionItem: For a dead string today, unplug it first, then press loose bulbs in firmly or swap in a spare.

p-349.title: Why a wide-mouth 'hah' feels warm and a pursed 'hoo' feels cool
p-349.summary: Breathing out with an open mouth feels warm, while breathing out through pursed lips feels cool.
p-349.principle: Pursed lips make a fast jet that pulls in surrounding air (entrainment). The mixed temperature falls to T=(m₁T₁+m₂T₂ / m₁+m₂), with a small extra cooling from expansion.
p-349.example: Breath at about 34°C mixed 1:1 with 20°C room air gives about 27°C, so the airflow on your hand feels about 7°C cooler.
p-349.actionItem: Today, blow on the back of your hand with a wide mouth and then with pursed lips and feel the difference.

p-350.title: Sled speed is set by height alone
p-350.summary: Without friction, a sled's speed at the bottom depends only on the drop height and not on body weight. In real life friction and air drag make it slower.
p-350.principle: Potential energy becomes kinetic energy, so mgh=12mv² gives v=√(2gh).
p-350.example: From a 5m drop, v=√(2 × 9.81 × 5) ≈ 9.9m/s, about 36km/h, and real speeds are lower.
p-350.actionItem: If you sled today, pick a gentle slope clear of obstacles and wear a helmet.

p-351.title: Lie on a mattress for 10 minutes and check the gap at your lower back
p-351.summary: When buying a mattress, lie down for about 10 minutes and see whether a hand slips easily under your lower back. A big gap leaves the back unsupported and concentrates pressure.
p-351.principle: Pressure is P=(F / A) and falls as the support area A grows. A mattress spreads load through its spring constant k and layer design.
p-351.example: A 70kg body (about 686N) on only 0.1m² gives about 6.9kPa, and spread over 0.3m² about 2.3kPa, one third as much.
p-351.actionItem: When testing a mattress today, also lie on your side for 10 minutes and check that shoulder, waist and hip are supported evenly.

p-352.title: A stove fan spins without electricity
p-352.summary: A fan on top of a stove spins from the stove's heat alone, with no cord or battery, and spreads warm air through the room.
p-352.principle: By the Seebeck effect, a temperature difference ΔT across junctions creates a voltage V=SΔT that drives a motor.
p-352.example: A thermoelectric module with a Seebeck coefficient of about 0.05V/K gives roughly 5V open-circuit at a 100K difference, with output of a few watts or less.
p-352.actionItem: Today, place a stove fan on a spot within its rated temperature range, out of reach of children.

p-353.title: A tealight and flowerpot heater cannot warm a room
p-353.summary: A heater made of a few tealights and a flowerpot cannot produce enough heat for a room and only adds fire and carbon monoxide risk.
p-353.principle: A candle gives only its combustion heat, P= m ΔH, and one tealight gives about 40W.
p-353.example: One tealight burns about 14g of wax (about 0.6MJ) over 4 hours, roughly 40W, so four give about 160W, a few percent of the 1-3kW a room needs.
p-353.actionItem: Today, seal gaps around windows instead of building a flowerpot heater.

p-354.title: A champagne cork flies at 50km/h
p-354.summary: A champagne bottle holds about 6atm of pressure, so a released cork can fly at nearly 50km/h and injure an eye.
p-354.principle: The pressure difference pushes with force F=ΔP · A, and the expanding gas does work that becomes kinetic energy 12mv².
p-354.example: With about 5bar of pressure difference over a cork cross-section of about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m², F ≈ 127N, and a 9g cork at 14m/s (50km/h) carries about 0.9J.
p-354.actionItem: When opening champagne today, tilt the bottle about 45°, hold the cork with your thumb and turn the bottle slowly, pointing it away from people.

p-355.title: White noise masks sudden sounds while you sleep
p-355.summary: Gentle white noise narrows the gap between a sudden sound and the background, which can help you wake less. Effects vary by person.
p-355.principle: In auditory masking, broadband noise raises the audibility threshold of other sounds. The contrast is ΔL=L_sound-L_bg.
p-355.example: A 70dB door slam over a 30dB background is a 40dB jump, but with 45dB white noise it is a 25dB jump and less startling.
p-355.actionItem: Tonight, play white noise quietly at about 40dB at your ear with a timer, and keep it well away from a baby's ears.

p-356.title: Crampons grip by mechanically biting into ice
p-356.summary: Crampons do not raise friction. Their sharp points dig into the ice and catch mechanically to prevent slipping.
p-356.principle: A shoe on ice slips at the limit θ=µ with a very small friction coefficient µ, but spikes engage the ice's shear resistance instead.
